Sūrat al-Nisā' is Madani, and it has one hundred and seventy-six verses.

﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿O mankind!﴾ This is an address whose ruling embraces all those obligated (mukallafun) at the time of revelation, and whoever will be included among them from those existing at that time and those who come into being after that until the Day of Resurrection, as they become included in it. However, this is not in the literal sense. The address directed to those present (khitab al-mushafahah) does not extend to those who have not reached the level of obligation, except according to the Hanbalis. Rather, it is either by way of predominance (taghlib) of the first group over the latter two, or by way of extending its ruling to them both through an external proof (dalil khariji). This is because there is an ijma' (scholarly consensus) that the last of the Community is obligated by what its first was obligated with, as indicated by his (ﷺ) saying: "What has come through my tongue is lawful until the Day of Resurrection, and what has come through my tongue is unlawful until the Day of Resurrection." This has been explained in its proper place. As for the nations that passed before the revelation, they have no share in the address, because the commands and prohibitions are specific to those from whom compliance can be conceived. As for their inclusion in the address concerning what is other than these two, which has a bearing on affirming the obligation and strengthening the imperative, you will come to know its status. The word "people" (al-nas) includes males and females in the literal sense. As for the masculine plural form in his, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Fear your Lord⁠﴾, it comes in the manner of predominance, since according to non-Hanbalis it does not literally include females. As for including them in the command to piety through the external proof mentioned, although it observes the aspect of the form, it requires restricting the word "people" to some of its individuals. And what is commanded is either absolute piety, which is abstaining from everything that incurs sin, whether an act or an omission, or piety concerning the rights of the members of the species (ibn al-jins), that is: fear Him in opposing His commands and prohibitions absolutely, or in opposing His obligations stated here. Whichever it is, the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), which indicates ownership and nurturing, together with its attribution to the pronoun of those addressed, serves to reinforce the command and to affirm the obligation of compliance with it, by way of encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib). ﴿Who created you from a single soul⁠﴾ is likewise a description of the Lord. His creating them in this wondrous pattern indicates a comprehensive power over all things that can be done, among which is punishing them for their disobedience, and a perfect blessing whose measure cannot be estimated, which is among the strongest motives for guarding against what brings about His wrath and the most complete deterrents from ingratitude for His blessing. Likewise, His making them as paired kinsfolk, derived from one root, which is the very soul of Adam (peace be upon him), is among the requirements for avoiding any neglect of the rights of brotherhood between them. The generalization of the address in "your Lord" and "created you" to the earlier nations as well, although it was earlier specific to those commanded, is based on the premise that reminding of the comprehensiveness of His Lordship and His creation of all is among the reinforcements of the command to piety and the requirements for complying with it. This is not a disruption of the noble arrangement, since His creating those commanded from the soul of Adam (peace be upon him), in that it occurred through the fathers and mothers between them and him (peace be upon him), means that mention of their creation includes mention of the creation of all the intermediaries. Likewise, mention of His Lordship over them includes mention of His Lordship over all their origins, especially since his, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying has expressed this: ﴿And from it He created its mate⁠﴾. Its clause, together with what is conjoined to it, is explicit in this. It is conjoined either to an implied element indicated by the flow of the discourse, because deriving branches from one origin necessarily requires the origin's own production, as if it were said: "He created you from a single soul which He created first, and from it He created its mate," and so on. It is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that comes to establish the unity of the origin and to explain the manner of their creation from it and to detail what was summarized first. Or it is an attribute of "soul," conveying this. Or it is conjoined to ﴿created you⁠﴾, lying within the scope of the relative clause together with it, establishing and explaining what was mentioned. Repeating the verb, although it is permissible to conjoin its object to the object of the first verb as in his, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you⁠﴾ etc., serves to show the difference between the two creations: the first is by way of derivation from the origin, and the second is by way of production from matter. He, the Exalted, created Eve from Adam's rib (peace be upon him). It is narrated that when He, the Mighty and Majestic, created him (peace be upon him) and settled him in the Garden, He cast sleep upon him. While he was between sleeping and waking, He created Eve from one of his ribs, the left one. When he awoke, he found her beside him. The postponement of the mention of her creation after the mention of their creation is because mentioning their creation is more effective in realizing the intended aim of moving them to comply with the command to piety than mentioning her creation. Fronting the prepositional phrase is for the sake of emphasizing that he (peace be upon him) was her origin, along with what that carries of suspense toward what is delayed. Mentioning her under the title of wifehood is a preparation for what follows of procreation.

﴿And He spread from both of them⁠﴾, that is: He scattered from that soul and its mate created from it, by way of procreation and multiplication.

﴿men in great number⁠﴾: "men" is an attribute of "men" (rijalan), emphasizing what the indefiniteness conveyed of multitude. The singular is in view of the meaning of the collective or the number. It has been said: it is an attribute of a verbal noun emphasizing the verb, that is: a great scattering.

﴿and women⁠﴾, that is: many. Leaving the explicit mention of them is for the sake of being sufficed by the mentioned attribute. Choosing the two (men and women) over "males and females" is to emphasize the multitude and to exaggerate it by highlighting each individual among the scattered ones for the originating status of the other. It was read as "khaliqun" and "bathththun" by omitting the subject, that is: and He is the Creator and the Scatterer.

﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another⁠﴾: this is a repetition of the command and a reminder of another of the requirements for complying with it. Their asking one another by God, the Exalted, by saying "I ask you by God" and "I adjure you by God" as an appeal for compassion, requires guarding against opposing His commands and prohibitions. Linking the piety to the Majestic Name serves to add emphasis and exaggeration in driving toward compliance, by instilling awe and introducing reverence, and because asking is done by Him and not by any of His other names and attributes. "tasa'alūna" originally was "tatasa'alūna", and one of the two tā's was dropped for lightness. It was also read with the assimilation of the tā' of the reflexive form into the sīn, because the two are close in being unvoiced (hams). It was read "tas'alūna" from the triliteral root, meaning: you ask others by Him. The first and second readings have been explained by this, and the use of the reciprocal form is taken as considering the plurality, as in your saying: "I saw the crescent and we saw it together," and by this was interpreted his saying "about what they ask one another" in one respect. It was read "tasalūna" by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the sīn.

﴿and the wombs⁠﴾: in the accusative, conjoined to the place of the prepositional phrase, as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd and 'Amr." It is supported by the reading "by whom you ask one another, and by the wombs," since they used to join them in asking and in adjuring by God, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: "I ask you by God and by the womb." Or it is conjoined to the Majestic Name, that is: fear God and the wombs, maintain them, and do not sever them, since severing them is among the things that must be guarded against. This is the statement of Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi permitted its accusative as an incitement (ighra'), that is: adhere to the wombs and maintain them. It was read in the genitive, conjoined to the pronoun in the genitive, and in the nominative as the subject of an omitted predicate, its estimation being: "and the wombs are likewise," that is: among what is guarded against or by which one asks. Indeed, by juxtaposing them with His Majestic Name, He, glory be to Him and exalted, drew attention to the fact that their connection has a place with Him, as in his, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Worship none but Him, and to parents show kindness⁠﴾. It is related from him (peace be upon him): "The womb is suspended from the Throne. It says: whoever joins me, God joins him, and whoever severs me, God severs him."

﴿Indeed God has been over you a watcher⁠﴾, that is: observing. It is an intensive form from "raqaba, yarqubu, raqban and raqaban," when one fixes the gaze on a matter one wishes to verify, that is: a guardian, fully aware of all deeds and sayings that proceed from you, and of what is in your hearts of intentions, intending to requite you for that. This is the justification for the command and the obligation to comply with it. The Majestic Name is made explicit for its emphasis, and the prepositional phrase is fronted to preserve the rhyme (fawasil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 2:

﴿And give to the orphans their property﴾. This begins the detailing of the sources and occasions of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety), by imposing what corresponds to them as commands and prohibitions, following the command itself time after time. The mention of matters concerning orphans is placed first to show the complete care for their affair and because of their connection with kinship, since the address is to the guardians and executors, and guardianship is rarely entrusted to strangers.

The orphan (yatim) is one whose father has died, from yutm, meaning solitariness; from it comes the unique pearl (durra yatima). Its plural is yatama, either because, having become like a noun, it was pluralized as yataatim and then inverted to become yatama; or because, being of the category of calamities (wadi al-afat), it was pluralized as yutma and then yutma was pluralized as yatama. Derivation requires the correctness of applying it to adults as well, and its restriction to children is based on custom (urf). As for his (peace be upon him) saying: ﴿There is no orphanhood after puberty (hulum)﴾, it is a legislative teaching and not a definition of the meaning of the word; that is, the ruling of orphans does not apply to the orphan after it. The meaning of giving them their property is: the addressees cutting off their empty greeds regarding it and restraining their snatching hands from appropriating it, and leaving it in its state, not touched by harm, until it comes to them and reaches them intact, as is indicated by what follows of the prohibition against exchanging. The eating is what is meant, not the actual giving, for that is conditioned on puberty and the perception of maturity (rushd), as indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿until they reach marriageable age﴾ and the verse. He expressed what was mentioned by "giving" metaphorically, to indicate that their intention with this should be to deliver it to them, not merely to abstain from touching it. So the referent of "them" is either children, as is most apparent, and the command is specific to whoever manages their affairs among the guardians and executors; and the inclusion of its ruling to the guardians of one who was an adult at the time of the revelation of the verse is by way of implication, not direct expression. As for one upon whom orphanhood has come in general, metaphorically, more broadly than whether he was so at the time of revelation or was adult, the command includes the guardians of both groups, in the form of an obligation upon them to guard their property and to be careful against its waste absolutely. As for the obligation of handing over to adults, it is derived from the command regarding it that comes later. It was also said that the referent is children, and "giving" means handing over in the future time; and it was said: their name was applied to adults by way of extension, due to the nearness of their having been orphans, to urge the guardians to hasten to hand over their property to them as soon as they reach maturity, before their known name departs from them. Giving then means handing over in deed, and the words of the Exalted ﴿And test the orphans﴾ etc. reject both views, for the command of handing over in it comes as an initial obligation, not merely as specifying its time or stating its condition, as the two opinions require. As for generalizing the name to children and adults metaphorically by way of predominance (taghlib), together with generalizing giving to giving in the present and giving in the future, and generalizing the address to the guardians of both groups, on the basis that whoever has reached maturity, his guardian is commanded to hand over to him in deed, and whoever has not yet reached it, his guardian is commanded to hand over to him upon his maturing with sound judgment, then with what preceded there is evident strain. Therefore the more fitting is what was previously stated: to understand giving them their property as what leads to leaving it untouched by harm, as the expression of giving in deed by handing over hints, whether the orphans are meant as children or as encompassing children and adults, as mentioned just above. As for what is related that a man from Ghatafan had a large property belonging to his nephew, and when he reached maturity he demanded his property from him, but he refused, and then it was revealed; when he heard it he said: "We obey God and we obey the Messenger; we seek refuge in God from the great sin" — this does not undermine that, since the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. This is a prohibition against taking the property of the orphan in the specific manner, after the implicit prohibition against taking it in general. Substitution (tabaddul) of one thing for another and exchanging it (istibdal) for it means taking the first in place of the second after it had been, or was about to be, in one's possession. Both are used always with their leading to what is obtained by themselves, and to what is lost by the preposition bi, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ etc., and the words of the Exalted: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾. As for tabdil, it is used sometimes in that way, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave them in exchange for their two gardens two gardens﴾ etc., and at other times in reverse, as in your saying: "I substituted the ring for the seal when you melted it and made it a seal," as stated by al-Azhari; and at other times by its leading to its two objects directly, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾. The meaning of the bad and the good, if they are the forbidden and the lawful, then what is prohibited is exchanging the property of the orphan for the property of themselves, in every case, as said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It was said: its meaning is: do not leave your lawful property and eat the unlawful from their property, so what is prohibited is eating their property in place of your property, whether actual or estimated. It was said: it is snatching his property in place of guarding it. Whichever it is, the expression of these two by these two is to make them abhorrent to what they took and to make attractive what they were given, and to depict their dealing in the form of what does not proceed from a rational person. If they are the inferior and the superior, then the object of the prohibition is what they used to do: taking the superior from the orphan's property and giving the inferior from their own property; this is what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and al-Suddi said. The restriction of this dealing to the prohibition is because it came out in the customary manner, not to permit what is other than it. As for expressing it by substituting the bad for the good, though it is actually substituting it with it or substituting the good for the bad, this is to indicate that the guardians ought, in exchanges, to act for the benefit of the orphan and not for themselves, being mindful of his side, intending to bring to him what is brought, whether as purchase or as price, and not to seize what is seized from him.

﴿And do not devour their property along with your property﴾. This is a prohibition against another evil they used to practice, that is: do not eat it combined with your property, nor equate the two, saying "this is lawful and that is unlawful." From this is excepted the amount of the equivalent wage when the guardian is poor.

﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, the eating understood from the prohibition.

﴿Is a great sin (huban)﴾, that is, a great wrong. It is read with the letter ha' vowelled with fatha, and it is a verbal noun: haba huban; it is also read "hab'an", which is likewise a verbal noun, like qala qawlan and qalan.

﴿Great (kabiran)﴾: an intensification in stating the greatness of the wrong of the aforementioned eating, as if it were said: it is among the great sins, not among the trivial ones.

**﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾.** *Al-iqsat* means justice (*al-'adl*). It was also read with a *fatha* on the *ta'* (*taqsatu*). Some said this is from *qasata*, meaning he acted unjustly (*jara*), and that *la* is extra (*mazida*), as in His saying, ﴿lest﴾ *li-'alla ya'lama* (﴿that he may not know﴾). Others said it means the same as *aqsata*, since al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH, grammarian) related that *qasata* is used in the sense of *aqsata*. The "fear" here means knowledge, as in His saying, ﴿Then whoever fears from a testator some deviation﴾ (2:182). It is expressed this way to signal that what is known is something feared and to be avoided, not its literal meaning. This is because the answer is conditioned on knowing that the feared injustice will occur, not on fear of it. Otherwise the command would not include someone who persists in injustice and does not fear it. This begins a prohibition of another wrong they used to commit, one that concerns the orphans themselves primarily and their property secondarily. It follows the prohibition concerning what relates to their property specifically. It is delayed after it because the prohibited act occurs less often than the first, and it descends from the first as a compound descends from a simple. They used to marry those orphan girls under their guardianship whom they were permitted to marry, but not out of desire for them; rather, out of desire for their wealth. They mistreated them in companionship and cohabitation and waited for them to die so that they could inherit from them. This is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri). It was also said: the orphan girl is under the guardianship of her guardian, who desires her wealth and beauty and wants to marry her for less than the customary bride-price of women like her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they gave them full bride-price, and they were commanded to marry other women. This is the view of al-Zuhri, transmitted from Urwa, from A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her). As for considering that a large number of them are gathered together, as most exegetes agree, saying: a man would find an orphan girl who had wealth and beauty, and he would be her guardian, so he would marry her to keep her from others. Thus it might happen that he had ten of them with him, etc., then the command does not support him in marrying others, because the harm is averted by reducing their number. That is: ﴿and if you fear that you will not be just toward orphans when you marry them﴾ through mistreatment in companionship or through diminishing the bride-price.

**﴿So marry what seems good to you﴾.** *Ma* is either a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) or a qualifying noun (*mawsufa*). What follows it is its complement (*silah*) or its qualifier (*sifah*). It was preferred over *man* in order to draw attention to the qualifying description and to signal that this is the primary intended meaning and the dominant consideration. This is not based on the view that women who are rational are treated like non-rational beings, since that would undermine the context of encouraging marriage to them. Ibn Abi 'Abla read *man tabā* (﴿whoever seems good﴾). The *min* in His saying ﴿from women﴾ is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*). It was also said to be partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), and the intended meaning of "them" is other than orphans, as indicated by the context. That is: marry those whom your souls find agreeable among foreign women. The preference for commanding marriage to them over prohibiting marriage to orphans, though the latter is the primary intended meaning, serves to gently steer them away from it. The soul is naturally inclined to desire what it is forbidden. Likewise, describing women as "good" in the manner indicated is an exaggeration intended to attract and encourage them. All of this aims at turning them away from marrying orphans. This is the secret behind directing the implicit prohibition at the anticipated marriage, even though the occasion of revelation was an actual marriage, because hastening to avert evil before it occurs is valuable, for many a thing that has occurred cannot be undone. There is also exaggeration in describing the situation of an actual marriage. The prohibition of the anticipated marriage stems from the anticipated injustice in it, so the prohibition of an actual marriage in which injustice is realized is even more fitting. It was also said that *al-tayyib* means lawful (*al-hill*), that is, what is lawfully permitted to you. This is because what they found agreeable includes forbidden things, and there is no specifier restricting it to women other than these. But this approach escapes one problem only to fall into something more grievous. What is lawful to them is general (*mujmal*), and it has been established that when a text is ambiguous between generality and specification, it is interpreted as the second, because a specified general statement is evidence outside the scope of the specification, whereas the ambiguous text is not evidence at all before clarification arrives. Even if His saying ﴿You are forbidden﴾ (4:23) etc. is taken as indicating detail, based on the claim that it was revealed earlier, it should still be taken as indicating specification.

**﴿Two, or three, or four﴾.** These are numbers in repeated form (*ma'dulah 'an a'dad mukarrarah*), not inflected (*ghayr munsarifah*), because they have two causes of deviation from their basic forms: deviation from their original patterns and deviation through repetition. It was also said that they are not inflected because of deviation and attributive use, since they were formed as adjectives even though their roots were not originally like that. It was also read *wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿa* with a short vowel (*qasr*) on the forms of *thulath* and *rubaʿ*. Their position is accusative, as they are a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of *tāba* (﴿seems good﴾), emphasizing what the description of goodness conveys regarding encouragement and attraction toward them, by widening the scope of permission. That is: so marry the good women for yourselves, in numbers of two two, three three, and four four, as you wish, meaning that each of them may choose whatever number he wishes from the mentioned numbers, not that some of them are assigned to some and others to others, as in your saying: "Divide this bag of money two dirhams each, three each, and four each." If they were mentioned alone, it would be understood as permitting combining these numbers but not distributing them. If they were mentioned with *aw* (or), the permission for variation in number would be lost. Some have said in interpreting this noble verse: when the verse about orphans was revealed, and about consuming their property being a grave sin, the guardians began to feel uneasy about their guardianship out of fear of incurring sin by failing to act justly. Yet they had not felt uneasy about failing to be just regarding women's rights, since a man might have ten wives. So it was said to them: if you fear failing to be just regarding the rights of orphans and feel uneasy about it, then also fear failing to be just among women, and reduce the number of wives you marry, because whoever feels uneasy about a sin or repents from it while committing a similar one is neither uneasy nor repentant. Others said: they did not feel uneasy about fornication, while they felt uneasy about guardianship of orphans. So it was said: if you fear injustice toward orphans, then fear fornication, and marry from the women who are lawful to you, and do not hover around what is forbidden. It is clear that the eloquence of this noble composition does not support these two views, because they rest on the first verse being revealed earlier and widely known among people, while it is evident that its ruling depends on what follows it: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ (4:5), up to His saying ﴿and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ (4:6).

**﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾**, that is, among them, even in the smallest of the mentioned numbers, just as you feared regarding orphans, or just as you have not been just toward them, or just as you have not been just regarding what exceeds these numbers.

**﴿Then one﴾**, that is: then adhere to one, or choose one, and leave aside all of them entirely. It was read in the nominative (*raf'*), meaning: then what is sufficient is one, or then one is enough for you.

**﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾**, that is: from the concubines (*sarari*, sing. *sarriyya*), of whatever number they may reach. This is coordinated with "one," in that adherence and choice in this case are by way of concubinage (*tasarri*), not by way of marriage as in what was coordinated with it. This is because it would necessitate that ownership by marriage be applied to ownership by right hand, given that the addressees are the same in both places. This differs from His saying later, ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then from what your right hands possess﴾ (4:25), where the one commanded to marry there is not the same as those addressed as owners of right hands. He equated in ease and convenience between one free wife and concubines without restriction to a number, because their responsibility is light, their burden is small, and there is no obligation of equal division (*qasm*) among them. It was also read as *aw man malakat aymanukum* (with *man*, for rational beings). The form in the well-known reading (*ma*) indicates that their rank is lower than that of rational beings.

**﴿That﴾** refers to choosing one wife and concubinage.

**﴿Is nearer to your not deviating﴾**. *Al-'awl* means inclination, from the expression *'ala al-mizan 'awlan* when the scale tilted, and *'ala fi al-hukm*, meaning he was unjust. Here it means forbidden inclination, which is the opposite of justice. That is: what has been mentioned, choosing one or concubinage, is closer than other options to your not inclining in a forbidden way, because such inclination is entirely absent: in the first case because its location is absent, and in the second because its danger is absent. This contrasts with choosing a number of wives in plural marriage, where forbidden inclination is anticipated because its location and danger are both present. From this it becomes clear that the basis of the matter is not achieving justice itself, as some have said, but avoiding *'awl*. It was explained as: that your dependents not increase, meaning that a man's dependents are his burden (*'ayal*, from *'ala ya'ulu*, i.e., he supports them). Thus increased dependents is expressed as increased expense, as a figure of speech (*kinayah*). This is supported by the reading *an tu'ilu* from *a'ala al-rajul* when his dependents increased. The reason concubinage is likely to mean fewer dependents, even though one may acquire many concubines, is that one may withdraw from them (*'azl*) without their consent, which is not the case with wives. The sentence is a new independent sentence (*mustaʾnafah*) that functions in relation to what precedes it as a causal explanation (*ta'lil*).

﴿وَآتُوا النِّساءَ﴾ أي: اللاتي أمر بنكاحهن.

﴿صَدُقاتِهِنَّ﴾ جمع *صَدُقَة* كـ*سَمُرَة*، وهي المَهْر (الصداق، أي المهر الذي يُعطى للزوجة). وقُرئ بسكون الدال تخفيفًا، وبضم الصاد وسكون الدال، جمعَ *صُدْقَة* كـ*غُرْفَة*، وبضمها على التوحيد، وهو تثقيل *صُدْقَة* كـ*ظُلُمَة* في *ظُلْمَة*.

﴿نِحْلَةً﴾ قال ابن عباس وقتادة وابن جريج وابن زيد: أي فريضة من الله، لأنها مما فرضه الله في *النِّحْلَة* (أي الملة والشريعة والدين). فانتصابها على الحالية من *الصَّدُقات*، أي: أعطوهن مهورهن حال كونها فريضة منه تعالى. وقال الزجاج: تَدَيُّنًا، فانتصابها على أنها مفعول لأجله، أي: أعطوهن ديانةً وشِرْعةً. وقال الكلبي: "نِحْلَةً" أي هبة وعطية من الله تعالى وتفضلًا منه عليهن، فانتصابه على الحالية منها أيضًا. وقيل: عطية من جهة الأزواج، من *نَحَلَه* كذا إذا أعطاه إياه ووهبه له عن طيبة من نفسه، *نِحْلَةً* و*نُحْلًا*. والتعبير عن إيتاء المهور بالنِّحْلَة مع كونها واجبة على الأزواج لإفادة معنى الإيتاء عن كمال الرضا وطيب الخاطر. وانتصابها على المصدرية، لأن الإيتاء والنِّحْلَة بمعنى الإعطاء، كأنه قيل: وانْحِلُوا النساءَ صَدُقاتهن نِحْلَةً، أي: أعطوهن مهورهن عن طيبة أنفسكم. أو على الحالية من ضمير *آتوا*، أي: آتوهن صدقاتهن ناحلين طيبي النفوس بالإعطاء، أو من *الصَّدُقات*، أي: مَنحولةً معطاةً عن طيبة الأنفس. فالخطاب للأزواج. وقيل: الخطاب للأولياء، لأنهم كانوا يأخذون مهور بناتهم، وكانوا يقولون: "هنيئًا لك النافجة" لمن يولد له بنت، يعنون: تأخذ مهرها فتَنْفِج به مالك، أي تُعظِّمه.

﴿فَإنْ طِبْنَ لَكم عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنهُ﴾ الضمير للصَّدُقات، وتذكيره لإجرائه مجرى ذلك، فإنه قد يُشار به إلى المتعدد، كما في قوله عز وجل: ﴿قُلْ أأُنَبِّئُكم بِخَيْرٍ مِن ذَلِكُمْ﴾ بعد ذكر الشهوات المعدودة. وقد رُوي عن رؤبة أنه حين قيل له في قوله:

﴿فِيها خُطُوطٌ مِن سَوادٍ وبَلَقْ ∗∗∗ كَأنَّهُ في الجِلْدِ تَوْلِيعُ البَهَقْ﴾

إنْ أردتَ الخطوطَ ينبغي أن تقول: *كأنها*، وإن أردتَ السوادَ والبلقَ ينبغي أن تقول: *كأنهما*. قال: لكني أردتُ: كأنّ ذلك. أو للصداق الواقع موقعه، صدقاتهن، كأنه قيل: "وآتوا النساءَ صداقهنّ"، كما في قوله تعالى: ﴿فَأصَّدَّقَ وأكُنْ﴾، حيث عطف *أكُنْ* على ما دلّ عليه المذكور ووقع موقعه، كأنه قيل: إن أخّرتني أصَّدَّقْ وأكُنْ. واللام متعلقة بالفعل، وكذا *عن*، لكن بتضمينه معنى التجافي والتجاوز. و*مِن* متعلقة بمحذوف وقع صفةً لـ*شيء*، أي: كائنٍ من الصَّداق. وفيه بعثٌ لهنّ على تقليل الموهوب.

﴿نَفْسًا﴾ تمييز، والتوحيد لما أن المقصود بيان الجنس، أي: إن وهبن لكم شيئًا من الصداق متجافيًا عنه نفوسُهنّ، طيباتٍ غيرَ مخبثات، بما يضطرهنّ إلى البذل من شكاسة أخلاقكم وسوء معاشرتكم. لكن عدل عن لفظ الهبة والسماحة إلى ما عليه النظم الكريم، إيذانًا بأن العمدة في الأمر إنما هو طيب النفس وتجافيها عن الموهوب بالمرة.

﴿فَكُلُوهُ﴾ أي: فخذوا ذلك الشيء الذي طابت به نفوسهن، وتصرفوا فيه تملّكًا. وتخصيص الأكل بالذكر لأنه معظم وجوه التصرفات المالية.

﴿هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا﴾ صفتان من *هَنُؤَ الطعامُ* و*مَرُؤَ*، إذا كان سائغًا لا تنغيص فيه. وقيل: *الهَنِيء* الذي يَلِذُّه الأكل، و*المَرِيء* ما يُحمد عاقبته. وقيل: ما يَنْساغ في مَجْراه، الذي هو *المَرِيء*، وهو ما بين الحُلقوم إلى فم المعدة، سُمّي بذلك لـ*مُروءِ* الطعام فيه، أي: انْسياغه. ونصبهما على أنهما صفتان للمصدر، أي: أكلًا هنيئًا مريئًا، أو على أنهما حالان من الضمير المنصوب، أي: كلوه وهو هنيءٌ مريءٌ. وقد يُوقف على *كلوه* ويُبتدأ *هنيئًا مريئًا* على الدعاء، وعلى أنهما صفتان أُقيمتا مقام المصدرين، كأنه قيل: هَنْأً ومَرْأً. وهذه عبارة عن التحليل والمبالغة في الإباحة وإزالة التبعة. ورُوي أن ناسًا كانوا يتأثمون أن يقبل أحدهم من زوجته شيئًا مما ساقه إليها، فنزلت.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 5:

﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth﴾ This is a return to explaining the remaining rulings concerning the wealth of orphans, and a detailing of what was stated in summary earlier concerning the condition, time and manner of handing it over. It comes after explaining some rulings concerning the orphan women themselves, namely their marriage, and explaining some rights concerning other women who are not related to them, in terms of both person and property, by way of digression (istitrad). The address is to the guardians (awliya'). They were forbidden to give the wasteful among the orphans their property, lest they squander it. It is attributed to them (the guardians), although it belongs to the orphans, not in view of it being under their guardianship, as has been said, for that is not valid given the attribute mentioned next, but rather by treating its being specific to its owners as if it were specific to the guardians. Thus their property is as if it were their own property, because of the generic and relational unity between them, as an intensification in urging them to safeguard it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill your own selves﴾, meaning: let not some of you kill others, where He expressed the human species by "your selves", as an intensification in restraining them from killing one another, so that their killing is as if it were the killing of their own selves. This has been reinforced by expressing its being the means of livelihood of its owners by making it the means of livelihood of the guardians. So it is said: ﴿which God has made for you a means of support﴾, meaning: God has made it something by which you stand and are sustained, with the first object omitted, so that if you waste it, you will be lost. Then the intensification was increased, until that by which one stands is itself called "standing", so that in itself it is your standing and your sustenance. It has also been said: it is attributed to the guardians only because it is of the kind by which people maintain their livelihoods, the intent not being personal specificity but generic specificity, which is the meaning of that by which livelihood is maintained, toward which hearts incline, and which is stored for times of need. In this sense it is not specific to orphans.

And you are aware that this is far from taking the guardians to the aforementioned safeguarding. How so? For the generic, monetary unity is not restricted to what lies between the orphans' property and the guardians' property, but is realized between their property and the property of strangers. Therefore there is no basis at all for considering it.

"اللّاتِي" and "اللَّواتِي" are read, and "قَيْمًا" is read with the meaning of "قِيامًا", just as "عَوْذًا" comes with the meaning of "عِياذًا". "قِوامًا" is read with a kasra on the qaf, which is that by which a thing is maintained, or the verbal noun of قاوم, and it is read with a fatha on it.

﴿And provide for them from it and clothe them﴾, meaning: make it a place for their provision and clothing, by trading and seeking profit, so that their expenses come from profits and not from the principal of the wealth. It has also been said: the address is to every person, whoever he may be, and the intent is the prohibition against entrusting the management of his wealth to someone without sound judgment, from among his wives, children, agents and others. It is not hidden that this detracts from the eloquence of the noble arrangement.

﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾, meaning: words that are gentle, by which their souls are made content. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj: promise them a fair promise, by saying: when you become righteous and sound of judgment, we will hand over your wealth to you. Whatever the soul finds comforting because of its goodness, in law or reason, from speech or action, is ma'ruf (recognized good), and whatever it rejects because of its ugliness, in law or reason, is munkar (reprehensible).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 6:

﴿And test the orphans⦆ This begins the specification of the time for handing over the orphans' property to them and the explanation of its condition, after the command to give it unconditionally and the prohibition against doing so while its owners are foolish. That is: test those among them who are not clearly foolish before puberty, by following up on their circumstances in the soundness of religion and their guidance to preserving property and handling it well, and try them with what suits their situation. If they are of the people of trade, then give them some of the property with which they may conduct buying and selling. If they are among those who have estates, households and servants, then give them some of it that they may spend on the maintenance of their slaves, servants, hired workers and all their other expenses, until the true state of their affairs becomes clear to you.

﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age⦆ That is, by reaching puberty, because at that point they are fit for marriage.

﴿And if you perceive⦆ That is, you witness and ascertain. It is also read as "aḥastum" (you sensed), in the sense of "aḥsastum," as in the saying of one who said:

"Except that the noble she-camels among the mounts / perceived him, and they were wary of him."

﴿in them maturity (rushd)⦆ That is, guidance towards the ways of handling affairs without incapacity or squandering. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the object is for emphasis on what is put first and to create anticipation for what is delayed, or to give weight to its being the starting point for it. The tanwin indicates sufficiency of some degree of maturity. It is also read with a fatha on the rā' and the shīn, and with a ḍamma on both.

﴿then hand over to them their property⦆ without delay beyond the limit of puberty. The choice of "daf'" (handing over) over the "itā'" (giving) occurring at the beginning of the matter indicates a difference between the two in meaning, as has been pointed out earlier. The structure of the noble verse is that "ḥattā" is the particle after which sentences occur, as in the line:

"The slain did not cease to pour out their blood / in the Tigris, until the water of the Tigris became discolored."

What follows it is a conditional sentence made the limit of the testing. The verb of the condition is "balaghū" (they reach), and its answer is the second conditional sentence. It is as if it were said: test the orphans until the time of their puberty and their becoming entitled to having their property handed over to them, on condition that maturity is perceived. The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that whoever reaches puberty without being mature, either through squandering or incapacity, is never to be given his property. This is the view taken by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu Hanifa said: he is to be waited for until twenty-five years of age, because puberty by age is eighteen years; when seven years are added to that, which is a period regarded in human conditions, on the basis of what the Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Command them to pray at seven," his property is handed over to him whether maturity is perceived in him or not.

﴿And do not devour it wastefully and hastily, before they grow up⦆ That is: wastefully and hastily, hurrying towards their growing up, or because of your wastefulness and your haste towards their growing up, you would overspend on it, saying "we spend as we wish before the orphans grow up, so they snatch it from our hands." The sentence is an emphasis on the command to hand over, a confirmation of it, and a preparation for what follows it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is rich, let him abstain﴾ etc. That is: whoever among the guardians and executors is rich, let him refrain from consuming it and be content with what God, exalted is He, has given him of wealth and provision, out of compassion for the orphan and preserving his property.

﴿And whoever is⦆ among the guardians and executors.

﴿poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner⦆ to the extent of his necessary need and the wage of his effort and service. In the wording "abstain" and "eat in a reasonable manner" there is an indication that the executor has a right because of his management of it. From the Prophet ﷺ: "A man said to him: I have an orphan in my care; may I eat from his property? He said: In a reasonable manner, without accumulating wealth, and without protecting your property with his property." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The guardian of an orphan said to him: May I drink from the milk of his camels? He said: If you are seeking its strayed ones, and mending its trough, and smearing its mangy ones, and watering them on the day of their coming, then drink without harming the offspring and without excessive milking." From Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "He is to be lean as an animal is lean, and to reduce himself to the status of a hired worker in what is absolutely necessary." From al-Sha'bi: "He eats from his property to the extent that is determined for him in it." And from him: "Like carrion, he takes it at times of necessity and repays it." From Mujahid: "He borrows, and when he becomes well-off, he repays." From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "If he wishes, he may drink the surplus milk, ride the animal's back, wear what covers him of clothing, and take sustenance, without exceeding it. If he becomes well-off, he repays it, and if he becomes destitute, he is free of it." From 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have placed myself, from the property of Allah, exalted is He, in the position of the guardian of an orphan: if I am rich, I abstain; if I am poor, I eat in a reasonable manner; and when I become well-off, I repay." The form "is'ta'affa" is more emphatic than "'affa," as if it seeks an increase in chastity.

﴿So when you hand over to them their property⦆ after you have observed the conditions mentioned. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the explicit object is for emphasis on it.

﴿then call witnesses against them⦆ that they have received it and taken possession of it, and that your obligations are discharged from it, since that is further from suspicion, more effective in avoiding disputes, more conducive to trustworthiness and clearing of reputation. Although this is not obligatory according to our companions, since the executor is believed in claiming delivery with an oath, contrary to the views of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both.

﴿And Allah suffices as a reckoner⦆ That is: as one who calls to account. So do not oppose what He has commanded you, and do not transgress the limits He has set for you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 7:

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave behind.﴾ This begins the explanation of the rules of inheritance (mawarith), after the explanation of the rules concerning the property of orphans that passes to them by inheritance. By "the close relatives" (al-aqrabun) is meant those among them who are entitled to inherit. The "min" in "mimma" is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier (sifah) of "nasib," meaning: for them there is a share existing from what was left behind. It has also been permitted for it to be connected to "nasib" itself.

﴿And for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave behind.﴾ The mention of their ruling separately, rather than weaving it into the rulings for them as in saying "for men and women, etc.," is for the sake of giving attention to their matter, announcing their independent entitlement to inheritance, and indicating from the outset the difference between the two groups' shares, and emphasizing the nullification of the judgment of the Jahiliyyah. For they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would say, "Only one who fights and defends the protected domain inherits." It is narrated that Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari (p-147) left behind his wife Umm Kuhhah and three daughters, and his paternal cousins Suwayd and 'Arfatah, or Qatadah and 'Arfajah, seized his inheritance from them according to the custom of the Jahiliyyah. Umm Kuhhah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him, and he said: "Return until I see what Allah the Most High brings about." Then the verse was revealed, and he sent to the two of them: "Allah has indeed made a share for them, but has not specified it, so do not distribute anything from Aws's property until it is specified." Then ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾ was revealed, etc., and he gave Umm Kuhhah the eighth, the daughters two-thirds, and the remainder to the two cousins. This is evidence for the permissibility of delaying the explanation (bayan) of a ruling beyond the address (khitab). His words, Exalted is He: ﴿of what little or much of it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the latter "ma," with the preposition repeated, and the pronoun in it refers back to it. This substitution is also intended in the first clause, though omitted for reliance on what is mentioned; its benefit is to remove the misconception that certain kinds of property are restricted to certain heirs, such as horses and weapons being for men, and to establish that each of the two groups has a right in everything, great or small.

﴿A share, obligatory﴾ is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid), like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾, as if it were said: a divided portion that is prescribed; or in the accusative of state (hal), since the meaning is: a share has been established for them existing from what the parents and close relatives leave behind, while it is prescribed; or in the accusative of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: I mean a fixed, prescribed share, obligatory for them. In this is evidence that if an heir turns away from his share, his right is not thereby forfeited.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 8:

﴿And when the division (qismah) takes place﴾, i.e., the division of the estate (tarikah). It has been placed first although it is the object (maf'ul), because it is the subject of inquiry, and because the agent (fa'il) is multiple; had the order been observed, the harmony of the parts of the speech would be lost.

﴿the near of kin﴾ among those who do not inherit.

﴿and the orphans and the needy﴾ from among the outsiders (ajanib).

﴿then provide for them out of it﴾, i.e., give them something from the property being divided, as indicated by the division. It has been said: the pronoun refers to "what" (ma), and it is a recommendation (amr nadb) imposed upon the adult heirs, to console the hearts of the mentioned groups and to give charity to them. It has also been said: it is a command of obligation (amr wujub), and then there was disagreement about its abrogation (naskh).

﴿and speak to them a kindly word﴾, which is that they should pray for them, make light of what they have given them (istiqlal), apologize for that, and not reproach them (la yamunnu 'alayhim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 9:

﴿And let those fear [God] who, if they had left behind them weak offspring, would have been apprehensive for them.﴾ This is a command to the guardians (al-awsiya') that they should fear God, Exalted is He, and be conscious of Him regarding the matter of orphans, so that they treat them as they would wish their own weak offspring to be treated after their death. Or it is addressed to those among the visitors who attend the sick person at the time of his bequest, that they should fear their Lord, or fear the children of the sick person and show them compassion as they would show compassion to their own children, so that they do not allow him to harm them by diverting the wealth away from them. Or it is addressed to the heirs, with compassion toward those weak relatives, orphans and needy persons who attend the division, imagining that if they were their own children who had been left behind them weak like them, would they permit their deprivation? Or it is addressed to the testators, that they should consider the heirs and not be extravagant in the bequest. And "if" (law) together with what is within its scope is a relative clause modifying "those," meaning: let those fear whose condition and attribute is that if they were about to leave behind heirs who are weak, they would fear their being lost. The placing of the command upon this condition indicates the intended purpose of it and its underlying reason, and it urges compassion and that one should love for the children of others what one loves for one's own children, and it is a warning to the violator through the state of his own children. It has also been read as "ḍu'afā'" (ضُعَفاءَ), "ḍi'āfā" (ضِعافى), and "ḍa'āfā" (ضَعافى).

﴿So let them be mindful of God﴾ in that matter; and the fa' (فَ) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes it.

﴿And let them speak words of appropriate justice﴾ He commanded them with taqwa (piety), which is the ultimate goal of fear, after He had commanded them with fear, observing both the starting point and the endpoint; for the first has no benefit without the second. Then He commanded them to say to the orphans what they would say to their own children, with compassion and good manners; or to the sick person, that which restrains him from extravagance in bequest and from wasting the heirs, and reminds him of repentance and the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahada); or to those present at the division, an excuse and a good promise; or that they should speak in the bequest in a manner that does not lead to exceeding one-third.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, Verse 10:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾, meaning: in the manner of injustice, or while being unjust. This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a sentence that begins a new statement while continuing the discourse), brought to confirm the content of the commands and prohibitions that were detailed earlier.

﴿They only consume fire into their bellies﴾, meaning: the full contents of their bellies.

﴿Fire﴾, meaning: that which leads to the Fire and results in it. It is narrated from Abu Barzah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, may He be exalted, will raise a people from their graves, their mouths blazing with fire." It was said: "Who are they?" He said, peace be upon him: "Have you not seen that Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾?"

﴿And they will burn in a blazing Fire﴾, meaning: they will enter a great Fire whose description is indefinite. It was recited with the *yā'* vowelled with a *ḍammah* (*yuṣlawna*), both lightened and intensified, from *al-iṣlā'* and *al-taṣliyah* (burning and being burned). It is said: *ṣaliya al-nār*, he endured its heat; *ṣalaytuhu*, I roasted it; and *aṣlaytuhu*, I cast him into it. *Al-sa'īr* is on the pattern *fa'īl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, from *sa'artu al-nār*, when I kindled the fire.

It is reported that the one who consumes the property of an orphan will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with smoke coming out of his grave, from his mouth, his nose, his ears and his eyes, so that people will know that he used to consume the property of an orphan in the world.

It is also reported that when this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on people, so they completely avoided mixing with orphans, and the matter became difficult for the orphans. Then the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them﴾, and so on.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 11:

﴿Allah enjoins upon you﴾ is the beginning of the detailing of the rulings on inheritance that were stated in summary in His words, exalted is He: ﴿For men there is a share﴾ and so on. The categories of heirs are three: a category that never falls away in any circumstance, namely the parents, the children and the spouses, so these are two categories; and the third is the kalalah (collateral heirs), that is, He commands you and charges you.

﴿concerning your children﴾, the children of each one of you; that is, concerning the matter of their inheritance. They are mentioned first because they are the closest of the heirs to the deceased and the most enduring after the one who leaves the inheritance.

﴿The male's share is equal to the portion of two females﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought to clarify and explain the injunction. It was said that its place in i'rab is in the accusative, dependent on "yuwsikum" (enjoins you), in the sense that He prescribes and legislates this ruling for you. This is close to what al-Farra' held, for he treats verbs that carry the meaning of "saying" as such in reporting the sentence that follows them, and its parallel is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness﴾ (p-149) and so on. As for His words, ﴿for the male﴾, it necessarily requires a pronoun referring back to the children, omitted on the basis of its being clear, as in the saying: "Butter is two manas for a dirham," meaning: for the male among them. It was also said that the definite article stands in place of the pronoun, and the original is: "for their male," and "mithl" (equal to) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: for the males among them there is a share equal to the share of two females. Beginning with the statement of the ruling for the male is to show his superiority over the female, just as the male is the basis for doubling his share. The choice of the terms "male" and "female" over what was mentioned first, "men" and "women," is to make explicit that the adults and the minors of both groups are equal in entitlement, without any consideration of puberty or adulthood in this at all, as is the claim of the people of ignorance, who did not give inheritance to children or to women.

﴿If they are women﴾, i.e., the children, and the feminine form is according to the predicate, which is His words, ﴿women﴾, meaning: purely female, with no male among them.

﴿more than two﴾ is a second predicate or an adjective of "women," meaning: women exceeding two.

﴿then for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, i.e., of what the deceased left, the deceased being understood from the context.

﴿But if she is one﴾, i.e., the one born.

﴿alone﴾, i.e., a single woman with no brother or sister with her; the omission of mention of the qualified noun is because it is clear from what preceded.

﴿then for her is half﴾ of what he left. "Wahida" was also read as "wahidatun" with "kana" as a complete verb. Scholars differed regarding two daughters. Ibn 'Abbas said: their ruling is the ruling of the single one, because He, exalted is He, assigned two-thirds to those above them. Al-Jumhur said: their ruling is the ruling of those above them, because when He, exalted is He, explained that the male's share is equal to the share of two females when there is a female with him, which is two-thirds, this required that their prescribed share be two-thirds; then, since this might imply that the share would increase with an increase in number, He rejected that with His words, ﴿If they are women more than two﴾. This is supported by the fact that a single daughter is entitled to a third alongside her brother, who is stronger than her in entitlement, so it is all the more fitting and more appropriate that she be entitled to it alongside one like her; and that two daughters are closer in kinship than two sisters, and Allah has prescribed for the two sisters two-thirds, where He said: ﴿then for the two of them is two-thirds of what he left﴾.

﴿And for his parents﴾, i.e., for the two parents of the deceased. The noble arrangement was changed because its ruling is not restricted to the preceding cases.

﴿for each one of them﴾ is a substitute for it by repetition of the governing element, placed between the subject, which is His words, ﴿the sixth﴾, and its predicate, which is "for his parents." The predicate was moved to it to specify that each of them is entitled to a sixth, and as emphasis for it by detailing after summary. It was also read "al-sudsu" with the letter dal sukun for lightness, and likewise "al-thuluth," "al-rub'," and "al-thumn."

﴿of what he left﴾ is related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause of "al-sudus," and the governing element is the stability implied in the predicate, meaning: being from what the deceased left.

﴿if he has children﴾, or a son's children, male or female, singular or plural; except that the father, in the case of the female line, after taking his mentioned share, takes what remains of the sharers by way of agnatic residuary entitlement.

﴿But if he has no children﴾ nor children of a son.

﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾ alone, ﴿then for his mother is a third﴾ of what he left, and the remainder is for the father. It was not mentioned because there is no need for it: since it was stipulated that the heirs are restricted to his two parents, and the mother's share was specified, it is known that the remainder is for the father. The singling out of the mother's side with mention, while leaving the father's side to be understood from the context, though the explanation is also achieved by the reverse, is because her share is more concise and her entitlement is more complete and more abundant; or because his entitlement is by way of agnatic residue rather than fixed share. This applies when neither of the spouses is with them. But when one of the spouses is with them, the mother has a third of what remains after the fixed share of one of them, not a third of the whole, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, for that would lead to preferring the mother over the father, although he is stronger than her in inheritance, as is evident from his taking double her share when they are alone without one of the spouses, and his being both a holder of a fixed share and an agnatic residuary; and that contradicts the established rule of the Shari'ah.

﴿If he has siblings﴾, i.e., a number of those who have brotherhood, without regard to the division into thirds, whether they are from both parents or from one of them, and whether they are males or females, mixed together, and whether they have a share of inheritance or are excluded by the father.

﴿then for his mother is a sixth﴾. As for the sixth from which they have excluded her, it is for the father when he exists, and for them when he does not; this is the view of the majority. According to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is for them in every case, except that this exclusion according to him is not realized by fewer than three siblings, nor by full sisters alone. It was also read "fa-li-immihi" with a kasra on the hamza, following the preceding letter.

﴿after a bequest﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the whole clause is connected to everything preceding it together, not to what immediately follows it alone, meaning: these shares are for the heirs after the removal of a bequest.

﴿which he bequeaths﴾, i.e., the deceased. It was also read passive with light doubling, and active with doubling. The benefit of the description is to encourage bequest and recommend it.

﴿or a debt﴾ is conjoined to "bequest," except that it is not restricted by the qualification that was applied to it; rather it is unrestricted, encompassing what is established by evidence or by acknowledgment during health. The choice of "aw" (or), which indicates permissibility, over the conjunction "wa" (and) is to show that both are equal in obligation, and that they precede the division, whether together or separately. The mention of the bequest before the debt, though it comes after it in ruling, is to show complete care for its execution, because it is prone to neglect in its fulfillment, and because it is not consistently observed, unlike the debt.

﴿Your parents and your children, you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾. The address is to the heirs, so "ababa'ukum" (your parents) is a subject, "abna'ukum" (your children) is conjoined to it, "la tadrun" (you do not know) is its predicate, "ayyuhum" (which of them) is a subject, "aqrabu" (nearer) is its predicate, and "naf'an" (in benefit) is in the accusative as a specification of it, and it is transferred from the agent, as though it were said: which of them is nearer to you in benefit? The clause is in the place of accusative governed by "la tadrun," and the large clause is parenthetical, emphasizing the obligation to execute the bequest, meaning: your ascendants and descendants who die, you do not know which of them is more beneficial to you: is it the one who bequeaths some of his wealth, thereby exposing you to the reward of the Hereafter by executing his bequest, or the one who bequeaths nothing, thereby leaving you the goods of this world in abundance? The denial of knowledge from them is not meant to explain that the matter is confused for them, nor that the beneficialness of each of the first and second is within the realm of possibility for them without one being preferred over the other, as in His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "The example of my community is like rain; one does not know whether its beginning is better or its end," for that has no bearing on the stated emphasis or the encouragement to execute the bequest. Rather, it establishes the beneficialness of the first within an implication that they hold a belief in the beneficialness of the second, based on lack of knowledge. This is indicated by the expression of beneficialness as nearness in benefit, to recall the basis of their assumption and to specify the source of their error, and as exaggeration in the stated encouragement by depicting the deferred reward in the form of the immediate, since human nature is inclined to love present good. It is as if it were said: you do not know which of them is more beneficial to you, so you judge, looking at the apparent circumstance and the nearness of attainment, that the second is more beneficial, although the matter is the opposite; for the reward of the Hereafter, given the certainty of its reaching its owner and the perpetuity of his enjoyment of it, together with the extreme brevity of the period between them of the worldly life, is nearer and more present, while the goods of this world, given the swiftness of their exhaustion and perishing, are farther and more remote. It was also said: the address is to the testators, and the meaning: you do not know who is more beneficial to you among those who inherit from you, of your ascendants and descendants, in this world and in the next; so strive in their matter as Allah, exalted is He, has enjoined upon you, and do not intend to prefer some and deprive others. It is narrated that when one of two related persons has a higher rank than the other in Paradise, he asks Allah, exalted is He, to raise his companion up to him, and he is raised up to him by his intercession. It was said: then the parenthetical clause is emphasizing the matter of the division. You should be aware that this indicates that the basis of inheritance is what has been mentioned of nearness in benefit, whereas the actual link is kinship.

﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a masdar emphasizing an omitted verb, meaning: Allah has obligated that as an obligation; or it is in agreement with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Allah enjoins upon you﴾, for it carries the meaning of: He commands you and imposes upon you.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾, i.e., of the interests and the ranks.

﴿Wise﴾ in all that He decrees and ordains, so the rulings mentioned enter into this in the first place.

(p-151) ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ of the wealth; this begins the explanation of the rulings concerning the second category of heirs. The reason for mentioning the ruling on men's inheritance first is something that needs no explanation.

﴿If they have no child﴾ i.e., no child who is an heir, whether from their womb or from the loins of their sons or the sons of their sons, however low, whether male or female, whether one or many, because the word "walad" (child) includes all of them, whether from you or from others. The remainder is for their heirs among the sharers (dhawu al-furud) and the agnates ('asabat) or others, and for the public treasury (bayt al-mal) if they have no other heir at all.

﴿But if they have a child﴾ in the manner detailed above. The fa' (then) indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes, for mentioning the supposition of there being no child and the statement of its ruling entails the supposition of its existence and the statement of its ruling.

﴿then for you is a quarter of what they leave﴾ of the wealth, and the remainder is for the rest of the heirs.

﴿after any bequest﴾ This is connected to both cases, not to what immediately precedes it alone.

﴿they bequeath﴾ is in the genitive position, being an attribute of "wasiyyah" (bequest). Its benefit is what has passed: encouraging the deceased to make a bequest and urging the heirs to carry it out.

﴿or a debt﴾ is conjoined to "bequest," whether its establishment is by evidence or by acknowledgment. The use of "aw" (or) rather than the conjunction "wa" (and) is because of what has been mentioned, namely to show the utmost concern for carrying it out.

﴿And for them is a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child﴾ according to the detail mentioned just above, and the remainder is for the rest of your heirs among the sharers and the agnates, or the dhawu al-arham (distant kindred), or the public treasury if you have no other heir at all.

﴿But if you have a child﴾ in the manner detailed, ﴿then for them is an eighth of what you leave﴾ of the wealth, the remainder going to the others.

﴿after any bequest you make or a debt﴾ The discussion of this is as detailed for its counterparts. He prescribed for the man, by virtue of the marital right, twice what He prescribed for the woman, as in lineage, because of his superiority over her and his evident nobility; for this reason he was singled out with the honour of direct address. The same analogy applies to every man and woman who share the same side and degree of kinship, and nothing is excepted from this except the uterine siblings, the male freed slave and the female freed slave. The single woman and the plural women are equal in the quarter and the eighth.

﴿And if a man﴾ is the beginning of the explanation of the rulings concerning the third category of heirs, which may be subject to exclusion. The reason for placing it after the first two is clear. The "man" here means the deceased. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿is inherited﴾ is in the passive voice from the verb waritha (to inherit), not from awratha (to bequeath), and is the predicate of kana (was), i.e., he is inherited from.

﴿kalalah﴾ Kalalah is originally a verbal noun meaning kalal, which is the loss of strength through weariness. It was borrowed for relationship not through the line of father or child, because it is weak in comparison with the relationship of those two. It is applied to one who leaves behind neither child nor parent, and to one among the deceased who is neither parent nor child, in the sense of one possessing kalalah, just as qarabah (kinship) is applied to kinsfolk. It has also been permitted that it be an attribute, like hajajah and faqaqah for a fool. Its accusative may therefore be either a object of purpose, i.e., he is inherited from for the sake of the said kinship; or a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in (p-152) "is inherited," i.e., while he is one with kalalah; or the predicate of kana, with "is inherited" being an attribute of "man," i.e., if there is a man who is inherited, having kalalah, who has no parent or child. It has been read as "yuwarrithu" in the active voice, both lightened and doubled, in which case the accusative of "kalalah" is either a circumstantial state of the verb's subject with the object omitted, i.e., he bequeaths for the sake of kalalah.

﴿or a woman﴾ is conjoined to "man," restricted by what it is restricted by, i.e., or a woman who is inherited in the same way. Perhaps the separate mention of her from his mention is to signal her nobility and originality in the rulings.

﴿And he﴾ i.e., the man. This contains emphasis, signalling the aforementioned, since she is not separately addressed after her mention has already run its course. It has been said that the pronoun refers to each of them. ﴿has a brother or a sister﴾ i.e., from the mother alone. It has been read so, for the rulings on full and consanguine siblings are those mentioned at the end of the noble surah. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "is inherited," or of "man" if "is inherited" is taken as an attribute of it. Its purpose is to depict the case, and the mention of "kalalah" is to confirm that the stated ruling applies even if other heirs of a different kind are present through kinship not of the kalalah type. As for its applying where the mother or the grandmother exists, though their kinship is not of the kalalah type, this is by consensus.

﴿Then each of them﴾ i.e., of the brother and the sister.

﴿receives a sixth﴾ without preference of the male over the female, because the connection to the deceased is through pure femaleness.

﴿But if they are more than that﴾ i.e., more than the single brother or sister, whether singly or more, and the fa' (then) indicates what has passed: that mentioning the possibility of single occurrence entails mentioning the possibility of plurality.

﴿then they are partners in the third﴾ dividing it equally, and the remainder goes to the rest of the heirs among the sharers and the agnates. This is the case. As for the permissibility that "is inherited" in the well-known reading be passive from awratha (to bequeath), with the meaning that the heir is made an heir for the sake of kalalah or as one with kalalah, i.e., not a father or child, and that heir has a brother or sister, so that each of that heir and his brother or sister receives a sixth; and if they are more than that, i.e., more than two, by being three or more, then they are partners in the third distributed between the two, with nothing added to it, this is far from correct. Firstly, because under that supposition what counts is the brotherhood between the heir and his partner in inheritance from his brother or sister, not the brotherhood between him and his testator, upon which the rule of inheritance is based and by which the depiction of the case is completed. What counts between them is inheritance by way of kalalah, which is general to all forms of kinship not through birth. Thus neither his share nor his partner's share is what has been mentioned exactly. Whoever claims that it is restricted to uterine siblings, relying on consensus, and that the kalalah here means the children of the mother, has thereby acknowledged the falsity of his opinion without realising it. How could it not be so? Its foundation is consensus that the brotherhood in His saying: ﴿and he has a brother or a sister﴾ means uterine siblings specifically, as the quoted reading and the verse at the end of the surah attest. Had the man not been a term for the deceased, and brotherhood not been considered between him and his heirs, it would not be possible for all to be children of the mother. Furthermore, kalalah, as I have pointed out, remains in its general sense with no trace of restriction to children of the mother, let alone consensus on that; otherwise the explanation would have been confined to the case where the heirs are limited to them. The consensus is only on what has been mentioned, that the brother and sister means one who is uterine only. You know well that this amounts to consensus that "is inherited" is from waritha, not awratha. So reflect. Secondly, it requires that the consideration in entitlement to the heirs in the stated share be the brotherhood of some of them to others through the mother, given the consensus mentioned, while entitlement holds on the supposition of brotherhood from both sides. Thirdly, the ruling for the case of the heir's sole existence apart from brother or sister would then remain unexplained, and it does not follow from each of them receiving a sixth by consensus that it is so when alone; do you not see that each of two sisters receives a third when together and a half when alone? Fourthly, singling out one heir for inheritance and making the others follow him in it, despite all sharing the same connection to the testator, is something unprecedented.

﴿after a bequest that is made or a debt﴾ The discussion of this is as in its counterparts, except that the debt here is described by the attribute of the bequest, following the principle that the conjoined is qualified by what qualifies the thing conjoined to, since the scholars agree that non-harm applies here too. That is only realised where the debt's establishment is by acknowledgment during illness, as if it were said: or a debt bequeathed.

﴿without causing harm﴾ is a circumstantial state of the subject of a hidden verb indicated by what is mentioned; what is omitted from the conjoined is understood from it, just as "men" in His saying: ﴿He is glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾ is, according to the passive reading, the subject of a verb implied by what is mentioned, and in the active reading the subject of the verb mentioned and the omitted verb is dispensed with. I.e., he bequeaths what has been mentioned, the bequest and the debt, while causing no harm to the heirs; that is, by bequeathing more than a third, or by making a bequest intended to harm them rather than for devotion, or by acknowledging a false debt during illness. The restriction of this condition to this place is because the heirs are the likely object of the deceased's neglect of their rights.

﴿as a commandment from God﴾ is an infinitive emphasizing a deleted verb, its tanwin signalling magnification, and "from" is connected to a hidden element that functions as an attribute of it, emphasizing its intrinsic majesty with the majesty of its origin. I.e., He commands you with that, a commandment issuing from God, like His saying: ﴿an obligation from God﴾. Perhaps the purpose of assigning each of the two terms its own place is to indicate the difference between the rulings concerning the roots and branches and those concerning others, following the difference between obligation and bequest, though both must be observed. Or it is in the accusative governed by "without causing harm" as an object, since it is an active participle relying on its noun of state, or negated in meaning, so it governs the explicit object. This is supported by the reading in the genitive construct: without causing harm to God's commandment and His covenant, not in the matter of children alone as has been said, since they have no connection to this context, but in the matter of the heirs mentioned here, for all the detailed rulings fall under His saying: ﴿God commands you﴾, serving as its explanation and clarification. Causing harm to them is undermining their rights by reducing them through bequeathing more than a third, or bequeathing with intent to harm rather than devotion, or acknowledging a false debt. Applying the term commandment to the bequest is though it actually falls on the heirs, as in the saying: "O thief of the night, the people of the house!", to intensify the warning against it by framing it as opposition to God's command. Making the bequest mean bequeathing a third or less requires that "without causing harm" be a state of the verb's subject connected to the bequest alone, which entails separating the state from its operator by a foreign element, namely what is conjoined to "a bequest," while the source of harm is not thereby cut off, since the acknowledgment of debt remains unrestricted.

﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾ of the one who causes harm and otherwise.

﴿Forbearing﴾ He does not hasten with punishment, so one should not be deceived by respite. The mention of the glorious Name, though a pronoun would suffice, is to instil awe and cultivate reverence.

(p-154) ﴿These﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned earlier concerning orphans, inheritance, and other matters.

﴿the limits of Allah﴾, that is, His prescribed laws, whose boundaries may not be transgressed.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in all the commands and prohibitions, among which are those detailed here. The mention of the Glorious Name explicitly is to draw attention to what was mentioned just before.

﴿He will admit him into gardens﴾: the word *jannāt* (gardens) is in the accusative. According to the majority of grammarians (*al-Jumhūr*) it is in the accusative of place (*al-ẓarfiyyah*, the adverbial accusative of place), while according to al-Akhfash (a grammarian of the Basran school) it is the direct object (*al-maf'ūliyyah*).

﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a descriptive clause (*ṣifah*) qualifying *jannāt*, and takes the same case as it does.

﴿abiding therein﴾ is an anticipated circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddarah*) from the object of *yudkhilhu* (He will admit him). The plural form is used in view of the plural sense of *man* (whoever) in meaning, just as the singular pronoun is used in view of its singular form in wording.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has preceded: admission into the gardens described with the qualities mentioned, to abide therein forever. The sense of distance in the demonstrative indicates the exceeding loftiness of its rank.

﴿the great triumph﴾, which has no triumph beyond it. The word *fawz*, meaning attaining success or good, is described as "great" either with regard to what it is connected to or with regard to its own essence, for winning something great is itself great. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 14:

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ even in some of the commands and prohibitions. Mujahid said: "In what He has apportioned of inheritances." 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever is not content with the apportionment of Allah, the Exalted, and transgresses what Allah, the Exalted, has said."
