Al-Kalbi said: "That is: whoever denies Allah's apportionment of the inheritances and transgresses His limits, deeming it permissible (istihlal)." The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to intensify the warning, by magnifying the matter and cultivating awe.

﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ His laws, which are bounded in all rulings, so that the matter at hand enters into it in the first place (dukhul awwaliyy).

﴿He will admit him﴾ It is also read with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) in both places.

﴿into a Fire﴾ that is, a great and terrifying one, whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿to abide therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), as has preceded. Perhaps the choice of the singular here is in view of the apparent wording, while the choice of the plural there (in view of the meaning) indicates that abiding in the abode of reward, in a state of togetherness, is more conducive to intimacy, just as abiding in the abode of punishment, in a state of isolation, is more intense in producing loneliness.

﴿And for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ that is, in addition to the punishment of the physical burning, there is another punishment, vague in its reality, whose true nature is known, namely the spiritual punishment, as its description indicates. The clause is circumstantial.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 15:

﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness (al-fahisha)﴾ This begins the explanation of another set of rulings concerning women, following the explanation of the rulings on inheritance. Al-lati is the plural of al-lati (the feminine relative pronoun) according to meaning rather than form. It has been said: it is a plural in a non-analogical form. Al-fahisha is the ugly deed, and by it is meant adultery (al-zina), because of the increased ugliness of that act. Al-ityan (coming to) means committing and engaging in the act; it is said: "atai al-fahisha," meaning he committed it and engaged in it, and similarly "jaaha," "rahaqaha," and "ghashiyaha." It has also been read as "bil-fahisha." So al-ityan has its well-known meaning, and "min" (of/from) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿yaʾtina﴾, meaning: those who commit adultery while being from your women, that is, from your husbands, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those of you who divorce their wives by zihar﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from your women with whom you have consummated marriage﴾. This is also the view of al-Suddi.

﴿Then call four witnesses against them from among you﴾ This is the predicate of the relative pronoun, and the fa' indicates that what falls within the relative clause is the cause of the ruling. That is: seek that four men from among the believing and free men testify against them to the act of adultery.

﴿And if they testify﴾ against them to that.

﴿Then confine them to the houses﴾ That is: detain them therein and make the houses a prison for them.

﴿Until death takes them﴾ That is: until it takes their souls in full.

﴿Death﴾ In this there is an intensification of the terror of death and its presentation in the form of one who takes charge of seizing and taking souls, or the meaning is: the angels of death take them.

﴿Or Allah ordains for them a way﴾ That is: He legislates for them a ruling specific to them. The expression of it as "the way" is perhaps to indicate that it is a path to be traversed, so there is no indication in it that it is lighter than confinement, as Abu Muslim said.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 16:

﴿And the two of you [male and female] who commit it among you﴾ refers to the male adulterer and the female adulterer, by way of taghlib (predominance of the masculine form, a rhetorical device in which the masculine gender is used to cover both sexes).

Al-Sindi said: By these two is meant the unmarried ones (al-bikran) among them, as is indicated by the fact that their punishment is lighter than perpetual confinement (al-habs al-mukhallad). With this, the repetition is removed. However, the ruling on the married adulterer (al-zani al-muhsan) remains unspecified, because the first punishment is specific to the married women (al-muhsanat), and the lack of clarity as to how he is to be attached to one of the two rulings is an indication of the hiddenness of the common ground in the basis for the ruling (al-manat).

﴿So harm them﴾ i.e., by rebuke and reproach. It is said: also by beating them with sandals. It is evident that the implementation of this ruling also takes place only after proof (al-thubut), but its mention has been omitted, relying on what was mentioned just before.

﴿And if they repent﴾ of what they did of the immorality, due to what they encountered of the deterrents of harm and the blows of reproach, as is indicated by the particle fa' (then). ﴿And reform﴾ i.e., their deeds. ﴿Then leave them alone﴾ by ceasing the harm and the reproach, for repentance and reform are among the things that prevent deserving blame and punishment. It has also been permitted that the address is to the witnesses who stood over their lapses, and that by harm is meant censuring them, rebuking them, and threatening them with referral to the rulers, and by leaving them alone is meant refraining from bringing them before the authorities. It is said: The punishment of the two groups mentioned was in the early days of Islam, as explained earlier, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the hadd (prescribed punishment), on the basis of what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Take from me, take from me; Allah has made a way for them: the married one is stoned and the virgin is flogged." It is also said: this verse precedes the first in revelation, and the punishment for fornicators in general was harm, then confinement, then flogging, then stoning. It has also been permitted that the command concerning confinement is not abrogated, by leaving out mention of the hadd because it is known from the Book and the Sunnah, and that they be directed to keep them in their houses after the hadd is carried out, to protect them from what happened to them through going out of their houses and exposing themselves to men. It is not hidden that this is something the noble text does not support. Abu Muslim said, attributing it to Mujahid: The first verse concerns female homosexuals (al-sahhaqat), and this verse concerns male homosexuals (al-lawwatin), and what is in Surat al-Nur concerns the male and female adulterers, holding that what is mentioned in the first is the feminine form specifically, and in the second the masculine form, and there is no necessity to resort to taghlib. Moreover, taghlib is not possible in the first, and the command to call four witnesses contradicts it, for that is not known in the Sharia except in the case of fornication (zina).

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Oft-Returning﴾ exceedingly accepting of repentance.

﴿Most Merciful﴾ of vast mercy; and this is the justification for the command to leave them alone.

﴿Indeed, repentance is with Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse), brought to explain that Allah's acceptance of repentance is not absolute, as His being described as Oft-Returning (Tawwab) and Most Merciful implies. Rather, it is restricted by what the noble text will go on to state. So His saying, ﴿repentance﴾, is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, ﴿for those who do evil﴾, is its predicate (khabar). His saying, ﴿with Allah﴾, is connected to what the predicate's connective meaning of "being established" (al-istiqrar) connects to. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its implicit governing element (al-'amil al-ma'nawi) is one whose permissibility is not disputed. The same applies to an adverb of time or place, or to something omitted that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the subject, hidden within what the predicate is connected to, according to the view of those who permit the fronting of a circumstantial clause before its implicit governing element when it is an adverb, or a prepositional particle, as was previously mentioned in the commentary on His saying, ﴿And for Allah is a pilgrimage to the House upon mankind﴾. (p-156) In any case, the meaning of repentance being "with Him" (ʿalayhi, subhanahu) is that acceptance proceeds from Him, Exalted. The word ﴿with﴾ ('ala) serves to indicate that it is definitely realized, by the established custom and the prior promise, to the extent that it is as though it were among the obligations upon Him, glorified is He. This is the intended meaning of those who said that the word "ʿala" means "min" (from). It was also said that it means "ʿinda" (with). Al-Hasan said: it means the repentance that Allah, Exalted, accepts. It was said: it is the repentance which Allah, Exalted, obligated upon Himself, by His bounty, to accept. This indicates that His saying, ﴿with Allah﴾, is a qualifier of "repentance," with its connected element being omitted and understood as definite, according to the view of those who permit omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause. That is: indeed, the repentance that is with Allah. By ﴿evil﴾ is meant disobedience, whether minor or major. It was said: the predicate is ﴿"with Allah"﴾. His saying, ﴿for those﴾, is connected to what the predicate is connected to, or to something omitted that stands as a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in the connected element of the predicate. There is not in it what is in the first aspect of fronting the circumstantial clause before the implicit governing element, except that what the context requires and the composition calls for is the first, because what precedes it, namely His being described as Oft-Returning and Most Merciful, only calls for explaining that the acceptance of repentance from Him, Exalted, is restricted to those mentioned. That can only be done by making His saying, ﴿for those﴾, etc., a predicate. Do you not see His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do bad deeds﴾, etc.? It clearly states what we have said, as though it were said: indeed, repentance is for these, not for those.

﴿in ignorance﴾ is connected to something omitted that stands as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they do," meaning: they do evil while being involved in it, that is, ignorant and foolish. Or it is connected to "they do," with the particle "bi" being causal, meaning: they do it because of ignorance, since committing sin is something ignorance prompts. The intended meaning is not lack of knowledge that it is evil, but the failure to reflect on its consequence, as the ignorant person does. Qatadah said: The Companions of the Messenger ﷺ gathered and held that everything by which one disobeys one's Lord is ignorance, whether intentionally or by mistake. It is related from Mujahid: "Whoever disobeys Allah, Exalted, is ignorant until he desists from his ignorance." Al-Zajjaj said: By His saying "in ignorance" He means their preferring fleeting pleasure over lasting pleasure.

﴿Then they repent soon﴾ means: within a short time, which is the time before the arrival of death, as is indicated by what will come later in His saying, Exalted: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾, etc., for it is explicit that the time of the death-throes is the time in which repentance is not accepted, so what lies beyond it remains within the scope of acceptance. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "before the authority of death descends upon him." It is related from al-Dahhak: "Every repentance before death" is "soon." It is related from Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi: "So long as it has not been seized by his throat," which is the passage of breath. Abu Ayyub related from the Prophet ﷺ: « "Indeed Allah, Exalted, accepts the repentance of the servant so long as he has not begun to death-rattle." » It is related from ʿAta': "Even if just before his death by the span of a she-camel's milking-pause." It is related from al-Hasan that Iblis, when he was sent down to the earth, said: "By Your might, I will not leave the son of Adam so long as his soul is in his body." So Allah, Exalted, said: "By My might, I will not close the door of repentance upon him so long as he has not begun to death-rattle." And "min" (from) is partitive, meaning: they repent within part of a short time. It is as though He named the period between the occurrence of the sin and the arrival of death a short time. So in whatever part of this period one repents, one is a penitent.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to those mentioned, in terms of their being characterized by what was mentioned. The distance implied in it is due to their being, by the completion of their mention, in the status of the distant. The address is to the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Allah accepts their repentance﴾. The repetition of the attribution in it is to strengthen the ruling. This is a promise of accepting their repentance right after stating that repentance is for them. The "fa" (then) indicates that it is the cause of acceptance.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾: exceeding in knowledge and wisdom, so He builds His rulings and actions upon the foundation of wisdom and benefit. The sentence is a parenthetical clause confirming the content of what precedes it. The expression of the Glorious Name in the place of the pronoun is to indicate the reason for the ruling, since divinity is the source of His being characterized by the attributes of perfection.

(p-157) ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who do evil deeds﴾ — an explicit statement of what was understood from restricting acceptance to the repentance of one who repents soon (min qarib), and an added specification by clarifying that the repentance of others is as if it did not exist. The plural "sayyi'at" (evil deeds) is used in consideration of their repeated occurrence over a long period of time, not because the intended meaning is all their kinds; and what has passed of wrongdoing (al-su') is one type of them.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "Indeed, I have repented now."﴾ "Hatta" is a particle of beginning (harf ibtida'), and the conditional clause after it is the terminus (ghayah) of what precedes it. That is: acceptance of repentance is not for those who do evil deeds up to the presence of their death and their saying at that time, "Indeed, I have repented now." The mention of "now" (al-an) serves to further specify the time. The choice of "qala" (he said) over "taaba" (he repented) serves to remove that [statement] from the level of consideration and to avoid calling it repentance.

﴿And nor [is repentance accepted from] those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ — a conjunction with the relative clause before it, meaning: acceptance of repentance is not for these nor for those. These [the second group] were mentioned, although there is no repentance for them at all, for the sake of emphasis in clarifying the non-acceptance of the repentance of procrastinators, and as a notice that their existence is like their non-existence. Moreover, the repetition of the negative particle in the conjoined clause implies a subtle indication that the state of the procrastinators, in failing to bring any benefit, is stronger than the state of those who die upon disbelief. By the two relative pronouns is meant either disbelievers specifically, or sinners alone; their being called "kuffar" (disbelievers) in the circumstantial clause is for emphasis of severity, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾. As for what encompasses both groups together, the designation is then by way of predominance (taghlib). It is also permissible that the first be meant as the wicked (fasaqa) and the second as the disbelievers (kafara), in which there is another emphasis.

﴿Those﴾ — a demonstrative referring to both groups, and the sense of distance in it is to notify the extreme heinousness of their state and the remoteness of their rank in evil. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿We have prepared for them﴾, i.e., We have readied for them.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ — the repetition of the predication is for the reinforcement of the ruling, as mentioned before. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object serves to show concern with the punishment being prepared for them, and the indefinite form of "punishment" along with its qualifier serves to express magnitude both intrinsically and descriptively.

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by force﴾. A man, when his relative died, would throw his garment over the widow or over her tent and say, "I inherit his wife just as I inherit his property." By this he would become more entitled to her than anyone else. Then, if he wished, he would marry her without a dowry other than the first dowry. If he wished, he would marry her to someone else and take her dowry, giving her none of it. If he wished, he would prevent her from remarrying (ʿaḍl) so that she would ransom herself with what she had inherited from her husband. And if the woman went back to her family before the garment was thrown, she had the better right to herself, but they were forbidden from doing this. It was said to them: "It is not lawful for you to take by way of inheritance, as you claim, as inheritances are seized, while they are unwilling to be so treated, or are compelled to it." It was also read as "تَحِلُّ" with a feminine (fawqāniyya) tā' (i.e., "تَحِلُّ"), on the basis that "أنْ تَرِثُوا" means "inheritance" (al-wirātha). It was also read as "كُرْهًا" with a ḍamma on the kāf, which is a dialect form like "الضَّعْف" and "الضُّعْف." When a man married a woman whom he did not need, he would detain her despite bad companionship and oppression, and restrict her so that she would ransom herself from him with her property and seek khul‘ (divorce in exchange for compensation). So it was said to them: ﴿And do not restrain them﴾, coordinated with "تَرِثُوا", with "لا" serving to emphasize the negation. The address is to the husbands. ʿAḍl means detention and constriction; from it comes "عَضَلَتِ المَرْأةُ بِوَلَدِها" when her womb is constricted so that part of the child emerges and part remains. That is: nor should you constrict them.

﴿That you may take away part of what you have given them﴾, i.e., part of the dowry, by their giving you some of it under compulsion, so that you take it from them. The verse does not mention their action, signifying that it is as if it did not exist, since it proceeds from them under compulsion. This is expressed as "taking away" (al-dhahāb) rather than "taking" (al-akhdh) or "causing to go" (al-idhhāb), in order to intensify its ugliness by showing that it includes two matters, each of which is forbidden: the abhorrent act of taking, and the removal from them, because it is an expression of going away while keeping hold of it.

﴿Unless they commit a clear immorality﴾. This is in the active form of "بَيَّنَ" with the meaning of "تَبَيَّنَ" (to become clear). It was also read in the passive form, and in the active form of "أبانَ" with the meaning of "تَبَيُّنْ," that is, manifestly ugly, consisting of rebelliousness (nushūz), bad temper, harming the husband and his family with abuse and foul speech. This is supported by Ubayy's reading: "إلّا أنْ يُفْحِشْنَ عَلَيْكُمْ" (unless they act immorally toward you). It was also said that al-fāḥisha means adultery (al-zinā). This is an exception from the most general of circumstances, or the most general of times, or the most general of causes. That is: it is not lawful for you to restrain them in any circumstance, or at any time, or for any cause, except in the circumstance of their committing an immorality, or except at the time of their committing it, or except because of their committing it, for then the cause comes from their side, and you are excused in seeking khul‘.

﴿And live with them in kindness﴾. This is addressed to those who mistreat them in companionship. Al-maʿrūf is what neither the Sharīʿa nor good manners reject. What is meant here is: equity in the sharing of nights, maintenance, and courtesy in speech, and the like.

﴿And if you dislike them﴾, and you tire of their company by the demands of natural inclination, without there being on their part anything that necessitates this from the matters mentioned. Then do not separate from them merely because of aversion of the soul, but be patient in living with them.

﴿Perhaps you dislike something and God places in it much good﴾. This is a reason for the condition, placed in its stead to signify the strength of its implication. As if it were said: If you dislike them, then be patient with them despite your aversion, for perhaps there is in what you dislike much good for you that is not in what you love. "عَسى" here is a complete verb, governing what follows and not requiring a predicate to be supplied, meaning: your dislike has brought near something, and God has placed in it much good. For the soul often dislikes what is more beneficial in religion, better in outcome, and closer to good, and loves what is contrary to it. So let your consideration be what contains good and righteousness, not what your souls desire. Mentioning the first verb while dispensing with it, and restricting causation to the second, is to serve as a means of generalizing its object, so as to convey that the bestowal of much good by God, exalted is He, is not specific to one disliked thing rather than another, but is a divine practice operating universally according to what wisdom requires, and that what we are dealing with is one instance of its instances. In it there is an emphasis on urging against separation and a generalization of guidance that is not hidden. It was also read as "وَيَجْعَلُ" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is then in the circumstantial position (ḥāl). Its assumed form is: "وهو أيْ ذَلِكَ الشَّيْءُ يَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ فِيهِ خَيْرًَا كَثِيرًَا" (and it, that thing, God places in it much good). It was also said that its assumed form is "واللَّهُ يَجْعَلُ," with the explicit noun placed in the position of the pronoun. The tanwīn on "خَيْرًَا" is for its intrinsic magnification, and describing it as "كَثِيرًا" is to show its descriptive grandeur. What is meant here is a righteous child. It was also said: affection and love.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 20:

﴿And if you desire to exchange a spouse﴾ i.e., to marry a woman you desire.

﴿in place of a spouse﴾ whom you turn away from by divorcing her.

﴿and you have given one of them﴾ i.e., one of the wives, for the word "spouse" here refers to the category (al-jins) [and the clause is circumstantial (hali), with qad implied, or it is coordinated (ma'tufah) with the conditional, meaning: and you have already given the one you wish to divorce].

﴿a great amount (qintar)﴾ i.e., a great amount of wealth.

﴿do not take back from it﴾ i.e., from that qintar.

﴿anything﴾ even a little, let alone much.

﴿Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) given to confirm the prohibition and to deter from what is forbidden, and the interrogative is for denunciation and reproach. I.e., would you take it while being slanderers and sinners, or for slander and sin? For one of them, when he married a woman, would slander the wife under him with an immoral act, until he compelled her to ransom herself from him with what he had given her, so that he could turn to marrying the new one. Hence they were forbidden from this. Buhtan is the lie that confounds and bewilders the one it is told about, and it may be used for a false action; for this reason it is interpreted here as injustice (zulm).

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿How can you take it?﴾ is a denunciation of taking it after a denunciation, and a repulsion from it after a repulsion. It is intensified by directing the denunciation at the manner of taking it, which signals that it is something for which there is no path to realization or occurrence at all. Whatever enters existence must be in some state of conditions, so if a thing has no state at all, it has no share of existence whatsoever.

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿while you have gone in unto one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "you take it." It serves to emphasize the reproach and affirm the improbability. That is, "in what manner or in what state would you take it," while the situation between you and them has been one of states contrary to it: seclusion, the fixing of the dower, the establishment of their right to service from you, and other things.

﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾ is conjoined to what precedes and falls under its ruling. That is, they have taken from you a firm pledge, which is the right of companionship and good living, or what Allah Most High made binding upon you concerning them by His saying: ﴿either retain them with kindness or release them with goodness﴾, or what the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated by his saying: "You took them as a trust from Allah, and made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah Most High."

﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾. This begins the explanation of which women are forbidden in marriage and which are not. This marriage is singled out for the prohibition, and was not included in the list of forbidden marriages that follows, in order to intensify the rebuke against it, since they persisted in practicing it. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir, Qur'anic exegesis) said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) used to marry the wives of their fathers, so they were forbidden from this. The term "fathers" (aba') includes grandfathers by metaphorical usage (majaz, figurative sense). Thus the prohibition on what they married is established both by explicit text (nass) and by consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). The marriage contract itself, if it is valid, is sufficient on its own to establish this prohibition. If it is invalid, however, establishing the prohibition requires intercourse (wati') or what takes its place, such as kissing, touching with desire, and the like. Indeed, it is intercourse that actually establishes the prohibition, so that if any of these occurs through ownership by right-hand possession (milk al-yamin) or in a forbidden manner, the prohibition is established by it according to us (the Hanafis), differing from al-Shafi'i regarding what is forbidden. That is: do not marry the woman whom your fathers married. The choice of "ma" (what) rather than "man" (whom) is to point to the attribute. It has also been said that "ma" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), taking the sense of the verbal noun, with the meaning of the object of the verbal noun.

﴿from women﴾ is an explanation of what was married, on both interpretations.

﴿except what has already passed﴾ is an exception from what was married. It serves to intensify the prohibition, by presenting the statement in the manner of a conditional tied to an impossibility, in the style of the poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords / are notched by the blows of the battalions."

The meaning is: do not marry the wives of your fathers, except whoever among them has died. The purpose is to completely close the path of permissibility. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. It has also been said that it is an exception from what the prohibition implies and what the act of the forbidden thing necessarily entails: as if it were said, "Do not marry what your fathers married of women, for it entails punishment, except what has already passed, for that is pardoned." It has also been said that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But what has already passed carries no blame," not that it is affirmed. Both of these are rejected by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination and hateful﴾, for this is a justification of the prohibition and an explanation that the forbidden thing is at the utmost ugliness, detested with the greatest hatred, and that it has always been described as such in the judgment and knowledge of God, exalted is He, even if He permitted it to one of the nations. Therefore it is not fitting that something which lessens its gravity, namely the absence of blame for what previously occurred, be placed between them.

﴿and evil is the way﴾. Regarding the word "sa'a" (evil was), there are two opinions. The first is that it functions like "bi'sa" (wretched was) in censure and in action, so in it is an implicit pronoun explained by what follows, and the object of the censure is omitted, its estimated sense being: "and evil is the way, the way of that marriage," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wretched is the drink﴾, meaning: that water. The second is that it is like the other verbs, and in it is a pronoun referring to what the pronoun of "innahu" (indeed it) refers to; "sabilan" is a specification (tamyiz), and the clause is either a new sentence with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), or it is conjoined to the predicate of "kana" (was), quoted by an implied verb of saying, which is in reality the conjoined element, its estimated sense being: "and said concerning it, evil is the way," for the tongues of all nations have never ceased to speak thus across ages and lands. It has been said: the degrees of ugliness are three: the legal ugliness (shar'i), the rational ugliness ('aqli), and the customary ugliness ('adi). God, exalted is He, has described this marriage with all of them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿an abomination﴾ is the degree of its rational ugliness; His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and hateful﴾ is the degree of its legal ugliness; and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and evil is the way﴾ is the degree of its customary ugliness. Whatever unites these degrees in it has reached the highest degree of ugliness.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 23:**

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters.﴾ The intended meaning is not the prohibition of their persons but the prohibition of marrying them, and of what is sought through them by way of enjoyment, and it explains the impossibility of marital ownership (milk al-nikah) being imposed on them and the complete absence of their being eligible for it. As for the prohibition of enjoying them through ownership by right hand (milk al-yamin) in those matters in which the continuance of ownership is conceivable, such as some of the items listed under the assumption of their being slaves, it is established by indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), because the underlying basis is the same, namely that their private parts are not eligible for ownership, and not by its explicit wording, as shown by the sequence and context of the noble composition. The stated basis did not necessitate the total impossibility of ownership by right hand, nor the prohibition of its cause, which is the contract or what takes its place, in the way that it necessitated the prohibition of the marriage contract and the impossibility of its ruling applying to them. This is because the object of ownership by right hand is not the genital organ, which is the object of marital ownership, such that it would cease with the cessation of eligibility for it, as marital ownership does. For where the object of marital ownership is that, it definitely ceases with the cessation of eligibility for it. Rather, its object is the person (raqabah) present in every slave, so it is realized with the realization of its place necessarily. Then it ceases upon the occurrence of manumission in those matters whose cause of prohibition is purely blood kinship, like the items mentioned, and it remains in the rest in its state, bringing with it all of its intended rulings prescribed by the Law. As for the permissibility of intercourse, it is not among those rulings, so there is no harm in its separation from it, as in the case of a Magian woman. "Mothers" includes grandmothers, however far up they go. "Daughters" includes their daughters, however far down they go. "Sisters" comprises sisters from the three lines (full, paternal and maternal), and likewise the rest. The paternal aunt is every female whom the one who begot your father has borne. The maternal aunt is every female whom the one who bore your mother has borne, whether near or distant. "Brothers' daughters" and "sisters' daughters" include the nearer and the more remote.

﴿And your mothers who have suckled you, and your milk-sisters﴾. God Most High has given suckling the status of lineage, so that the wet-nurse is called "mother" to the nursling and the nursling's co-nursed is called "sister." Likewise, the husband of the wet-nurse is his father, his parents are his grandparents, and her sister is his aunt. Every child born to him from someone other than the wet-nurse, whether before or after the suckling, is his brother or sister on the father's side. The mother of the wet-nurse is his grandmother, and her sister is his maternal aunt. Every child born to her from this husband is his brother or sister on both the father's and the mother's side, and whoever she bore from another is his brother or sister on the mother's side. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by suckling," and this is a universal rule that applies in its generality. As for the mother of his brother on the father's side, the sister of his son on the mother's side, the mother of his son's mother, the mother of his paternal uncle, and the mother of his maternal uncle on the father's side, their prohibition is not on account of lineage, such that it would be permitted by its generality, as is necessary for their permissibility in cases of suckling. Rather, it is on account of affinity (musahara). Do you not see that the first is the wife of his father, the second is the daughter of his wife, the third is the mother of his wife, the fourth is the wife of his grandfather by a valid marriage, and the fifth is the wife of his grandfather by an invalid marriage?

﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. This begins the explanation of the prohibitions arising from affinity, following the explanation of the prohibitions arising from suckling, which have a bond like the bond of lineage. By "wives" is meant those married in general, whether or not they have been consummated with, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said concerning a man who married a woman and then divorced her before consummating the marriage: "There is no harm in his marrying her daughter, but it is not lawful for him to marry her mother." It is related from Umar and Imran ibn Husayn, may God be pleased with them both, that the mother becomes prohibited by the contract itself. It is related from Masruq that it is a loose statement (mursalah), so let go what God has let go. It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Leave unspecified what God has left unspecified." Except that it is related from him, and from Ali, Zayd, Ibn Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with them, that they read: "And the mothers of your wives with whom you have consummated." It is related from Jabir in two reports. It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from Zayd, that if she died while he was married to her and he took her inheritance, he disliked marrying her mother, and if he divorced her before consummation, then he might do so if he wished. He treated death as occupying the place of consummation in this matter, just as it occupies its place in the matters of the dower and the waiting period (iddah). Those with whom intercourse has occurred in any of the ways counted previously, and those who have been touched (mamsusat) and their like, are also attached to them. "Mothers" includes the wet-nurses just as it includes the grandmothers, as has been mentioned.

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾. "Rabaib" is the plural of "rabibah," a form in the sense of "maf'ulah," and the feminine ending is for transferring it to the status of a noun. The "rabib" is the child of a woman by another husband. He is so named because he is usually raised (yarubbuhu) by the stepfather, just as he raises his own child, although this is not a consistent rule. Their being "in the guardianship" refers to this, for their customary and usual state is that they are in the custody of their mothers, under the protection of their husbands, and that is how they are in fact. The purpose of describing them thus is to strengthen and complete the cause of the prohibition, just as it is the reason for their being mentioned by the name "stepdaughters" rather than "daughters of women." For their being in the position of being raised by them and under their protection and upbringing, and the nobility of being turned over in their guardianship, strengthens the closeness and resemblance between them and their own children, and calls for treating them in the way of their daughters. It does not restrict the prohibition to their being in their guardianship in fact. This is as is related from Ali, may God be pleased with him. Dawud adopted this view, and it is the position of the majority of scholars: the prohibition stated first applies whether or not they are in their guardianship. This is unlike the words of God Most High: "from your women with whom you have consummated," for this is definitely a restriction. The word "min" (from) relates to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "your stepdaughters," or from its pronoun that is concealed in the adverbial phrase, because when it occurred as a relative clause it bore a pronoun. That is, "And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, being from your women…" and so on. There is no justification for making it a circumstantial clause from "mothers," nor from what it is specifically attached to, and this is clear and has no covering. Nor is there any justification for making it a circumstantial clause from the first one (stepdaughters), because the circumstantial status of it from "your stepdaughters" or from a pronoun requires that the word "min" be for beginning, while its circumstantial status from "mothers" or from "your women" requires that it be explanatory. Claiming that it is connective, comprising the meaning of both beginning and explanation, or making the relative clause a qualifier of the women while the two governing elements differ, is something that must be kept far from the sanctity of the revelation. Moreover, it is an attempt to silence what the Prophet ﷺ pronounced and on which the majority agreed, as has been mentioned earlier. As for what has been transmitted of a reading, its transmission is weak, and on the assumption of its authenticity it is to be understood as abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). The meaning of "having consummated with them" is bringing them behind the curtain, and the particle "bi" is for transitivity, and it is a metaphor for sexual intercourse, like the people's saying: "He built upon her" and "He drew the veil over her." Touching and its like are included in its ruling, as has passed. ﴿But if you have not consummated with them﴾, that is, previously.

﴿You have consummated with them﴾ at all.

﴿Then there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, in marrying the stepdaughters. This is an explicit statement of what was implied by what precedes. The first "fa" (then) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, for explaining the ruling on consummation entails explaining the ruling on its absence.

﴿And the wives of your sons﴾, that is, their wives. The wife is called "halilah" because she is lawful (halal) for the husband or because she settles (hulul) in his place. It is said that it is because each of the two spouses unlaces the other's garment. Included in their ruling are those with whom they have committed adultery, and those who are in their position among those who have been touched and their like. God Most High's words, ﴿who are of your loins﴾, serve to exclude adopted sons, but not the sons of sons nor the sons from nursing, for although they are far removed, they are in the position of biological sons.

﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ is in the position of the nominative case, as a conjunction with what precedes of the prohibitions. What is intended by it is combining them in marriage, not in ownership by right hand. As for combining them in intercourse through ownership by right hand, it is attached to it by way of indication, because the two share the same basis. This is also due to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not deposit his water in the womb of two sisters." This is unlike the very ownership by right hand, for it does not have the meaning of marriage in leading to intercourse, nor does it necessarily entail it. For this reason, it is valid to buy a Magian woman but not to marry her. Thus, if he has intercourse with both, it is lawful for him to have intercourse with one of them until intercourse with the other becomes forbidden to him through some cause. Likewise, if he marries the sister of his concubine with whom he has had intercourse, it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with either of them until the other becomes forbidden to him, because the married woman is in legal effect one who has been had intercourse with, so it is as if he combined the two in intercourse. The prohibition is attributed to the combining of the two, not to the second of them, by saying, "and the sisters of your wives," in order to avoid conveying a perpetual prohibition as in the earlier prohibited persons, and because this wording is far from indicating the prohibition of combining the two together simultaneously. This same ruling is shared by combining a woman with her paternal aunt and their like, for the basis of the prohibition of combining two sisters is that it leads to severing what God has commanded to be joined, and this is realized in combining these persons, and even more so, for the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt are in the position of the mother. Thus his saying, peace be upon him: "A woman shall not be married to her paternal aunt, nor to her maternal aunt, nor to her brother's daughter, nor to her sister's daughter," is by way of explaining the meaning, not by way of abrogating the ruling. It is said that it is a well-known report, by which addition may be made to the Book.

﴿Except what has already passed﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), that is, but what has already passed, you will not be held accountable for. There is no way to make it a connected exception for the purpose of emphasis and exaggeration, as has passed earlier, because God Most High's saying, ﴿Indeed, God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, is a justification for what the exception conveys, so disconnection is definitive. Ata and al-Suddi said its meaning is: except what was from Ya'qub, peace be upon him, for he combined between Leah, the mother of Yahudha, and Rachel, the mother of Yusuf, peace and blessings be upon them. But the justification does not support this, because what Ya'qub, peace be upon him, did was lawful in his law. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to prohibit what God prohibited (p-163) except the wife of the father and the combining of two sisters. Hisham ibn Abd Allah related from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to recognize these prohibitions except two: marrying the wife of the father, and combining two sisters. Do you not see that the prohibition regarding each of these two is followed by God Most High's saying, ﴿except what has already passed﴾? This indicates that the exception in both of them follows one pattern, and the difference in the two justifications contradicts this.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 24:**

﴿Wal-muhsanat﴾ (with the *sad* vowelled with a *fatha*). These are the married women. They are made chaste (*ahsanahunna*) by marriage, or by their husbands, or by their guardians; that is, they are kept chaste from falling into what is forbidden. It is also read in the form of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), *fa-innahunna ahsanna furujahunna 'an ghayri azwajihinna* ("for they have guarded their private parts from other than their husbands"), or *ahsanna azwajahunna* ("they have guarded their husbands"). It has been said that the form is active (*li-l-fa'il*) even on the first reading, and that the *fatha* on the *sad* is treated as an anomaly (*shudhudh*), as in its two parallels *mulqah* and *musheb*, from *alqaha* and *asheba*. It has been said: the word *ihsan* occurs in the Qur'an with four meanings. The first is marriage, as in this noble verse. The second is chastity, as in His saying ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾. The third is freedom, as in His saying ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾. The fourth is Islam, as in His saying ﴿And when they are made chaste (*uhsinna*)﴾. It was said in its interpretation, that is: when they embrace Islam. And it is coordinated with the previously mentioned forbidden women. His saying ﴿min al-nisa'﴾ ("from among the women") is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it, meaning: "being from among the women." Its purpose is to emphasise its generality, not to rule out the possibility that it includes men, on the basis that it is an attribute of *anfus* (persons), as was imagined.

﴿Illa ma malakat aymanukum﴾ ("except what your right hands possess") is an exception from *al-muhsanat*, an exception of a type from a genus, meaning: what you own. The attribution of ownership to the right hands is because its usual cause is the condition connected with them. This is well known regarding slaves, especially their females, and they are the ones meant here, in keeping with the contrast between it and the ownership of marriage (*milk al-nikah*) which applies to free women. The expression about them with *ma* ("what") is to lower them, because of the deficiency of slavery in them from the rank of rational beings. It is either general according to the generality of its relative clause, in which case the exception is not to remove all its members from the ruling of prohibition by way of the scope of negation, but by way of negating the comprehensiveness, which entails the exclusion of some of them. That is: the married women are forbidden to you in general, except the married women whom you own, for they are not forbidden absolutely; rather among them are those whose marriage is not prohibited in general, namely the captives whose husbands are not with them, or absolutely, according to the difference of the two opinions. Or it is specific to those mentioned, and the meaning is: the married women are forbidden to you except those who were taken captive, for their marriage is permitted in general, that is, to others than their owners. As for their being lawful to them by the ruling of ownership of the right hand, it is understood by the indication of the text (*dalalat al-nass*), because the basis (*manat*) is unified, not by its expression, as you know, since the purpose of the noble arrangement is to explain the prohibition of enjoying the forbidden women listed under the ruling of ownership of marriage. The prohibition of enjoying them under the ruling of ownership of the right hand is established by way of the indication of the text, and this is something in which exception definitely does not apply. As for counting them among those with husbands, while separation between them and their husbands has definitely occurred, either by alienation or by captivity, according to the difference of the two opinions, it is based on the belief of people, since at that time they were unaware of the separation. Do you not see what was narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "On the day of Awtas we captured captives who had husbands, and we disliked having intercourse with them. So we asked the Prophet (ﷺ) — and in another narration from him, we said: O Messenger of Allah — how can we have intercourse with women whose lineages and husbands we know? Then this was revealed: ﴿And the married women, except what your right hands possess﴾, so we made them lawful to us." In another narration from him: "The caller of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proclaimed: 'Let no pregnant woman be had sexually until she gives birth, nor any non-pregnant woman until she menstruates.'" Thus he permitted intercourse with them after the waiting period (*istibra'*). There is nothing in the arrangement of this ruling upon the revelation of the noble verse that indicates that the verse was intended for it, for that depends on its conveying it in one of the ways of indication, by way of expression or something similar.

This is so. It has been narrated from Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It was revealed concerning women who used to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while they had husbands, and some Muslims would marry them, then their husbands would come as emigrants, so He forbade marrying them." Then "the married women" at that time is an expression for emigrant women whose husbands are expected or certain to embrace Islam and emigrate. For this reason the name of *ihsan* did not leave them. The prohibition is for the certain case and to ascertain the situation of the expected case. Otherwise, the others are far from prohibition and from deserving the application of the name to them. How could they not be? When the bond between the captive woman and her husband was severed even though they shared the same religion, then the severing of the bond between the emigrant woman and her husband is more appropriate and preferable, as His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He, makes clear: ﴿If you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful to them, nor are they lawful to them﴾ — the verse.

﴿Kitaba Allah﴾ ("the Book of Allah") is an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*), meaning: Allah prescribed (*kataba*).

﴿'Alaykum﴾ ("upon you") — the prohibition of these people is a prescription (*kitaban*), and He obligated it as an obligation (*farDan*). It has been said: it is in the accusative as a call to attention (*al-igra'*) with an implied verb, meaning: "Hold fast to the Book of Allah," and "upon you" is connected either to the verbal noun or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from it. It has been said: it is another call to attention, emphasising what precedes it, its object having been omitted because of what is mentioned indicating it; or it is with "upon you" itself, according to the opinion of one who permits fronting the accusative in the case of the call to attention, as in the line of poetry:

*O drawer of water, my bucket is yours,*
*Indeed I have seen the people praising you.*

It is also read as *kutubu Allah* in the plural and nominative, meaning: these are the obligations of Allah upon you. And it is read as *kataba Allah* with the verbal form.

﴿Wa uhilla lakum﴾ ("and it is made lawful for you") is coordinated with ﴿Forbidden to you are﴾ and so on. The placement of His saying ﴿the Book of Allah upon you﴾ between them is for the sake of emphasis in urging the preservation of the aforementioned prohibited ones. It is also read in the active voice, so it is coordinated with the omitted verb. It has been said: rather it is coordinated with ﴿Forbidden﴾ and so on, for they are two contrasting sentences founding prohibition and permission, which depend on the command of Allah, Exalted. There is no harm in the difference of the subject apparently, especially after the first has been emphasised by what indicates that the one who prohibits is Allah, Exalted.

﴿Ma wara'a dhalikum﴾ ("what is beyond that for you") refers to what was mentioned of the counted prohibited ones, meaning: the marriage of others than them is made lawful for you, individually and collectively. Perhaps the choice of the demonstrative, which points to the described and named referent, over the pronoun, which refers only to the essence, is to remind of the title in each one of them on which the ruling of prohibition turns, so that the sharing of those who are in their meaning in it is understood by way of indication. The prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt, or with her maternal aunt, is not by way of expression but by way of indication, as already passed. It has been said: the intended meaning of permission is not permission absolutely, that is, in all circumstances, so that it would be objected that it entails the permissibility of combining a woman with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt. Rather, it is their permission in general, that is, in some circumstances. There is no doubt about the permissibility of marrying them individually, and this is not harmed by their prohibition when combined. Do you not see that the prohibition of marrying a woman in her waiting period, a woman divorced three times, a fifth wife, marrying a slave woman over a free woman, or marrying a woman who has been cursed through li'an, impairs the lawfulness of marrying them after the waiting period, after halala (the intermediate marriage), after the fourth divorce and the end of the waiting period, after divorcing a free woman, and after the one who performed li'an retracts his statement? You know well that the permission must here attach to what the prohibition attached to above, and here it has attached to combination, so the permission must also attach to it.

﴿An tabtaghu﴾ ("that you seek") is connected to the two verbs mentioned, as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), but not in consideration of the two themselves, rather in consideration of their explanation and clarification, meaning: He made clear to you the prohibition of the counted prohibited ones and the permission of others, wishing that you seek with your wealth. The object is omitted, meaning: that you seek women; or it is left unstated, meaning: that you perform the seeking.

﴿Bi-amwalikum﴾ ("with your wealth") — by spending it on their dowries; or it is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from ﴿ma wara'a dhalikum﴾ with an implied pronoun of the object.

﴿Muhsinin﴾ ("chaste") is a circumstantial clause from the subject of *tabtaghu*. *Ihsan* is chastity and guarding oneself from falling into what entails blame and punishment.

﴿Ghayra musafihin﴾ ("not fornicators") is a second circumstantial clause from it, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *muhsinin*. *Sifah* is adultery and debauchery, from *safh*, which is pouring out semen; it was named so because that is its purpose. The object of the two verbs is omitted, meaning: "chaste, guarding your private parts, not fornicating with prostitutes." This is in reality an emphatic circumstantial clause, because one who is chaste is never a fornicator. As for what is in His saying ﴿So for whichever of them you have enjoyed﴾, it is either an expression for the women or for what is connected to them of actions. In either case, it is either a conditional, in which what follows it is its condition, or a relative pronoun, in which what follows it is its relative clause. And whichever it is, it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate, if it is conditional, is either the verb of the condition or its response or both, according to the well-known disagreement. If it is a relative pronoun, the predicate is His saying ﴿give them their wages﴾, and the *fa'* is for the relative pronoun's implying the meaning of a condition. Then, if it is an expression for the women, the returning pronoun to the subject is the pronoun in the accusative in ﴿fa-atuhunna﴾, whether it is conditional or relative. And *min* is explanatory or partitive, its place being accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive in *bihi*. The meaning is: whichever individual you have enjoyed, or the individual whom you have enjoyed being of the kind of women or some of them, then give them their wages. The consideration of the wording was observed at times, so the pronoun was made singular at first, and at other times the consideration of meaning, so it was made plural in the second and third places. As for it being an expression for what is connected to them, then *min* is inceptive, connected to the enjoyment, and the returning pronoun to the subject is omitted. The meaning is: whatever action you have enjoyed from their side, from marriage or seclusion or the like, or the action which you have enjoyed from their side of the mentioned actions, then give them their wages for it, or in exchange for it. The intended meaning of *ujur* is dowries, for they are the wages of their private parts.

﴿Faridatan﴾ ("as an obligation") is a circumstantial clause from *ujur* in the sense of "obligated", or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a given obligation; or an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: that was obligated as an obligation, that is, it is due to them from you.

﴿Wa la junaha 'alaykum fima tara 'adtum bihi﴾ ("And there is no blame upon you regarding what you mutually agree upon") means: there is no sin upon you regarding what you mutually agree upon of reduction of the dowry or release from it, in the manner of His saying ﴿But if they give you willingly of it, then eat it﴾, following His saying ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, and His saying ﴿unless they forgo it﴾. Its generality to include increase over what was named is supported by the removal of blame from the men, for it is not a place of blame except that the address is made to the husbands by way of predominance (*taghlib*), for taking an increase over what was named is a place of blame upon the wife. It has been said: regarding what you mutually agree upon of maintenance and the like. It has been said: of residence or separation. But His saying ﴿after the obligation﴾ does not support it, since they have no connection to the obligation unless separation is by way of *khul'* (divorce by wife's request). It has been said: it was revealed concerning *mut'a* (temporary marriage), which is marriage for a known term, a day or more. It was named so because its purpose is merely enjoyment of the woman and her enjoyment of what is given. It was permitted for three days when Mecca was conquered, may Allah honour it, Exalted, and then it was abrogated (*nusikhat*), because it was narrated that he, peace be upon him, permitted it, then in the morning he said: "O people, I had commanded you to enjoy these women. Indeed Allah has prohibited that until the Day of Resurrection." It has been said: it was permitted twice and prohibited twice. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he retracted the view of its permissibility at his death, and said: "O Allah, I repent to You from my statement about *mut'a* and my statement about *sarf* (exchange of currency)."

﴿Inna Allaha kana 'aliman﴾ ("Indeed Allah is ever Knowing") of the interests of the servants.

﴿Hakiman﴾ ("Wise") in what He legislated for them of rulings; and for this He legislated for you these rulings suited to your condition.

(p-166)﴿وَمَن لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ مِنكُمْ﴾ "Man" (مَن) is either a conditional particle, whose following clause is its condition, or a relative pronoun, whose following clause is its relative clause (ṣila). The prepositional phrase "minkum" (مِنكُمْ) is related to an omitted verb and functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "yastaṭi'" (يَسْتَطِعْ), meaning: "while being one of you." ﴿طَوْلا﴾ "ṭawlan" means wealth, abundance or ample means, i.e. ascendancy and attainment; its root meaning is increase and excess. It is the object (mafʿūl) of "yastaṭi'." ﴿أنْ يَنْكِحَ المُحْصَناتِ المُؤْمِناتِ﴾ "an yankiḥa al-muḥṣanāti al-mu'minat" ("that he marry the chaste believing women") may be: (a) the direct object of "ṭawlan," since the implementation of a nunated verbal noun (maṣdar) is common and well known, as in His words ﴿أوْ إطْعامٌ في يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ﴾ "or feeding on a day of hunger" ﴿يَتِيمًا ذا مَقْرَبَةٍ﴾ "an orphan near of kin" (Q. 90:14–15), as if it were said: "and whoever among you cannot attain their marriage"; or (b) with a preposition omitted, meaning: "and whoever among you lacks the means for their marriage" or "for marrying them," in which case the prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a qualifier (ṣifa) of "ṭawlan," meaning: "ṭawlan conveying him to it, or belonging to him, or for their marriage," on the basis that "ṭawl" means power. In the Qamus (the classical lexicon): "al-ṭawl, al-ṭā'il and al-ṭā'ila: excess, power, wealth and ampleness." The position of "an" after the omission of the preposition is accusative according to Sibawayh and al-Farra', and genitive according to al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It may also be (c) a substitute (badal) for "ṭawlan," since ṭawl is excess and nikah is power; or (d) the object of "yastaṭi'," with "ṭawlan" as an emphatic verbal noun for it, since it has the same meaning, because istiṭā'ah (capacity) is ṭawl; or (e) a specification (tamyīz), meaning: "whoever among you cannot marry them by capacity, or from the side of ṭawl and wealth," i.e. not from the side of natural disposition and temperament, since the lack of capacity from that side has no connection to the context. The term "al-muḥṣanāt" (المُحْصَناتِ) means free women (al-ḥarā'ir), as shown by their contrast with the enslaved women (al-mamlūkāt), since their freedom protects them from the humiliation of slavery, from being demeaned and from other attributes of deficiency and shortcoming. ﴿فَمِن ما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾ "famin mā malakat aymānukum" ("then from what your right hands possess") is either the response to the condition or the predicate of the relative clause; the "fa'" (فَ) is present because the clause includes the meaning of a condition. The prepositional phrase is related to an omitted verb whose object is omitted, and "mā" is a relative pronoun, meaning: "then let him marry a woman or a slave-girl of the category that your right hands possess." In reality it is related to an omitted element functioning as a qualifier of that omitted object. "Min" here is partitive (tab'īḍiyya), meaning: "then let him marry a woman who is of that category." It is also said that "min" is superfluous and the relative pronoun is the object of the omitted verb, meaning: "then let him marry what your right hands possess." ﴿مِن فَتَياتِكُمُ المُؤْمِناتِ﴾ "min fatayātikumu al-mu'minat" ("from your believing slave-girls") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun understood in "malakat," which refers back to "mā." It is also said that it is the object of the omitted verb, with "min" superfluous, and "mimmā malakat" is related to the verb itself, with "min" indicating the starting point (ibtidā' al-ghāya); or it is related to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause from "fatayātikum," with "min" partitive, meaning: "then let him marry your slave-girls being some of what your right hands possess." "Al-mu'mināt" is a qualifier of "fatayātikum" under every interpretation. It is also said that it is the object of the omitted verb, with "mimmā malakat" as explained above, and "min fatayātikum" a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun.

The apparent meaning of this noble text indicates that marrying a slave-woman is not permissible for one who is able, as al-Shafi'i, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, held, and that marrying a slave-woman who is a People of the Book is not permissible at all, which is the view of the people of the Hijaz. Abu Hanifa, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, permitted both, relying on the general wording. Thus the conditional and descriptive wording is understood as indicating preference, and there is no dispute about that among anyone. It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "Among what God has granted this Ummah in ease is marrying a slave-woman, a Jewish woman or a Christian woman, even if one is wealthy."

﴿واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِإيمانِكُمْ﴾ "And Allah is most knowing of your faith" is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tariḍa), brought to make them comfortable with marrying slave-women and to lower them from the rank of disdain for it, by stating that the basis of distinction and the axis of pride is faith, not lineage and ancestry, as expressed in His words: ﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ إنّا خَلَقْناكم مِن ذَكَرٍ وأُنْثى وجَعَلْناكم شُعُوبًا وقَبائِلَ لِتَعارَفُوا إنَّ أكْرَمَكم عِنْدَ اللَّهِ أتْقاكُمْ﴾ "O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you" (Q. 49:13). The meaning is that He, the Exalted, knows your ranks in faith better than you do, the faith by which the affairs of servants are ordered and around which revolves the orbit of benefits in this life and the next. It has no connection to freedom or slavery specifically, for a slave-woman's faith may surpass the faith of free women. His words ﴿بَعْضُكم مِن بَعْضٍ﴾ "some of you are from some others" — if by this is meant connection in terms of religion, then it is an explanation of their kinship from that aspect, following the explanation of their differing in that respect; if by it is meant connection in terms of lineage, then it is another parenthetical sentence, emphasizing the comfort from another angle. The address in both places is either to the believing men addressed in the preceding context, as in the address that follows, where the wording was observed in what preceded, while here the meaning is observed, and the turn of address (iltifāt) is for the purpose of concern with encouragement and comfort; or it is to others among the Muslims, like the preceding addresses, since encouragement is achieved by addressing them as well. Whatever the case, the repetition of the command to marry in the form of direct address in His words ﴿فانْكِحُوهُنَّ﴾ "so marry them," although it is understood from His words ﴿فَمِن ما مَلَكَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾ as mentioned, is for the increase of encouragement to marry them. It is restricted by His words ﴿بِإذْنِ أهْلِهِنَّ﴾ "with the permission of their families," and its beginning with "fa'" indicates that it follows from what precedes, meaning: "Since you have come to know the clear matter, then marry them with the permission of their masters, and do not look down upon them." The stipulation of their masters' permission rather than their direct conduct of the contract indicates that they may directly conduct it.

﴿وَآتُوهُنَّ أُجُورَهُنَّ﴾ "And give them their wages," i.e. their dowries (mahr).

﴿بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ "bil-ma'rūf" ("with fairness, in the customary manner") is related to "ātūhunna," meaning: pay them their dowries without delay, harm, or forcing them to demand and press for them, as required by the Shari'a and custom. It necessarily follows that the payment is to be made to them with the permission of their masters; so the mention of giving them is to explain the permissibility of paying them directly, not to show that the dowries belong to them. It is also said that the original is "ātū mawālayhunna" ("give their masters"), with the modified noun omitted and the verb transferred to the noun it was attached to.

﴿مُحْصَناتٍ﴾ "muḥṣanāt" ("chaste") is a circumstantial clause from the object of "fa-nkiḥūhunna," meaning: being chaste, protected from fornication.

﴿غَيْرَ مُسافِحاتٍ﴾ "ghayra musāfiḥāt" ("not openly fornicating") is an emphatic circumstantial clause, meaning: not openly committing it.

﴿وَلا مُتَّخِذاتِ أخْدانٍ﴾ "wa lā muttakhidhāt akhdān" ("nor taking secret lovers") is coordinated with "musāfiḥāt," and "lā" is to emphasize the negation contained in "ghayr." "Al-khidn" means companion. Abu Zayd said: "al-akhdān are friends in sin; the singular is khidn or khadīn." The plural is used in contrast by way of division, meaning that none of them should have a single lover, not that none of them should have lovers. That is, not openly committing fornication, nor secretly doing so. In the pre-Islamic period, fornication was divided into these two kinds.

﴿فَإذا أُحْصِنَّ﴾ "fa-idhā uḥṣinna" ("then when they are protected") means by marriage. It was read in the active form, meaning: "they guarded their chastity or their husbands."

﴿فَإنْ أتَيْنَ بِفاحِشَةٍ﴾ "fa-in atayna bi-fāḥisha" ("then if they commit an immorality") means they committed a grave sin, which is fornication.

﴿فَعَلَيْهِنَّ﴾ "fa-'alayhinna" ("then upon them") means: then it is legally incumbent upon them.

﴿نِصْفُ ما عَلى المُحْصَناتِ﴾ "niṣfu mā 'alā al-muḥṣanāt" ("half of what is upon the chaste women") means the free virgins.

﴿مِنَ العَذابِ﴾ "min al-'adhāb" ("of the punishment") means of the prescribed penalty (ḥadd), which is one hundred lashes, so its half is fifty, as it is likewise before marriage. The purpose is to show that their penalty is not made different by marriage, just as the penalty of free women is not different. Thus "fa" in "fa-in atayna" is the response to "idhā," and the second "fa" is the response to "in." The second condition with its response depends on the existence of the first, as in your saying: "If you come to me, and if I do not honor you, then my slave is free."

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ "dhālika" ("that") means the marrying of slave-women.

﴿لِمَن خَشِيَ العَنَتَ مِنكُمْ﴾ "liman khashiya al-'anata minkum" ("for whoever among you fears falling into sin") means for whoever fears falling into the sin to which overpowering desire leads. The original meaning of "al-'anat" is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, and it is used figuratively for every hardship and harm that befalls a person after his condition has been sound. No harm is greater than falling into sins by committing the most vile abominations. It is also said that it means the prescribed penalty, because if one is attached to her, he fears he will commit the act and be punished with the ḥadd. The first meaning is more fitting to the condition of a believer than the second, since the second suggests that what is feared is the penalty itself, not what necessitates it.

﴿وَأنْ تَصْبِرُوا﴾ "wa an taṣbirū" ("and that you be patient") means: refrain from marrying them, being chaste and restraining yourselves from what desire inclines you toward among the sins.

﴿خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ "khayrun lakum" ("is better for you") than marrying them, even though the permission to do so has been expressed, because it exposes the child to slavery. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whichever free man marries a slave-woman has enslaved half of himself." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Marrying a slave-woman is nothing but close to fornication." Also, the right of the master over her is stronger, so she is not wholly devoted to her husband as free women are. Also, the master can use her as he wishes, while traveling and at home, and can sell her to whoever is present or absent, and in this there is an extreme disruption to the husband's condition and his children's. Also, she is humiliated and debased, going out and coming in, and all of this is abasement and humiliation which spreads to the one who marries her, while dignity is what befits believers. Also, her dowry belongs to her master, so she cannot enjoy it nor give it to her husband, and thus the affairs of the household are not ordered. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Free women are the well-being of the house, and slave-women are the ruin of the house."

﴿واللَّهُ غَفُورٌ﴾ "wa-llāhu ghafūr" ("and Allah is Forgiving") means He is intensely forgiving, so He forgives whoever is unable to be patient regarding marrying them, and what is in that of matters contrary to the condition of believers.

﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ "raḥīm" ("Merciful") means He is intensely merciful, and for this reason He has permitted you to marry them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ — this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought in to confirm the rulings mentioned earlier and to show that they run along the paths of the rightly guided among the prophets and the righteous. It is said: the original structure of the noble statement is "Allah desires that He make clear to you" (yurīdu Allāhu an yubayyina lakum). The lam (lām) was inserted to emphasize the meaning of futurity (istiqbāl) that is necessary to the act of desiring. The object of "yubayyina" (makes clear) is omitted, relying on what the preceding and surrounding context indicates. That is: Allah desires to make clear to you what is hidden from you of your own interests and the best of your deeds, or what He has obligated you to of the lawful and the unlawful. It is also said: the object of "yurīdu" (desires) is omitted, its implied sense being: Allah desires the legislating of what He has legislated of prohibition and permission, for the sake of making it clear to you. This is the view of the Basran grammarians and is attributed to Sibawayh. It is also said: the lam itself governs the verb directly without the implied "an," and it together with what follows it is the object of the preceding verb. For the lam may stand in place of "an" with verbs of desiring and commanding; one says: "I desired (aradtu) li-adhhaba" and "an adhhaba," and "I commanded you (amartuka) li-taqūma" and "an taqūma." God Most High said: ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ (yurīdūna li-yuṭfi'ū), and in another place ﴿they desire to extinguish﴾ (yurīdūna an yuṭfi'ū). And God Most High said: ﴿And we have been commanded to submit﴾ (wa-umirnā li-nuslima), and in another place ﴿and I have been commanded to submit﴾ (wa-umirtu an uslima), and in another ﴿and I have been commanded to do justice among you﴾ (wa-umirtu li-a'dila baynakum), i.e., an a'dila baynakum. This is the view of the Kufan grammarians, while the Basran grammarians rejected it and said: the function of the lam is jarr and naṣb, and in these cases the "an" is implied: "we have been commanded with what we were commanded so that we submit," and "they desire what they desire so that they extinguish." It is also said: the verb preceding the lam is interpreted as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the nominative, with what follows it made its predicate, as in "You hear of the Mu'aydi that he is better than that you see him," i.e., that you hear of him. This opinion is attributed to some of the Basran grammarians.

﴿and guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you﴾ — of the prophets and the righteous, that you may follow them.

﴿and turn to you in forgiveness﴾ — when you turn to Him, Exalted is He, from what occurs from you of shortcoming and negligence in observing what you have been charged with of the laws, for the one under obligation rarely is free of a shortcoming that calls for its remedy through repentance. And He forgives you your sins, or guides you to what restrains you from sins and urges you to repentance, or to what serves as expiation for your misdeeds. The address is not to all the obligated so that His purpose would be defeated by His will regarding those among them who do not repent; rather it is to a specific group for whom this repentance has been realized.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ — intensive in knowledge of things, among which is what He has legislated for you of rulings.

﴿All-Wise﴾ — observant in all His acts of wisdom and benefit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 27:

﴿And Allah wishes to accept your repentance﴾ is an independent (ibtida'iyya) sentence, brought in to show the full benefit of what Allah the Exalted wills and the full harm of what the wicked (fajara) desire, not to state His willing of their repentance, which would make it a matter of repetition for the sake of confirmation (al-takrir li-l-taqrir). For this reason the construction was changed to a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya), to indicate the permanence (dawam) of the willing. This was not done in His words: ﴿But those who follow their lusts desire﴾, in order to indicate occurrence (al-huduth) and to hint at the complete contrast (al-mubayana) between the meanings of the two sentences, as was explained earlier in His words: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾, and so on. By "those who follow lusts" (muttabi'i al-shahawat) is meant the wicked (al-fajara), for following them means acting upon them. As for one who partakes of the desirable things (al-mushahhiyat) that the Sharia has permitted, and not others, he is following the Sharia, not the lusts. It was said: they are the Jews and the Christians. It was said: they are the Magians, since they used to permit marriage to sisters from the father's side, daughters of a brother, and daughters of a sister. When Allah the Exalted forbade these, they said: "You permit the daughter of your maternal aunt and the daughter of your paternal aunt, although the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt are forbidden to you; so marry the daughters of a brother and of a sister." Then the verse was revealed.

﴿That you incline﴾ away from the truth by agreeing with them in following lusts and making lawful what is forbidden, and that you become fornicators like them. It was also read with the yaa' (ya') at the beginning (bi-l-ya' al-tahtaniyya), with the pronoun referring to "those who follow lusts."

﴿A great inclination﴾, i.e., in comparison with the inclination of one who commits a sin occasionally without considering it permissible.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 28:

﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you﴾ by [the concessions] already mentioned, [relieving you of] the hardships of the obligations that fall upon you. The sentence is resumed (mustanafa), and it has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

﴿And man was created weak﴾, unable to oppose his desire, not able to withstand his impulses and faculties, since he cannot restrain himself from following his appetites and does not employ his faculties for the hardships of acts of obedience. It is reported from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is weakness of constitution, but the context does not support this, for the sentence is an interjected conclusion (i'tiraD tadhyiliyy), brought to affirm what precedes it of lightening [the burden] through the concession regarding marrying female slaves. Physical frailty has no bearing on this; what the lightening relates to is the difficult acts of worship. It has also been said: the intended meaning is his weakness in matters concerning women in particular, since he cannot restrain himself from them.
