And it is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: Satan never despaired of the children of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I am squinting with the other, and the thing I fear most for myself is the temptation of women.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, read "وَخَلَقَ الإنْسانَ" (and He created man), with the active voice, the pronoun referring to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He.

It is also reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him: "Eight verses in Surat al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than everything upon which the sun rises and sets": ﴿Allah wishes to make clear to you﴾, ﴿And Allah wishes to accept your repentance﴾, ﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you﴾, ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] even by the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾, ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾, ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe?﴾.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 29:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾ This begins an account of some of the sanctities relating to wealth and lives, following the account of the sanctities relating to sexual matters. The address is introduced with the vocative and the attention-drawing particle to show the utmost concern for its content. By "unjustly" (bil-batil) is meant what contradicts the Sharia, such as usurpation, theft, embezzlement, gambling, usurious contracts and other things the Sharia has not permitted; that is, let none of you consume the property of another by a means that is not lawful under the Sharia.

﴿except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), and "an" (from) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of "trade" (tijaratan). That is: except that the trade be trade proceeding from mutual consent, as in the line of poetry:

"When there is a day with stars, most dreadful"

meaning: when the day is a day such-and-such, etc. Or: except that the wealth be wealth of trade. It is also read as "tijaratun" in the nominative, with "kana" as a complete verb (kana tammah), meaning: but intend the occurrence of trade by mutual consent; or: but the existence of trade by mutual consent is not forbidden. Its specific mention, among the other causes of ownership, is because it is the most common and frequent of them in occurrence and the most suitable for people of honour. By "mutual consent" is meant the satisfaction of the two contracting parties with what they agreed upon during the transaction, at the time of offer and acceptance according to us, and according to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it is at the moment of separation from the contract session.

﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ That is: whoever among you is of your kind, from among the believers, for all of them are like a single soul. It is related from al-Hasan: "do not kill your brothers." The expression of them as "selves" is for emphasis in forbidding their killing, by portraying it in the form of what a sane person hardly would do. Or: do not destroy yourselves by exposing yourselves to punishment by committing what leads to it, for that is the true killing of them, as its placement directly after the prohibition of consuming what is unlawful indicates, so it confirms the earlier prohibition. It has been said: do not kill yourselves by starving oneself to death, as some ignorant people do, or by committing offences that lead to killing. It has been said: do not throw yourselves into destruction. This is supported by what is related from 'Amr ibn al-'As, that he interpreted it as permitting tayammum (dry ablution) out of fear of cold, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not object to him. It is also read "wa la tuqattilu" with the intensive doubling, for multiplicity. In this exhortation, the preservation of life has been combined with the preservation of property, because property is its sibling in that it is a means of its sustenance, of attaining its perfections, and of acquiring its virtues. The prohibition of attacking life is placed first because it is more frequently committed.

﴿Indeed, God is ever Merciful to you﴾ This is a justification of the prohibition by way of a fresh sentence (isti'naf), that is: exceedingly merciful and compassionate. For this reason He has forbidden you what He has forbidden, for that is a great mercy to you by restraining you from sins, and to those who are exposed to being harmed by the preservation of their property and their lives. It has been said: its meaning is: indeed He has been merciful to you, O community of Muhammad, in that He commanded the Children of Israel to kill themselves, so that it would be a repentance for them and an expiation of their sins, and He did not impose on you those arduous obligations.

﴿And whoever does that﴾: a reference either to killing specifically, or to what precedes it, namely consuming one another's wealth unjustly. The sense of distance in the demonstrative (dhalika) serves to signal how far removed these two acts are in corruption.

﴿out of transgression and wrongdoing﴾: that is, excessive overstepping of the limit and doing what one does not deserve. It has been said that "transgression" (ʿudwān) refers to aggression against others through injustice, and "wrongdoing" (ẓulm) refers to wronging oneself by exposing oneself to punishment. Its place in the sentence is accusative, either as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "as an aggressor and a wrongdoer," or as a causal accusative (ʿilliyyah), meaning "for transgression and wrongdoing." It has also been read as ʿidwānan, with a kasra on the ʿayn.

﴿then We will cause him to burn﴾: this is the answer to the conditional clause, meaning "We will cause him to enter." It has been read with a shaddah on the lām, from ṣallā, and with a fatḥah on the nūn, from ṣalāhu, yaṣlīhi, from which comes the expression shāh maṣliyyah (a roasted sheep). It has also been read with a yā' as yuṣlīhi. The pronoun refers either to God Most High, or to that act insofar as it is a cause of burning.

﴿in a Fire﴾: that is, a particular Fire, terrifying and severe in its punishment.

﴿And that is﴾: that is, his being made to burn in the Fire.

﴿for God easy﴾: because the motive is certain, nothing prevents it, and the Sublime Name is mentioned explicitly through the shift in grammatical person (iltifāt, a shift in address from one grammatical person to another) to inspire awe and to emphasize the independent force of the concluding parenthetical statement (tadhyīl, a closing sentence that reinforces the preceding meaning).

(p-171) ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden⁠—﴾ that is, the major sins of wrongdoing that the Law has forbidden you, whether those mentioned here or not. It is also read as "kabīra" (singular), taking it as a generic noun.

﴿We will remove from you﴾ with the first-person plural (the "plural of majesty"), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person); it is also read with the yā' (third person), attributing the act to Him, may He be exalted. Takfīr (expiation) is the removal of what is deserving of punishment by means of a greater reward or by repentance; that is, "We will forgive you."

﴿your misdeeds﴾, meaning your minor sins, and We will efface them from you. The exegetes said: prayer to prayer, Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan are expiations for what lies between them of minor sins, provided major sins are avoided. There is disagreement concerning what constitutes major sins. The more likely view is that a major sin (kabīra) is every sin for which the Lawgiver has prescribed a fixed penalty (ḥadd) or explicitly threatened punishment. It has been said: it is whatever is known to be forbidden by a definitive proof. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are seven: associating partners with Allah, the Most High; killing a soul which Allah, the Most High, has forbidden; slandering chaste women; consuming the property of orphans; usury (ribā); fleeing from the battlefield; and disobedience to parents. It is narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that apostasy after emigration (al-taʿaqqub baʿda al-hijra) replaces disobedience to parents. Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) added sorcery and the violation of the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Ḥarām). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that a man said to him, "The major sins are seven"; he said, "They are closer to seven hundred than to seven." It is also narrated from him that they are up to seventy, since there is no minor sin with persistence and no major sin with seeking forgiveness. It has also been said that what is meant is the kinds of shirk, based on His saying, the Most High: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. It has also been said: the smallness and greatness of sins is relative to what is above and below them, and according to their doer, and indeed according to times and places as well. So the greatest of major sins is shirk, and the smallest of minor sins is mere inward thought, and what lies between them are intermediate degrees to which both descriptions apply. Whoever is faced with two of these, and his soul is inclined towards both in such a way that he cannot restrain himself, but he restrains himself from the greater of the two, then what he committed is expiated for him, in return for the greater reward he deserves for avoiding the greater sin.

﴿and We will admit you﴾ with a ḍamma on the mīm, a noun of place meaning Paradise.

﴿with honour (karīman)﴾, that is, a good and pleasing [entrance], or it is a mīmī verbal noun, meaning admission together with honour. It is also read with a fatḥa on the mīm, which likewise may be a place or a verbal noun. If it is the verbal noun, it is in the accusative by an implied verb that is a consequence of the mentioned one, meaning: "We will admit you, so you will enter an entrance, or a noble entering," as in the verse:

Wa ʿaḍḍatu dahrin yā ibna Marwāna lam tadaʿ / min al-māli illā mushtatun aw mujallafu
("And the bite of time, O son of Marwān, has left of wealth only the stripped or the shaven")

That is: it has left, so there remains only the stripped one, etc.

﴿And do not wish for what Allah has favoured some of you with over others﴾, that is, over you. Perhaps the choice of the indefinite (بعضكم, "some of you") rather than a more specific form was to avoid direct confrontation with what would grieve them. Al-Qaffal said: When Allah the Exalted forbade them to consume one another's wealth falsely and to kill souls, He followed this with a prohibition against what leads to it, namely covetousness toward their wealth and wishing for it. It was also said: He first forbade them from encroaching on their wealth with their limbs, and then from encroaching on it in the heart through envy, so as to purify their outward and inward deeds. The meaning, then, is: Do not wish for what Allah the Exalted has given some of you of worldly matters, such as standing and wealth and other things over which people compete, instead of you. That is a apportionment from Allah, issuing from a management suited to the circumstances of His servants and grounded in comprehensive knowledge of the great and minute affairs of their lives. Therefore each of those who have been given less must be content with what Allah has apportioned to him, and must not wish for the portion of the one who has been favoured, nor envy him for it, because that opposes the ruling of divine decree, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom. (This is not because its absence would be better for him, nor because, if it were otherwise, it would be harmful to him, as has been said. For that would not be supported by what follows, the command to ask Allah for His bounty, since that clearly indicates that what is forbidden is wishing for another's share, not wishing for whatever exceeds one's own share absolutely.) This is the statement. It has also been said: When Allah the Exalted made the share of a male in inheritance equal to the share of two females, the women said: "We are more in need that we should have two shares and men one share, because we are weak and they are strong and more capable of seeking livelihood than we are." So this was revealed. This is the most fitting reading in light of the prohibition being explained by His saying, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned﴾. For this is explicit that wishing occurs between the two groups, men and women. Perhaps the masculine form of the prohibition is used because "some" (بعض) referred to them. The meaning: For each of the two groups in inheritance there is a share fixed in amount from what has befallen it according to its capacity. This is expressed with "earning" by way of a subordinate metaphor (al-istiʿara al-tabaʿiyya, i.e., a metaphor in which the verb or verbal notion is borrowed), based on likening the requirement of one's condition for his share to earning it, to affirm the entitlement of each of them to his share and to strengthen its exclusivity to him, such that it does not go beyond him to another. For this is among what the cessation from the aforementioned wishing necessitates. And His saying, Exalted: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty﴾ is coordinated with the prohibition, and the placement of the explanatory clause between them serves to confirm the cessation, along with the encouragement to comply by means of the command, as if it were said: Do not wish for what belongs exclusively to others of their earned share, and ask Allah the Exalted from the treasuries of His blessings, which never run out. The second object is omitted for generality, that is: Ask Him for whatever you desire, for He, Exalted, will give it to you; or because it is understood from the context, that is: Ask Him for the like of it. It has also been said that "min" (من) is superfluous and the sense is: Ask Him for His bounty. And it has come in a hadith: «"Let none of you wish for his brother's wealth, but let him say: O Allah, provide for me; O Allah, give me the like of it."» And from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Ask Allah of His bounty, for He loves to be asked, and the best worship is waiting for relief﴾. As for interpreting "share" as the otherworldly reward and keeping "earning" in its literal sense, by making the occasion of revelation what has been related: that Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I wish Allah had prescribed jihad upon us as He prescribed it upon men, so that we would have a reward like theirs." On this reading the meaning is: For each of the two groups there is a share of reward specific to it, consequent upon its deeds. So men have a reward corresponding to what is fitting for them of deeds, such as jihad and the like, and women have a reward corresponding to what is fitting for them of deeds, such as safeguarding the rights of their husbands and the like. Thus women should not wish for the specific reward of men, but should ask from the treasuries of His mercy, Exalted, what is fitting for their condition of reward. This is not supported by the context of the noble text, which concerns inheritance and the merits of men.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾. For this reason He placed people in ranks and raised some of them above others in degrees, according to the levels of their capacities, which overflow upon them in accordance with a will founded on lofty wisdoms.

﴿وَلِكُلٍّ جَعَلْنا مَوالِيَ مِمّا تَرَكَ الوالِدانِ والأقْرَبُونَ﴾ ("And for every one We have appointed heirs (mawali) to what the parents and close relatives leave behind") is a new independent sentence that confirms the meaning of what precedes it. "Li-kull" (لِكُلٍ) is the second object of "ja'alna" (جَعَلْنا), and it is placed before the verb to emphasize comprehensiveness and to block the assumption that the appointment applies only to some and not to others, as in His saying: ﴿لِكُلٍّ جَعَلْنا مِنكم شِرْعَةً ومِنهاجًا﴾ ("For each of you We have appointed a law and a way"). The meaning is: for every estate We have appointed heirs who differ in rank, who take possession of it and receive their shares according to their entitlement, which depends on the relationship between them and the deceased. "Mimma taraka" (مِمّا تَرَكَ) is an explanation of "li-kull" (لِكُلٍ), and the two are separated by what governs it, (p-173) just as they are separated in His saying: ﴿قُلْ أغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أتَّخِذُ ولِيًّا فاطِرِ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ ("Say: Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?"), where the divine name is separated from its attribute by the governing word of what is annexed to it, namely "ghayr" (غَيْرَ) or "awliya" (أوْ). Or the meaning is: for every people We have appointed them heirs (mawali), i.e., inheritors with a specific share different from the share of other people, from what the parents and close relatives leave behind. This is on the basis that "ja'alna mawali" (جَعَلْنا مَوالِيَ) is an attribute of "li-kull" (لِكُلٍ), and the returning pronoun referring to it is omitted, so the sentence is a subject and predicate, following the pattern of your saying: "For everyone whom Allah has created as a human being, a portion of Allah's provision," meaning: a share of it. As for what has been said, that the meaning is "for each person We have appointed heirs (mawali) to what he leaves behind," meaning inheritors of it, with "min" (مِن) being a complement of "mawali" because it carries the sense of "heir (warith)," and with a concealed pronoun in "taraka" (تَرَكَ) referring to "kull" (كُلٍّ), and His saying: ﴿الوالِدانِ والأقْرَبُونَ﴾ ("the parents and close relatives") is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining "mawali," as if it were said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "The parents," and so on, then this involves a disruption of the noble arrangement, because by explaining "mawali" in the manner mentioned, the vagueness that justifies considering the variation among them is lost, whereas with the first arrangement the order is achieved, as was indicated in the explanation of the first two interpretations, together with what it entails: children are excluded from the "mawali," since "the close relatives" does not include them, just as it does not include the two parents.

﴿والَّذِينَ عَقَدَتْ أيْمانُكُمْ﴾ ("And those with whom your oaths have bound you") refers to the "mawali of alliance" (mawali al-muwalat). The ally used to inherit a sixth (sudus) of his ally's property, and this was abrogated (nuskh) by His saying: ﴿وَأُولُو الأرْحامِ بَعْضُهم أوْلى بِبَعْضٍ﴾ ("And blood relatives are closer to one another"). According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, if a man embraces Islam at the hand of another man and the two make a contract that he will inherit from him and pay his blood money (aql) on his behalf, it is valid; the blood money is then his obligation, and he inherits from him if the deceased has no heir at all. The attribution of the contract to the oaths is because the customary practice was to wipe hands (al-mumasaha) upon them at the time of the contract. The meaning is: "Your oaths have bound their pledges," so "pledges" (uhud) is omitted and the annexed noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is put in its place. It is also read as "'aqqadat" (عَقَّدَتْ) with a doubled letter, and as "'aqadat" (عاقَدَتْ), meaning "your oaths have contracted with them," and "masahtumuh" (ماسَحْتُمُوهُ), "you have wiped hands upon it." The phrase is a topic (mubtada') that implies the sense of a conditional. For this reason the predicate, namely His saying: ﴿فَآتُوهم نَصِيبَهُمْ﴾ ("then give them their share"), is introduced with "fa" (فَ), or it is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb that the following clause explains, as in your saying: "Zayd, so strike him," or it is in the nominative and coordinated with "the parents and close relatives." His saying: ﴿فَآتُوهُمْ﴾ ("then give them") and what follows is a sentence that clarifies the preceding sentence and emphasizes it, and the pronoun refers to the "mawali."

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("Indeed Allah is over all things") among the things, of which giving and withholding are part.

﴿شَهِيدًا﴾ ("Witness"). Therein is a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 34:

﴿The men are the protectors and maintainers of the women﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to explain the reason why men deserve a greater share in inheritance, in detail, after the general statement of the difference in their entitlements. The sentence is nominal (ismiyyah), and its predicate is in the intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah, the emphatic pattern), to indicate that they are long-established in the attribute ascribed to them and firmly rooted in it. The meaning is: it is their custom to maintain authority over them through commanding and forbidding, as rulers maintain authority over their subjects. He explains this by two matters: one innate (wahbi) and one acquired (kasbi). So it is said: ﴿by what Allah has preferred some of them over others﴾. The bi is causal (sababiyyah), connected to "qawwamun" or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its pronoun. The "ma" is verbal-masdarial (masdariyyah), and the pronoun that is expressed refers to both groups by way of predominance (taghlib). That is: they are maintainers over them because of Allah the Exalted's preferring them over women, or they are connected with Allah the Exalted's preference of them, and so on. Placing "some" (ba'd) in the position of the two pronouns indicates that the matter is extremely evident and that there is no need to state explicitly either the one preferred or the one over whom he is preferred. For the same reason, the attributes of perfection by which the preference occurs are not stated explicitly. These are perfection of intellect, good management, soundness of judgment, and greater strength in actions and acts of obedience. For this reason they were singled out for prophethood, leadership of the community (imamah), guardianship (wilayah), leading the ritual observances, testimony in all matters, the obligation of jihad, the Friday prayer, and other things besides that.

﴿and by what they spend from their wealth﴾ The bi is connected to the same element to which the first bi is connected. The "ma" is either masdariyyah or a relative pronoun (mawsulah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted from the relative clause (silah). The "min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah) or initial (ibtida'iyyah), connected to "anfaqu" or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun. That is: and because of their spending from their wealth, or because of what they have spent from their wealth, or existing from their wealth, and this is what they spent of the dower and maintenance. It is narrated that "Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', one of the chiefs (nuqaba') of the Ansar, may Allah be pleased with them, had a wife, Habibah bint Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr, who showed disobedience (nashazat) toward him, so he struck her. Her father set out with her to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained. He said, peace be upon him: 'Let her retaliate against him.' Then the verse was revealed. He said, peace be upon him: 'We wanted one thing and Allah wanted another, and what Allah wanted is better.'" ﴿So the righteous women﴾ begins the detailed explanation of their conditions and the manner of maintaining authority over them according to the differences in their conditions. That is: so among them the righteous women.

﴿are devoutly obedient﴾ That is, they are obedient to Allah the Exalted, standing in fulfilment of the rights of their husbands.

﴿guarding in the absence [of their husbands]⁠﴾ That is, guarding what is due of the absence, meaning what it is obligatory for them to guard during the absence of their husbands, of their chastity and their property. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of women is the woman who, when you look at her, pleases you; when you order her, she obeys you; and when you are absent from her, she guards you in her property and herself." Then he recited the verse. It is also said: [guarding] their secrets. The attribution of the property to them indicates that the husband's property, with regard to the right of disposal, is in the status of her property, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿and do not give the foolish your property﴾, and the verse continues.

﴿by what Allah has guarded﴾ The "ma" is masdariyyah, meaning: by Allah the Exalted's guarding them through commanding them to guard what is hidden, urging them to it by promise and threat, and granting them success in it. Or it is relative (mawsulah), meaning: by that which Allah has guarded for them against men, namely the dower, maintenance, maintaining their protection, and defending them. It is read "bima hafiza Allaha" with the accusative, by omitting the genitive-annexed noun (mudaf), meaning: by the matter which guarded the right of Allah the Exalted and His obedience, namely chastity and compassion toward men.

﴿And those [women] from whom you fear disobedience⁠﴾ This is addressed to the husbands and is guidance for them to the way of maintaining authority over them. Fear (khawf) is a state that arises in the heart when something disliked occurs, or upon suspicion or knowledge of its occurrence. It may mean one of these two: you suspect their disobedience and their rising above your obedience; nushuz is elevation from the ground.

﴿then admonish them﴾ That is, advise them, by encouragement and warning.

﴿and forsake them﴾ after that, if admonition and advice do not benefit.

﴿in the beds﴾ That is, in the sleeping places, so do not let them under the covers, and do not have intercourse with them. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for joining them. It is said: "al-madaji'" means the places of spending the night, that is, do not spend the night with them. It is read "fi al-madja'" and "fi al-mudtaja'".

﴿and strike them﴾ if what you have done of admonition and forsaking does not succeed, a beating that is not severe (ghayr mubarrih) and not disfiguring (la shain).

﴿Then if they obey you﴾ in that, as is evident, because it is the final limit of what is counted as a deterrent.

﴿then do not seek against them a way⁠﴾ by rebuke or harm. That is, remove from them the act of confronting them, and treat what came from them as though it had not happened, for the one who repents of a sin is like one who has no sin.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Exalted and Great⁠﴾ So beware of Him, for He the Exalted is more capable over you than you are over those under your hands. Or: He the Exalted, with the loftiness of His station, overlooks your misdeeds and accepts your repentance when you repent, so you are more deserving of pardoning your wives when they obey you. Or: He exalts and magnifies Himself above wronging anyone or diminishing his right. The absence of mention of their disobedience toward them is to indicate that this is not something that should come about or be supposed to come about, and that what is expected from them and befits their station, especially after the deterrents that have occurred, is obedience. For this reason the conditional clause is introduced by fa', which indicates that what precedes it is the cause of what follows.

(p-175) This is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), directing the speech to the arbitrators (al-hukkam). It is based on a tacit assumption (al-taqdir al-maskut 'anhu), namely non-compliance, which leads to dispute and to bringing the matter before them. Al-shiqaq means opposition, either because each of the two wants what harms the other, or because each is on a side (shiqq), that is, a direction, other than the other's side. Here "fear" (al-khawf) means knowledge, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas. Asserting that the breach exists does not contradict sending the two arbitrators, because they are sent in hope of removing it, not to learn whether it actually exists.

It has also been said that "fear" means suspicion (al-zann). The dual pronoun refers to the spouses, although no prior mention of them has been made, because what refers to them has been mentioned. The attribution of shiqaq to the time expression (al-zarf) is either treating it as an object, as in the line of poetry, "O thief of the night" (ya sariqa al-laylata), or treating it as a subject, as in your saying, "its day is fasting" (nahāruhu sā'im). The meaning is: if you know or suspect that the opposition has become so firm that the husband cannot remove it.

﴿Then send﴾, that is, to the spouses, for the reconciliation of the matter (li-islah dhat al-bayn).

﴿an arbiter﴾, a man who is moderate (wasat), fit for judgment and reconciliation.

﴿from his family﴾, from the husband's family.

﴿and an arbiter﴾, another, of the same description as the first,

﴿from her family﴾, for relatives know the inner circumstances better and are more eager for reconciliation. This is by way of recommendation (istihbab), so if they are appointed from outsiders, it is permitted. Scholars differ on whether the two may join or separate the couple if they see that to be right. It has been said that they have that authority, and this is what is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Sha'bi also said it. It is narrated from al-Hasan that they may join the couple but may not separate them. Malik said that they may arrange a khul' (divorce by the wife's compensation) if reconciliation lies in it.

﴿if they both intend﴾, that is, the two arbitrators,

﴿reconciliation﴾, that is, if they intend to reconcile the couple, their intention is sound and their hearts are sincere for the sake of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾, that is, He will create agreement and affection between the spouses and place in their hearts love and compassion. The omission of mention of their not intending reconciliation, as stated, implies that such a thing is not to be assumed of them, and that what befits their position and is expected of them is the intention to reconcile. This contains a further encouragement to the arbitrators toward reconciliation and a warning against laxity, so that the failure of the matter is not attributed to their lack of intention. Thus the conditional "if" (in) states that the occurrence of harmony depends on the occurrence of the intention, and indicates that its non-occurrence depends on the absence of that intention. It has been said that both pronouns refer to the arbitrators, meaning: if they intend reconciliation, Allah will bring about harmony between them, so that their word becomes united and their aim is achieved. It has also been said that both refer to the spouses, meaning: if they intend to reconcile what lies between them of opposition, Allah, exalted is He, will create familiarity and accord between them. This contains an indication that whoever makes his intention right in what he seeks, Allah grants him success in what he desires.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Acquainted﴾ with outward and inward matters, so He knows how to remove opposition and bring about accord.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 36:

﴿And worship Allah, and do not associate anything with Him.﴾ This is an independent statement, brought forward to explain the rulings related to the rights of parents, relatives, and others, following the explanation of the rulings related to the rights of spouses. It is introduced with what pertains to the rights of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which are the most emphatic and greatest of rights, as a reminder of the exalted status of the rights of parents by arranging them in the same sequence, as is the case in all other passages. "Shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative because it is an object: that is, do not associate with Him anything among things, whether an idol or other than it; or it is an infinitive: that is, do not associate with Him any form of association (ishrak), whether manifest or hidden.

﴿And to parents, good treatment.﴾ That is: treat them both well. (p-176) ﴿And to the near relative﴾ That is: to the one who has a kinship, such as a brother, an uncle, a maternal uncle, or the like.

﴿And the orphans and the needy﴾ from among outsiders.

﴿And the neighbor who is near (dhi al-qurba)﴾ That is: the one whose neighborhood is close. It is said: the one who, besides being a neighbor, has closeness and connection through lineage or religion. It is also read in the accusative, as a particularization, to magnify the right of the near neighbor.

﴿And the neighbor who is distant (al-junub)﴾ That is: the distant one, or the one who has no kinship. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, from him: "Neighbors are of three kinds: a neighbor who has three rights: the right of neighborhood, the right of kinship, and the right of Islam; a neighbor who has two rights: the right of neighborhood and the right of Islam; and a neighbor who has one right, which is the right of neighborhood, and this is the neighbor from among the People of the Book." It is also read as "wal-jari al-junubi."

﴿And the companion at your side﴾ That is: the companion in a good matter, such as learning, business, a trade, or travel, for he has accompanied you and is at your side. Among them are those who sat beside you in a mosque, a gathering, or otherwise, of any slight companionship that joined you and him. It is said: this is the wife.

﴿And the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil)﴾ is the traveler who has been cut off, or the guest.

﴿And what your right hands possess﴾ from among the slaves, male and female.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love one who is arrogant (mukhtal)﴾ That is: proud, who disdains his relatives, neighbors, and companions and does not turn to them.

﴿Boastful (fakhur)﴾ who boasts over them. The clause is a justification for the preceding command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 37:

﴿Those who are miserly and bid people to be miserly﴾ with a damma on the bāʾ and a sukūn on the khāʾ (yabkhulūna, pronounced with dammah and sukun), and it is also read with a fatha on the first letter, with fatha on both, and with damma on both. The relative clause is either a substitute (badal) for His words, exalted is He, ﴿whoever is﴾, or it is put in the accusative to express censure (naṣb ʿalā al-dhamm), or in the nominative for the same purpose, i.e., "they are the ones who...". Or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: "Those who are miserly, and act, and make [such things] are deserving of every reproach."

﴿And conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, i.e., of wealth and riches, or of his attributes, peace be upon him, which He had made clear to them in the Torah. The latter is more fitting to their bidding people to be miserly, for their rabbis used to conceal them and bid their descendants to conceal them.

﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that whoever has this characteristic is a disbeliever in the blessing of Allah, exalted is He, and whoever is a disbeliever in the blessing of Allah, exalted is He, for him is a punishment that will humiliate him, just as he humiliated the blessing by miserliness and concealment. The verse was revealed concerning a group of the Jews, who used to say to the Ansar, by way of advice: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you." It is also said: it was revealed concerning those who concealed the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding statement (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī) confirming what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 38:

﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by the people﴾, i.e., for boasting and so that it may be said, "How generous and how bountiful they are!", not seeking the Face of Allah, the Exalted. This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "those who are stingy" (alladhina yabkhaluna) or upon "the disbelievers" (al-kafirin). They were made to share in the blame and the threat because stinginess and extravagance, which is spending on what is not fitting, are, insofar as both are extremes of negligence and excess, equal in ugliness and in bringing upon oneself reproach and blame. It is also permissible that the conjunction is based on treating a descriptive difference as if it were an essential difference, as in his saying:

To the stout-hearted king and the son of the lofty one,
And the lion of the battalions in the crowded press.

Or it is an inchoative (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion﴾ etc., as if it were said: ﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by the people.﴾ ﴿And they do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾ (p-177), so that by spending they might seek out His good pleasure and His reward. They are the polytheists of Makkah who spent their wealth in hostility to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: they are the hypocrites.

﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is the companion he has﴾. I.e., their companion is Satan. It was omitted to signal that it is evident and needs no explicit mention. What is meant is Iblis and his helpers, since they drove them to those ugly deeds and adorned them for them, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils.﴾ It is also permissible that this is a threat to them, that Satan will be joined with them in the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 39:

﴿And what would it have been upon them﴾ i.e., upon those of the groups mentioned.

﴿If they had believed in God and the Last Day and spent from what God has provided them﴾ i.e., seeking the Face of God Most High. The phrase was not made explicit, relying on the preceding detail (tafsil) and being content with mentioning belief in God and the Last Day, for this implies that spending be undertaken absolutely seeking His Face and desiring His reward. That is: what harm or burden would there be upon them in believing in God and spending in His way? This is a rebuke to them for their ignorance of the place of benefit and their belief in a thing contrary to what it is, and an exhortation to reflect in order to seek the answer, so that it may lead them to knowledge of the great benefits and fine rewards it contains. It is also an admonition that one invited to a matter in which there is no harm should be inclined to respond to it out of caution; how much more so when it contains countless benefits. The mention of belief in these two first is due to its importance in itself, and because spending is not counted as valid without it. As for placing their spending for show before their not believing in these two, although the latter is worse than the former, this is for the sake of preserving the connection between their spending of that kind and what precedes it, namely their stinginess and their commanding people to it.

﴿And God is ever of them﴾ and of their actual conditions.

﴿Knowing﴾. So this is a threat to them of punishment, or regarding their deeds that were required; thus it is an explanation of His reward to them had they believed and spent, as His saying Most High indicates: *

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (even) an atom's weight﴾. *Al-mithqāl* (مِثْقال, weight) is a *mif'āl* pattern noun from *al-thiql* (ثِقْل, heaviness), like *al-miqdār* (مِقْدار, measure) from *al-qadr* (قَدْر, extent). Its accusative case (*intiṣāb*, انتصاب) is because it is an epithet (*na't*, نَعْت, adjective) standing in place of the object (*maf'ūl*, مفعول). This holds whether *al-zulm* (wronging) means diminishing or placing a thing in other than its proper place. The meaning is: He does not diminish from the reward or add to the punishment by even the weight of an atom. Or it is an epithet of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*, مصدر), which stands in its place, meaning: He does not wrong with a wronging equal to the weight of an atom. The atom (*dharra*, ذرّة) is the tiny ant, or every particle of the motes of dust seen in a window's light, and this is the most fitting for the context of hyperbole (*mubālagha*, مبالغة), since its smallness in weight is more evident than the smallness of the ant in weight. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he put his hand into the dust, then blew on it, and said: "Each one of these is a *dharra*."

﴿And if it is a good deed﴾: that is, and if the weight of an atom is a good deed. The feminine *ḥasanatan* (حَسَنَة) is used because the predicate (*khabar*, خبر) is feminine, or because it is attached to *dharra*. The nun of *takun* (تَكُ) is deleted without analogical rule, modeled on the weak letters (*ḥurūf al-ʿilla*, حروف العلة) and for lightness due to frequent use. It was also read *ḥasanatun* (حَسَنَةٌ) with the nominative, taking *kāna* (كان) as complete (*tāmmah*, تامّة).

﴿He multiplies it﴾: that is, He multiplies its reward. He made this a multiplication of the good deed itself, to indicate the complete connection between them, as if they were one thing. It was read *yuḍʿifhā* (يُضْعِفْها), and both have one meaning. It was read *nuḍāʿifhā* (نُضاعِفْها) with the plural of majesty, following the manner of *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person, التفات). From ʿUthmān al-Nahdī that he said to Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him: "It has reached me that you say, 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, gives His believing servant a thousand thousand good deeds for one good deed.'" Abū Hurayra said: "No; rather I heard him (ﷺ) say: 'He gives him two thousand thousand good deeds.'" Then he recited this noble verse. What is meant is abundance, not a precise limit. (p-178)

﴿And gives from Himself﴾: and gives its possessor from His presence, in the manner of bounty, beyond what He promised in return for the deed.

﴿A great reward﴾: a generous, abundant gift. He called it a *ajr* (أجر, reward) because it follows the reward and is added to it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 41:**

﴿Then how﴾ Its position (i'rab) is either the nominative, as a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or the accusative, by an omitted verb, by analogy with the circumstantial accusative (hal), as is the view of Sibawayh; or by analogy with the adverbial accusative of place or time (zarf), as is the view of al-Akhfash. That is: "Then how is the state of these disbelievers, from among the Jews, the Christians and others, or how will they act?"

﴿when We bring﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿from every nation﴾ from among the nations.

﴿a witness﴾ who will bear witness against them concerning what they were upon of corrupt beliefs and foul deeds, and he is their prophet, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I was a witness over them while I was among them﴾. The element governing the adverbial phrase (zarf) is the meaning contained in the subject and predicate, namely the terror of the matter and the greatness of the affair; or it is the implied verb, and "from" (min) is connected to "We bring."

﴿And We bring you﴾ O Muhammad ﴿against these﴾ — a reference to the witnesses indicated by what was mentioned.

﴿as a witness﴾ bearing witness to their truthfulness, since you have knowledge of their beliefs, because your law comprises the essentials of their fundamental principles. It has been said: [the reference is] to the deniers, whose condition is being asked about; you bear witness against them of disbelief and disobedience, just as all the prophets bear witness against their nations. It has been said: [the reference is] to the believers, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 42:

﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their condition, the severity and dreadfulness of which was alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿how [will it be]﴾. If by them are meant those who denied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then the expression of them by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), especially after pointing to them with "these" (ha'ula'), serves to censure them by what is within the scope of the relative clause (silah), and to indicate the cause of the dreadful condition and the tremendous matter that befell them. And mentioning him (peace be upon him) by the title of Messengership is to honour him and to increase the ugliness of the state of those who denied him, for the right of the Messenger is that he be believed in and obeyed, not that he be disbelieved and disobeyed. If, however, by them is meant the category of disbelievers, then they are included within their ranks by primary inclusion (dukhulan awwaliyyan), and the word "the Messenger" then means the genus that encompasses the Prophet (peace be upon him) by primary inclusion. Whichever is the case, there is in it such a magnification of the matter and such an awfulness of the state that its extent cannot be measured.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and disobeyed﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon ﴿disbelieved﴾ and is included with it within the relative clause. The meaning is their acts of disobedience distinct from their disbelief. In this there is an indication that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the sharia (furu' al-shara'i') with respect to being held accountable.

It has been said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿disbelieved﴾. It has also been said: it is a relative clause (silah) for another relative pronoun, meaning: they will wish on that day, those who combined disbelief with disobedience of the Messenger, or those who disbelieved while having disobeyed the Messenger, or those who disbelieved and those who disobeyed the Messenger.

As for "law" (lau) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if the earth were levelled over them﴾, if it is made a verbal (masdariyya) particle, then the clause is the object of "will wish", meaning: they will wish that they were buried so that the earth would be levelled over them like the dead. It has been said: they will wish that they had not been resurrected or had not been created, and that they and the earth were equal. It has been said: the beasts will become dust, so they will wish for their condition. If it is made to retain its own function (jariya 'ala babiha), then the object is omitted, being indicated by the clause, meaning: they will wish for the levelling of the earth. The answer of "law" is also omitted, to signal its utmost clarity, meaning: they would be gladdened by that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not hide from Allah any statement﴾ is coordinated upon "will wish", meaning: and they will not be able to conceal it, because their limbs will bear witness against them. It has been said: the waw is for the circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they will wish to be buried in the earth while they hide from Him, exalted is He, no statement and do not lie to Him by their saying: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists," for it is narrated that when they say that, Allah sets a seal upon their mouths, so their limbs bear witness against them, and the matter becomes severe for them, so they wish that the earth were levelled over them.

It is read "tassawwa" (تَسَّوّى), the original being "tatasawwa", with the ta assimilated into the sin. And it is read "tasawwa" (تَسَوّى) with the second ta omitted, from "sawwaytuhu, fa-tasawwa" (one says: I levelled it, so it became levelled).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 43:**

﴿O you who believe, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying﴾. Since they had been forbidden, in what preceded, from associating anything with Him, Exalted is He, they are forbidden here from what leads to that, from a direction they do not expect. It is related that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, prepared food and drink at a time when wine was permitted, and he invited a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. They ate and drank until they became intoxicated. When the time for the Maghrib prayer came, one of them went forward to lead them in prayer and recited "Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship" (Qur'an 109:1-2), and then this verse was revealed. The opening of the speech with the two particles of address and alerting (ya and ayyuha) is for emphasis, in urging them to act upon the implication of the prohibition against approaching the prayer, although the intended meaning is the prohibition against performing it, for the sake of emphasis in this matter. It has been said that the intended meaning is the prohibition against approaching the mosques, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "Keep your mosques away from your children and your insane." But his saying, Exalted is He, "until you know what you are saying," contradicts this. The meaning then is: do not perform it in the state of intoxication, until you know, before beginning, what you are saying, for through that test it becomes evident that they know what they will recite in the prayer. Taking "what you are saying" to mean what is in the prayer requires that the beginning of the prayer precede the ultimate point of the prohibition. And taking knowledge to refer to "what" in potential, to mean "until you are in a condition in which you know what you will recite in the prayer," is needless prolixity, because that condition only becomes evident through the test mentioned. Moreover, preferring "what you are saying" over "what you recite" would then be devoid of a motive. It has also been said that the intended meaning of intoxication is the intoxication of drowsiness and the overpowering of sleep. In any case, the prohibition does not return to the restricted (the prayer) while the restriction remains and the permission stays as it is; rather, it is the restriction itself while the restricted remains in its state. ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been a decreed obligation upon the believers, at fixed times﴾ (Qur'an 4:103). It is as if it were said: O you who believe, do not become intoxicated during the times of the prayer. It has been related that after this verse was revealed, they did not drink wine during the times of the prayer, and when they had prayed the 'Isha, they would drink it, so they would not wake up except that the intoxication had left them and they knew what they were saying.

﴿And not in a state of janabah﴾. This is a conjunction with His saying, Exalted is He, "while you are intoxicated," for it is in the domain of accusative. It is as if it were said: do not approach the prayer intoxicated or in a state of janabah. The janabah (ritual impurity from sexual intercourse or seminal emission) is the one afflicted by janabah. In it the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural, are equal, because it functions in the manner of a verbal noun.

﴿Except as travelers in passing﴾. This is an exception that is "emptied" (istithna' mufarragh, an exception in which the excluded element is not stated and the sentence is read as if the exception were the only element) from the most general of states. Its position is the accusative, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "do not approach," in consideration of its being restricted by the second state and not the first. The governing element in it is the verb of prohibition. That is: do not approach the prayer in a state of janabah in any circumstance, except while you are travelers. The meaning is that in the state of travel the ruling of the prohibition ends, but not by way of universal negation covering all its forms; rather, by way of negating universality in general, without any indication of the negation of the specific character of the part that is negated, nor of the persistence of the specific character of the remaining part, nor of the establishment of its contradictory, neither totally nor partially. For the exception does not indicate that expressly. Yes, it does point to the ruling of what follows differing from what precedes, with a general allusion that is sufficient in rhetorical contexts, but not in establishing the legal rulings of the Shari'ah. For the criterion in that matter is the evidence, and it has come after it in the manner of explanation. It has been said that it is an attribute of "janaban" (in a state of janabah), on the basis that "illa" (except) means "ghayr" (other than). That is: "and not in a state of janabah other than as travelers in passing." Whoever takes the prayer to mean its places interprets passing through (ubur) as crossing through them, and permits the one in janabah to cross through the mosque. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. According to us, this is not permitted except where water or a path is located within it. It has been said that some men of the Ansar had their doors opening onto the mosque, and janabah would befall them, and they would find no passage except through the mosque, so this was granted to them as a concession.

﴿Until you wash﴾. This is the ultimate point of the prohibition against approaching the prayer in the state of janabah. Perhaps the placing of the exception before it is to announce from the outset that the ruling of the prohibition in this case is not absolute, as in the case of intoxication, in order to create suspense toward the explanation and to fix it more firmly in minds. In the noble verse there is an indication that the one who prays should be careful to avoid what distracts him and occupies his heart, and should purify himself from what defiles him, and should not settle for the lowest degrees of purification when its higher degrees are possible.

﴿And if you are sick﴾. This begins the detailing of what was summarized in the exception, and the explanation of what is in the ruling of the excepted matters, among the excuses. In what came before, the mention was limited to the exception of travel, while the rest share with it the ruling of concession, to indicate that it is the most common excuse, which signals the necessity around which the matter of the concession revolves. It is as if it were said: nor in a state of janabah except when compelled. To this return the statements that "travelers in passing" was made a metaphor for all those excused. By sickness is meant what prevents the use of water absolutely, whether that is by being unable to reach it or by being unable to use it.

﴿Or on a journey﴾. This is a conjunction with "sick," that is: or you are on a journey, whether long or short. Its explicit mention, although it was already mentioned by way of exception, is for the building of the legal ruling upon it and the explanation of its manner, for the exception, as has been indicated, is far from indicating its establishment, let alone indicating its manner. The placing of sickness before it is to announce its primacy and its independence with rulings that do not exist in other cases, such as the requirement of using water and the like.

﴿Or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾. The ghā'iṭ is the low, depressed ground. Coming from it is a metaphor for minor impurity (hadath), because it is customary that one who intends to relieve himself goes to it in order to conceal his person from people's eyes. The attribution of coming from it to one of you, from among the addressees and not to all of them, is to avoid explicitly attributing them to what is shameful or what it is disgraceful to state explicitly. Likewise is the preference for metaphor in what is conjoined to it, from His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ over explicit mention of intercourse. Their being placed together in the chain of two causes of the removal of purity and the resort to tayammum (dry ablution with earth), although they are causes of the obligation of purification, is not by consideration of themselves but by consideration of their qualifier derived from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you find no water﴾. Rather, it is the true cause, and they were mentioned only as a preparation for it and as an alert that it is a cause of the concession after the establishment of the causes of minor and major purity. It is as if it were said: or you were not sick nor travelers, but you were lacking water for some reason, while what requires its use was established. The specification of its mention in this case, even though it is also considered in the case of sickness and travel, is because its occurrence in them is rare, and because those two are independent of its mention, either because janabah is definitely considered in them, so the ruling of minor impurity is known from its ruling by the indication of the text, since the structure of the verse is: do not approach the prayer in the state of janabah except as travelers; so if you are such, or you are sick, and so on. Or because of what has been said: that the general scarcity of water is frequent in the case of the traveler, and inability to use water, which takes the place of its absence, in the case of the sick, is sufficient to dispense with its mention verbally. And what has been said, that this qualifier refers to all, and that the qualifier of the obligation of purification, indicated by coming from the place of relieving oneself and touching, is considered in all, is not supported by the noble structure.

﴿Then perform tayammum with clean earth﴾. Then intend a clean portion of the surface of the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: the sa'id is the surface of the earth, whether dust or something else, even if it is a rock with no dust on it. If the one performing tayammum strikes his hand on it and wipes, that would be his purification. This is the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, some dust must adhere to the hand.

﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands﴾. That is, up to the elbows, because it has been related that "he, peace be upon him, performed tayammum and wiped his hands up to his elbows," and because it is a substitute for wudu' (ablution), so it is measured by its measure.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾. This is a reason for the concession and the facilitation and an affirmation of them, for whoever's constant practice is to pardon the erring and forgive the sinners must be one who makes things easy and not one who makes them difficult. It has been said that this is a metaphor for both of them, for leniency and indulgence are among the followers of pardon and the attendants of forgiveness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 44:

﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to make the believers marvel at their bad condition and to warn against allying with them. The address is to everyone among the believers who is capable of seeing (this), and it is directed here specifically to him, while later it is directed to all of them together, to signal the full fame of the ugliness of their condition and that it has reached such a level of manifestness that everyone who sees it marvels at it. The seeing is visual, meaning: Have you not looked at them? For they are more deserving that you witness them and marvel at their states. As for the permissibility that it be a seeing of the heart, with "ila" (to) carrying the sense of reaching (al-intiha') to what they did, this is rejected by the context of publicizing their vile acts and by placing it in the row of matters that are witnessed. The intended people are the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning two rabbis of the Jews who used to come to the chief of the hypocrites, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, and his group, discouraging them from Islam. And also from him, may Allah be pleased with him, it was revealed concerning Rifaʿa ibn Zayd and Malik ibn Dukhshum, who, whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke, would twist their tongues and find fault with him. By "the Scripture" is meant the Torah; and taking it to mean the genus of scripture that encompasses it in an initial arrangement is a lengthening of the distance. By "what they were given" is meant what was made clear to them therein of rulings and knowledge, among which is what they knew of the descriptions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the reality of Islam. Expressing it as "a portion" (nasib), which indicates that it is a right among their rights that must be observed and preserved, is to signal the complete flimsiness of their opinions, since they wasted it utterly. Its tanwin is for magnification (tafkhim), supporting the reproach against them and the marvel at their state. Thus expressing them by the relative pronoun serves to alert to the full extent of their ugliness by what is in the relative clause, and to indicate the place of what has been omitted in the transaction ascribed to them, namely the guidance which is one of the two counter-values (ʿiwadayn).

The word "min" is connected either to "utu" (were given) or to an omitted element that falls as a qualifier of "nasiban" (a portion), specifying its relative magnitude after specifying its intrinsic magnitude; i.e., a portion existing from the Scripture.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They buy error﴾ — it has been said: it is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the waw of "utu". There is no doubt that considering their buying, as mentioned, to be included in the giving is not fitting for the context. It has also been said: it is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, i.e., Have you not looked at them in the state of their buying? And you know that this is devoid of conveying that the substance of the reproach and marvel is the mentioned buying and what is conjoined to it. What the splendor of the noble composition requires is that it is a resumed statement explaining the ground of reproach and the focus of marvel, which were understood from the opening of the speech in a general and ambiguous manner, and it is founded on a question that arises from it, as if it were said: What do they do such that they are looked at? It is said: They take error and leave what they were given of guidance. The left-out element was omitted because the matter is extremely evident, especially after the mentioned allusion. The expression of that by "buying," which is a metaphor for exchanging a commodity for a price, i.e., taking it in place of it, a taking arising from desire for it and turning away from the other, is to signal the complete eagerness of theirs for error, which should be turned away from entirely, and their turning away from guidance, for which competitors compete. In this there is, of what is not hidden, a recording of the extreme frivolity of their minds and the utter flimsiness of their opinions, since their condition is depicted in a form that hardly anyone with even minimal discernment would undertake. The intended meaning of "error" is not its genus already present in them beforehand, which would disturb the sense of "buying" indicating its being later than it; rather it is its perfect instance, namely their obstinacy and persistence in disbelief after they knew the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and became certain of the truth of his religion and that he is the Arab Prophet announced in the Torah. There is no doubt that this rank was not attained by them before that, and this has passed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara.

﴿And they wish﴾ — a conjunction upon "yashtaruna" (they buy), a partner to it in specifying the locus of reproach and marvel. The form of the present tense in both serves to indicate renewed continuity, for the renewal of the ruling of their mentioned buying and the repetition of acting according to its requirement is, in effect, a renewal of itself and its repetition. That is: they are not content with the error of themselves, but they wish, by what they did of concealing his descriptions (peace be upon him), [that...].

﴿that you too go astray﴾ — you also, O believers.

﴿the way﴾ — the straight path that leads to the truth.

﴿And Allah knows best﴾ — that is, better than you do.

﴿about your enemies﴾, all of them, and these are among them. He has already told you of their enmity toward you and what they intend for you, so that you may be on guard against them and against associating with them. Or He knows best their condition and the outcome of their affair. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) that affirms their intention mentioned above.

﴿And Allah is sufficient as a protector﴾ in all your affairs and interests.

﴿And Allah is sufficient as a helper﴾ in every circumstance. So trust in Him, be content with His guardianship and His support, do not take them as allies, and do not concern yourselves with them or with the evil they inflict upon you, for He, exalted is He, will suffice you against their scheming and their harm. Thus there is in this both a promise and a warning. The particle ba' (al-bāʾ al-mazīda, the superfluous ba') is added to the subject of kafā (ʾafā, "suffices") to emphasize the connection of the predicate to its subject through the connection of the genitive. The repetition of the verb in both clauses, along with the use of the divine name in a place where a pronoun would ordinarily stand, serves to strengthen the independence of each clause, which suits the parenthetical structure, and to emphasize His sufficiency, mighty and majestic is He, in both guardianship and support, and to hint that each of these is the cause of the other, since divinity (al-ulūhiyyah) necessarily requires both.

﴿From among those who are Jews﴾. It is said: this is an explanatory clarification of "your enemies," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ). But there is an objection to this: there is no basis for restricting His knowledge, glorified is He, to a group among their enemies, especially in the context of a parenthetical interjection, which by its nature should be general and unrestricted, and should cover what is the intended meaning in the context in a primary way, as has been indicated.

It is also said: it is a relative complement (ṣilah) to "a helper" (naṣīran), meaning: He will help you against those who are Jews, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who will help me against God?﴾. There is in this what there is of restricting the wide scope of His help, glorified and exalted is He. Moreover, there is no need to place the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun referring to the enemies, because what is in the sphere of the relative clause is not a fitting description for help.

It is also said: it is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada'), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ occurs as a description of it, meaning: from among those who are Jews are a people or a group who distort words, etc. But there is an objection to this: it requires that the preceding group be entirely free of distortion, which is the actual referent of their "buying" (the error). So what befits the dignity of the noble revelation is that it is a clarification of the first relative pronoun, which in meaning includes the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitābayn). Between them was placed what was placed, for the greater importance of clarifying the point of censure and wonder, and for the swiftness of making the believers averse to them and warning them against associating with them, and for the concern to make them rely on God, glorified and exalted is He, and suffice with His guardianship and help. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They distort﴾ and what is conjoined to it is a clarification of their aforementioned "buying" and a detailing of the varieties of their misguidance. In the noble composition, the method of explanation after vagueness and detail after summary has been observed. The particle "mā" (in "mā yuḥarrifūna") is for added emphasis required by the situation. "Al-kalim" is a collective noun whose singular is "kalimah," like "tamr" and "tamrah." The pronoun referring to it is masculine in consideration of its singular form, and "mawāḍi'ihi" is plural in consideration of its multiplicity in meaning. It has also been read with a kasra on the kāf and sukūn on the lām (kilm), the plural of kilmah, as a lightened form of kalimah. It has also been read "yuḥarrifūna al-kalām." The intended meaning of it here is either what is in the Torah specifically, or what is more general than that and includes what will be related of them, the known words that issued from them during their dialogue with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). There is no room for taking those words alone as the intended meaning, by making the conjunction of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they say: We hear and we disobey﴾ etc. to what precedes it an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsīrī) for what you will come to know of its secret. So if by "it" (the distortion) is meant the first (the Torah), as is the opinion of the majority, then its distortion is removing it from the places where God, exalted is He, placed it in the Torah, like their distortion regarding the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) as "dark-complexioned, of medium build," by putting in its place "light-skinned, tall." And like their distortion of stoning (rajm) by replacing it with the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), or by diverting it from the meaning God, exalted is He, revealed in it to what has no validity, through deviant interpretations suited to their false desires. And if by "it" is meant the second (the words), then there must be intended by "its places" whatever is fitting for it absolutely, whether that is by God's explicit specification, like the places of what is in the Torah, or by the specification of reason or religion, like the places of other things. In any case, their saying "we hear and we disobey" should be applied in its generality, without restriction to a time or place, and without specifying one matter over another. Rather, it should be understood to include what is more general than actual speech, and what their obstinacy and stubbornness expresses, so that what their tongues of condition spoke when distorting the Torah is included. For whoever does not utter that great thing hardly dares such a crime. Otherwise, restricting it to what they said in the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ) of abominations alone would require restricting the ruling of the following conditional clause and what follows it to those words alone, without addressing their distortion of the Torah, although that is the greatest of their enumerated crimes. From here the promised secret has been revealed to you, so reflect. That is: they say, in every matter contrary to their corrupt desires, whether in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) or not, with the tongue of speech or of condition, "We hear and we disobey," in obstinacy and in establishing opposition.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And hear, not made to hear﴾ is a conjunction to "we hear and we disobey," included under the speech. That is: they say this during his address (ﷺ) specifically. It is a statement with two meanings, admitting of an evil sense: that it be understood as "hear, while you are one not made to hear anything at all, by deafness or death," meaning: may you be called upon without hearing, or "not made to hear a word you would be pleased with." In that case its accusative may be a direct object. It admits of a good sense as well: that it be understood as "hear from us, not made to hear anything disliked," which they would address to the Prophet (ﷺ) mockingly, displaying to him (ﷺ) the intention of the last meaning, while they inwardly intend the first meaning and are content with it.

﴿And "rāʿinā"﴾ is a conjunction to "not made to hear." That is: they also say this during their address to him (ﷺ). Here they bring each of the three great matters in its place. It too is a word with two meanings: it admits of a good sense by understanding it as "watch us (irqubnā) and look at us (unẓurnā), and we will speak to you," and an evil sense by understanding it as a curse with ruʿūnah, meaning foolishness; or by treating it as analogous to a similar word in Hebrew or Syriac, which they used to revile one another with, namely "rāʿīnā." They would address the Prophet (ﷺ) with it intending insult and contempt while showing reverence and respect. Their course, in the last two senses, is the path of hypocrisy, while in the first they openly disobey, because they said that all the unbelievers would confront him with unbelief and disobedience, but would not confront him with cursing and calling for evil. It is also said: they would say the first in private among themselves. It is also said: it is possible that they did not utter it, but since they did not believe in him, they were treated as if they had uttered it.

﴿Twisting their tongues﴾: that is, twisting them with them, and diverting speech from its course toward ascribing cursing, in that they placed "not made to hear" in the place of "may you not be made to hear anything disliked," and treated "rāʿinā," resembling "rāʿīnā," as "look at us." Or, twisting with them and bending what they display of calling and reverence toward what they conceal of cursing and contempt.

﴿And as a slander upon the religion﴾: that is, a disparagement of it through mockery and derision. Both are in the accusative as causes (ʿilliyyah) for "they say," in terms of its connection to the last two statements, meaning: they say that to divert speech from its proper sense toward cursing and slander against the religion. Or they are in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), meaning: twisting and slandering the religion.

﴿And if they had﴾: when they heard some of God's commands and prohibitions.

﴿Said﴾: with the tongue of speech or the tongue of condition, in place of their saying "we hear and we disobey."

﴿"We hear and we obey"﴾: "we hear" is repeated though it is already realized in their speech. The need is only to place "we obey" in place of "we disobey," not to alert to disregarding it, but to indicate the consideration of its absence. How could it not be so? Their hearing is the hearing of rejection, and their intention in relating it is to announce their disobedience to the command after hearing it and knowing it. So it is necessary to remove that and establish the hearing of acceptance in its place.

﴿And hear﴾: that is, if they had said, when addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), "hear" instead of their saying "hear, not made to hear."

﴿And look at us﴾: that is, if they had said that instead of their saying "rāʿinā," and had not concealed under their speech evil and corruption. That is, if it were established that they had said this in place of the sayings they uttered.

﴿It would have been﴾: their saying that.

﴿Better for them﴾: than what they said.

﴿And more upright﴾: that is, more just and more correct in itself. The comparative form is either on its proper basis, with consideration of the basic superiority in the one being compared, according to their belief, or by way of sarcasm. Or it is in the sense of the active participle. The description of its status in relation to them is put before its status in itself, because their aims are confined to what benefits them.

﴿But God has cursed them for their disbelief﴾: that is, but they did not say that, and persisted in their disbelief, so God, exalted is He, forsook them and removed them from guidance because of their disbelief in this.

﴿So they do not believe﴾ after that.

﴿Except a few﴾: it is said: that is, except a faith that is few and of no account, which is belief in some of the books and messengers. Or, except for a short time, which is the time of dying, for they believe when faith will not benefit them. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾. Both of these are certainly not faith. It has also been permitted that by the fewness is meant complete absence, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death﴾. That is: if the nonexistent faith is faith, then they produce some faith, and this in meaning is a suspension upon the impossible.

You know that all of this is rejected by what follows it of the command to believe in the Qur'an, which speaks of this, because it leads to imposing what is impossible, namely their believing in the continued non-belief of themselves. As for the last interpretation, it is evident. As for the first two, their being commanded to believe in all the books and messengers is an obligation on them to believe, while in fact they do not believe in some of the books and messengers and do not believe until the time of dying. Therefore the correct view is that the few are understood as those who believe after that, but the exception should not be made from the subject pronoun in "they do not believe," because that leads to the occurrence of faith by one whom God, exalted is He, cursed and forsook. Along with that is the attribution to the readers of agreement on what is not the chosen reading. Rather, it is made from the object pronoun in "cursed them." That is: but God has cursed them, except a small group, for He, exalted is He, did not curse them, so the door of faith was not closed to them. And a group of the rabbis did believe after that, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Kaʿb, and their likes, as will come.

(p-185) "O you who have been given the Book" (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ أُوتُوُا الكِتابَ﴾) is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab) and a redirection of it, either to those whose conditions and statements have been related, specifically by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and whose description is at times "given the Book," i.e., the Torah, and at times "given a portion of it," so that each of the two situations is given its due. For what is intended in what preceded is the explanation of their taking up misguidance and the removal of what they were given, by contrasting it with distortion. Not all of the Book was removed by that, so they are not described as "given it" in full; rather, part of it was removed, so they are described as "given it." Here, however, what is intended is to emphasize the obligation of compliance with the command that follows, and to warn against opposing it, on the basis that belief in the one who confirms (the Qur'an) necessitates belief in what it confirms (the Torah), while disbelief in the latter definitely entails disbelief in the former.
