There is no doubt that what they feared was the necessary consequence of disbelieving in the Torah itself, not in some part of it, and this is realized by making the Qur'an a confirmer of all of it, even if the basis of confirmation is some part of it, since the confirmer of a part is necessarily a confirmer of the whole that contains it. Or it is addressed to them and to others altogether, which is the more apparent reading. In any case, the detailing of what was detailed: since this was among the likely grounds for each of the two groups to give up the misguidance they were upon, he followed this with a command to hasten to the path of guidance, accompanied by a severe threat against opposing it, so it is said: ﴿آمِنُوا بِما نَزَّلْنا﴾ "Believe in what We have sent down," from the Qur'an. He expressed it by the relative pronoun, to honour it with what is in the clause of the relative, and to affirm that it is from Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِما مَعَكُمْ﴾ "confirming what is with you," from the Torah. He expressed it thus to signify their complete awareness of the reality of the situation, for the "being with" (ma'iyyah), which calls for continuous recitation of it and repeated reference to it, is among the causes of finding what is in its folds, which leads to knowledge that the Qur'an confirms it. The meaning of its confirming it is its descent in the manner described for them in it, or its agreeing with it in the stories, the promises, the call to monotheism, justice among people, and the prohibition of sins and abominations. As for what appears to be its opposition to it in particular rulings due to the differences among nations and eras, this is not in reality opposition; rather it is the very agreement, since each of them is true relative to its own age, containing the wisdom upon which the revolution of legislation turns. Even if the earlier revelation had been delayed, it would have descended in accordance with the later one; and if the later had preceded, it would necessarily have agreed with the earlier. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Had Moses been alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me." ﴿مِن قَبْلِ أنْ نَطْمِسَ وُجُوهًا﴾ "before We obliterate faces," is connected to the command, indicating haste in complying with it and earnestness in refraining from opposing it, with the severe threat it contains, delivered in the most emphatic and forceful manner, since the threatened outcome is not conditioned upon opposition and is not explicitly stated to occur upon it, as an alert that this is a certain matter, needing no report, and that it is on the verge of befalling those addressed. The indefiniteness of "faces" (wujuh), which indicates multiplicity, conveys the gravity of the matter, and its vagueness is a kindness to those addressed and a good inducement to them to believe. The root of "tams" is the erasing of traces and the removal of features; i.e., believe before We erase the outline of their forms and remove their traces. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: We will make them like the hoof of a camel or the hoof of a beast. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: We will blind them, as in His saying: ﴿فَطَمَسْنا أعْيُنَهُمْ﴾ "and We obliterated their eyes." It was also said: We will make them like the places where hair grows, like the faces of monkeys.

﴿فَنَرُدَّها عَلى أدْبارِها﴾ "and turn them back upon their backs," so that We make them in the shape of their backs and their napes, obliterated like them; here the "fa'" indicates causation. Or: We reverse them after the obliteration, so that We return them to the place of the napes and the napes to their place, and only the more severe of the two is mentioned; here the "fa'" indicates sequence. It was also said: the intended meaning of "faces" is the notables, with "tams" taken in the sense of general alteration, i.e., before We alter the conditions of their notables, stripping them of their prominence and standing, and clothing them in humiliation and retreat, or We return them whence they came, which is the region of Adhri'at in Syria; the intended meaning of this would then be the exile of the Banu al-Nadir. It is not hidden that this does not suit the context of intensifying the threat and generalizing the warning to all; therefore the first of the stated meanings is the correct one. Scholars have differed as to whether the threat was to take effect in this world or in the Hereafter. It is said it was to take effect in this world, and this is supported by what is related that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam (may Allah be pleased with him), when he came from Syria, having heard this verse, went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before reaching his family, embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not think I would reach you until my face turned to my nape." In another narration, he came to the Prophet ﷺ with his hand upon his face, embraced Islam, and said what he said. Likewise, it is related that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) recited this verse to Ka'b al-Ahbar, and Ka'b said: "O Lord, I believe; O Lord, I submit," fearing that its threat would befall him. Then they differed. It was said that it is still awaited, and that there must be an obliteration and a transformation among the Jews; this is the view of al-Mubarrad. Its objection is that the averting of the promised punishment from their forerunners, who were directly involved in the causes of its descent and the grounds of its arrival, having witnessed the signs of prophethood in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and denied them, and having distorted them in the Torah, and persisted in disbelief and misguidance, and upon whom the direct address of threat was directed, and then its descent upon those who were found after hundreds of years among their misguided descendants, who misled the worlds by the laws of error they had laid down, is far from the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. It was also said: its occurrence was conditional upon non-belief, and some of their scholars mentioned (above) and their like did believe, so it did not occur. Its objection is that if the embracing of Islam by some of them was not a cause for the descent of punishment to be made certain upon the rest, due to their intensified denial and obstinacy after the truth had become clearer and the proof had been established against them by the testimony of their noble and trustworthy men, then at least it should not be a cause for lifting it from them. It was also said: the threat was of the occurrence of one of the two matters, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿أوْ نَلْعَنَهم كَما لَعَنّا أصْحابَ السَّبْتِ﴾ "or We curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath." So if the first matter did not occur, there is no dispute over the occurrence of the second; how could it not be, when they are cursed in every tongue in every age? Interpreting the curse as transformation is by no means established. You know that what is understood from the curse likened to the curse of the people of the Sabbath is transformation, and there is no hint in its being coordinated with the obliteration and the return upon the backs indicating that transformation is not intended, since it is a change distinct from what it is coordinated with. Moreover, the threatened matter must be a newly occurring event consequent upon the threat, feared by them, so that it serves as a deterrent from opposing the command; and it is not known that a curse of this description befell them. What befell them is only the continuous curse upon their tongues, which they have grown accustomed to, and this is far from being fit to be the outcome of this threat or a deterrent for the obstinate. It was also said: the threat was of the occurrence of what was mentioned in the Hereafter, at the Gathering, and one or both of the two matters will certainly occur in it, by way of distribution. As for what is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Ka'b, it is based on the caution fitting their standing. The truth is that the noble wording is not explicit in either of the two views; rather, what is understood from it according to the context is the first, since it is more effective in deterrence, and what is related from the two scholars is based on it. But since its occurrence was not clearly established, it is known that the intended meaning is the second. And Allah, Most High, knows best. In any case, perhaps the secret in singling them out with this punishment among the punishments is the observance of correspondence between it and what necessitated it, namely their offence, which is distortion and alteration. And Allah is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

﴿وَكانَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ "And the command of Allah was": i.e., what He commands, whatever it is, or His command to bring about some thing among things.

﴿مَفْعُولا﴾ "executed": carried out, certainly occurring, so that what you were threatened with is included in it primarily. Thus the sentence is a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tiraz tadhyili) confirming what preceded. The placement of the noble name in place of the pronoun by way of iltifat serves to nurture awe, to give the reason for the ruling, and to strengthen the independence contained in the parenthesis.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with partners.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʼnaf), brought to confirm what precedes it of threat and to affirm the obligation of compliance with the command to believe, by showing that forgiveness is impossible without it. They used to do what they did of distortion (tahrif) and still hoped for forgiveness, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them an successor who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life﴾, meaning: by means of distortion.

﴿And they say: "We shall be forgiven."﴾ The intended meaning of "association" (shirk) is absolute disbelief (kufr), which encompasses the disbelief of the Jews in a primary sense, for the Law has explicitly stated the association of the People of the Book altogether, and has decreed the eternal abiding of the categories of disbelievers in the Fire. Its revelation concerning the Jews is as Muqatil said, and it is the most fitting with the context of the noble composition. Its context does not necessitate that it be restricted to their disbelief; rather, it suffices that it definitively includes them. Indeed, there is no basis for it at all, since it would imply the permissibility of forgiving what is lesser than their disbelief in severity among the kinds of disbelief. That is: He does not forgive disbelief for one who is characterized by it without repentance and faith, because the legislative wisdom requires closing the door of disbelief, and permitting its forgiveness without faith would lead to opening it. Also, the darknesses of disbelief and sins are only covered by the light of faith; so whoever has no faith, nothing of disbelief and sins is forgiven for him.

﴿And He forgives what is less than that﴾ is coordinated with the predicate of "inna." "That" is a reference to association and what it contains of the meaning of distance, despite its proximity in mention, to indicate the remoteness of its rank and that it is at the extreme of ugliness. That is: He forgives what is less than it in ugliness among sins, whether minor or major, out of His bounty and grace, without repentance from them. However, not for everyone, but ﴿for whom He wills﴾, that is, for whomever He wills to forgive from among those characterized by it, and only that, not what is above it. For the forgiveness of both for those characterized by them is equal in the impossibility of falling under the will that is based on legislative wisdom. The restriction of forgiveness of sins without repentance to the people of faith is part of encouragement toward it and deterrence from disbelief. Whoever ties the will to both acts, and makes the first relative pronoun refer to one who did not repent and the second to one who repented, has strayed from the right path. How so? Since the purpose of the noble composition is to show the full greatness of the crime of disbelief and its distinction from all other sins, by stating the impossibility of its forgiveness and the permissibility of the forgiveness of the others. If the permissibility were conditional upon repentance, no difference would appear between them, since there is consensus on their forgiveness by repentance, and the intended aim of a forceful deterrence from disbelief and rebellion, and of driving toward repentance and faith, would not be achieved.

﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah﴾: the mention of the noble Name in place of the pronoun serves to intensify the reprehensibility of association and to make abhorrent the state of one who is characterized by it.

﴿has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin﴾: that is, he has invented and fabricated, committing a sin whose magnitude cannot be measured, and in comparison to which all other sins are considered trivial, so forgiveness definitely does not apply to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 49:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their state, which is contrary to what they are upon of disbelief and transgression. The intended people are the Jews, who say, "We are the sons of God and His beloved." It has also been said: some of the Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with their children and said, "Is there any sin upon these?" He (ﷺ) said, "No." They said, "We are only like them. We did a deed by day and were expiated for it by night, and did a deed by night and were expiated for it by day." That is: look at them and marvel at their claim that they are pure before God the Exalted, despite what they are upon of disbelief and great sin; or at their claim of expiation, given that it is impossible for anything of a disbeliever's disbelief or sins to be forgiven. In this there is a warning against a person's self-admiration and admiration of his own deeds.

﴿Nay, God purifies whom He wills﴾ This is a conjunction with an implied clause that the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "They do not really purify themselves, because of their lying and the falsity of their belief. Rather, God purifies whom He wills," that is, grants purification to those among His servants, the believers, who are worthy of it and whom He approves, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware of what humans harbor of good and evil. God has described them by the vile qualities they possess. The root of purification (tazkiyah) is the negation of what is abhorrent, either by deed or by speech.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ This is a conjunction with a clause "qad" that has been omitted, relying on the indication of the situation upon it and as a notice that it is independent of mention. That is: they will be punished for that vile deed, and they will not be wronged in that punishment.

﴿a fatil﴾ That is: the least and smallest injustice, which is the thread in the split of a date-stone, a thing used as a proverb for paucity and insignificance. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who purify themselves will be rewarded, and nothing whatsoever will be diminished from their reward; and the context of warning does not support this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 50:

﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah!﴾ "Kayfa" is in the accusative case, either by analogy with an adverb of place (ẓarf) or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), according to the well-known difference of opinion between Sibawayh and al-Akhfash. The governing element is "yaftarūna" (they invent), and "ʿalā" is connected to it. The meaning is: in what state, or in what condition, do they invent lies against Him, exalted is He? The purpose is to show the abominableness of that state and the complete extent of its monstrousness. The clause is in a place of accusative after the removal of the preposition, and the verb "al-naẓar" (look) is connected to it. This is an expression of wonder upon wonder, and an alert that what they committed includes two great matters, each of which calls for astonishment: their claim to be characterized by what is the opposite of what they actually are, and their inventing lies against Allah, glorified is He. Their claim of purity in His sight includes their claim that Allah accepts and approves of them, exalted is He far above that by a great elevation. And because this is more heinous in crime and greater in ugliness than the first, since it involves attributing to Him, glorified and exalted is He, something that is utterly impossible for Him, namely accepting disbelief, approving it for His servants, and forgiving the disbelief of the disbeliever and all his sins, the gaze has been directed to its manner, to intensify the reproach and emphasize the wonder. The explicit mention of "lies," although inventing (iftirāʾ) can only be lying, is for the sake of emphasis in condemning their state.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾: that is, their inventing this, insofar as it is an invention against Him, exalted is He, is sufficient on its own, setting aside its being accompanied by the purification of their own selves and their other great sins. Its being a sin is clear and evident. The meaning is: that alone is sufficient for them to be more sinful than every sinning disbeliever, or for them to deserve the most severe punishments, for reasons whose secret has already passed. Making the pronoun refer to their claim is untenable, since it undermines the awe-inspiring magnitude of the act of invention, so reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 51:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at another state of theirs, and a description of them with what was mentioned of being given a portion, because of its incompatibility with what proceeded from them of ugly deeds. And the statement of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They believe in jibt and taghut﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the substance of the wonder, built upon a question that the speech leads to, as if it were said: "What do they do when they are looked at?" So it is said: "They believe..." etc. The jibt (jibt: idols and everything that is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted). It is said that its origin is al-jibs (jibs: that which has no good in it), and the sin was changed into a ta'. It is also said: al-jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and al-taghut is the devil. It is said: it is in origin everything that causes a person to transgress. It is narrated that Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the two Jews, went out to Makkah with seventy riders from the Jews, to form an alliance with the Quraysh against fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to break the covenant that was between them and him (ﷺ). They said: "You are the people of the Scripture and you are closer to Muhammad than we are, so we do not feel safe from your deception. Prostrate to our gods so that we may be reassured by you." So they did it. This is their belief in jibt and taghut, because they prostrated to idols and obeyed Iblis in what they did. Abu Sufyan said to Ka'b: "You are a man who reads the Scripture and knows, while we are unlettered and do not know. So which of us is more rightly guided on the path, we or Muhammad?" He said: "What does Muhammad say?" He said: "He commands the worship of Allah alone and forbids associating partners with Him." He said: "And what is your religion?" They said: "We are the custodians of the House; we give drink to the pilgrims, we host the guest, and we free the captive," and they mentioned their deeds. He said: "You are more rightly guided in the way." And that is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., concerning them and regarding them.

﴿These⁠﴾ meaning them.

﴿are better guided than those who believe, as to the way﴾, i.e., more upright in religion and more correct in method. Their being mentioned under the title of belief is not from the side of the speakers, but from the side of Allah, the Exalted, as a way of identifying them by the beautiful description, and as a refutation of those who prefer over them those characterized by the ugliest of ugly deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 52:

﴿Those﴾ is a pointer to the speakers. The sense of distance in it, despite their closeness in mention, serves to signal how far their station is in misguidance. It is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate is His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, meaning: He removed them far from His mercy and expelled them. The clause is resumptive (mustani'afa), explaining their condition and displaying their outcome and final destination.

﴿And whoever Allah curses﴾, meaning: He removes him far from His mercy.

﴿you will never find for him a helper﴾ who will ward off punishment from him, whether worldly or otherworldly, neither by intercession nor by anything else. In it is an explicit statement of their being deprived of what they sought from the Quraysh. In the word "لَنْ" (lan, "never"), in directing the address to everyone who is capable of being addressed, in making "نَصِيرًا" (nasiran, "helper") indefinite and singular, and in expressing its absence by "عَدَمِ الوِجْدانِ" (adam al-wijdan, "not finding"), which indicates that a seeking had preceded, attributed to the general addressee, there is an indication, not hidden, of their perpetual and total deprivation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, Verse 53:**

﴿Or do they have a share of the dominion?﴾ This begins a specification of another of their vices. "Am" (أمْ) here is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, introducing a new topic), and what it contains of *bal* (بَلْ) signals *idrab* (a turn away from the previous subject, a change of topic). The speech shifts from blaming them for their self-praise and other things related about them to blaming them for claiming a share of the kingdom and for their extreme stinginess and profound miserliness. The *hamza* (الهَمْزَةُ) is for denial that they have what they claim, and for nullifying their assertion that the kingdom would come to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they would not give people even a speck (naqir)﴾ is an explanation that they do not deserve it. Rather, they deserve to be deprived of it, because of their meanness and baseness: were they given any of it, they would not give people even the least bit of it. Whoever is given dominion ought to grant others some of it. The *fa'* (الفاءُ) here indicates causation with a consequent (*al-sababiyya al-jaza'iyya*), for an elided condition, meaning: if a share of it were given to them, then they would not give people even the quantity of a *naqir*. The *naqir* is the small pit on the back of a date stone, and it is used as a proverb for smallness and worthlessness. This is the explanation that reveals the reality of their state. If their condition is like this while they are kings, then what do you think of them when they are humble and destitute?

It is also permissible that the *hamza* is not for denying the occurrence, but for denying what has occurred and rebuking them for it, i.e., considering it an abhorrent thing unworthy of occurring. Moreover, the *fa'* is for coordination (*al-'atf*), and the denial is directed at both coordinated clauses together, with the meaning: Do they have a large share of the kingdom, since they were owners of wealth, gardens and lofty palaces like kings, so that they do not give people even a *naqir* despite that? This is like saying to a wealthy man who does not show consideration to his father: Do you have this amount of wealth, so that you spend nothing on your father?!

The benefit of *idhan* (إذَنْ) is the emphasis of denial and rebuke, since they make the existence of the share a cause for withholding, although it is a cause for giving. It is *mulgha* (nullified from operating), as if it were said: "So they would not give people," then. It has been read as "*fa-idhan la yu'tu*" (فَإذَنْ لا يُؤْتُوا) with the accusative, by making it operative.

﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾ This is also a disjunctive (*munqati'a*) question, shifting from rebuking them for what came before to rebuking them for envy, which is the worst and most ugly of the vices, especially since they are far from deserving it. The "al" in ﴿al-nās﴾ (the people) is for specific reference (*li-l-'ahd*), pointing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. Taking it as generic (*al-jins*), to indicate that they possess all human perfections so that they are, as it were, "the people" and no one else, does not suit the mention of the story of the family of Abraham, for that serves to remind of the connection between the two groups, which necessitates that both share in deserving grace. The hamza is for denouncing the actual event and deeming it ugly, for they used to hope that the promised Prophet would come from among them. When Allah, Exalted is He, singled out others for that honour, they envied them. That is: "Rather, do they envy them?"

﴿for what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ means prophethood, the Book, and the increase of honour and victory day by day. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We gave﴾ is a justification for the denial and condemnation, an obligation upon them with what they themselves accept, and a cutting off of the root of their envy and their disdain, both of which rest on the delusion that the envied one does not deserve the bounty he was given. It shows that he deserves it by inheritance, elder after elder. The discourse follows the style of majesty by way of *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person), to show full concern with the matter. The meaning: their aforementioned envy is utterly ugly and baseless, for We have indeed given before this.

﴿the family of Abraham﴾ are those who are the ancestors of Muhammad (ﷺ) or the sons of his paternal uncles.

﴿the Book and the wisdom﴾ i.e., prophethood.

﴿And We gave them﴾ in addition to that.

﴿a great kingdom﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. So how do they find his prophethood unlikely and envy him for being given it? The repetition of "gave" is required by the context of preference, along with an indication of the difference between prophethood and kingship. If "giving" is meant directly, then "the family of Abraham" refers only to their prophets, and the pronoun in the second verb refers to some of them, either by elision of a modifier or by *istikhdam* (a device in which one word carries two senses), since kingship was not given to all of them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the kingship among the family of Abraham is the kingship of Yusuf, Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them.

If it is meant to include that and other kinds of giving through intermediaries, which is the most fitting for the context and the most consistent with what precedes regarding the attribution of bounty to people, then "the family of Abraham" means all of them. Honouring some of them with the prophethood and kingship mentioned is an honour to all, since they are concerned with its traces and draw from its lights. In detailing what they were given, the repetition of the verb, describing the kingship as great, and its indefinite form for magnification, there is clear emphasis on the binding nature of the argument and the intensification of the denial. This is the most apparent meaning of the noble wording, and the majority of the imams of tafsir (exegesis) inclined to it. But the apparent reading in that case is that His saying, Exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 55:

﴿Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it.﴾ This is a report of what their forefathers did after the event being related occurred, without it having any bearing on the rebuke for which the speech was brought. That is: among the kind of these envious people and their forefathers were those who believed in what was given to the family of Abraham, and among them were those who turned away from it. As for making the two pronouns refer to what was mentioned of the story of the family of Abraham, that requires the noble verse to be distant in revelation from what precedes it. How could it not? For the report of their believing in the aforementioned narrative and their turning away from it, in the past tense, is only conceivable after the occurrence of the later belief and turning away, which come after hearing the narrative that is itself later than its revelation. Likewise, making them refer to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would also require this. The apparent meaning is the description of their state after this rebuke, and taking it as a report of their earlier state is supported by the fa' (فَ, "so"), which links what follows to what precedes it. It is not far-fetched at all that the hamza (أ, the interrogative particle) is for affirming their envy and rebuking them for it. Then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ (4:54), is a justification for it by its indication of their turning away from what the family of Abraham was given, even though it is not stated that this was by way of envy. It is as if it were said: "Rather, do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty, and not believe in it? That is their constant habit. For We have indeed given the family of Abraham what We gave, so among them, that is, among their kind, were those who believed in what We gave them, and among them were those who turned away from it and did not believe in it." God, glorified is He, knows best. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿And Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ That is, a kindled fire by which they will be punished. The sentence serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾ If by them is meant those who disbelieved in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then by the signs (ayat) is meant either the Qur'an, or what encompasses all of it and part of it, or what also encompasses all the other miracles of his. And if by them is meant the category (jins) that includes them in a primary sense, then by the signs is meant what encompasses the aforementioned and all the other proofs (shawahid) which the prophets, peace be upon them, were given.

﴿We will surely cause them to burn in Fire﴾ Sibawayh said: "Sawfa" is a word used for threat and warning, and the sin (sin) takes its place; and both may be mentioned in promise, in which case they convey emphasis. That is: We will cause them to enter a great and terrifying Fire.

﴿Every time their skins are roasted﴾ That is, they are burnt. "Kullama" is a temporal adverb, and its governing element is ﴿We will replace them with other skins﴾. It is of the type of "he replaced his fear with security" (badhdhalahu bi-khawfihi amnan), not of the type of "Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds" (yubaddilu Allahu sayyi'atihim hasanat). That is: We will give them, in place of every skin that is burnt when it burns, a new skin that differs from the burnt one in form, even though it is identical in substance, by removing the burning from it so that its sensation of the punishment returns. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "We will cause them to burn". It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause for "Fire", with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: every time their skins are roasted in it. So the meaning of His, exalted is He, saying ﴿so that they may taste the punishment﴾ is that its tasting may endure and not cease, like your saying to the honoured one: "May Allah honour you." It was also said: He creates another skin in its place, and the punishment is for the disobedient soul, not for the instrument of its perception. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: They are replaced with white skins like sheets of paper. It is also narrated that this verse was recited in the presence of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said to the reciter: "Repeat it," and he repeated it. Mu'adh ibn Jabal was present and said: "I have its explanation: it is replaced a hundred times in an hour." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Thus I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say." Al-Hasan said: The Fire consumes them every day seventy thousand times, each time it has consumed them. It is said to them: "Return," and they return as they were. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the distance between the shoulders of the disbeliever is a three-day journey for a swift rider. And from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The molar of the disbeliever, or the fang of the disbeliever, is like Uhud, and the thickness of his skin is a three-day journey." The expression of the perception of punishment as "tasting" is not to indicate its smallness, but (p-192) to indicate that their sensation of the punishment each time is like the sensation of one who tastes what is tasted, in that it does not suffer diminishment, owing to the continuity of the contact; or to convey the bitterness of the punishment together with its pain; or to draw attention to the intensity of its effect, since the faculty of taste is the most affected of the senses; or to its penetration to the interior. Perhaps the secret in replacing the skins, although He is able to keep the perception of punishment and its taste in its state along with the burning, and to keep their bodies in their state preserved from burning, is that the soul may imagine that perception ceases with burning, and does not regard as wholly improbable that it be preserved from pain and punishment by the preservation of its body from burning.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Mighty﴾ Nothing He wills is out of reach for Him, and no one can prevent Him.

﴿Wise﴾ He punishes whom He punishes in accordance with His wisdom. The clause gives the reason for what precedes it, namely the burning and the replacing. The mention of the Exalted Name by way of iltifat serves to magnify the matter, to cultivate awe, and to give the reason for the judgment, for the title of Divinity (al-uluhiyyah) is the basis of all the attributes of His perfection, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 57:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ The explanation of the bad state of the disbelievers is followed by the explanation of the good state of the believers, to complete the distress of the former and the delight of the latter. That is: those who believed in Our signs and acted in accordance with their requirements. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿We shall admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. It has been read as "sa-yudkhiluhum" with the yā' (third person), referring back to the Majestic Name, and the sīn (sa-) adds emphasis to the promise.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun in the accusative in "sa-nudkhiluhum". And the statement of the Mighty and Exalted: ﴿for them therein are spouses purified﴾ means: free from what is in the women of this world of disgusting bodily conditions and natural impurities. It is in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "gardens", or as a second circumstantial clause from the accusative pronoun, or as an adjective of "gardens" following another adjective; or it is in the nominative position, as the predicate of the relative pronoun following a predicate.

﴿And We shall admit them to a shade, deep and extended﴾ That is: a shade that is spreading, with no heat in it, lasting forever, which the sun does not nullify. O Allah, grant us that by Your grace and generosity, O Most Merciful of the merciful. The word "zalil" is an adjective derived from the word "zill" (shade) for emphasis, as in "laylun alyal" and "yawmun aywam". It has been read as "yudkhiluhum" with the yā', and it is coordinated with "sa-yudkhiluhum", not on the basis that it is different from the first admission in essence, but rather in its designation, as in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 58:**

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts (amanat) to their rightful owners.﴾ The opening of the speech with the particle of emphasis (kalimat al-tahqiq, the emphatic particle *inna*), the mention of the Majestic Name, and the presentation of the command in the form of a report, together contain the utmost grandeur, the affirmation of the obligation to comply with it, and an indication of the great concern for its matter, beyond which there is no further degree. It is an address whose ruling encompasses all the responsible persons (mukallafun) without exception, just as "trusts" encompass all the rights attached to their obligations, whether the rights of Allah the Exalted or the rights of His servants, whether they are actions, statements, or beliefs. It was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn Talha ibn 'Abd al-Dar, the custodian (sadin) of the Holy Ka'bah. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, closed the door of the Ka'bah, climbed onto the roof, and refused to hand the key to him, saying: "Had I known that he was the Messenger of Allah, I would not have prevented him." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib twisted his hand, took the key from him, opened the door, and the Prophet ﷺ entered and prayed two rak'ahs. When he came out, al-'Abbas asked him to give him the key and to combine for him the watering of the pilgrims (siqayah) and the custodianship (sidanah). So this verse was revealed, and he commanded 'Ali to return the key to 'Uthman and apologize to him. 'Uthman said to 'Ali: "You have humiliated and harmed me, and then you come to make amends." 'Ali said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted has revealed a Qur'an concerning your matter," and he recited the verse to him. 'Uthman said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Then Jibril, upon him be peace, descended and informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that the custodianship belongs to the descendants of 'Uthman forever.

The word "al-amanat" is also read in the singular (al-amanah), and the intended meaning is the generic category, not a specific referent. It has also been said: this is a command to rulers (wulat) to render the rights attached to their obligations, such as offices and other positions, to those who deserve them. Likewise, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ is a command to them to deliver the rights attached to the obligations of others to their owners. Since the command here is specific to the time of litigation (murafa'ah), it was restricted to that time, unlike the command mentioned first, which was not tied to any particular time and was therefore stated in an unrestricted form. Thus the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿an tahkumu﴾ (that you judge) is coordinated with "an tu'addu" (that you render), and the conjunction and the conjoined have been separated by the adverbial phrase that governs the verb according to the Kufans, while according to the Basrans the implied element indicates it, because what follows *inna* does not govern what precedes it in their view. That is: "and that you judge when you judge," and so on. The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿bil-'adl﴾ (with justice) is connected to "tahkumu," or to an implied element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of its subject, meaning: "while being characterized by justice and equity."

﴿Indeed, how excellent is what Allah instructs you with.﴾ "Ma" is either an accusative noun described by "ya'izukum bihi" (what He instructs you with), or a nominative relative pronoun connected to it, as if it were said: "an excellent thing with which He instructs you," or "the excellent thing with which He instructs you." The subject of praise (al-makhsus bil-madh) is omitted, meaning: "how excellent is what He instructs you with, that is, this, which is the command to render trusts and to judge with justice." It has been read as "ni'imma" with a fatha on the nun, and the sentence is then a resumptive clause that confirms what precedes it, containing additional kindness toward the addressees and a good invitation to them to comply with the command. The mention of the Majestic Name serves to cultivate awe.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of your statements.

﴿Seeing﴾ of your deeds. So this is both a promise and a warning. The mention of the Majesty is for what was mentioned just before, since it contains an affirmation of both the promise and the warning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 59:

﴿O you who have believed﴾. After commanding the rulers, generally or specifically, to render trusts and to be just in judgments, He commanded all people to obey them, but not absolutely; rather, within the obedience of Allah the Exalted and the obedience of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as it is said: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾. They are the rulers of truth and the governors of justice, such as the Rightly-Guided Caliphs and those who follow their guidance among the rightly guided. As for rulers of tyranny, they are far from deserving to be joined with Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) in the obligation of obedience to them. It has also been said that they are the scholars of the Shari'ah, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who derive it from them would have known it﴾. But this is contradicted by His saying: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah﴾, since it is not permissible for the layman (muqallid) to dispute with the mujtahid over his ruling, unless the address is directed to those in authority by way of iltifat (a shift in address), and this is far-fetched. The conditional clause is introduced with the fa' (فاء) because it follows from what precedes: the explanation of the ruling on obeying those in authority, when it agrees with the obedience of Allah the Exalted and the obedience of the Messenger (ﷺ), calls for the explanation of its ruling when they differ, i.e., if you and those in authority among you dispute over a matter of the affairs of religion, then refer it back to the Book of Allah.

﴿And the Messenger﴾, i.e., to his Sunnah. The deniers of qiyas (analogy) have used this as evidence, though in reality it is evidence for its authority. How could it not be? Referring what is disputed to what is explicitly stated can only happen through analogy and building upon it, and this is what is meant by qiyas. It is supported by the command to it after the command to obey Allah the Exalted and obey His Messenger (ﷺ), for it indicates that the rulings are of three kinds: what is established by the Book, what is established by the Sunnah, and what is established by referring to these two through qiyas.

﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is connected to the last command mentioned in the matter of dispute, since it is what requires warning against opposition. The apodosis of the condition is omitted according to the majority of the Basran grammarians, relying on what is mentioned as indicating it, i.e., if you believe in Allah and the Last Day, then refer it, etc., for belief in both necessitates this. As for belief in Allah the Exalted, it is evident; and as for belief in the Last Day, it is because of the punishment for opposition that it contains.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the referral commanded.

﴿is better﴾ for you and more beneficial.

﴿and best﴾ in itself.

﴿in outcome (ta'wil)﴾, i.e., in consequence and final result. The mention of its being better for them before its being best in itself is because their attention is attached to what benefits them. The intended meaning is to show that it is in itself characterized by complete goodness in its essence, without considering its superiority over something that shares with it the basic goodness and excellence, as the preceding warning indicates.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 60:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you?﴾ This is a shift in the mode of address, directing it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to express wonder at the state of those who oppose the decisive command that has already been mentioned and who obey neither Allah nor His Messenger. Describing them as claiming belief in the Qur'an and in what was revealed before it, namely the Torah, serves to emphasize the wonder and to intensify the reproach and censure, by showing the complete contradiction between their claim and what actually proceeds from them. The two verbs are also read in the active voice. The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They desire to seek judgment from the taghut (false object of worship)﴾ are a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new clause) brought in to explain the locus of the wonder. It is based on a question arising from the opening of the speech, as if it had been said: "What do they do?" So it was said: "They desire..." etc.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that a hypocrite had a dispute with a Jew. The Jew invited him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hypocrite invited him to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Then the two of them went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for judgment, and he ruled in favor of the Jew. The hypocrite was not content with this, so he invited him to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. The Jew said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled for me, but he refused his judgment." 'Umar said to the hypocrite: "Is it so?" He said: "Yes." 'Umar said: "Wait here until I come out to you." He went in, took up his sword, then came out and struck the hypocrite's neck with it until he was dead. Then he said: "This is how I judge for the one who is not content with the judgment of Allah and the judgment of His Messenger." So this was revealed. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said: "Indeed 'Umar has distinguished between truth and falsehood." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are al-Faruq (the Distinguisher)."

So the taghut here is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. He was named by it because of his excess in rebellion and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or it is used figuratively, by likening him to Satan and naming him with his name. Or the choice of seeking judgment from someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ), over seeking judgment from him, is treated as seeking judgment from Satan.

Al-Dahhak said: The intended meaning of the taghut is the soothsayers (kahanah) of the Jews and their sorcerers. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that the hypocrite invited his opponent to a soothsayer in Juhayna, and they went to him for judgment. It is reported from al-Suddi that the incident occurred concerning a slain man between the Banu Qurayza and the Nadir. The Muslims from both groups sought judgment from the Prophet (ﷺ), but the hypocrites from both groups refused except to seek judgment from Abu Burda the soothsayer of the Aslam tribe, and so they went to him for judgment. In that case, restricting the statement to the desire to seek judgment, without the act itself, is within the context of wonder and censure, while the act also occurred, to alert that merely desiring it is itself a cause for wonder, and it should not even come into being; so what then is the case with the act itself? This is more fitting to the description of the hypocrites as claiming belief in the Torah, for just as it implies that they are hypocrites among the Jews, it also implies that what proceeded from them of seeking judgment is clearly incompatible with their claim of believing in the Torah. Seeking judgment from Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf is not so manifestly contradictory. Furthermore, what is understood from the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they were commanded to reject it﴾ is that they were commanded to reject it in both books, and that refers only to Satan and his allies who are well known for his guardianship, such as the soothsayers and their like, not to others who are not known for that. It is also read as ﴿to reject them﴾, with taghut being a plural noun, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Their allies are the taghut, who bring them out﴾ (2:257). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they desire," serving to emphasize the wonder and intensify the censure, like the preceding description.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and Satan desires to lead them far astray﴾ are a conjunction with ﴿they desire﴾, falling under the ruling of wonder. For their following of one who desires to lead them astray, and their turning away from one who desires to guide them, is more wondrous than anything wondrous. And "far astray" (dalalan ba'idan) is either a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the mentioned verb by dropping its extra letters, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and made it grow a good growth﴾ (3:37), meaning: "a far misleading," or it is a verbal noun emphasizing its own verb implied by the mentioned verb, meaning: "so that they go astray with a going astray." Whichever it is, describing it as "far" (ba'id), which is the attribute of its modified noun, is for emphasis; and the words of the Exalted:*

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 61:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger"﴾ is a continuation of the theme of astonishment, by explaining their explicit turning away from seeking judgment by the Book of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, following the explanation of their turning away from that within the context of seeking judgment from the tyrant (al-taghut). It is also read as "ta'alaw" with a damma on the lam, on the basis that the lam of the verb has been dropped for lightness (takhfif), as in the saying of the Arabs: "ma baliytu balatan" (I did not care at all), whose original form is "baliyatun," like "'afiyatin." And as they said regarding "ayatin" (sign): its original form is "ayyatun," so the lam was dropped, and the waw of the plural came after the lam in "ta'ala," so it was given a damma, and it became "ta'alaw." From this is the saying of the people of Makkah to the woman, "ta'ali" with a kasra on the lam. Upon this is the verse of Abu Firas al-Hamdani:

Ya jaratī mā anṣafa al-dahru baynanā ... ta'ālī uqāsimki al-humūma ta'ālī

﴿You saw the hypocrites﴾: the explicit mention of "the hypocrites" in place of a pronoun serves to record hypocrisy against them, to censure them for it, and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The "seeing" is visual. His words, the Exalted: ﴿turning away from you﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the hypocrites." It has been said that the seeing is of the heart and the clause is a second object of it, but the first is more fitting given the manifestness of their condition. His words, the Exalted: ﴿with aversion﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing its verb, meaning: they turn away from you with aversion, and what aversion! It has been said that it is a noun for the verbal noun, which is "al-sadd," but the more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun of the intransitive "sudud," while "al-sadd" is the verbal noun of the transitive. It is said: "sadda 'anhu sududan," meaning he turned away from him, and "sadahu 'anhu sadda," meaning he prevented him from it.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, verse 62:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then how﴾ begins an explanation of the gravity of their wrongdoing reported here and the wretchedness of its consequence. That is, how will their condition be?

﴿When a calamity strikes them﴾ means at the time the calamity befalls them, which is their exposure through the manifestation of their hypocrisy.

﴿because of what their hands have put forward﴾ means because of the wrongful deeds they committed, among which is seeking judgment from the taghut (every object of false worship, or any figure of defiance against God), and turning away from your judgment.

﴿Then they come to you﴾ to offer excuses for the vile deeds they committed (p-196). This is conjoined to "strikes them." The purpose is to magnify their condition and to convey the enormity of the affliction that overtook them and the severity of the matter that seized them at the moment the calamity struck and at the moment they came to offer excuses.

﴿swearing by Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of "come to you."

﴿We intended nothing but good and reconciliation﴾ means: we did not intend, by seeking judgment from someone other than you, anything but a just settlement in a good manner and reconciliation between the two parties. We did not intend to oppose you or to be displeased with your judgment, so do not hold us accountable for what we did. This is a warning to them for what they did, and that they will regret it when regret will not benefit them and excuses will not avail them. It is also said: the kinsmen of the hypocrite came seeking his blood, though Allah, Exalted is He, had declared it forfeit. They said: "We intended nothing," meaning: our companion, who was killed, intended by seeking judgment from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, nothing but that he would be kind to him and bring about reconciliation between him and his adversary.

**﴿Ulā'ika﴾** ("Those") is a demonstrative referring to the hypocrites, and the distance implied in it serves to draw attention to how far removed their rank is in disbelief and hypocrisy. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is **﴿alladhīna ya'lamu Allāhu mā fī qulūbihim﴾** ("those whom God knows what is in their hearts"), that is: of the various kinds of evil and corruption that contradict what they showed you of falsehoods.

**﴿Fa-a'rid 'anhum﴾** ("So turn away from them") is the response (jawab) to an elided conditional clause, meaning: if their state is such, then turn away from accepting their excuse. It has also been said: turn away from punishing them, for the sake of a benefit in sparing them; and do not let them know that you are aware of what is in their inner selves, and do not expose their concealment, so that they remain in apprehension and wariness.

**﴿Wa-'iẓhum﴾** ("And admonish them"), i.e., restrain them from hypocrisy and scheming.

**﴿Wa-qul lahum fī anfusihim﴾** ("And speak to them concerning their own souls"): concerning their own wicked selves and their hearts folded upon the evils which God, exalted is He, knows; or, "in their own souls," meaning privately with them, with no one else present with them, speaking to them secretly with counsel, since counsel given in secret is more effective.

**﴿Qawlan balīgha﴾** ("a far-reaching word"): effective, reaching the very core of the intended meaning, corresponding to the purpose for which it was directed. The adverbial phrase, under both interpretations, is connected to the command. It has also been said that it is connected to **"balīgha"** according to the view of those who permit the fronting of the complement of an adjective before the noun it modifies, meaning: say to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves, effective upon their hearts, by which they seize the opportunity eagerly and sense fear keenly; and it is a threat of killing and annihilation, and an announcement that what is in their hearts of hidden evils and hypocrisy is not hidden from God, exalted is He, and that this warrants the most severe punishments, and that this reprieve and delay are only for their showing faith and obedience while concealing disbelief. And if they display discord and emerge in their persons from the tunnel of hypocrisy, then **﴿la-yamassannahumu al-'adhāb﴾** ("the punishment will surely touch them"), **﴿inna Allāha shadīdu al-'iqāb﴾** ("indeed, God is severe in retribution").

This is an independent opening statement, introduced as a preface to explain their error in occupying themselves with concealing their wrongdoing through false excuses, and in not making amends for it through repentance. That is, "We did not send any messenger from among the messengers for any purpose except to be obeyed, by the permission of Allah, the Exalted, in His obedience and in His command to those to whom he was sent, that they should obey and follow him, because he conveys from Him, the Exalted. So his obedience is the obedience of Allah, the Exalted, and his disobedience is disobedience to Him, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [4:80]." Or it means: by Allah's facilitation and His enabling of obedience to him.

﴿And if they, when they wronged themselves﴾, and exposed themselves to punishment in addition to the punishment of hypocrisy, by abandoning obedience to you and seeking judgement from others.

﴿came to you﴾ without delay, as the fronting of the adverbial phrase makes clear, seeking your intercession in disavowing their past and present wrongdoing, and they did not add wrong upon wrong by intending to conceal it (p-197) with false excuses and wicked oaths.

﴿So they sought Allah's forgiveness﴾ through repentance and sincerity, and they earnestly pleaded with you, until you stood as an intercessor for them before Allah, the Exalted, and asked forgiveness for them. The statement ﴿and the Messenger asked forgiveness for them﴾ was phrased in the manner of *al-iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, from address to third-person narration), to magnify the rank of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to exalt his seeking forgiveness, and to draw attention to the fact that his intercession is accepted.

﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾: they would have known Him to be exceedingly accepting of their repentance and bountiful to them with mercy. If *al-wijdan* (finding) is interpreted as "coming upon," then His words ﴿Accepting of repentance﴾ are a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject), and ﴿Merciful﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, apposition) for it, or a *hal* from the pronoun within it. Whichever is the case, there is in this a great encouragement for the listeners to hasten to repentance and seeking forgiveness, and a further rebuke of those hypocrites for what they did, because the first signs of the acceptance of repentance and the attainment of mercy, and their witnessing of the effects of these, are a blessing added to them both, which necessitates complete desire to attain them and perfect regret at missing them.

﴿فَلا ورَبِّكَ﴾ That is: "فَوَرَبِّكَ" (by your Lord). The "لا" is redundant (zā'idah), used to emphasize the meaning of the oath, not to emphasize the negation in its answer, namely His words ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (they do not believe). This is because it is also used with affirmation, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿فَلا أُقْسِمُ بِمَواقِعِ النُّجُومِ﴾ (So I swear by the setting-places of the stars), and similar examples.

﴿حَتّى يُحَكِّمُوكَ﴾ That is: they seek judgment from you and bring their disputes before you. The form of "tahkim" (making someone arbiter) was used even though he ﷺ is a judge by the command of Allah, subhanahu, to indicate that it is their duty to make him an arbiter among them and to be content with his ruling, even if one sets aside the consideration that he is a judge in an absolute sense.

﴿فِيما شَجَرَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ That is: in what has become disputed and confused among them of matters. The word "shajar" (tree) comes from it, due to the interlacing of its branches.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يَجِدُوا﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon an implied clause that the speech leads to, meaning: "so you judge between them, then they do not find". ﴿فِي أنْفُسِهِمْ حَرَجًا﴾ (any discomfort in themselves), that is, constriction.

﴿مِمّا قَضَيْتَ﴾ That is: from what you have decided, or from your judgment. It was said: "shakā min ajlihi" (he complained because of it), since the doubter is in constriction over his matter.

﴿وَيُسَلِّمُوا﴾ That is: they submit to your command and yield to it.

﴿تَسْلِيمًا﴾ This is an emphasis of the verb, in the position of repeating it. That is: complete submission, outwardly and inwardly. It is said: "sallama li-amr Allāh" and "aslama lahu" with the same meaning. Its real meaning is that he surrendered himself to Him when he made himself wholly safe for Him and purely His. That is: they yield to your ruling with a yielding free of any doubt, outwardly and inwardly.

It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrite and the Jew. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Zubayr and a man from the Ansar when they disputed before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over watercourses from al-Harrah, by which they were irrigating palm trees. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then send the water to your neighbour." The Ansari became angry and said: "Because he is the son of your paternal aunt?" The face of the Messenger of Allah changed. Then he said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the walls, and take your full right, then send it to your neighbour." He had given Zubayr an opinion that had leeway for him and for his opponent. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pressed, he gave Zubayr his full right in a explicit ruling. Then they went out and passed by al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, who said: "For whom was the judgment?" The Ansari said: "He judged for the son of his paternal aunt," and twisted his cheek. A Jew who was with al-Miqdad noticed this and said: "May Allah fight these people! They testify that he is the Messenger of Allah, then they accuse him in a judgment he makes between them. By Allah, we once committed a sin in the lifetime of Musa, and he called us to repent from it and said: 'Kill yourselves,' so we did, and our slain reached seventy thousand, in obedience to our Lord, until He was pleased with us." Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas said: "By Allah, Allah knows of me the truth: if Muhammad commanded me to kill myself, I would have killed myself." It is narrated that Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Ammar ibn Yasir (p-198) (may Allah be pleased with them) said this. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, among my nation are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the firm mountains." Then it was revealed concerning these people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 66:

﴿And if We had decreed for them: "Kill yourselves, or leave your homes,"﴾ That is: if We had obligated upon them the like of what We obligated upon the Children of Israel, namely killing themselves or leaving their homes, when they were made to repent of worshipping the calf. The "an" (أنْ) is either a verbal particle (مَصْدَرِيَّةٌ, masdariyyah, introducing the verbal noun) or an explanatory particle (مُفَسِّرَةٌ, mufassirah, "that"), because kataba ("decreed") here carries the meaning of amara ("commanded").

﴿They would not have done it﴾ That is: the thing decreed, indicated by "kataba," or one of the two verbal nouns of the two verbs.

﴿except a few of them﴾ That is: except a few people among them, and they are the sincere believers. It is related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "By Allah, if our Lord had commanded us, we would have done it, and all praise is due to Allah who did not do that to us." It was also said: the meaning of "kill yourselves" is: expose yourselves to being killed through jihad, but this is far-fetched. It is also read "illa qaliilan" (إلّا قَلِيلًا) in the accusative as an exception, or "illa fi'lan qaliilan" (إلّا فِعْلًا قَلِيلًا, "except a little action").

﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with﴾ namely following the Messenger (ﷺ), obeying him, and submitting to what he sees and rules, outwardly and inwardly. The commands and prohibitions of Allah the Exalted are called admonitions (مَوَاعِظ, mawa'iz) because they are coupled with promise and threat.

﴿it would have been better for them﴾ That is: their doing that.

﴿and stronger in firmness﴾ for them in faith, further from wavering in it, and more firmly establishing the reward of their deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 67:

﴿And then We would surely have given them from Us a great reward﴾ is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "And what would they have after being made firm?" So it is said: "And then, if they had remained steadfast, We would have given them..." Indeed, "idhan" (then/in that case) is both a response and a condition.

﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path﴾ — by following it they would reach the world of holiness (ʿālam al-qudus), and it would open for them the gates of the unseen. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah the Exalted will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he does not know."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 69:

﴿Whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʼnaf) containing a great deal of encouragement to obedience and an increased stirring of desire for it, by making clear that its outcome is the furthest that the aspirations of nations reach and the highest that their resolves stretch toward: being in the company of the greatest of creation in rank and the most exalted of them in standing. It includes an explanation of what was left ambiguous in the answer of the preceding conditional sentence and a detailing of what was stated in summary there. What is meant by obedience (taʻah) is complete submission and perfect compliance with all commands and prohibitions.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those who obey. The plural is used in view of the meaning of "man" (whoever), just as the singular is used in the verb of the condition in view of its wording. The sense of distance together with nearness in mention is for signalling the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in nobility. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿with those whom Allah has blessed﴾. The clause is the answer of the condition. Leaving out mention of what the blessing was is for indicating that expression falls short of detailing and explaining it.

﴿of the prophets﴾ is an explanation of those blessed. The mention of the company of all the prophets, peace be upon them, although the discourse is about explaining the ruling on obedience to our Prophet ﷺ, is because their mention occurred in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), together with what it contains of an indication that his ﷺ obedience includes obedience to them, since his ﷺ law encompasses their laws, which do not change with the changing of ages. It has been narrated that a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Prophet of Allah, if we enter Paradise, you will be raised above us in the degrees of prophethood, and we will not see you." Al-Sha'bi said: A man from the Ansar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was weeping. He said: "What makes you weep, so-and-so?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, other than whom there is no god, you are dearer to me than my own self, my family, my wealth and my children. I remember you while I am with my family and I am seized as if by madness until I see you. And I remembered my death, and that you will be raised with the prophets, and that if I enter Paradise I would be in a station lower than your station." The Prophet ﷺ did not answer, and then this verse was revealed. It has also been narrated that Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, had an intense love for him, peace be upon him, and little patience in being apart from him. One day he came to him with his face changed, his body emaciated, and sorrow visible in his face. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him about his condition. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have no pain, but when I do not see you I long for you and feel a severe loneliness until I meet you. Then I remembered the Hereafter and feared that I would not see you there, because I know that you will be raised with the prophets, and if I enter Paradise I would be in a station below your station, and if I do not enter, then that is the time I will never see you again." Then this verse was revealed. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no servant believes until I am dearer to him than his own self, his parents, his family, his child, and all people." This has been related from a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It has been narrated that "Anas said: O Messenger of Allah, a man loves a people but has not yet joined them. He, peace be upon him, said: 'A person is with whom he loves.'"

﴿and the truthful ones﴾ meaning those who excel in their affirmation of truth (taṣdiq), who are most emphatic in truthfulness and sincerity in words and deeds. They are the excellent companions of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the most distinguished of their close intimates, such as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿and the martyrs﴾ are those who gave up their lives in obedience to Allah the Exalted and in raising His word.

﴿and the righteous﴾ are those who devoted their lives to His obedience and their wealth to His good pleasure. The intended meaning of "company" is not unity in rank, nor mere sharing in entering Paradise, but rather that they are in it in such a way that each of them can see the other and visit him whenever he wishes, even if the distance between them is great.

﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾. The rafiq is the companion (ṣāḥib), derived from rifq, which is softness of side and gentleness in association, in speech and in deed. If "those" is taken as referring to the prophets and those after them, on the basis that the sense of distance in it is as previously mentioned many times, then "rafiqan" is either a specification (tamyiz) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), in the sense that they are described as excellent from the standpoint of being companions to the obedient, or in the state of being companions to them. Its being singular is because it is like "ṣiddīq," "khalīṭ," and "rasūl," which applies to the single and the plural alike, or because the meaning is: each one of them was excellent as a companion. If "those" is taken as referring to the obedient, then it is a specification in the sense that they are described as having an excellent companion from among the prophets and those after them, not as being excellent in themselves, so "min" cannot be placed before it, as it could in the first case. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming what precedes and emphasizing the encouragement and stirring of desire. It has been said: it carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How excellent are those as companions!" And because it stands alone with the meaning of wonder, it has been read as "wa-ḥasna" with the sin sukun.

ذَلِكَ ("That") is a demonstrative referring to what the obedient receive of great reward and increased guidance, and companionship with those upon whom Allah has bestowed blessings; or it refers to their excellence and distinction. The sense of distance in it (ma fihi min ma'na al-bu'd) is to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station in nobility. It is the subject (mubtada'), and the words of the Exalted, ﴿الفَضْلُ﴾ ("the bounty"), are its attribute (sifah), and the words of the Exalted, ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("from Allah"), are its predicate (khabar). That is: that great bounty is from Allah (p-200) the Exalted, not from anyone else. Or, "al-fadl" is the predicate and "min Allah" is related to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to it, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the demonstrative; that is: that which has been mentioned, the bounty, existing from Allah the Exalted, not that the deeds of the responsible persons necessitate it.

﴿وَكَفى بِاللَّهِ عَلِيمًا﴾ ("And Allah suffices as Knower") of the reward of whoever obeys Him, and of the measures of the bounty and of what its recipients deserve.

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾. Al-hidhr (الحِذْرُ) and al-hadhar (الحَذَرُ) are one and the same, like al-ithr (الإثْرُ) and al-athar (الأثَرُ), and al-shibh (الشِّبْهُ) and al-shabah (الشَّبَهُ). That is: be alert and guard yourselves against the enemy, and do not let him gain access to you. It is said: "He took his precaution (akhadha hadhrahu)" when he became alert and guarded himself against what he feared, as if he made caution his instrument by which he protects himself. It was also said: it is what one is cautious with, namely weapons and resolve, meaning: prepare yourselves for the enemy.

﴿Then go forth﴾ with a kasrah on the fa', and it has been read with a dammah on it, meaning: set out for jihad when you set out.

﴿in groups﴾. Thubat (ثُباتٍ) is the plural of thubah (ثُبَةٍ), which is a company of men numbering more than ten. Its original form is fu'alah (فُعَلَةٌ), like huthamah (حُطَمَةٌ), whose lam has been deleted and the feminine ta' (تاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ) substituted in its place. Is the deleted letter a waw or a ya'? There are two opinions. It was said: it is derived from tha-ba yathbu (ثَبا يَثْبُو), like hala yahlu (حَلا يَحْلُو), meaning "to gather." It was said: it is from thabayta 'ala al-rajul (ثَبَيْتَ عَلى الرَّجُلِ), when you praise a man, as if you gathered his good qualities. It is also pluralized as thubin (ثُبِينَ), a compensatory plural for what was deleted from its end. Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl, حال) construction, meaning: go forth in scattered groups, one company after another.

﴿Or go forth all together﴾, meaning: gathered as one single troop, and do not hold back and abandon one another, lest you cast yourselves into ruin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 72:

﴿And indeed, among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾ That is: will certainly be slow and hold back from jihad. It is from baṭṭaʾa, which has the meaning of abṭaʾa (to delay), like ʿattama with the meaning of aʿtama (to be late for the ʿatama prayer). The address is to the whole army of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), both its believers and its hypocrites. The ones who lag behind (al-mubaṭṭi'ūn) are their hypocrites, who were sluggish and held back from jihad. Or the meaning is: he will certainly cause others to lag and discourage them, from baṭṭaʾa as a transitive form derived from baṭuʾa, like thaqqala from thaqula, just as Ibn Ubayy caused some people to lag on the day of Uhud. The first is more fitting for what follows. The first lam is the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtida'), which entered upon the subject of inna to separate it from the predicate. The second is the answer to an omitted oath, and the oath with its answer forms the relative clause of man, and the returning pronoun is the one concealed in "la-yubaṭṭi'anna." The estimated sense is: "And indeed among you is one for whom I swear by God that he will certainly lag behind."

﴿Then if a calamity strikes you﴾ such as killing and defeat.

﴿He says﴾ That is: the one who lags, rejoicing in his conduct and praising his own opinion.

﴿God has indeed blessed me﴾ That is: by staying behind.

﴿in that I was not present with them as a witness﴾ That is: not present in the battle, so that I would be struck by what struck them. The fa' in the conditional clause indicates that its content follows from what precedes it, for mentioning the lagging entails mentioning what follows from it, just as the lagging itself calls for something the one who lags awaits to happen.

﴿And if there befalls you a bounty﴾ such as a conquest and spoils.

﴿from Allah﴾ is related either to "أصابَكُمْ" (befalls you), or to an omitted word that serves as an attribute (ṣifah) of "فَضْلٌ" (bounty), meaning: "existing from Allah, exalted is He." Attributing the befalling of bounty to the Exalted Majesty, while not attributing the befalling of calamity to Him, is one of the noble customary usages (al-ʿādāt al-sharīfah al-tanzīliyyah), as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who heals me﴾. The conditional clause of the first kind is placed first because its content is more in accord with their aim, and the effect of their hypocrisy is more evident in it.

﴿They will surely say﴾ out of regret for his (the hypocrite's) holding back and his sitting idle, and out of avid greed for the trappings of this world and grief over missing it. It is also read "لَيَقُولُنَّ" (layaqūlunna) with a ḍammah on the lām, returning the pronoun to the meaning of "مَن" (whoever). His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿as if there had never been between you and him any affection﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ, an interjected clause) placed between the verb and its object, which is ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so that I would have achieved a great achievement"﴾. This is so that it is not understood from the opening of his speech that his wish is to be with the believers in order to support and aid them, as the affection between them would require. Rather, it is out of greed for wealth, as its ending makes clear. The affirmation of affection between them is not meant as a factual statement but in a mocking manner (tahakkum, sarcasm).

It is said: the comparative clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "لَيَقُولَنَّ", meaning: "he will surely say while being likened to one with whom you have no affection." It is also said: it is included within what is said, meaning: the one who holds back says to whoever he holds back among the hypocrites and weak believers: "as if there had never been between you and Muḥammad any affection, since he did not take you along in the campaign so that you could win what he won." His aim is to sow enmity between them and him, upon him be prayers and peace, and to reinforce it. The "كَأنْ" (ka’anna, as if) is a lightened form of the heavy one (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), and its subject is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), which is omitted. It is also read "لَمْ يَكُنْ" with the yāʾ. The vocative in "يالَيْتَنِي" (yā laytanī, "Oh, I wish") is omitted, meaning "yā qawm" (O people). It is said: "yā" is used to draw attention to the expansiveness (of the matter). His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿so that I would win﴾ (fa-afūza) is in the accusative as an answer to the wish (jawāb al-tamannī). It is also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "so I would win at that time," or as conjoined to "كُنْتُ" (kuntu, I was), included with it under the wish.
