﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah﴾. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*, a prepositional or adverbial complement) is placed before the agent (*fa'il*, the doer of the action) to give it emphasis.

﴿who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter﴾. That is, they sell it in exchange for it, and they are the believers. The *fa'* (the particle *fa*) is the answer to an implied condition (*shart muqaddar*), meaning: if these people hold back from fighting, then let the sincere ones, who spend themselves in seeking the Hereafter, fight. Or it refers to those who buy it and prefer it over the Hereafter, and they are the ones who hold back. In this case the *fa'* indicates sequence (*ta'qib*): let them abandon the hesitation and hypocrisy they were engaged in, and follow it with fighting in the way of Allah.

﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah, then is killed or overcomes, We shall give him﴾. It is with the nun of majesty (*nun al-'azama*), a shift in grammatical person (*iltifat*).

﴿a great reward﴾, whose measure cannot be estimated. The placing of fighting alongside one of the two outcomes indicates that the warrior should prepare himself for one of the two good things, and the third possibility should not occur to his mind at all. The mention of being killed first signals that it precedes the other in bringing about the reward.

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, has guaranteed for the one who strives in His way, and whose only motive for going out is striving in His way and belief in His word, that He will either admit him to Paradise or return him to the dwelling from which he went out, together with whatever reward and spoils he has gained."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 75:

﴿Why should you not﴾ is an address to those commanded to fight, in the manner of iltifat (the shift from third person to second person), for the sake of exaggerating the incitement to it and emphasizing its obligation. It is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿not fighting in the way of Allah﴾ is a hal (circumstantial clause) whose governing element is what the adverbial phrase contains of the meaning of a verb. The interrogative is for denial and negation, meaning: "What is wrong with you that you are not fighting?", i.e., you have no excuse for abandoning fighting.

﴿And of the oppressed﴾ is conjoined to the word "Allah", meaning: in the way of the oppressed, which is their liberation from captivity and their protection from the enemy. Or it is conjoined to "the way" with the elision of the noun it modifies, meaning: in (p-202) the liberation of the oppressed. Its being in the accusative is permissible as an object of specification (ikhtisas), for the way of Allah encompasses the doors of good, and the liberation of weak believers from the hands of the disbelievers is the greatest and most specific of them.

﴿Of the men, the women, and the children﴾ is an explanation of "the oppressed," or a hal from them; they are the Muslims who remained in Mecca, either to be held back by the polytheists, or because of their weakness in emigrating, being humiliated and abused. The children were mentioned along with them to complete the appeal for compassion and the drawing of mercy, and to alert to the extremity of the polytheists' oppression, such that their harm reached the children, to coerce their fathers and mothers, and to announce the answering of the forthcoming supplication and the nearness of the time of deliverance, by explaining their participation in humbly supplicating to Allah Most High. All of this is for the sake of exaggerating the urging to fight. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the children" is the male and female slaves, since they are called al-walid and al-walida; the males have been given precedence over the females, so "the children" was applied to the female slaves as well.

﴿Who﴾ has a place in the genitive, as it is an attribute of "the oppressed," or of what is in the scope of explanation; or it is in the accusative as an object of specification.

﴿Who say: "Our Lord, bring us out from this town whose people are oppressors"﴾ — with polytheism, which is a great wrong, and with harming the Muslims. It is Mecca, and "oppressors" (al-zalim) is its attribute. Its masculine form is to match what is attributed to it, for when the active or passive participle is applied to something other than its possessor, it behaves like a verb in masculinity and femininity according to what it governs. ﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a protector﴾ — both prepositional phrases are connected to "appoint" because their meanings differ. The fronting of the two prepositional phrases before the direct object serves to show concern for them and to reveal the desire for what is postponed, by placing before it its circumstances; for postponing what should be first behind what is among its desirable circumstances, as it produces the hearer's longing for its arrival, indicates the speaker's complete desire for it and his concern for its attainment without doubt. The fronting of the lam before "min" hastens to reveal that what is asked is beneficial to them and desired by them. It is also permissible for the word "min" to be connected to an elided element that serves as a hal from "waliyyan" (a protector), being fronted on it because it is indefinite; and likewise the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: meaning, appoint over us a ruler from among the believers, who will be a friend to us, will manage our interests, will guard our religion and our law for us, and will support us against our enemies. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, indeed answered their supplication, for He facilitated for some of them the departure to Medina, and He made for those who remained among them the best of protectors and the mightiest of helpers, so He opened Mecca at the hands of His Prophet ﷺ; He then took charge of them in the best manner and gave them a signal victory, then He appointed 'Attab ibn Asid over them, and he protected and supported them until they became the most honored of its people. It has been said: the intended meaning is: "and appoint for us from Yourself a guardianship and a victory," i.e., be Yourself our protector and our helper. The repetition of the verb and its complements is for exaggeration in humble supplication and pleading.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 76:

﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah﴾ is an independent statement, brought to encourage the believers to fight and to hearten them by showing the perfection of their strength through the support and help of Allah the Exalted and the extreme weakness of their enemies. That is: the believers fight only for the true religion of Allah, which leads them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and for raising His word; so He is their Patron and their Helper without doubt.

﴿And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of al-Taghut﴾ — that is, in that which leads them to Satan, so they have no helper other than him. The fa' (فَ) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So fight the friends of Satan﴾ indicates that what precedes it results in what follows it. Mentioning them with this title serves to show that this is a consequence of their fighting in the way of Satan, and it gives the sense that the believers are the friends of Allah the Exalted, since their fighting is in His way. All of this is to affirm the believers' eagerness for fighting and to strengthen their resolve upon it, for the friendship of Allah the Exalted is a sign of might and strength, just as the friendship of Satan is a symbol of humiliation and weakness. It is as if it were said: since the matter is so, then fight, O friends of Allah, the friends of Satan. Then the reason is stated explicitly, so it is said: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan has always been weak﴾, that is: in itself, so how much more so in comparison with the power of Allah the Exalted. He did not undertake to explain the strength of His own side, the Exalted, as an announcement of its manifestness. They said: the benefit of introducing "kāna" (كانَ) in such contexts is emphasis, by showing that since it has existed, it has been so; so the meaning is: the plot of Satan, since it has existed, has always been characterized by weakness.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 77:**

﴿Have you not seen those to whom it was said, "Restrain your hands"﴾ is an expression of wonder addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at their holding back from fighting, although before that they were eager for it and keen upon it, to the point that they almost engaged in it, as the command to "restrain the hands" indicates, since that implies they were about to extend their hands against the enemy, so that they nearly fell upon them. Al-Kalbi said: A group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), among them ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf al-Zuhri, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad al-Kindi, Qudama ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi and Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with them, used to suffer severe harm from the polytheists of Makkah before the Hijrah, so they complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Permit us to fight them." The Prophet (ﷺ) would say to them: "Restrain your hands."

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: for I have not been commanded to fight them. The verb "it was said" is in the passive form, although the speaker was the Prophet (ﷺ), to indicate that this is by the command of Allah, glorified and exalted, and because what is intended in itself and what is considered in the wonder is the completeness of their desire for fighting and their being in a state that required that they be forbidden from it. The command to "restrain the hands" is mentioned within the relative clause only to confirm and depict it by way of metonymy (kināya), so there is no purpose in specifying who issued the command. They remained in this state during their residence in Makkah. When they emigrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Madinah and were commanded to fight at the Battle of Badr, some of them disliked it and it was hard upon them. Yet this was not from doubt in the religion nor aversion to it, but from recoiling from risking their lives and from fear of death, by the requirement of human nature. This is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them﴾, etc., which is conjoined to ﴿it was said to them, "Restrain your hands"﴾ in terms of its metonymic meaning; for then the difference between the meanings of the two conjoined clauses is realized, and on this the matter of the wonder turns, as if it were said: "Have you not seen those who were eager for fighting, but when it was prescribed for them, some of them disliked it?"

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Behold, a party of them fear men﴾ is the answer to "lamma" (when), with "a party" as the subject, "of them" as a complement attached to an omitted element that stands as its qualifier, and "fear" as its predicate. Beginning it with "idha" of suddenness indicates how quickly they hastened to fear, the most immediate of the immediate, without hesitation or wavering; that is: a party of them was suddenly overtaken by fear of the unbelievers, that they might kill them. Perhaps directing the wonder at all of them, although the fear issued from only some of them, is to indicate that it should not have proceeded from any one of them what contradicts their former state.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿as the fear of Allah﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object, in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "fear", meaning: they fear them resembling the people of the fear of Allah, the Exalted. His saying: ﴿or even greater fear﴾ is conjoined to it, meaning "or even greater fear than the people of the fear of Allah"; or it is an emphatic verbal noun, treating the fear as possessing fear for the sake of intensification, as in "jadda jidduhu" (his effort was truly effort), meaning: they fear them with a fear like the fear of Allah, or with a fear more intense than the fear of Allah. In either case, the particle "aw" is either for classification, meaning that the fear of some of them is like the fear of Allah and the fear of some of them is greater than it, or it is for obscuring to the hearer, which is close to what is in His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾, meaning that whoever sees them would say they are a hundred thousand or more.

﴿And they said﴾ is conjoined to the answer of "lamma": that is, when fighting was prescribed for them, a party of them was suddenly overcome by fear of the people, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?﴾ at this time, not by way of objection to His ruling or denial of its obligation, but by way of wishing for lightening.

﴿Why did You not defer us to a near term?﴾ is a request for an extension of the period of restraint and a plea for a later time, out of fear of death. It has been permitted that this may be among what the tongues of their states spoke without their uttering it explicitly.

﴿Say﴾: that is, to make them lose desire for what they hope to gain by remaining seated, of fleeting enjoyment, and to encourage them toward what they will attain through fighting, of lasting bliss.

﴿The enjoyment of this world﴾: that is, what is enjoyed and benefited from in this world.

﴿is little﴾: swift to pass away, imminent in its cessation, even if you are deferred to that term.

﴿But the Hereafter﴾: that is, its reward, of which the reward attached to fighting is part.

﴿is better﴾: that is, for you than that little enjoyment, for its abundance, its non-cessation, and its purity from turbidity. It is only said ﴿for the one who fears Allah﴾ to urge them toward guarding against disobedience and falling short of the obligations of the duty.

﴿And you will not be wronged a whit﴾: conjoined to an implied element that the speech extends to, that is: you will be recompensed therein and not diminished the least bit of the rewards of your deeds, of which your striving in the matter of fighting is part, so do not turn away from it. The "fatil" is the thread in the split of a date-stone, a proverb for paucity and insignificance. It is also read as "yuzlamun" with the ya', returning the pronoun to the apparent antecedent of "man" (those who).

﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ is a fresh statement, introduced by Him, Exalted is He, by way of changing the address and turning it away from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to those being addressed. This is to emphasize binding them to it, following the explanation, through him (ﷺ), of the lowliness of this world and the exalted rank of the Hereafter. It therefore has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), or it is in the accusative position, falling under the speech that was commanded. That is: wherever you are, whether at home or on a journey, death will overtake you, the death from which you flee to fighting, supposing it is among its sources, and you love to sit back from it, supposing that it is a means of escape from it. In the word "overtake" (yudrik) there is an indication that they are fleeing from death while it is diligent in pursuing them. It was also read in the nominative, by omitting the fa' (the conjunctive particle), as in his saying: "Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them." Or by considering that "wherever you are" takes the place of "wherever you may be." Or by considering it a fresh statement, with "wherever you may be" connected to "you will not be wronged," meaning: you will not be deprived of anything of what has been decreed for your lifetimes, wherever you are, in the clashes of wars and the battlefields of calamities.

﴿Even if you were in towers built up high﴾: in lofty fortresses or fortified palaces. Al-Suddi and Qatada said: "towers of the sky." It is said: he built the building (shada al-bina'a), made it high (ashadahu), and plastered it (shayyadahu): he raised it. It was also read "mushayyadah" with a kasra on the ya', as an adjective describing it by the action of its doer, metaphorically, as in "a poem that is poetic" (qasida sha'ira). And "mashidah," from shada al-qasr when he raised it or plastered it with al-shid, which is gypsum. The answer to "law" (even if) is omitted, relying on the indication of what precedes it upon it. That is: even if you were in towers built up high, death would overtake you. The clause is conjoined with another similar to it, that is: even if you were not in towers built up high, and even if you were, and so on. Its omission has become common because the mentioned part clearly indicates it, for if a thing is realized when an obstacle is present, it is all the more realized when that obstacle is absent. On this point turns the emphasis and intensification found in the connective "law" (al-law al-wasliyya, the "even if" particle), and its verification has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers had no understanding at all, nor were they guided?﴾

﴿And if good befalls them, they say: "This is from God"﴾: a fresh statement, brought after what was related about the Muslims, because of the connection between them in that both include ascribing what they dislike to certain matters and their disliking it for that reason. The pronoun refers to the Jews and the hypocrites. It is narrated that provision had been extended to them, but when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina and invited them to faith, and they disbelieved, he withheld from them some of what he had given. So they said: "We have continued to notice a shortfall in our fruits and our fields since this man and his companions came." And that is His saying: ﴿And if evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you"﴾. That is: if blessing and ease befall them, they attribute it to God, Exalted is He; and if calamity from drought and high prices befalls them, they attribute it to you, as was related about their predecessors in His saying: ﴿And if evil befalls them, they consider it an omen from Musa and those with him﴾. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to refute their false claim, guide them to the truth, and silence them by explaining that the whole of it is ascribed to Him, Exalted is He, in general terms, since they do not dare to oppose the command of God, Mighty and Majestic, where it was said: ﴿Say: "All is from God."﴾ That is: each of blessing and calamity is from God, Exalted is He, in creation and origination, without my having any part in the occurrence of either of them in any way, as you claim. Rather, the occurrence of the first is from Him, Exalted is He, directly, by way of grace, and the occurrence of the second is through the sins of the one afflicted with it, as a punishment, as its explanation will come. So this general answer has the same meaning as what was said in refutation of their predecessors in His saying: ﴿Surely their omen is with God﴾. That is: the cause of their good and their evil, or the cause of the befalling of the evil, which is their sins, is with God, Exalted is He, and not with anyone else, so that they might attribute it to him and take omens from him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with these people﴾ and so on, is an interjected statement between the thing explained and its explanation, sent from Him, Exalted is He, to reproach them with ignorance, to denounce their condition, and to express wonder at the completeness of their dullness. The "fa'" (so) is for its sequence upon what precedes it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They scarcely understand any statement﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "these people," and what operates in it is the meaning of settledness within the adverbial phrase. That is: since the matter is so, what has happened to them while they are far removed from understanding any statement? Or it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), built upon a question arising from the interrogation, as if it was said: "What is their state, and what are they doing, that one should wonder at it or ask about its cause?" So it was said: "They scarcely understand any statement at all, from among the statements, so they say what they say. For if they understood anything of that, they would understand this text, and what has the same meaning as it, and what is clearer than it, from among the Qur'anic texts that declare plainly that the whole is overflowing from God, Exalted is He, that blessing is from Him, Exalted is He, by way of grace and kindness, and calamity by way of punishment for the sins of His servants." Especially the text that came to them in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim, which fulfilled that "no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (Qur'an 53:38), and they did not ascribe the crime of their own selves to others.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾ and so on, is an explanation of the general answer that was commanded and whose implementation was on the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ. Then the explanation is delivered from Him, Mighty and Majestic, by way of varying the address and directing it to each one of the people, and by iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), for greater attention to it and concern to refute their false statement, and to announce that its content is based on a subtle wisdom, truly worthy that the Knower of the unseen should undertake its explanation. The address is directed to each one of them rather than to all of them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you, it is for what your hands have earned﴾, for emphasis in affirmation, by cutting off the possibility that the disobedience of some of them is the cause of punishment for the others. That is: whatever blessing of the blessings befalls you.

﴿Then it is from Allah﴾, i.e., it is from Him, Exalted is He, essentially, by way of bounty and kindness, without its being owed to you on your part. How could it not be? For every act of obedience that a person performs, which is supposed to be a means to attaining some blessing, is such that it hardly compensates for the blessing of his life that accompanies its performance, nor for the blessing of His empowering him, Exalted is He, to perform it, let alone for its meriting another blessing. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "No one enters Paradise except by the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He." It was said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I."

﴿And whatever evil befalls you﴾, i.e., a calamity of the calamities.

﴿Then it is from yourself﴾, i.e., it is from you, because of your committing the sins that necessitate it, even though in terms of its existence it is attributed to Him, Exalted is He, descending from Him as a punishment, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you, it is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾. And from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "No Muslim is afflicted with fatigue or hardship, even a thorn that pricks him, or even the cutting of his sandal-thong, except that it is for a sin; and what Allah pardons is more."

It was said: The address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as is the case with what precedes and follows it, but not to explain his state ﷺ; rather, to explain the state of the disbelievers by way of depiction. Perhaps this is to show complete displeasure and anger toward them, and to indicate that they, because of their extreme ignorance and dullness, are far from deserving the address, especially with such an elegant wisdom.

﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾: an explanation of the loftiness of his station ﷺ and his standing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after the explanation of the falsity of their corrupt claim concerning him ﷺ, based on their ignorance of his sublime status. The definite article in "mankind" (an-nās) denotes totality, and the prepositional phrase is either related to "a messenger," placed before it to indicate exclusivity, looking at the restriction of universality, i.e., sent to all people, not to some of them only, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾. Or it is related to a verb, so "a messenger" is an emphatic circumstantial accusative. It has also been permitted that it be an emphatic verbal noun, as in the verse:

*They have indeed lied, the slanderers, that I divulged to them a secret, nor did I send them as a messenger.*

That is: by a sending, in the sense of a message.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾, i.e., to your messengership, by establishing the miracles, among which is this clear text and the true revelation. The shift (iltifat) is to instill awe and strengthen the testimony. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 80:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ is an explanation of the rulings of his messengerhood (ﷺ), following the explanation of its being established and confirmed. That is so because the one who commands and forbids in reality is Allah, the Exalted, and he (ﷺ) is only the conveyor of His command and His prohibition; so the return of obedience and disobedience is to Allah, glorified is He. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: ﴿Whoever loves me has loved Allah, and whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah﴾. Then the hypocrites said: "Do you not hear what this man says? He has indeed fallen into associating partners, for he forbids that anything other than Allah be worshipped; he only wants us to take him as a lord, just as the Christians took Jesus." Then it was revealed. The expression of him (ﷺ) by "the Messenger" rather than by direct address is to signal that the basis for his obedience being obedience to Him, the Exalted, is not the particularity of his person (ﷺ) but rather from the aspect of his messengerhood. And the display of the Divine Majesty (al-Jalala) is for cultivating awe and for emphasizing the obligation of obedience by mentioning the title of divinity (al-Uluhiyya). And taking "the Messenger" to be the genus that includes him (ﷺ) in an initial inclusion is rejected by the specification of address to him (ﷺ) in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ (p-207). The conditional's answer is omitted, and what is mentioned is its justification; that is: "And whoever turns away from obedience, then turn away from him; We have only sent you as a messenger conveying (the message), not as a guardian watching over them, who keeps account of their deeds, calls them to account for them, and punishes them according to them." "Ḥafīẓan" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf (of "arsalnāka"), and "ʿalayhim" is connected to it, placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila). The plural of the pronoun is in consideration of the meaning of "man," just as the singular in "tawalla" is in consideration of its wording.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 81:

﴿And they say﴾ This begins an account of their dealings with the Messenger (ﷺ) after the explanation of the obligation to obey him; that is, they say when you command them to something.

﴿Obedience﴾ That is: our affair and our matter is obedience, or from us is obedience. The original form is the accusative (naṣb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the nominative (raf') is used to indicate permanence, as in salāmun (peace).

﴿When they go out from your presence﴾ That is: they leave your assembly.

﴿A group of them plots by night﴾ That is: a group of them, meaning the aforementioned speakers, and they are their leaders.

﴿other than what you say﴾ That is: a group of them fabricates and arranges the opposite of what they told you of acceptance and pledging obedience, because they are persistent in rejection and disobedience, and they only show what they show out of hypocrisy, or [they arrange] the opposite of what you said to them. Tabyīt (plotting by night) is either from baytūtah (passing the night), because it is the carrying out and planning of a matter at night; it is said: "This is a matter that was planned (bayyita) at night." Or it is from bayt al-shi'r (a line/verse of poetry), because the poet composes and arranges it. The verb is masculine because the feminine of ṭā'ifah (group) is not real (ḥaqīqī). It has also been read with the assimilation of the tā' into the ṭā' because the points of articulation are close. Its attribution to a group of them is to show that they are the ones who directly take charge of it, while the rest are followers of them in this matter, not because the rest are steadfast in obedience.

﴿And Allah records what they plot﴾ That is: He records it among what is revealed to you, so He informs you of their secrets, so that they do not suppose that their scheme is hidden from you, whereby they might find a way to harm you; or He records it in their scrolls, and He will recompense them for it. In either case, the sentence is parenthetical (i'tirāḍiyyah).

﴿So turn away from them﴾ That is: do not concern yourself with them and with what they have done; or overlook them and do not seek to take revenge upon them. The fa' indicates that what precedes is the cause of what follows.

﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾ in all that you do and all that you leave undone, especially regarding their affair. The mention of the Divine Name (al-jalālah) in the place of the pronoun is to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Guardian﴾ So He will suffice you in knowing them, and He will avenge you upon them. The explicit mention here too is for the reason mentioned, and to draw attention to the independence of the sentence and its being self-sufficient from everything else in every respect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 82:

﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ This is a rebuke and a condemnation of their failure to reflect upon the Qur'an and their turning away from contemplating what it contains of the grounds for faith. Tadabbur (reflection) of a thing means contemplating it and considering its back-ends (adbar), that is, what it leads to, its outcome and its end. The term was then used for every kind of reflection and consideration. The fa' (then) is a conjunction (lil-'atf) connecting to an implied premise, meaning: "Do they turn away from the Qur'an and not contemplate it, so that they might know that it is from Allah the Exalted, by observing the signs it contains, among which is this truthful revelation and the explicit text that exposes their hypocrisy as it is described?"

﴿And had it been﴾, that is, the Qur'an,

﴿from other than Allah﴾, as they claim,

﴿they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾, by some of its reports not conforming to reality, since no one other than Him, glory be to Him, has knowledge of unseen matters, whether past or future. And since its reports conform to reality, it is necessarily established that it is from Him, the Exalted.

Al-Zajjaj said: Had it not been from Allah the Exalted, what it contains of reports of the unseen, which the hypocrites conceal and plot in secret, would have been mixed, some of it true and some of it false, because none knows the unseen except Allah the Exalted.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: These hypocrites used to conspire secretly in many kinds of deceit and cunning, and Allah the Exalted would inform the Messenger (ﷺ) of that and tell him of it in detail. So it was said to them: If that had not come about through the information of Allah the Exalted, the truthfulness of it would not have been consistent, and discrepancy would have occurred in it. Since that never happened at all, it is known that it was by His informing. This is what the sublimity of the noble composition (nazm) requires.

As for interpreting "discrepancy" as contradiction, or as variation in eloquence (balaghah), such that some of it indicates a correct meaning according to the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulama al-ma'ani) while some indicates a corrupt meaning that does not cohere, and some of it reaches the limit of inimitability (i'jaz) while some falls short of it and can be countered, as the majority have inclined to, this is something that neither the context of the preceding verses (siyaq) nor the wider flow of the discourse (siyaq al-kalam in the sense of its sequence) supports. Whoever pursues this approximation and says: "Perhaps its mention here is to alert to the fact that the difference among the rulings mentioned earlier is not due to contradiction in the ruling, but to difference in the wisdoms and benefits that necessitate them," has strayed far from the truth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 83:

﴿When there comes to them a matter concerning security or fear, they spread it about.﴾ It is said: *adhā'a al-sirr* and *adhā'a bihi* mean he spread it and made it public. It is also said that the meaning of *adhā'ū bihi* is that they performed *al-idhā'a* (the act of spreading), which is more emphatic than *adhā'ūhu*. This statement is made to dispel what might be suspected in some matters, namely a trace of disagreement, on the basis that the intended meaning was not understood. It explains that this was because they did not grasp the meaning of the statement, not because its implication differed from it. Some of the weaker Muslims, who had no experience of affairs, would spread whatever the Messenger ﷺ informed them had been revealed to him, whether a promise of victory or a warning from the disbelievers, without understanding its meaning or grasping its import, according to what they understood and the interpretations they gave it. Even if they did understand it, it might be conditional on factors that are lost through spreading it, so its expected effect would not appear, and this would become a cause of suspicion of disagreement. Therefore He reproached them for this. It is also said that ﴿if they had referred it﴾ means: that matter which came to them.

﴿to the Messenger﴾ means: they presented it to his opinion ﷺ, seeking to uncover its meaning and what should be done about it, and the proper planning and attention it requires, since the title of Messenger necessitates referring and returning matters to his judgment ﷺ.

﴿and to those in authority among them﴾ means: the senior Companions, who were perceptive in affairs, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿would have known it﴾ means: those who referred it would have known its meaning and its planning. The relative form was used in place of their pronoun, so it says ﴿those who draw conclusions from it among them﴾, to indicate that their purpose in referring it to them should be to seek its meaning and clarify its import. That is: those referrers would have known it, those who draw conclusions from it (*yastanbitūnahu*, i.e. they receive it and extract its knowledge and planning) from them, that is, from the side of the Messenger ﷺ and the Companions in authority among his Companions, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all. Since they did with regard to it what they did, what occurred of confusion and suspicion of disagreement did not happen. It is also said: those who would have known it are those who extract its planning by their acumen, their experience, and their knowledge of war and its stratagems. In this case the word *min* in *minhum* is explanatory. It is also said: when news reached them of the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whether of safety and security or of fear and disorder, they would spread it, and their spreading was corrupting. Had they referred that news to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to those in authority, those who draw conclusions from it, that is, who extract its planning by their acumen, their experience, and their knowledge of war and its stratagems, would have known the planning of what they were informed of. It is also said: (p-209) they used to stand before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those in authority with security and confidence of triumph over some enemies, or with fear, and they would spread it, so it would circulate and reach the enemies, and their spreading would become corrupting. Had they referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority and entrusted it to them, and acted as though they had not heard it, those who draw conclusions from it would have known how to plan it and what they should do and refrain from doing in it. It is also said: they would hear from the mouths of the hypocrites some report about the expeditions, conjectural and not certainly authentic, and they would spread it, so that became a calamity for the believers. Had they referred it to the Messenger ﷺ and to those in authority, and said: "We will remain silent until we hear it from them and know whether it is something to be spread or not," those who would spread it, namely those who draw conclusions from the Messenger and those in authority (i.e. receive it from them and extract its knowledge from them), would have known whether it was authentic and whether it was something to be spread or not. So the sense of the noble composition at that point is to explain the offence of that group and their poor judgment, following the explanation of the offence and deceit of the hypocrites. The address in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾, is to the aforementioned group, by way of *iltifāt* (a shift in address), that is: were it not for His grace upon you, Exalted is He, and His mercy in guiding you to the path of truth, which is referring to the Messenger ﷺ and those in authority in matters of uncertainty.

﴿you would have followed Satan﴾ and acted upon the opinions of the hypocrites in what you do and what you leave undone, and you would not have been guided to the ways of rightness.

﴿except for a few﴾ who are those in authority who comprehend the secrets of the Book and are firmly grounded in knowledge of its rulings. The exception is therefore *munqaṭi'* (disjunctive). It is also said: and were it not for His grace upon you and His mercy by sending the Messenger and sending down the Book, you would have followed Satan and remained in disbelief and error, except for a few among you, who were granted a sound intellect by which they were guided to the path of truth and rightness and preserved from following Satan, such as Quss ibn Sa'ida al-Iyadi, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqa ibn Nawfal and their like. The address is then to all, and the exception is *muttasil* (connected). It is also said: the intended meaning of grace and mercy is victory and triumph over the enemies, that is: were it not for the attainment of victory and triumph in succession and continuity, you would have followed Satan and abandoned the religion, except for a few among you, who are people of penetrating insight, strong resolve and firm determination, from the outstanding believers who comprehend the truth of the religion and have reached the degree of certainty of knowledge, being independent of witnessing the signs of its truth through conquest and victory. It is also said: except for a little following.

﴿So fight in the way of Allah﴾ is a change of address (*talwin al-khitab*), directed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by way of *iltifat* (a shift from third person to second person). It is the answer (*jawab*) to an omitted conditional clause that the noble composition implies. The meaning is: if the matter is as has been related, with the hypocrites' disobedience and their scheming, and the others' negligence in observing the rulings of Islam, then fight, you alone, paying no heed to what they have done.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You are not charged except with yourself﴾, meaning "except with the act of yourself", is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that confirms what precedes it. The restriction of the Prophet's ﷺ obligation to his own act is among the consequences of his fighting alone. This indicates that the discouragement they produced does not harm him ﷺ and that he is not held accountable for it. It has been said that this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "fight", meaning: fight, not being charged with anything except yourself. It was also read as "you are not charged" (*la tukallif*) with the jussive, as a prohibition (*nahy*). It was said that it is the answer to the imperative. It was read with the royal "we" (*nun al-'azamah*), meaning: We do not charge you with anything except the act of yourself, not in the sense that We do not charge anyone except yourself.

﴿And urge the believers﴾ is a conjunction (*'atf*) with the preceding command and falls under its ruling. The situation of the two groups as related is the cause of the command to fight alone and to urge on the sincere believers. *Tahrid* (urging) upon something means exhorting to it and encouraging it. Al-Raghib said: "It is as if, originally, it is the removal of *haras*, which is what has no good in it and is not considered." That is: encourage them to fight, and do not be harsh with them. The one urged to it is not mentioned because it is so evident.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It may be that Allah will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾, is a promise from Him, glorified and exalted, whose fulfillment is certain, to restrain the violence and scheming of the disbelievers. What begins with "la'alla" and "'asa" is certainly established from Him, mighty and majestic, and so it was. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ promised Abu Sufyan, after the battle of Uhud, a meeting at the season of Badr al-Sughra in Dhu al-Qa'dah. When the appointed time arrived, he called the people to go out, but some of them disliked it, and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out with seventy riders, and they arrived at the appointment. Allah cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, and they turned back from Marr al-Zahran. It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Badr with his army and remained there eight nights. They had merchandise with them, which they sold, and they gained much good. This has been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.

﴿And Allah is stronger in might﴾, meaning: than Quraysh.

﴿And stronger in punishment﴾, meaning: in torment and chastisement that deters whoever witnesses it from doing what leads to it. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD tadhyili*) that confirms what precedes it. The mention of the majestic Name serves to instill awe, to give the reason for the ruling, to strengthen the independence of the sentence, and the repetition of the predicate serves to emphasize the severity.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, verse 85:

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share in it﴾. That is, a share of its reward. This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah), brought to explain that the Prophet ﷺ himself has a abundant share in what he was commanded to do, namely urging the believers on. For intercession (shafa'ah) is mediation by speech in securing for a person some benefit, whether worldly or otherwise, or in rescuing him from some harm of a similar kind, as if the one interceded for were a single (fard) and the intercessor made him a pair (shaf'). A good intercession is one made in a lawful matter, by which the right of a Muslim is observed, seeking the Face of God Most High, without including any worldly aim. And what benefit is greater than that which the believers obtained through his ﷺ urging them to jihad, both worldly and otherwise? And what harm is greater than that from which they were delivered by it, namely being discouraged from it? Included in this is supplication for a Muslim, for it is an intercession addressed to God, Glorified is He, and the verse of greeting that follows is brought in this context. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever supplicates for his Muslim brother in his absence, it is answered for him, and an angel says to him: 'And for you is the like of that.'" This is an explanation of the measure of the share promised.

﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession﴾: this is what is contrary to the good one.

﴿will have a portion of its burden (kifl)﴾: that is, a share of its sin equal to it in measure, without anything being diminished from it.

﴿And God is ever Omnipotent over all things (muqit)﴾: that is, Capable (muqtadir), from aqata 'ala al-shay' when one is capable of it; or Watchful (shahid), Preserver (hafiz). Its derivation is from qut (sustenance), for it strengthens the body and preserves it. The sentence is a concluding statement confirming what precedes it under both meanings.

﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ This is an exhortation to a common instance of the good intercession (*shafa'ah*, "intercession" or "mediation"), following the general exhortation to it and the warning against its opposite, the evil intercession. It also directs one to fulfil the right of the one who intercedes and to the manner of discharging it, for the greeting of Islam from a Muslim to his brother is an intercession from him to Allah, exalted is He.

"*Al-tahiyyah*" (greeting) is a verbal noun of *hayya*, whose original form is *tahiyyah*, like *tasmiyah* from *sammā*. (p-211) The root of the root is *tahayyi*, with three *yā'*s; the last was deleted and replaced by the feminine *tā'*, and the first was assimilated into the second after its vowel was transferred to the *ḥā'*.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: The original sense of *al-tahiyyah* is the invocation of life and its prolongation, then it came to be used for every invocation. The Arabs, when one of them met another, would say: "May Allah grant you life" (*ḥayyāka Allāh*). Then the Sharī'ah employed it for greeting with peace, and this is the greeting of Islam. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their greeting therein is peace﴾, and He said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace﴾, and He said: ﴿So greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾. They said: Peace has a distinction over *tahiyyah*, because it is an invocation for safety from religious and worldly calamities, and this entails the prolongation of life, whereas the invocation for prolonged life does not contain that. Moreover, "al-Salām" is one of the names of Allah, exalted is He, so beginning with the mention of it is something whose excellence and distinction are beyond doubt. That is: when greeting is offered to you from the direction of the believers.

﴿Then return it with something better than it﴾, that is: with a greeting better than it, by saying: "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah," if the Muslim has confined himself to the first, and by adding "and His blessings" (*wa barakātuh*) if the Muslim has combined them. This is the utmost, since it encompasses all the aspects of what is sought, which are safety from harms, attaining benefits, their continuation, and their increase.

﴿Or return it﴾, that is: respond to it with its like. It is narrated that men came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and one of them said: "Peace be upon you," and he (ﷺ) said: "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah." Another said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah," and he said: "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." Another said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings," and he said: "And upon you." The man said: "You have diminished me, so where is what Allah the Exalted said?" and he recited the verse. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You did not leave me any excess, so I returned to you its like." The response to the greeting is obligatory, and the choice lies only between adding to it and leaving it as it is. It is related from al-Nakha'i that the greeting is a sunnah while the response is an obligation. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: The response is obligatory, and there is no man who passes by a company of Muslims, greets them, and they do not return his greeting, except that Allah strips from them the Spirit of Holiness (*Rūḥ al-Qudus*), and the angels return the greeting to him. It is not returned during the sermon, during the open recitation of the Qur'an, during the narration of ḥadīth, during the study of knowledge, during the call to prayer (*adhān*) and the iqamah, and one does not greet a player of backgammon (*nard*) or chess (*shiṭranj*), a singer, a man sitting to relieve himself, a keeper of pigeons, or a naked man in the bath, and others. They said: A man greets his wife, but not a non-Mahram woman. The Sunnah is that one walking greets one seated, one riding greets one walking, the rider of a horse greets the rider of a donkey, the young greets the elder, the few greet the many, and when two meet, each greets first. It is related from Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him: One does not return the greeting aloud, meaning loudly. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿When the People of the Book greet you, say: "And upon you"﴾, that is: "And upon you what you have said," since some of them would say "al-Sām 'alaykum" (death be upon you). It is narrated: Do not begin a Jew with the greeting, and if he begins with you, say: "And upon you." It is related from al-Hasan that it is permissible to say to a disbeliever: "And upon you be peace," without the addition. It has also been said: the greeting with what is better applies when the one greeting is a Muslim, and the return of its like applies when he is a disbeliever.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Accountable over all things﴾, so He will call you to account for every one of your deeds, among which is what you have been commanded regarding greeting. So be vigilant in observing it as you have been commanded.

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him﴾ is a *mubtada'* (nominal subject) and *khabar* (predicate). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, He will surely raise you from your graves for the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection." It has been said that "إلى" here means "فِي" (in), and the oath clause is either a new independent sentence with no place in the i'rab, or a second predicate of the *mubtada'*, or it is itself the predicate, with ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ as a parenthetical insertion. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ means: about the Day of Resurrection, or about the gathering. It is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from "the Day," or an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning: a gathering about which there is no doubt.

﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ This is a denial that anyone could be more truthful than Him, exalted is He, in His promise and in all His other reports (p-212), and it is a demonstration of the impossibility of such a thing. How could it be otherwise, since lying is impossible for Him, glorified is He, and not for anyone else?

**﴿فَما لَكُمْ﴾** (*fa-ma lakum*, "so what is wrong with you") is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa-khabar*). The interrogative is for denunciation (*inkar*) and negation (*nafy*). The address is to all the believers, but the rebuke it carries is directed at some of them.

**﴿فِي المُنافِقِينَ﴾** (*fi al-munafiqin*, "concerning the hypocrites") may be connected in one of three ways:

1. To what the predicate (*khabar*) depends on. The meaning is: "What thing is there for you concerning them," that is, concerning their affair and their state. The governed noun (*mudaf*) has been deleted and the governing noun (*mudaf ilayhi*) has taken its place.
2. To what the phrase **﴿فِئَتَيْنِ﴾** (*fi'atayn*, "two groups") implies of separation (*iftiraq*). The meaning is: "Why do you separate into groups concerning the hypocrites?"
3. To an implied word that functions as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of **"فِئَتَيْنِ"**. The meaning is: "being in the case of the hypocrites." This is because it was originally an adjective (*sifah*), and when it was placed first it became accusative as a state, as is the general rule for adjectives of indefinite nouns. Alternatively, it is a state of the pronoun in **"تَفْتَرِقُونَ"** (*tafarriqun*, "you separate").

According to the Basrans, **﴿فِئَتَيْنِ﴾** is accusative as a state of the addressees (*mukhatabin*), and the governing element is the sense of the verb contained in **"لَكُمْ"** (*lakum*). This is like the verse **﴿فَما لَهم عَنِ التَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ﴾** ("What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the reminder?"). According to the Kufans, it is the predicate (*khabariyyah*) of a hidden *kana* (*kuntum*), meaning: "What is wrong with you concerning the hypocrites, that you (were) two groups?"

The purpose is to deny that the addressees have any justification for disagreeing about the matter of the hypocrites. It also explains that it is obligatory to decide definitively on their disbelief and to treat them in all rulings as open disbelievers. They are mentioned by the title of hypocrisy because of their earlier attribute.

It is reported that they were a group of hypocrites who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to go out to the desert (*al-badw*), making the excuse that they found Medina unhealthy (*ijtiwa' al-Madinah*). When they went out, they kept travelling stage after stage until they joined the polytheists, and the Muslims disagreed about their status.

It is also said that they were people who had emigrated from Mecca to Medina, then changed their minds and returned, and wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We are upon your religion; what drove us out was only the unhealthiness of Medina and longing for our homeland."

It is also said that they were people who displayed Islam and sat back from emigration (*hijrah*).

It is also said that they were people who went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud and then turned back. But this is rejected by what follows, which makes their emigration the limit (*ghayah*) of the prohibition against taking them as allies.

It is also said that they were the people of ʿUrayna (*al-ʿUraniyyun*), who raided the herd (*al-sarh*) and killed the shepherd of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). But this is rejected by the subsequent verses that explain how they are to be treated, whether in peace or in war. Those people were seized and treated with what was done to them, namely mutilation and killing, and no disagreement among the believers concerning their matter is reported.

**﴿واللَّهُ أرْكَسَهُمْ﴾** (*wa-llahu arkasahum*, "and Allah has returned them [to the state of disbelief]") is a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the hypocrites. It serves to reinforce the earlier denunciation and to make the occurrence of the denounced act seem unlikely, by stating that what is left after the absence of any motive still exists. It is also said that it is from the pronoun of the addressees, and the linking element is the *waw*. The meaning is: "What motive calls you to disagree about their disbelief, when there is what requires your agreement on their disbelief, namely that Allah, exalted is He, has returned them to disbelief as they were?"

**﴿بِما كَسَبُوا﴾** (*bima kasabu*, "because of what they earned") means: because of what they brought upon themselves of apostasy, joining the polytheists, and plotting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The returning pronoun to the relative (*'a'id ila al-mawsul*) is deleted. It is also said that **"ما"** is a verbal-source particle (*masdariyyah*), meaning "because of their earning."

It is also said that the meaning of **"أرْكَسَهُمْ"** (*arkasahum*) is: "He overturned them," by making them into fuel for the Fire. The root *raks* means returning a thing upside down (*maqlub*). It is also read as **"رَكَّسَهُمْ"** (*rakkasahum*, with doubled letter) and **"رَكَسَهُمْ"** (*rakasahum*, without doubling).

**﴿أتُرِيدُونَ أنْ تَهْدُوا مَن أضَلَّ اللَّهُ﴾** (*aturidun an tahdu man adalla Allah*, "Do you want to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?") strips the address of its general sense and restricts it to those among the two groups who affirm their faith. It rebukes them for their supposition, and suggests that it leads to attempting the impossible, namely guiding one whom Allah, exalted is He, has led astray. This is because ruling that they are believers and claiming that they are guided, when they are far from that, is an effort toward their guidance and a desire for it.

The relative construction (*al-mawsul*) is placed in the position of the pronoun for the hypocrites, to intensify the denunciation and emphasize the impossibility of guidance by what is mentioned in the relative clause (*sillah*). The denunciation is directed at the wanting itself, not at its object. The wording is not "Will you guide...?" but "Do you want to...?", for the sake of exaggeration in denying it, by showing that it is something whose wanting is impossible, let alone its occurrence.

Interpreting guidance and misguidance as ruling that someone is guided or misguided is refuted by the verse **﴿وَمَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلَنْ تَجِدَ لَهُ سَبِيلا﴾** (*wa-man yudlili Allahu falan tajida lahu sabilan*, "And whoever Allah sends astray, you will not find for him any way"). That is: whoever Allah creates misguidance in, whoever he may be, you will not find for him any path among the paths, let alone that you could guide him to it. This contains a clearer expression of the complete impossibility than the verse **﴿وَمَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَما لَهُ مِن هادٍ﴾** ("And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide") and similar verses.

Interpreting Allah's misguidance as His judgment and decree of misguidance spoils the good correspondence between the condition and its consequence.

Addressing each one of the addressees individually indicates that the absence of finding (guidance) includes each of them, in detail. The sentence is either a circumstantial state of the subject of **"تُرِيدُونَ"** (*turidun*, "you want") or of **"تَهْتَدُوا"** (*tahtadu*, "you be guided"), with the linking element being the *waw*. Or it is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ tadhyili*) that establishes the earlier denunciation and affirms the impossibility of guidance. In that case, the address may be to anyone suitable among the original addressees and others besides them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 89:

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve just as they disbelieve, so that you would be equal.⟩ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to explain their extremism, their persistence in disbelief, and their eagerness to lead others astray, following the explanation of their own disbelief and misguidance. The word "law" (lau) here is verbal (masdariyyah), needing no answer (ghaniyyah ʿan al-jawab), and it together with what follows it is in the accusative position as an object (mafʿul), meaning: they wish that you would disbelieve. The phrase of the Most High, ﴿just as they disbelieve﴾, is in the accusative either as a qualifier (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning "disbelieve the disbelief of theirs," or as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun of that verbal noun, as is the view of Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian). The phrase of the Most High, ﴿so that you would be equal﴾, is coordinated (ʿatf) upon ﴿you would disbelieve﴾ and falls under its ruling, meaning: they wish that you would disbelieve, so that you would be equal, alike in disbelief and misguidance. It has been said: the word "law" retains its conditional sense, and its answer is omitted, serving as the object of "they wish," with the estimate: they wish your disbelief—if you were to disbelieve as they disbelieved, they would be delighted by that.

﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾. The fa' is the answer of an omitted condition, and the plural "allies" (awliyaʾ) is in consideration of the plural of those addressed, since the intended meaning is a prohibition that any one of those addressed should take one of them as an ally. That is: when their state is as mentioned, namely wishing your disbelief, then do not befriend them.

﴿Until they emigrate in the way of God﴾. That is: until they believe and realize their faith by an emigration (hijrah) done for God the Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ), not for any of the worldly aims.

﴿But if they turn away﴾. That is: from belief manifested by sound and upright emigration.

﴿Then seize them﴾. That is: when you are able over them.

﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾, whether within the sacred territory or outside it, for their ruling is the ruling of all other polytheists, both in captivity and in killing.

﴿And do not take from among them any ally or helper﴾. That is: keep away from them with complete avoidance, and do not accept from them any guardianship or support, ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 90:

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ This is an exception from His words, exalted is He: ﴿So take them and kill them﴾. That is: except those who connect with and reach a people who have made a covenant with you and did not fight you. These are the Aslamiyyun. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out from Makkah, he had made a truce with Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, on condition that he would not help him nor help against him, and that whoever reached Hilal and sought refuge with him would have the same protection as Hilal has. It was also said: they are the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat. And it was said: they are Khuza'ah.

﴿Or who come to you﴾ is a conjunction upon the relative clause (silah), meaning: or those who come to you, withholding themselves from fighting you and fighting their own people. Two groups are excepted from those ordered to be seized and killed: one of them is those who left the fighters and joined the covenanted ones, and the other is those who came to the believers and refrained from fighting both groups. Or it is in the description of a people, as if it were said: except those who join a people who are covenanted, or a people who withhold from fighting you and fighting against you. The first is the more apparent, because of His words, exalted is He, that follow: ﴿Then if they withdraw from you﴾ etc., for it is explicit that their restraint from fighting is one of the two causes that entitle them to the absence of any harm to them. It was also read "jA'uukum" without the conjunction, as a description following a description, or as an explanation of "yasiluna", or as a resumptive clause.

﴿Their breasts are constricted﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, as evidenced by its being read "ḥaṣiratun ṣudūruhum", "ḥaṣirātun ṣudūruhum" and "ḥāṣirātun ṣudūruhum". It was also said: it is a description of an omitted noun that is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "jA'uu", i.e.: or they came to you as a people whose breasts are constricted. It was also said: it is an explanation of "jA'uukum", and they are the Banu Mudlij, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ not fighting. Al-haṣar: constriction and restraint.

﴿That they fight you or fight their people﴾ i.e.: from fighting you, or because they would fight you, or out of aversion to fighting you, etc.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾ is an independent sentence serving as a reason for excepting the last group from the ruling of seizing and killing, and for placing them in the same category as the first group, which stands in the position of covenanted ones, although they are not connected to us nor to those with whom we have a covenant, like the first group. That is: and if Allah had willed, He would have empowered them over you by expanding their breasts, strengthening their hearts, and removing terror from them.

﴿Then they would have fought you﴾ immediately after that, and not withheld from you. The lam is the answer of "law" (if), repeated or substituted for the first. "Falaqatalukum" was also read with light and heavy pronunciation.

﴿Then if they withdraw from you﴾ and do not molest you.

﴿And do not fight you﴾ despite what you know of their ability to do so by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿And offer you peace﴾ i.e. submission and surrender. It was also read with the lam sukun.

﴿Then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾ a path, by capture or by killing, for their withholding from fighting you, their not fighting their own people, and their offering you peace, even if they have not made a covenant with you, are sufficient for their entitlement to your not molesting them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 91:

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people.﴾ They are a people from Asad and Ghatafan who, whenever they came to Madinah, embraced Islam and made covenants so that they would be secure from the Muslims; then whenever they returned to their people, they disbelieved and broke their covenants, in order to be secure from their people. It is also said: they are the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, and their habitual conduct was what has been mentioned.

﴿Whenever they are returned to temptation﴾ i.e., they are called to disbelief and to fighting the Muslims.

﴿they are plunged back into it﴾ i.e., they are overturned in it in the most vile and hideous manner, and they were in it worse than any hostile, malicious enemy.

﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾ by refraining from confronting you in any way.

﴿and offer you peace﴾ i.e., they do not offer you reconciliation and a treaty, but rather they throw it back at you.

﴿and restrain their hands﴾ i.e., they do not restrain them from fighting you.

﴿then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾ i.e., wherever you gain power over them.

﴿Against these﴾ those described by the repulsive qualities that have been enumerated.

﴿We have given you clear authority﴾ a manifest proof for overpowering them, by killing and taking captives, because of the clarity of their enmity and the exposure of their state in disbelief and treachery and their harm to the people of Islam; or a manifest dominion, since We have permitted you to seize them and kill them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 92:

﴿And it is not for a believer﴾ i.e., it is not proper for him, nor befitting his state.

﴿to kill a believer﴾ unjustly, for faith restrains him from that.

﴿except by mistake﴾ for it may occur, since complete avoidance of it does not fall within human capacity. Its accusative (intisab, i'rab) may be either as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., "it is not for him to kill a believer in any state except in the state of mistake"; or as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., "it is not for him to kill him for any cause except by mistake"; or as an attribute of the verbal noun (sifah lil-masdar), i.e., "except a killing by mistake." It has been said that "illa" (except) here means "wa la" (and not), and the sense is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer, either intentionally or by mistake." It has also been said that the negation carries the meaning of a prohibition, and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but if he kills him by mistake, then his recompense is what is mentioned." Mistake (khata') is that which is not accompanied by the intention either to the act or to the person, or in which the killing is not intended to cause the taking of life generally, or in which no forbidden act is intended, such as shooting a Muslim among the disbelievers' ranks while unaware of his Islam. It is also read "khata'an" with a long vowel, and "khata" (like "asa") with the hamza lightened. It is narrated that 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, who was the maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl, embraced Islam and emigrated to Madinah out of fear of his family, and this was before the Hijrah of the Prophet (ﷺ). His mother swore that she would neither eat nor drink, nor would any roof shelter her, until he returned. So Abu Jahl set out, accompanied by al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah, and they came to him while he was in a fortress. Abu Jahl seized him by the top and back of the neck and said: "Is it not Muhammad who urges you to maintain the ties of kinship? Return and be kind to your mother, while you remain upon your religion." Until he descended and went with them. When they had gone some distance from Madinah, they bound him and flogged him. Then he said to al-Harith: "This is my brother; so who are you, O Harith? By Allah, if I find you alone, I will kill you." They brought him to his mother, and she swore that his bonds would not be undone until he apostatized. He did so with his tongue. Afterwards he emigrated and embraced Islam, and al-Harith also embraced Islam and emigrated. 'Ayyash met him at the outskirts of Quba' without knowing of his Islam, and he struck him down and killed him. Then he was informed of his Islam, and he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I killed him without knowing of his Islam." Then this verse was revealed.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, [then the freeing of a believing slave]﴾ i.e., upon him, or its requirement, is the freeing of a slave, that is, the setting free of a soul, which is expressed by "neck" just as it is expressed by "head."

﴿a believing [slave]﴾ i.e., one judged to be Muslim by her faith, even if she is a child.

﴿and a blood-money [diyah] paid to his family﴾ delivered to his heirs, who divide it like other inheritances, based on the statement of Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to me instructing me to give the wife of Ashyam al-Dabbabi an inheritance from the blood-money ('aql) of her husband."

﴿unless they remit it﴾ i.e., unless his family give it up as charity to him. Forgoing it is called charity (sadaqah) to urge towards it and to draw attention to its merit. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every good deed is a charity." It is also read "illa an yassaddaqu" (with the doubling of the sad). The phrase is connected either to "upon him" or to "delivered," meaning: the blood-money is due, or he delivers it to his family except at the time of their giving it up as charity, in which case it is in the accusative place as a time adverb; or except as a circumstance in which they are giving it up, in which case it is a circumstantial state of the family or the killer.

﴿If he was﴾ i.e., the slain.

﴿from a people hostile to you﴾ disbelievers at war.

﴿and he was a believer﴾ and the killer did not know of it, because he was among his people, having embraced Islam among them without departing from them, or because he came to them after leaving them for some important matter.

﴿then [the freeing of] a believing slave﴾ i.e., upon his killer is expiation, not blood-money, since there is no inheritance between him and his family, as they are combatants.

﴿And if he was﴾ i.e., the slain believer.

﴿from a people﴾ of disbelievers.

﴿between you and them is a covenant﴾ i.e., a treaty, either limited in time or perpetual.

﴿then a blood-money﴾ i.e., upon his killer is blood-money.

﴿delivered to his family﴾ from among the people of Islam, if they are found. Perhaps the mention of this ruling here, while it was deferred earlier, is to indicate haste in delivering the blood-money, to avoid the suspicion of breaking the covenant.

﴿and the freeing of a believing slave﴾ as is the ruling for all Muslims. Perhaps its separate mention, though it falls under the ruling previously stated in His words ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾ etc., is to clarify that his being among those bound by treaty does not prevent the obligation of blood-money, as his being among combatants did prevent it. It has also been said that the intended slain is a dhimmi or a mu'ahad, lest the repetition be without benefit, and lest there be inheritance between a Muslim and a disbeliever; and you have known that it is not obligatory.

﴿And whoever does not find﴾ i.e., a slave to free, by not owning one nor the means of obtaining one through its price.

﴿then fasting﴾ i.e., upon him is fasting.

﴿two consecutive months﴾ in which no breaking of the fast intervenes between any two of their days.

﴿as a repentance﴾ it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, i.e., this was legislated for you as repentance, meaning acceptance of it, from "Allah accepted his repentance" when He accepted his repentance; or it is a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, i.e., "He turned to you in repentance." It has also been said that it is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "upon him," with an omitted modifier, i.e., "upon him is fasting for two months, being a repentance." His words, exalted is He, ﴿from Allah﴾ are connected to an omitted element that falls as an attribute of "repentance," i.e., proceeding from Him, exalted is He.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of all things, of which His own state is part.

﴿Wise﴾ in all that He legislated and decreed of laws and rulings, of which is what He legislated concerning this matter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 93:

﴿Whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾. When he had explained the ruling on killing by mistake and detailed its three categories, he followed this with an explanation of intentional killing, except that its worldly ruling had already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah, so here he restricted himself to its otherworldly ruling. It is narrated that Maqis ibn Dubabah al-Kinani, who had embraced Islam together with his brother Hisham, found his brother slain among the Banu al-Najjar. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him the story. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) sent with him Zubayr ibn 'Iyad al-Fihri, who was among the companions of Badr, to the Banu al-Najjar, instructing them to hand over the killer to Maqis so that he could take retribution from him if they knew who he was, or to pay the blood-money if they did not know. They said: "We hear and obey Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (peace be upon him). We do not know of any killer of his, but we will pay his blood-money." So they brought him one hundred camels. The two returned toward Madinah, and when they were on part of the road, Satan came to Maqis and whispered to him, saying: "Will you accept the blood-money of your brother, so that it becomes a disgrace upon you? Kill the one who is with you, so that it becomes a soul for a soul, and the surplus of the blood-money is yours as well." So he caught al-Fihri off guard, struck him with a rock and crushed him. Then he mounted one of the camels, drove the rest of them, and returned to Makkah as an unbeliever, saying:

Poetry:
"I killed Fihr for his sake, and I carried his blood-price, the chiefs of the Banu al-Najjar, the companions of Qari'."
"I attained my vengeance and lay down at ease with a pillow, and I was the first to return to the idols."

Then this verse was revealed. He is the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) excepted on the day of the Conquest from those he had granted safety, and he was killed while clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah.

As for His saying ﴿intentionally﴾, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "yaqtul" (kills). It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he read the taa' with a sukun, as if he fled from the succession of vowels (tawālī al-ḥarakāt).

﴿Then his recompense﴾ is what he deserves for his crime, ﴿is Hell﴾. His saying ﴿therein he will abide forever﴾ is a predicated circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah) referring to the subject of an implied verb which the context requires, as if it were said: "His recompense is that he enters Hell, abiding therein forever." It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yujzāhā" (He will recompense him with it). It was also said that it is from the object of "jāzāhu" (He recompensed him), and this was supported by the claim that it is more suitable for the coordination of what follows it to it, because it corresponds to it in form. It is not hidden that what is supposed for the circumstantial clause or for its coordination should be something the context requires clearly, and that the statement indicates clearly. It is evident that the fact that his recompense is what has been mentioned does not necessarily entail that the recompense actually occurs at all, as you will come to understand, so that one would have to suppose "yujzāhā" or "jāzāhu" in the sense of informing about its occurrence. As for His saying ﴿and Allah is angry with him﴾, it is coordinated upon an implied element indicated clearly by the conditional structure, as if it were said by way of resumption (isti'nāf), confirming and emphasizing its content: "Allah has decreed that his recompense is that, and He is angry with him," that is, He takes vengeance upon him.

﴿And He has cursed him﴾, that is, He has removed him far from mercy by making his recompense what has been mentioned. It was also said that this and what follows it are coordinated upon the predicate (khabar) with the supposition of "an" (that), and the past tense is taken in the sense of the future, as in His saying ﴿and the Horn is blown﴾ and its parallels, meaning: "So his recompense is Hell, and that Allah becomes angry with him, etc."

﴿And He has prepared for him﴾ in Hell,

﴿a great punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. Because of the severe threat, the firm warning, and the various kinds of lightning and thunder that you see in this noble verse, it is reinforced by the severe reports that have been narrated, such as his (ﷺ) saying: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, the passing away of this world is less grave before Allah than the killing of a believer." And his (ﷺ) saying: "If a man were killed in the east and another were pleased with it in the west, he would be made a partner in his blood." And his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever helps in the killing of a believer, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'Despairing of the mercy of Allah the Exalted.'" With such thunderbolts, the Khawarij (a sect that declared grave sinners unbelievers) and the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) held fast to this verse for the eternal abiding of the one who intentionally kills a believer in the Fire. They have no proof in it except what has been said, that it concerns one who considers the killing lawful, as is the view of 'Ikrimah and his like, based on the fact that it was revealed concerning Maqis ibn Dubabah al-Kinani, the apostate, as his story has passed. For the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. Moreover, "khulud" (abiding) here means a long stay, not perpetual duration, because of the many texts clearly stating that the punishment of believing sinners does not last forever.

As for what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that there is no repentance for one who intentionally kills a believer, and likewise what is narrated from Sufyan that the scholars, when asked, would say: "He has no repentance," it is to be understood as following Allah's Sunnah in severity and harshness.
