Upon this is understood what is narrated from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah refuses to grant repentance to the killer of a believer." How could it not be so, when it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that a man asked him: "Is there repentance for the killer of a believer?" He said: "No." Another asked him: "Is there repentance for the killer of a believer?" He said: "Yes." It was said to him: "You said this to one and that to another?" He said: "The first had not yet killed, so I said what I said so that he would not kill; and this one had killed, so I said to him what I said so that he would not despair." It is also narrated from him the permissibility of forgiveness without repentance, when he said concerning His saying ﴿Then his recompense is Hell﴾, the verse: "That is his recompense; if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him." It is narrated with a raised (marfu') chain from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "That is his recompense, if He recompenses him." Likewise said 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Salih, saying: "A person may say to one whom he is restraining from a matter: 'If you do it, your recompense is death or beating,' and then if he does not recompense him with that, it is not a lie from him." Al-Wahidi said: "The principle in this is that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may break a threat, though it is impossible for Him to break a promise. On this basis the Sunnah came from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever Allah promises a reward for his deed, He will certainly fulfil it for him; and whoever He threatens with punishment for his deed, He has the choice.'"

The verification is that there is no need to derive what we are discussing from the principle mentioned, because it is an information from Him, exalted is He, that his recompense is that, not that He will recompense him with it. How could it not be so, when Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾? If this were information that He, exalted is He, recompenses every evil deed with its like, it would contradict His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He pardons much﴾.

﴿O you who have believed﴾, after he had explained the ruling on killing in its two categories, and that what can be imagined to proceed from a believer is only killing by mistake, he began to warn against what leads to it: carelessness about matters.

﴿When you go forth in the cause of Allah﴾, i.e., you travel out on a military campaign (ghazw). Because *idhā* (إذا, "when") carries the sense of a condition, His saying ﴿investigate﴾ is introduced with the *fa'* (فـ, "then"). That is: seek clarity regarding the matter in everything you do and everything you leave undone, and do not hasten in it without reflection and deliberation. It is also read *fatathabbatū* (فَتَثَبَّتُوا, "be certain"), i.e., seek its confirmation. His saying ﴿and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace﴾ is a prohibition against what results from abandoning the commanded action, and a specification of one important case among the matters in which clarification is obligatory. It is also read *al-silma* (السِّلْمَ) without an *alif* and with a *kasra* on the *sīn* and a *sukūn* on the *lām*, i.e., do not say, without deliberation, to whoever greets you with the greeting of Islam, or to whoever hands you the keys of submission and compliance.

﴿You are not a believer﴾, and you only displayed what you displayed seeking refuge. Rather, accept from him what he displays and deal with him according to its requirement. It is also read *mu'manan* (مُؤْمَنًا) with a *fatḥa*, i.e., safety has been granted to you. This reading is more fitting with the other two readings. Limiting the mention to the greeting of Islam in the first reading, although it is accompanied by the two words of testimony, as will come in the occasion of revelation, serves to intensify the prohibition and rebuke, and to draw attention to the complete clarity of their error, by explaining that the greeting of Islam was sufficient to restrain and deter people from harming its bearer, so how much more when it is combined with them.*

His saying ﴿seeking the goods of worldly life﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of *lā taqūlū* (لا تَقُولُوا, "do not say"). It indicates what drives them to haste and to abandoning deliberation. But the prohibition does not refer only to the condition, as in your saying: "Do not seek knowledge seeking status through it," but rather to both together. That is: do not say this to him while you are seeking his property, which is a fleeting trifle that quickly perishes.

His saying ﴿with Allah are abundant spoils﴾ is a reason given for the prohibition against seeking his property, through the implicit promise it contains, as if it were said: do not seek his property, for with Allah are abundant spoils which He will grant you, and so He will make you independent of committing what you have committed.

His saying ﴿thus you used to be [in the past], but Allah conferred favor upon you﴾ is a reason given for the prohibition against the aforementioned saying. Its being placed later may be because it contains a kind of detailed explanation, which placing it earlier might disrupt the harmony of the parts of the noble composition, along with the consideration of comparison between the earlier reason and what is given as the reason here. This is like His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turned black...﴾ etc. The predicate of *kāna* (كانَ) is placed first for restriction (qaṣr), which serves to affirm the resemblance between the two sides of the comparison. "That" (ذَلِكَ) refers to the one to whom you gave the greeting of peace, in terms of his being characterized by what is in the relative clause. The *fa'* in *fa-manna* (فَمَنَّ) is for coordination with *kuntum* (كُنْتُمْ). That is: like that one to whom you gave the greeting of peace, you too were, at the beginning of your Islam, displaying to people something other than what was apparent from you, such as the greeting of Islam and the like. So Allah conferred favor upon you by accepting that rank from you, and by it He protected your blood and your property, and did not command an investigation into your inner selves.

The *fa'* in His saying ﴿then investigate﴾ (p-219) is *faṣīḥah* (فَصِيحَةٌ, an expressive *fa'* that signals an implied condition). That is: if the matter is as described, then seek clarity about this clear matter, measure his situation against yours, and treat him as you were treated at the beginning of your affairs, by accepting the outward state without verifying whether the outward and inward are in agreement. This is what the eloquence of the revelation requires and what the grandeur of its exalted matter demands.

Whoever supposes that the meaning is: "When you first entered Islam, the words of testimony were heard from your mouths, and thus they safeguarded your blood and property without waiting to ascertain whether your hearts agreed with your tongues; so Allah conferred favor upon you by steadfastness, by being known for faith and by preeminence in it; and if you have become leaders in it, then you must treat those who enter Islam as you were treated, and regard the outward profession of Islam in matters of general application, and do not say..." etc., has strayed from the truth. For, as you have come to know, the intended meaning is to clarify that safeguarding blood and property is a ruling that follows from the mere utterance of the testimony, which is what makes them equal to him in that respect. The declaration that its consequence applies to them also implies that it applies to him, as a binding argument against them and a demonstration of their error. It should not be overlooked that this can only be achieved through an explanation from Him, exalted is He, regarding them, which follows from their being like him, namely the safeguarding of their blood and property, as mentioned; so that the obligation to safeguard his blood and property may become clear to them as well, by the rule of shared inclusion in what makes it obligatory. Since He did not do this, but instead explained it by what He explained, nothing remains in the noble composition that indicates the consequence of safeguarding their blood and property as he claimed. So from where does he get the statement "so I safeguarded your blood and property," in order for the explanation to be possible? And the supposition of such an implied element, based on the requirement of what was mentioned in the explanation of the favor, is built on a weak foundation.

How could it not be? The mention of it is in the context of explanation, and although it is a matter branching from what involves equality and is based upon it regarding them, it is not a ruling whose establishment for him is intended on the basis of its establishment for them, like the aforementioned safeguarding, so that it deserves to be addressed. Nor is it a matter with any bearing on the obligation to regard the outward Islam of those who enter it, such that it could be properly arranged in the chain of what is made a consequence by His saying "then you must do..." etc. And interpreting the statement to mean that "at first you were like him in the deficiency of rank in Islam, then Allah conferred favor upon you and you attained this lofty rank from Him, so do not belittle his state by looking at your present state, but rather count it great by looking at your former state," is refuted by the fact that his killing was not due to the deficiency of his Islam, but rather due to the suspicion that his heart did not agree with his tongue.

The noble verse was revealed concerning Mirdās ibn Nahīk, from the people of Fadak, who had embraced Islam, and none of his people had embraced it besides him. A *sariyyah* (سَرِيَّةٌ, a small expedition sent out by the Prophet) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raided them, led by Ghālib ibn Faḍālah al-Laythī. They fled, but Mirdās remained, trusting in his Islam. When he saw the horsemen, he drove his sheep to a steep place on the mountain and climbed up. When they caught up with him and shouted "Allahu akbar," he also shouted "Allahu akbar" and said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you." Usāmah ibn Zayd killed him and seized his sheep. They informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was deeply grieved and said: "You killed him, seeking what he had with him?" Usāmah ibn Zayd said: "He said it with his tongue but not with his heart." — In another narration: "He only said it out of fear of the weapons." — The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why did you not split open his heart?" — In another narration: "Did you not split open his heart?" Then he recited the verse to Usāmah. Usāmah said: "O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for me." He said: "How [will you do] with 'There is no god but Allah'?" Usāmah said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) kept repeating it until I wished that I had not embraced Islam until that day. Then he asked forgiveness for me and said: 'Free a slave.'"

It was also said: the verse was revealed concerning a man who said: "O Messenger of Allah, we were pursuing a people, and Allah had routed them. I targeted a man, and when he sensed the sword he said, 'I am a Muslim,' but I killed him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Did you kill a Muslim?" He said: "He was only seeking refuge." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Did you not split open his heart?"

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ of deeds, outward and hidden, and of their manners.

﴿Acquainted﴾, so He will reward you according to them: if good, then good; if evil, then evil. So do not be lax in killing, and be cautious regarding it. The sentence is an explanatory reason for what precedes it, by way of a resumptive statement (isti'nāf). It is also read with a *fatḥa* on (p-220) *inna* (إنَّ), so that it is governed by *tabayyanū* (تَبَيَّنُوا, "investigate"), or with the omission of the *lām* of causation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 95:

﴿Those who sit at home are not equal﴾ This explains the difference in ranks among the believers according to the differences in their efforts in jihad, after the command to fight and the exhortation of the believers to it had already been mentioned. The purpose is that the one who sits back may be ashamed of it and raise himself above the lowering of his rank, so that he is stirred with desire for the elevation of his station. By them is meant those who were given leave to stay behind from jihad, being satisfied with others. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: they are those who stayed behind from Badr and those who went out to it. This is the apparent meaning, consistent with the chronology of the revelation, not what is reported from Muqatil, that they are those who went out to Tabuk, for history does not agree with that and the circumstances do not support it, since the ones who stayed behind on that day did not have this concession.

His saying, ﴿from among the believers﴾ (min al-mu'minin), is connected to an omitted element that stands as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of "al-qā'idūn" (those who sit back), meaning: being among the believers. Its benefit is to announce from the outset that the attribute of sitting back does not undermine their faith, and to indicate the reason for their deserving what is coming of the good reward (al-ḥusnā).

﴿other than those with a harm﴾ (ghayr ūlī al-ḍarar) is a ṣifah (adjective, qualifier) of ﴿al-qā'idūn﴾, since it functions in the manner of an indefinite noun, as no specific people are intended by it, or it is a badal (substitute) of it. It has also been read in the accusative, as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of it or as an exception (istithnā'), and in the genitive, as a ṣifah of ﴿al-mu'minin﴾ or a badal of it. Al-ḍarar means illness or a defect, such as blindness, lameness, chronic disability or the like. In its meaning is also inability to obtain the necessary equipment.

On the authority of Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: I was beside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the tranquility (sakīnah) overcame him, and his thigh fell upon my thigh, until I feared it would be crushed. Then it passed from him, and he said: "Write." So I wrote: "Those who sit back among the believers and those who strive are not equal." Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about one who is unable to strive among the believers?" Then the tranquility overcame him again in the same way, and then it passed from him, and he said: "Write: ﴿Those who sit back among the believers, other than those with a harm, and those who strive are not equal﴾."

Their mention with this title, rather than with "those who went out" which corresponds to the attribute of the conjoined term, as occurs in the wording of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), is likewise; and so is the restriction of the striving by its being (in the cause of Allah).

﴿in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves﴾ is for praising them by it and indicating the reason for their deserving elevated rank. Also, "the way" (al-sabīl) has a fine placement in contrast with sitting back. The mention of "those who sit back" first, and the announcement from the outset that the deficiency indicated by the non-equality is on their side and not on the side of those who are compared with them, is significant. The concept of non-equality between two things that differ in excess and deficiency, although it may be considered according to the excess of the one who exceeds, the more evident sense is to consider it according to the deficiency of the deficient one. On this is His saying: ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ and other similar verses. As for His saying: ﴿Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾ the placing of the superior first there is perhaps because its attribute is a habit that corresponds to the attribute of the inferior.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their selves over those who sit back by a degree﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'nāf) brought to explain the kind and quantity of the superiority between the two groups, which was understood in general from the mention of their non-equality. It is built upon a question that the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "How did that happen?" So it was said: "Allah has preferred..." and so on. As for estimating "what is with them that they are not equal," this is only suitable if the resumptive statement is taken as an explanation of the non-equality, directed toward proving it, and this involves an obvious reversal, for what ought to be intended in itself is the explanation of the superiority of the two groups in varying degrees. As for the non-equality of the two, its best is that it serves as a preparation for mentioning it. The definite article in "al-mujāhidīn" and "al-qā'idīn" is for specificity (al-'ahd), so the condition that the striving be in the way of Allah is taken into account in the first, just as the condition of no harm is taken into account in the second.

"Darajatan" (by a degree) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), since it stands in the position of the single instance of the verb of preference, meaning: Allah gave a preference of a preference; or by removing the preposition, meaning: by a degree. It was said: it is in the accusative as a tamyīz (specification). It was also said: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of "al-mujāhidīn," meaning: possessors of a degree. Its tanwīn (nunation) is for magnification.

His saying, ﴿and all﴾ (wa-kullan), is the first object of the verb that follows it, and it is placed before it to give the force of restriction (qaṣr), as an emphasis of the promise, meaning: each one of the strivers and the ones who sit back.

﴿Allah has promised the best reward﴾ (wa'ada Allāh al-ḥusnā), meaning: the good reward, which is Paradise, not just one of the two as in His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾, where the lam is connected to "rasūlan" (as a messenger). The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), brought to remedy what the preference of one of the two groups over the other might seem to imply, namely the deprivation of the lesser one. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Allah has preferred﴾ and so on, and the lam in "al-farīqayn" (the two groups) replaces for them the mention of the conditions that were left out by way of gradual progression.

His saying, ﴿a great reward﴾ (ajran 'aẓīman), is a verbal noun emphasizing "faḍḍala" (preferred), on the basis that it carries the meaning of "ajara" (rewarded). Its choice over the verbal noun that derives from the verb is to indicate that this preference is a reward for their deeds. Or it is a second object of it, by including in it the meaning of giving, meaning: He gave them, over those who sit back, a great reward. It was also said: it is in the accusative by removing the preposition, meaning: He preferred them with a great reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 96:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Darajat﴾ (degrees) is a substitute (badal) for "ajran" (a reward), a substitution of the whole (badal al-kull) that specifies the quantity of the preference. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿minhu﴾ (from Him) is connected to an omitted element (mutaʿallaq bi-mahdhuf) that occurs as a qualifier (sifah) of "darajat," indicating its magnificence and the greatness of its rank; that is: degrees proceeding from Him, Exalted is He. Ibn Muhayriz said: they are seventy degrees, between each two degrees being the distance of a swift, well-trained horse running for seventy autumns. And al-Suddi said: they are seven hundred degrees. And on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah, Exalted is He, has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two degrees is as the distance between the heaven and the earth." It is also permissible that the accusative of "darajat" be an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), as in your saying, "He struck him with whips" (darabahu aswatan), meaning: strikes; as if it were said: He preferred them with preferences. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa maghfiratan﴾ (and forgiveness) is a substitute for "ajran," a substitution of a part (badal al-baʿd), because part of the reward is not of the category of forgiveness; that is: forgiveness for the sins that proceed from them, which the other good deeds performed by those who remain behind do not expiate, so that these are counted among their distinctive features. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa rahmah﴾ (and mercy) is a substitution of the whole for "ajran," like "darajat," and it is permissible that the accusative of both be by means of an implied verb of each, that is: He forgave them with forgiveness and showed them mercy with mercy. This is so; and perhaps the repetition of the preference by way of conjunction, which indicates difference, and its restriction at one time with "darajah" (a degree) and at another with "darajat" (degrees), while the preferred and the one preferred over are the same, as the context requires and the excellence of arrangement demands, is either to treat the difference in designation between the two preferences and between the degree and the degrees as if it were an essential difference, as a preparation for adopting the method of ambiguity followed by explanation, for the sake of greater verification and confirmation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment﴾. It is as if it were said: Allah preferred the strivers over those who remain behind by a degree whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be reached; and since the realization of this vast gap between them would suggest the deprivation of those who remain behind. It has been said: "And to each Allah has promised the best," then the explanation of what the indefiniteness (tankir) conveyed by way of ambiguity was intended, in a manner that cuts off the possibility that it denotes unity, so it was said what was said; and to Allah belongs the excellence of the Revelation's style. Or it is for the difference in essence between the two preferences and between the degree and the degrees, on the basis that what is meant by the first preference is what Allah granted them immediately in this world of booty, victory, and good remembrance, which is fitting to be a single degree; and by the second preference what He bestowed in the Hereafter of lofty degrees that cannot be counted, as is indicated by the placing of the first first and the second last, and the mention of the promise of Paradise between them; as if it were said: He preferred them over those who remain behind in this world by one degree, and in the Hereafter by degrees that cannot be numbered. Between them in mention is placed what is intermediate between them in existence, namely the promise of Paradise, to clarify their state and as a hastening to console the one who is preferred less. And Allah, Glorified is He, knows best. This is the account concerning the strivers and those who remain behind other than those with a harm. As for those with a harm, they are equal to the strivers according to those who hold the doctrine of the implication of the qualifier (mafhum al-sifah) and that an exception from a negation is an affirmation; but according to those who do not hold this, there is no indication of it in the wording of the text. It has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed, you have left behind in Medina people who, whenever you journeyed any journey or crossed any valley, were with you." They are those whose intentions were sound, whose hearts were sincere, and whose hearts inclined towards jihad, but who had something preventing them from setting out, such as harm or other reasons. In another wording: "Indeed, in Medina there are people who, whenever you journeyed any journey or crossed any valley, were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, while they are in Medina?" He said: "Yes, while they are in Medina; excuse has held them back." They said: "This equality is conditioned by another condition besides harm, which has been mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or the ill﴾ up to His saying ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾." It has also been said: the first "those who remain behind" are the afflicted (al-adrarr), and the second are others; and in this there is a disjointing of the noble arrangement that is not hidden. And there is no doubt that the afflicted are more excellent in degree than others, just as there is no doubt that they are below the strivers in worldly rank.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾: a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming what was promised of forgiveness and mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 97:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ is an explanation of the state of those who stayed back from emigration (hijra), following the explanation of the state of those who stayed back from jihad. The verb "tawaffahum" may be past tense, and this is supported by the reading "tawaffathum." It may also be present tense, with one of the two taa's omitted, its original form being "tatawaffahum," in the narrating of a past state and with the intention of bringing its image to mind. This is reinforced by the reading of one who recited "tuwaffahum," the present tense of "wuffiyat," meaning that God Most High causes the angels to fulfil their souls, so they fulfil them; that is, He enables them to take them in full, so they take them in full.

﴿wronging themselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "tawaffahum." Although it is grammatically attached to a definite noun (in construct), it is in reality indefinite, because the meaning is one of separation, even though in form it is joined, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿not violating the sanctity of game﴾ and ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'ba﴾, and "thani 'itfihi" meaning "muhillin al-sayd" and "balighan al-Ka'ba," and "thaniyan 'itfahu," as if it were said: "wronging themselves." This is by abandoning emigration and choosing to dwell among the disbelievers, which necessarily leads to neglecting the matters of religion. It was revealed concerning a group of people from Mecca who had embraced Islam but did not emigrate when emigration was obligatory.

﴿They say﴾: that is, the angels say to the dying, as a confirmation to them of their shortcoming in manifesting their Islam and upholding its rulings, such as prayer and the like, and as a rebuke to them for it.

﴿"In what state were you?"﴾: that is, in what matters of your religion were you?

﴿They say﴾: this is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) founded upon a question arising from the narration of the angels' question, as if it were said: "What did they answer?" So it is said: they answered, evading a plain acknowledgment of their shortcoming (p-223) and making excuses by what they thought necessitated it.

﴿"We were oppressed in the land"﴾: that is, in the land of Mecca, unable to carry out the duties of religion among its people.

﴿They say﴾: refuting their excuse and rebuking them.

﴿"Was not God's earth spacious, so that you could have emigrated therein?"﴾: to another region of it where you could uphold the matters of religion, as those did who emigrated to Medina and to Abyssinia. As for taking their excuse to be a claim of inability to emigrate, and making the angels' reply a denial of that, this is refuted by the fact that the cause of inability to emigrate is not confined to the absence of a place of emigration; it may also be lack of ability to leave due to poverty, or the disbelievers not allowing it. So the statement of the spaciousness of the earth is not a denial or refutation of them, but rather it is necessary to show their ability as well, so that the rebuke is complete. It was also said: that group had gone out with the polytheists to Badr, among them Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughira, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their like, and they were killed there. The angels struck their faces and their backs and said to them what they said. So this would be a reproach and rebuke to them for their support of the disbelievers and their enrolment in their army. Their answer of being oppressed would be an excuse, claiming that they were subdued under their hands and were taken out unwillingly. It was refuted by saying that they had a way of escape from their subjugation and were able to emigrate.

﴿Those﴾: those whose dreadful states have been related.

﴿Their abode﴾: that is, in the Hereafter.

﴿is Gehenna﴾: just as their abode in this world was the abode of disbelief, because they abandoned the obligatory duty. So "mawahum" is the subject (mubtada') and "Jahannam" its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "ula'ika," and this clause is the predicate of inna, and the fa' in it is because its subject contains the meaning of a condition. And His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "In what state were you?"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the angels," with "qad" implied according to those who require it, or it is the predicate, and the returning pronoun in it is omitted, that is: they said to them. The sentence introduced by the fa' is conjoined to it and derived from it and from what falls within its scope.

﴿and evil is it as a destination﴾: that is, their destination, namely Gehenna. In this noble verse there is guidance to the obligation of emigrating from a place where a person cannot carry out the matters of his religion, for whatever reason. And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever flees with his religion from land to land, even if it were a span of land, Paradise is made obligatory for him, and he shall be the companion of Abraham and of his Prophet Muhammad ﷺ."

﴿Except the oppressed﴾ is an exception of the *istithna' munqati'* type (disconnected exception, where the excluded item does not belong to the category of what precedes it), since they are not included in the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, "those who") or its pronoun, or in the demonstrative referring to it. The word "مِن" (*min*, "from") in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from among the men and the women and the children﴾, is related to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of ﴿the oppressed﴾, meaning: being among them. The mention of "الوِلْدانِ" (*al-wildan*, "the children") is clear if by them are meant the slaves (*al-mamalik*) or those approaching puberty (*al-murahiqun*). But if by them are meant young children (*al-atfal*), then it is for emphasis on the matter of emigration (*hijrah*), and to imply that it is of such a nature that, if those not yet obligated (*ghayr al-mukallafin*) were able to perform it, it would be obligatory upon them; and to indicate that there is no escape for them from it at all, so that it is obligatory upon them once they reach maturity, as if it were already obligatory upon them before puberty if they were able; and that their people are obligated to emigrate with them whenever it is possible.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿who cannot devise a plan, nor are they guided to a way﴾, is a descriptive clause (*sifah*) of ﴿the oppressed﴾, since the "اللام" (*al-lam*) in it is not the definite article (*lam al-ta'rif*); or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of them, or of the concealed pronoun (*damir al-mustakinn*) within it. It has been said that it is an explanation (*tafsir*) of the oppressed themselves, due to the many aspects of their oppression. The ability to devise a plan (*istita'at al-hilah*) means finding the means and causes of emigration, and its beginnings; and being guided to the way (*ihtida' al-sabil*) means knowing the route to the place to which one emigrates, either by oneself or by a guide.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 99:

﴿Those⁠﴾ (p-224) refers to the weak ones described with the qualities of incapacity that were mentioned.

﴿It may be that Allah pardons them﴾ The word of hope (ʿasā, "it may be") and the term of pardon (ʿafw) are used to indicate that emigration is of such emphatic obligation that abandoning it, on the part of one for whom its non-obligation has been definitively established, should be considered a sin that calls for seeking pardon, out of hope and longing, not with certainty and conviction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 100:

﴿And Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) that confirms what came before it.

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find in the earth many a refuge and abundance﴾ is an encouragement to emigration (targhib fi al-muhajara) and a consolation for it. That is, he will find in it a place to move to (mutahawwal) and a place of emigration (muhajar). He expressed it this way to emphasize the encouragement, because it implies that in that place of move the emigrant will attain such good and blessing that it becomes a cause for humbling the noses of the people he left behind. Al-rughm means humiliation and abasement; its original sense is the sticking of the nose to al-raghaam, which is dust. It has also been said: he will find in it a path by which he humbles his people through his conduct, i.e., he separates from them in spite of their noses (ala raghm unufihim).

﴿And abundance﴾ means: of provision.

﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him﴾ means: before he reaches the destination, even if that occurs outside his home's threshold, as is indicated by the choice of "leaving his home" over "emigrating." It is coordinated (atf) with the conditional verb. It has also been read with a nominative ending (raf'), on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that it is the vowel of the ha' transferred to the kaf in the intention of pausing, as in the verse:

Of the Anazi who insulted me, I did not strike him; I was amazed, while time is full of wonders.

It has also been read with the accusative (nasb), with the particle "an" (that) being implied, as in the verse: [And I shall join the Hijaz and find rest].

﴿Then his reward has fallen upon Allah﴾ means: that is established with Him, exalted is He, with the firmness of a binding matter. It was reported that when the aforementioned verses were revealed to the Muslims of Mecca, Jundub ibn Damra said to his sons, and he was a very old man: "Carry me, for I am not among the oppressed, and I am indeed able to find the way. By Allah, I will not spend the night in Mecca." So they carried him on a litter heading toward Medina. When he reached al-Tan'im, he was at the point of death, so he clapped his right hand upon his left and said: "O Allah, this is for You and this is for Your Messenger; I pledge allegiance to You upon what Your Messenger pledged to You." Then he died in a praiseworthy state. The news reached the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "Had he died in Medina, his reward would have been more complete." Then this was revealed. They said: every emigration undertaken for a religious purpose, whether seeking knowledge, pilgrimage, jihad, or the like, is an emigration to Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and to His Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, intensive in forgiveness, so He forgives him whatever lapses he committed, among which is remaining behind from emigration until the time of departure.

﴿Merciful﴾, intensive in mercy, so He shows him mercy by completing the reward of his emigration.

﴿And when you travel in the land﴾: this begins the explanation of how prayer is performed in the case of the necessities that arise from travel, from encountering the enemy, from illness, and from rain. It also contains an affirmation of the resolve of the emigrant (muhajir) to emigrate and an encouragement to him to do so, because of the ease it brings in reducing hardship. That is, if you travel on any kind of journey whatsoever. For this reason it is not restricted by the conditions that were attached to emigration.

﴿then there is no blame upon you﴾: that is, no sin or wrongdoing.

﴿if you shorten﴾: that is, in shortening. Qasr (shortening) is the opposite of madd (lengthening). One says qasartu al-shay', meaning "I made the thing short" by removing some of its parts or attributes. Strictly speaking, the object of qasr is that thing itself, not a part of it, since a part is the object of the removal, not of the shortening. On this basis, the saying of the Exalted: (p-225) ﴿of the prayer﴾ should be the object of "taqsuru" if min is taken as an extra particle, as al-Akhfash held. But if min is taken as partitive and the object is omitted, as is the view of Sibawayh, meaning "some of the prayer," then either the part must be described with the attribute of the whole, or qasr is taken in the sense of restraining (habs), as one says qasartu al-shay' when I restrained it, or the prayer is taken as a genus, so that what is shortened is a part of it, namely the four-rak'ah prayers. That is: there is no blame upon you in shortening some of the prayer by halving it. It is also read as tuqsiru (from iqsar) and tuqassiru (from taqsir), and all of them have the same meaning.

The minimum duration of travel that makes shortening applicable is, according to Abu Hanifa (ra), three days and their nights at the pace of camels and walking on foot at a moderate speed. According to al-Shafi'i, it is two days. The apparent meaning of the noble verse is optionality (takhyir) and the superiority of completing the prayer, and al-Shafi'i relied on this. He also relied on what is narrated: "From the Prophet (ﷺ) that he completed (the prayer) during travel." And from Aisha (ra) that she sometimes completed it and sometimes shortened it. And from Uthman (ra) that he would complete and shorten. According to us, shortening is obligatory without doubt, except that some of our shaykhs called it 'azimah (the firm, default ruling), and some called it a rukhsah of removal (rukhsat isqat), such that there is no room for completing it. It is not a rukhsah of ease, for there is no sense in offering a choice between the lighter and the heavier. This is the view of Umar, Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Jabir, may Allah be pleased with them all. It was also said by al-Hasan, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Qatada, and it is the view of Malik. It has been narrated from Umar (ra): "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, complete and not shortened, on the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ)." And from Anas (ra): "We went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) from Madinah to Makkah, and he would pray two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, until we returned to Madinah." And from Imran ibn Husayn (ra): "I never saw the Prophet (ﷺ) pray during travel except two rak'ahs, and he prayed two rak'ahs in Makkah, then said: 'Complete it, for we are a traveling people.'" And when Ibn Mas'ud heard that Uthman (ra) had prayed four rak'ahs at Mina, he said the words of istirja' (inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un), then said: "I prayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Mina two rak'ahs, and I prayed with Abu Bakr (ra) at Mina two rak'ahs, and I prayed with Umar (ra) at Mina two rak'ahs. So would that my share of four rak'ahs were two accepted rak'ahs." Uthman (ra) excused his completing the prayer by saying that he had settled in Makkah. And it is narrated from al-Zuhri that he completed it only because he had resolved to reside in Makkah. And from Aisha (ra): "The first time the prayer was enjoined, it was enjoined as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs. Then it was confirmed for travel and increased for residence." In the Sahih of al-Bukhari she said: "Allah enjoined the prayer when He enjoined it as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, both in residence and travel. Then the prayer of travel was confirmed and it was increased in the prayer of residence." As for what is narrated from her about completing it, she offered an excuse for it and said: "I am the mother of the believers, so wherever I alight, it is my home."

The reason this was expressed with the negation of blame is that they had become accustomed to completing the prayer, so they were likely to think that there was a deficiency upon them in shortening. Therefore the negation of blame was stated explicitly, so that their souls would be content with it and be reassured by it, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So whoever makes the pilgrimage to the House or performs the 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between the two﴾, even though that circumambulation is obligatory according to us and a pillar according to al-Shafi'i.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve will afflict you﴾, its answer (jawab) is omitted, the preceding context indicating it. That is: if you fear that they will confront you with what you dislike of fighting and other things, then there is no blame upon you, etc. This is a condition that is considered for the legislation of what is mentioned after it, namely the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) performed in congregation. As for the shortening in general, there is no consideration of this condition, by consensus, because the Sunnah is abundantly clear on its legislation, as far as I have come to know its details. Al-Tahawi, in his Sharh al-Athar, mentioned with a chain going back to Ya'la ibn Umayya that he said: "I said to Umar ibn al-Khattab (ra): 'Allah only said: ﴿there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve will afflict you﴾, and people are now secure.' Umar (ra) said: 'I was amazed at what you were amazed at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: ﴿It is a charity which Allah has granted you, so accept His charity.﴾'" (p-226) In this there is evidence that it is not permissible to complete (the prayer) in full, because giving charity of something that does not admit of transfer of ownership is a pure remission that does not admit of rejection, as has been verified in its proper place. Let it not be supposed that this contradicts the Book, for restriction by a condition, according to us, only indicates the establishment of the ruling when the condition exists. As for its absence when the condition is absent, it is silent on that, so if there is other evidence for it, it is established by that evidence as well, and otherwise it remains in its original state, because the evidence for it has not been established, not because evidence for its absence has been established. It is enough for you what you have heard of the clear evidences. As for those who hold the doctrine of mafhum (implicative meaning), it indicates the negation of the ruling when the condition is absent only when it has no other purpose. The condition here came out in the manner of what is most usual, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity﴾. Rather, we say that the noble verse is general (mujmal) regarding the extent of shortening and its manner, regarding what is connected to it of prayers, and regarding the duration of travel to which shortening is attached. So everything that has come from him (ﷺ) about shortening in a state of security, and its restriction to four-rak'ah prayers by way of classification, and to travel of a specified duration, is an explanation of the generality of the Book.

It has also been said that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿if you fear﴾ etc. is connected to what follows of the prayer of fear and is separate from what precedes it. For it has been narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (ra) that he said: "The saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾. Then they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after a year, and it was revealed: ﴿if you fear﴾ etc." That is: if you fear that those who disbelieve will afflict you, then there is no blame upon you, etc. It has also been read: "of the prayer, that they afflict you," without ﴿if you fear﴾, as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for what the speech indicates, as if it were said: "He legislated that for you out of aversion to their afflicting you," etc. For the continuation of engagement in prayer is a likely occasion for their ability to bring about affliction. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers have been to you a manifest enemy﴾ is the justification for that, in terms of the justification being what has been mentioned, or what is understood from the speech, namely that their affliction is anticipated, for the full extent of their enmity toward the believers is among the things that make it likely they will be harmed.

The utterance of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, namely the general text, which came in the derivative manner concerning the legislation of shortening (the prayer), and a depiction of how it is performed in the case of complete necessity. The explanation is restricted to this form, while the explanation of other forms is left to the Sunnah, because of the greater need for it, since such forms involve many changes from the original configuration. From here it becomes clear to you that the noble text is primarily about the shortened prayer, and the ruling on other cases is derived from its ruling. The address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is in the manner of tajrid (addressing the Prophet as a representative of the community), and by its apparent meaning it concerns those who do not hold that the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) continues after his death ﷺ. There is no doubt that the imams after him are his deputies ﷺ, who carry out what he used to carry out, so the ruling of the address that came to him ﷺ applies to them, as in His utterance, exalted is He: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾. It has been narrated that when Sa'id ibn al-'As (p-227) wanted to lead the people at Tabaristan in the prayer of fear, he said: "Who among you witnessed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and described it to him, and he prayed with them as he had described. This took place in the presence of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and none of them objected, so it attained the status of consensus (ijma'). And it is related in the Sunan that they fought alongside 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah at Babil, and he led them in the prayer of fear.

﴿So you established the prayer for them﴾: that is, you intended to lead them in the prayer.

﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾: after you have divided them into two groups, and let the other group stand facing the enemy so that they may guard you against them. It was not stated explicitly because it is evident.

﴿And let them take﴾: that is, the group standing with you.

﴿their weapons﴾: that is, they should not put them down nor throw them away. He expressed this by "taking" to indicate the importance of keeping them at hand, as if they were taking them up at the start.

﴿Then when they have prostrated﴾: that is, those standing with you, and they have completed the rak'ah.

﴿let them be behind you﴾: that is, let them turn toward facing the enemy to guard.

﴿And let another group come who have not prayed﴾ yet, namely the group standing facing the enemy for guarding. It was not identified earlier because it had not been mentioned before.

﴿so let them pray with you﴾ the remaining rak'ah. The noble verse does not specify the status of the remaining rak'ah for each of the two groups, and this has been explained by the Sunnah, where it is related from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, that "the Prophet ﷺ, when he prayed the prayer of fear, prayed with the first group one rak'ah and with the second group one rak'ah, as in the noble verse. Then the first group went away and this group went to face the enemy, until the first group completed the last rak'ah without recitation and they gave the salam. Then the second group came and completed the first rak'ah with recitation, so that each group had two rak'ahs." ﴿And let them take﴾: that is, this group.

﴿their precaution and their weapons﴾. Perhaps the increase in the command to take precaution this time is because this is the point where the disbelievers may realize that the group standing with the Prophet ﷺ is occupied with something preoccupying, whereas before this they may have thought them to be standing ready for battle. The obligation on each of the two groups to do what was mentioned is because occupation with prayer is a cause for laying down weapons and turning away from other things, and a cause for the enemy's attack, as His utterance, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would be unmindful of your weapons and your belongings, so that they might attack you in a single assault﴾. This is an resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for the aforementioned command, and the address is to both groups by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), meaning: they wish to gain an opportunity and seize a chance, so that they may fall upon you in one single onslaught. By "belongings" is meant what one uses for enjoyment in war, not in general. This command is obligatory, as indicated by His utterance, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons due to rain or if you are ill﴾, where permission is granted to them to put them down when carrying them has become burdensome due to rain or sickness, and they are nevertheless commanded to remain alert and cautious. Then it is said: ﴿And take your precaution﴾ lest the enemy fall upon you suddenly. Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ campaigned against Muharib and Banu Anmar, and they camped, and the people did not see any of the enemy, so they put down their weapons, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out for a need of his, having put down his weapon, until he crossed the valley while the sky was sprinkling rain. The valley came between him ﷺ and his companions, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat down. Ghawrath ibn al-Harith al-Muharibi saw him and said: 'May Allah kill me if I do not kill you!' Then he descended from the mountain with his sword, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not notice him until he was standing over his head with his sword drawn from its sheath. He said: 'O Muhammad, who will protect you from me now?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic.' Then he said: 'O Allah, suffice me against Ghawrath ibn al-Harith however You will.' Then he swung the sword at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to strike him, but he fell on his face from a sudden weakness that struck him between his shoulders, and his sword slipped from him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up, took it, and said: 'O Ghawrath, who will protect you from me now?' He said: 'No one.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and I will give you your sword.' He said: 'No, but I testify that I will never fight you nor help an enemy against you.' (p-228) So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave him his sword. Ghawrath said: 'By Allah, you are better than me.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I am more deserving of that than you.'" Ghawrath then returned to his companions and related his story to them, and some of them believed. He said: The valley subsided, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ crossed over to his companions and informed them of the news.

His utterance, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ is a reason for the command to take precaution: He has prepared for them a humiliating punishment by forsaking them and granting you victory over them. So be attentive to your affairs and do not neglect the taking of means, so that His punishment may descend upon them at your hands. It has also been said: since the command to be cautious of the enemy might give the impression of expecting their dominance and their power, this impression is removed by stating that Allah, exalted is He, will grant them victory and humiliate their enemy, so that their hearts may be strengthened.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 103:

﴿So when you have finished the prayer﴾ i.e., the prayer of fear, that is, you have performed it in the manner explained and have finished with it.

﴿then remember Allah, standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾ i.e., persist in the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, and maintain your awareness of Him, your intimate conversation with Him, and your supplication to Him in all circumstances, even in the midst of sword-fighting and battle, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you encounter a company, stand firm, and remember Allah much, that you may prosper﴾.

﴿Then when you are secure﴾ i.e., when your hearts are calm from fear and you are safe, after the war has laid down its burdens.

﴿then establish the prayer﴾ i.e., the prayer whose time has then come; perform it with the proper completion of its pillars and the observance of its conditions. It has been said: the intended meaning of "remembrance" in the three states is the prayer performed in them, i.e., when you intend to perform the prayer, then pray standing during close combat, sitting on the knees while shooting arrows, and on your sides, wounded by injuries. Then, when you are secure in general, make up what you prayed in those states, which are states of anxiety and distress. This is the opinion of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and there is in it much remoteness, which is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, the prayer has been, for the believers, a decree of specified times﴾ i.e., an obligation with a set time. Mujahid said: Allah has fixed its times for them, so it must be established even in a state of fear, in the manner described. It has also been said: it is an obligation prescribed with a fixed measure in the state of residence, four rak'ahs, and in travel two rak'ahs, so it must be performed at every time according to what has been determined for it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 104:**

﴿And do not falter in pursuit of the people﴾, that is, do not weaken or slacken in pursuing the disbelievers, by fighting them and confronting them with weapons. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer, and you hope from Allah what they do not hope﴾, is a justification for the prohibition and an encouragement to them. That is: what you endure of pains is not specific to you; rather it is shared between you and them. Then they endure that, so why do you not endure, when you are more deserving of it than they are, since you hope from Allah, for the making of your religion prevail over all other religions, and for a reward in the Hereafter beyond anything that occurs to their minds? It was also read as ﴿أن تكونوا﴾ (*an takunu*), with the hamza vowelled with a fatha, meaning: do not falter, because you are suffering. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed they﴾ (*fa-innahum*), is a justification for the prohibition against weakness on account of it. The verse was revealed concerning Badr al-Sughra (the Minor Badr).

﴿And Allah was ever All-Knowing﴾, exceedingly so in knowledge, so He knows your deeds and your inner intentions.

﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He commands and prohibits. So strive diligently in complying with that, for it has praiseworthy outcomes.

(p-229) ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. It is related that "a man from the Ansar called Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, of the clan of Zafar, stole a coat of mail from his neighbour Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, in a bag of flour. The flour began to scatter from a tear in it, so he hid it with Zayd ibn al-Samin the Jew. The coat of mail was searched for at Tu'mah's, but it was not found, and he swore that he had not taken it and had no knowledge of it. So they left him and followed the trail of the flour until it led to the Jew's house, and they seized it. He said: 'Tu'mah gave it to me,' and some people from the Jews testified on his behalf. Then the clan of Zafar said: 'Come with us to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ,' and they asked him to argue on behalf of their companion. They also testified to his innocence and to the Jew's theft. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was inclined to do so, and then this was revealed." It is also related that "Tu'mah fled to Makkah and apostatised, and he dug through a wall in Makkah in order to steal from its people, but the wall fell on him and killed him. It was also said: he stayed with a man of the Banu Sulaym from the people of Makkah called al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat, and he dug through his house, but a stone fell on him, and he could neither enter nor leave. He was seized to be killed, but it was said: 'Leave him, for he has sought refuge with you.' So he was left, and they expelled him from Makkah. He joined merchants from Quda'ah heading towards Syria, and they stopped at a station, and he stole some of their goods and fled. They seized him and stoned him with stones until he died. It was also said: he boarded a ship to Jeddah, stole a purse in it containing dinars, was seized, and was thrown into the sea."

﴿So that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you﴾, i.e., by what He has made you know and revealed to you.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾, i.e., do not argue on their behalf and defend them, and they are Tu'mah and those who support him from his people, or he and whoever follows his conduct.

﴿Disputing﴾ i.e., contending on behalf of the innocent; that is, you should not dispute with the Jews on their behalf. The prohibition is coordinated with a command that the noble discourse implies, as if it were said: "So judge by it, and do not be..." etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 106:

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾ for what you had intended, relying on their testimony (ta'wil).

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, exceeding in forgiveness and mercy toward whoever seeks His forgiveness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 107:

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. That is, they betray themselves by sinning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. The sins of the sinners have been made a betrayal of themselves by them, just as they have been made a wrong done to themselves, because their harm returns to them. The relative clause (al-mawsul) may refer either to Ṭu'mah and those like him, or to him and whoever supported him and bore witness to his innocence from among his people, for they are partners with him in the sin and the betrayal.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love one who is ever a betrayer﴾, excessive in betrayal and persistent in it.

﴿Sinful﴾, immersed in it. The attaching of the absence of love, which is a metaphor for hatred and wrath, to one who is extreme in betrayal and sin is not to restrict it to him; rather it is to show the excess of Ṭu'mah and his people in both.

﴿They hide themselves from the people﴾: they conceal themselves from them, out of shame and fear of their harm.

﴿And they do not hide themselves from Allah﴾: that is, they feel no shame before Him, glorified and exalted is He, though He is more worthy that they be ashamed before Him and fear His punishment.

﴿And He is with them﴾: knowing of them and of their circumstances. So there is no way to concealment (p-230) except by abandoning what He finds abhorrent and holds them accountable for.

﴿When they devise by night﴾: they plot and fabricate.

﴿Such speech as He does not approve﴾: such as casting accusation at the innocent, false oath, and false testimony.

﴿And Allah is ever, of what they do﴾: of the actions, both apparent and hidden.

﴿Encompassing﴾: nothing of them escapes Him or eludes Him.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 4, verse 109:

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ is a shift in address (talwin lil-khitab) and a turning of the speech toward them by way of iltifat (the shift from third person to second person), signalling that enumerating their crime necessitates addressing them directly with rebuke and reproach. The phrase is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar), and His words, exalted is He, ﴿argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ form a clause that explains the occurrence of "ula'" as the predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "ula'" to be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) meaning "those who," with "argued" and what follows as its relative clause (silah). Mujadalah (argument) is the most intense form of contention (mukhasamah). The meaning is: suppose that you contended on behalf of Tu'mah and his like in the world.

﴿Who then will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: who will contend on their behalf on that day, at the time of their punishment and their chastisement?

﴿Or who will be a guardian (wakil) over them?﴾ That is: a protector and defender against the might (ba's) and retribution of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 110:

﴿And whoever does an evil﴾: a foul deed whose harm extends to another, as Ta'mah did to Qatadah and the Jew.

﴿Or wrongs himself﴾: by that which is specific to himself, such as a false oath. It is said: "evil" refers to what is less than shirk, and "wronging" refers to shirk. It is also said: they are the minor sin (saghirah) and the major sin (kabirah).

﴿Then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾: through sincere repentance (tawbah).

﴿He will find Allah Forgiving﴾: of his sins, whatever they may be.

﴿Merciful﴾: bestowing favour upon him. In this there is further encouragement for Ta'mah and his people to repent and seek forgiveness, since witnessing the traces of forgiveness and mercy by the one who repents is an added blessing, as has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 111:

﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾ of the sins.

﴿then he earns it only against himself﴾ inasmuch as its harm and its consequence do not extend to anyone else; so let him guard against exposing himself to punishment and torment, both in this world and in the next.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ intensively so in knowledge.

﴿Wise﴾ observing wisdom in everything He decrees and decides; and for this reason He does not burden a bearing soul with the burden of another.

﴿And whoever commits a sin﴾ (*khaṭī'ah*), meaning a minor sin, or a wrong done without deliberate intent among the sins. It is also read as "wa-man yakessib" (وَمَن يَكِسِّبْ), with a kasra on the kaf and a shadda on the sin, and its original form is *yaktasib* (يَكْتَسِبُ).

﴿or a grave sin﴾ (*ithm*), meaning a major sin, or one committed deliberately.

﴿then throws it﴾, meaning he hurls it or attributes it to someone. The singular pronoun, despite the plural reference, is due to the position of "or" (أوْ), and its masculine form is to give precedence to the sin (*ithm*) over the minor wrong (*khaṭī'ah*), as if it were said: "then throws one of the two." It is also read as "yarmi bihimā" (يَرْمِ بِهِما), with the dual pronoun. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the act of earning (*kasb*) indicated by His words ﴿earns﴾, and "then" (ثُمَّ) indicates delay in rank.

﴿an innocent one﴾, meaning someone innocent of what he attributed to him, so as to impose on him its immediate punishment, as Ṭu'ma did to Zayd.

﴿then he has borne﴾, meaning by what he did of transferring his offence onto the innocent one.

﴿a calumny﴾ (*buhtān*), which is a lie told against another person by which the hearer is struck dumb and bewildered because of its enormity and horror. It has also been said that it is a lie whose greatness leaves one bewildered.

﴿and a manifest sin﴾, meaning clear and gross. It is an adjective of "sin" (*ithm*). The indefinite form, which conveys magnification, is sufficient to express the greatness of the calumny, as if it were said: a calumny whose extent cannot be measured, and a manifest sin. The description of the sin with what has been mentioned is equivalent to the description of the calumny with it, because both are expressions of one matter, namely throwing an innocent person with the offence of one's own self. He has expressed it by both, to magnify the matter and make his condition appear appalling. The basis of the greatness and grandeur is that what is thrown belongs to the thrower. For throwing an innocent person with any offence, whether it is a minor sin or a grave one, is a calumny and a sin in itself. As for it being a calumny, this is obvious. As for it being a sin, this is because the offence being a minor sin with respect to the one who committed it does not necessarily make it so with respect to the one who attributed it to the innocent person. Indeed, that is definitely not permissible. How could it not be? It is a lie forbidden in all religions, so it is in itself without doubt a calumny and a sin. That the offence belongs to the thrower only intensifies it further and increases its ugliness. However, this is not because his acquired offence is added to the throwing of the innocent person; otherwise throwing without any offence would be equal to it in magnitude. Nor is it merely because it includes clearing his own sinful self; otherwise throwing without offence together with clearing himself would likewise be equal in magnitude. Rather, it is because it includes the intention of imposing his offence on the innocent one and making him bear its punishment, as is indicated by the preference for "bearing" (*iḥtimāl*) over "earning" (*iktisāb*) and the like, for it contains an indication of the reversal of his assessment, along with what it implies of the heaviness of the burden and the difficulty of the matter. Yes, by what has been mentioned, namely the combination of his earning and clearing his own self together with throwing the innocent person, the offence becomes more ugly. But that increase is a description of the whole, not of the sin alone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 113:

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ by informing you, through revelation, of what they were plotting, and alerting you to the truth. It is also said: by prophethood and infallibility (ʿiṣmah).

﴿A group of them had resolved﴾ i.e., of the Banu Zafar, who were the ones defending Ṭuʿma (Ṭuʿmah). It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "a group" is all of them, with the pronoun referring to the people. It is also said: they were the delegation of the Banu Thaqif, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "We have come to you so that you will pledge allegiance to us on condition that you do not break our idols and do not impose the tithe (ʿushr) on us." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rejected them.

﴿To lead you astray﴾ i.e., by leading you astray from judging with the truth, while they know the reality of the matter. The clause is the answer to "were it not" (lawla). He negated their resolve, although what is negated is only its influence, to signal that its influence is entirely absent. It is also said: the intended meaning is the resolve that has an effect, and there is no doubt that it is absent in reality. It is also said: the answer is omitted, i.e., "they would have misled you." And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿had resolved﴾ is a resumed (independent) clause, i.e., "indeed a group had resolved," etc.

﴿Yet they mislead none but themselves﴾ because the evil consequence of their scheming falls only upon them, without any of it striking you. The clause is a parenthetical insertion. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they cannot harm you in any way﴾ is coordinated with it. The prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-al-majrūr) is in the accusative position as an infinitive of manner (maṣdariyyah), i.e., "and they cannot harm you with any kind of harm," because He, Exalted is He, is your protector. As for what occurred to your mind, it was an action on your part based on outward appearance, out of trust in the words of those who spoke, without it occurring to your mind that the reality was contrary to that.

﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾ i.e., the Qur'an, which combines both titles. It is also said: the intended meaning of "wisdom" is the Sunnah.

﴿And taught you﴾ through revelation, from the hidden matters, among which are the ways of nullifying the plot of the hypocrites, or from the matters of religion and the rulings of the Law.

﴿What you did not know﴾ until the time of teaching.

﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been immense﴾ for there is no greater grace than general prophethood and complete leadership.

(p-232) ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾, i.e., in much of the private conversation of people.

﴿except for one who enjoins﴾, i.e., except in the secret talk of one who enjoins

﴿charity or what is right﴾. It has been said that the word "secret talk" is used figuratively to mean those who engage in it. It has also been said that *najwa* (secret talk) is the plural of *najiyy* (confidant), as related by al-Kirmani. In either case, the exception (*istithna'*) is connected (*muttasil*). It is also permissible for it to be disconnected (*munqati'*), in the sense: "But whoever enjoins charity, etc., in his secret talk there is good." The *ma'ruf* (what is right) is everything that the Sharia approves of and that reason does not reject, so it encompasses all kinds of beauty and all branches of righteous deeds. It has been interpreted here as lending, relieving the distressed, and voluntary charity, with the understanding that "charity" here means obligatory charity.

﴿or reconciliation between people﴾, when hostility and enmity arise among them, without exceeding the bounds of the noble Sharia. The word "between" (*bayn*) may either be related to the noun "reconciliation" (*islah* itself), as one says, "I reconciled between the people," or to an omitted word that is its adjective, meaning: "existing between the people."

It was narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Shall I direct you to a charity better for you than red camels?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Reconcile between people when they become corrupted, and bring them closer when they become estranged."

They said: Perhaps the secret of mentioning these three categories specifically is that a good deed which extends to people is either to convey benefit or to repel harm. Benefit is either physical, like giving wealth, to which the words of Allah the Exalted refer: ﴿except for one who enjoins charity﴾; or spiritual, to which the enjoining of what is right refers. As for repelling harm, it is indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾.

﴿And whoever does that﴾ is a reference to the matters mentioned, namely charity, what is right, and reconciliation, for it is pointed to with a demonstrative used for a plurality. The sense of distance in it, despite the recency of mention, is to signal the elevated rank of these deeds and the greatness of their status. The promise is attached to doing them immediately after explaining the excellence of enjoining them, because the primary aim is to encourage the act itself, while explaining the excellence of enjoining it serves to indicate its excellence all the more, since the basis of the goodness or ugliness of an enjoining is the goodness or ugliness of what is enjoined. Hence, when the excellence of enjoining the matters mentioned is established, the excellence of performing them is even more established. In this there is an incitement to enjoin them, and to perform them, or it is an allusion to enjoining them, as if it were said: "And whoever enjoins them." The discussion regarding the attaching of the promise to performing them is like that which preceded regarding excellence, for the reward being great in consequence of enjoining them is only because it is a means to performing them, so its being consequent upon the performance is more fitting and more deserving.

﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ is the reason for the act, and the restriction to it is because deeds are by intentions, and whoever does good for other than that reason deserves nothing from it but deprivation.

﴿then We will give him﴾, with the *nun* of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*) by way of *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person). It has also been read with the *ya'* (third person).

﴿a great reward﴾, which description falls short of describing it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 115:**

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾: The mention of the title "the Messenger" serves to display the full heinousness of the opposition and defiance they dared to commit, and to give the reason for the ruling that follows.

﴿After guidance has become clear to him﴾: The truth became manifest to him through becoming acquainted with the miracles that indicate his prophethood.

﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾: That is, other than what they are steadfast upon in belief and practice, which is the upright religion (al-din al-qayyim).

﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to﴾: That is, We shall make him a guardian (wali) over the misguidance he has taken up, and abandon him by leaving him to what he has chosen.

﴿And burn him in Hell﴾: That is, We shall cause him to enter it. It is also read with a fathah on the nun, from sala (ṣalā).

﴿And evil it is as a destination﴾: That is, Hell. In this there is an indication of the authority (hujjiyyah) of consensus (ijma') and the prohibition of opposing it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. Its interpretation has already passed earlier, and it is a repetition for emphasis and stress, or it refers to the story of Ṭu'mah, and his death as a disbeliever has already been mentioned. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that an old man from among the Arabs came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I am an old man deeply immersed in sins, but I have never associated anything with Allah since I knew Him and believed in Him, I have not taken any protector besides Him, and I have not committed sins out of boldness toward Allah, the Exalted. I never imagined, even for the blink of an eye, that I could escape Allah by fleeing. Indeed, I am remorseful, repentant, and seeking forgiveness. So what do you think of my state with Allah, the Exalted?" Then it was revealed:

﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah has certainly strayed into a far-off error﴾ from the truth, for association is the greatest kind of error and the furthest from correctness and uprightness, just as it is a slander and a great sin. For this reason the consequent in this conditional is stated as "then he has certainly strayed," etc., and in what preceded it is "then he has certainly committed a great sin," as the context of the noble composition requires, and its context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 117:

﴿They invoke nothing besides Him﴾ i.e., they worship nothing besides Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Only females﴾ meaning al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat and the like. It is related from al-Hasan that there was no tribe of the Arabs but that it had an idol which they worshipped, which they called "the female of the so-and-so clan." It was said: this is because they used to say of their idols, "They are the daughters of Allah." It was also said: this is because they used to dress them in various kinds of jewelry and adorn them in the forms of women. It was also said: what is meant is the angels, because of their saying, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It was also said: calling them "females" is due to the feminine gender of their names, or because they are in origin inanimate objects, and inanimate objects are made feminine insofar as they resemble females in being acted upon (passive). Designating them by this name serves to draw attention to the extreme foolishness of their worshippers and the utmost depth of their ignorance. "Al-Inath" is the plural of "unthā," like rabab and ruba. It was also read in the singular (as "unthā"), and "unuthan" also, as the plural of "anīth," like qalīb and qulub, or as the plural of "inath," like thimar and thumur. It was read "wuthunan" and "uthunan," with and without emphasis (tashdid), as the plural of "wathan," like your saying "usud, usd and asud" according to the original form, with the waw converted to alif, as in ujuh for wujuh.

﴿And they invoke only﴾ and they worship, by worshipping them.

﴿Only a rebellious devil﴾ for he is the one who commanded them to worship them and incited them to it, so their obedience to him was a form of worship. "Al-Marid" and "al-Marid" (the rebellious one): it is the one who does not cling to any good. The root meaning of the word is smoothness, and from it come "sarhun mumarrad" (a smooth-polished palace) and "shajarah mardā'" (a tree whose leaves have fallen off).

﴿Whom Allah cursed﴾ is a second description of "a rebellious devil" (shayṭānan).

﴿And he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion"﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause. That is, [he is] a rebellious devil (shayṭānan marīdan) who combines Allah's curse with this vile statement issued by him at the time of being cursed. And [Allah] has demonstrated that the worship of idols is the utmost error, through the causal argument (ta'līl) that those who worship them are acted upon and do not act, performing no voluntary action, and this completely contradicts divinity (al-ulūhiyyah). Then it is inferred that this is worship of Satan, which is the most heinous error in three respects. The first: he is immersed in misguidance and scarcely clings to anything of good or guidance, so obeying him is a far-off error, distant from the truth. The second: he is cursed for his misguidance, so obeying him entails nothing but curse and misguidance. The third: he is at the utmost pains to destroy and mislead them, so allying with one of this character is the utmost error, let alone worshipping him. And "mafrūḍ" means decided and cut off, i.e., a portion that was determined and specified for me, from their saying: "he imposed (faraḍa) for him in the allotment."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 119:
