﴿And I will surely lead them astray, and I will surely arouse in them false desires﴾ — the false wishes, such as prolonging life, the denial of resurrection and of punishment, and the like.

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely slit the ears of cattle﴾ — i.e., they will surely cut them, in compliance with my command, and split them without hesitation or delay. This is what the Arabs used to do with the baheera and the sa'iba (the she-camel whose ears were slit and which was set free).

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely alter﴾ — complying with it,

﴿the creation of Allah﴾ — from its natural form, either in appearance or in attribute. What has been said about gouging out the eye of the protective camel (al-hami), castrating slaves, tattooing, and filing the teeth (al-washr), and the like, falls under this. The general wording prohibits castration absolutely, but the jurists permitted it in animals because of the need (li-makan al-haja).

These statements reported of the accursed one are among what his tongue uttered, whether in speech or in state. All the lam particles in them are for oath, and the object of the command in both places is omitted, relying confidently on what the composition indicates.

﴿And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah﴾ — by preferring what he calls to over what Allah the Exalted has commanded, and by overstepping obedience to Allah the Exalted in favour of obedience to him.

﴿has surely suffered a clear loss﴾ — because he has entirely squandered his capital and exchanged his place in Paradise for his place in the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 120:

﴿He promises them﴾, i.e., [promises] what he is hardly able to fulfill.

﴿And arouses in them desires﴾, i.e., empty desires; or [it means] he makes the promise and the desire-arousing [itself] follow the pattern of the saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds." The two pronouns refer to "man" (man), and the plural [in "they"/"them"] is in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular in "yattakhidh" (﴿takes﴾) and "khasira" (﴿lost﴾) is in consideration of its wording.

﴿And Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾, which is showing benefit in what contains harm. This promise is either by casting corrupt thoughts (khawatir, "passing thoughts") or through the tongues of his allies. "Ghuruuran" (delusion) is either a second object of "yaʿidu" (promises), or an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), or an adjectival qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "a promise that is deluding"; or it is a verbal noun not of the same root as the verb, since "yaʿiduhum" carries the force of "yaghurrahum bi-waʿdihi" ("deceives them with his promise"). The clause is a parenthetical interjection. The commentary does not address "tamniyah" (desire-arousing) separately, because it is a branch of promising.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 121:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the allies of Satan, and the sense of distance contained in it (ma fihi min ma'na al-bu'd) serves to indicate how far removed their rank is in loss. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿their abode﴾ is a second subject (mubtada' thani), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿is Hell﴾ is the predicate of the second, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first.

﴿and they will not find for themselves any escape from it﴾: that is, no way of deviation (ma'dilan) and no place of flight (mahraban), derived from hasa al-himar (the donkey swerved) when it deviated. It was said: (mahis) means being freed and escaping. It was also said: al-hays is swerving away in aversion. The phrase ﴿from it﴾ (anha) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying ﴿mahisan﴾, meaning: existing away from it. Its connection to ﴿mahisan﴾ is not permissible, whether mahis is a noun of place, where it is obvious, or a verbal noun, because a verbal noun does not govern what precedes it.

(p-235) ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ He has coupled the threat against the disbelievers with the promise to the believers, to increase the joy of these and the distress of those.

﴿The promise of Allah is true.﴾ That is: He promised a promise, and He made that true, a truth. Thus the first (waAd Allah) is emphatic of itself, because the content of the nominal sentence is a promise, and the second (haqqan) is emphatic of something other than itself. It is also permissible that the relative clause be governed by an implied verb that the following words explain, and that "waAd Allah" be governed by His saying, ﴿We shall admit them﴾, since it carries the sense of "We promise them the admission into gardens," and "haqqan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the verbal noun (masdar).

﴿And who is truer in speech than Allah?﴾ This is an emphatic and eloquent sentence. The purpose of the verse is to set against the false promises of Satan to his companions the true promise of Allah to His friends, and the intensification of its emphasis is to encourage the servants to attain it. "Al-qil" is a verbal noun like "al-qawl" and "al-qal"; Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-qil" and "al-qal" are two nouns, not verbal nouns. Its accusative is as a specifier (tamyiz). It has been recited with ishmam of the sad (sad), and likewise every quiescent sad followed by a dal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 123:

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾. That is: what Allah the Most High has promised of reward is not attained by your wishful thinking, O Muslims, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; rather it is attained by faith and righteous deeds. Perhaps the juxtaposition of the wishful thinking of the People of the Book with the wishful thinking of the Muslims, despite the clear state of the former, is to signal that the wishful thinking of the Muslims is likewise of no benefit at all, as in His saying, the Most High: ﴿Nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾, as has passed.

From al-Hasan: "Faith is not by wishful thinking, but it is what settles in the heart and is confirmed by deeds. Indeed, there are people whom the hopes of forgiveness distracted until they left this world without any good deed, and they said: 'We have good expectations of Allah,' and they lied; had they had good expectations of Him, they would have done good deeds."

It has been said: the Muslims and the People of the Book boasted, and the People of the Book said: "Our prophet is before your prophet, and our book is before your book, so we are closer to Allah the Most High than you are." The Muslims said: "We are closer than you. Our prophet is the Seal of the Prophets, and our book overrides the earlier books." So this was revealed.

It has also been said: the address is to the polytheists, and this is supported by their having been mentioned earlier. That is: the matter is not by the wishful thinking of the polytheists, which is their saying: "There is no Paradise and no Fire," and their saying: "If the matter is as these people claim, we will surely be better than them and in a better state," and their saying: "I will surely be given wealth and children." Nor is it by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, which is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾, and their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few countable days﴾. Then He affirmed this by His saying, the Most High: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, because it is reported that when this was revealed, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Then who will be saved after this, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Does not grief afflict you, or sickness, or does not hardship befall you?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "That is it."

﴿And he will not find for himself, besides Allah﴾: that is, one who goes beyond the allegiance of Allah and His support.

﴿any guardian﴾: one who will be his ally.

﴿or any helper﴾: one who will help him in repelling the punishment from him.

(p-236) ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾, meaning some of them or a portion of them, for no one is able to perform all of them, nor is anyone obligated to all of them.

﴿of either male or female﴾: this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "yaʿmal" (does). "Min" here is either explanatory (li-l-bayān), or, if attached to "al-ṣāliḥāt" (righteous deeds), then "min" indicates the starting point (li-l-ibtidāʾ). That is: being from a male or female, etc.

﴿while he is a believer﴾: this is a circumstantial clause that makes the accompaniment of the deed with faith a condition for the stated reward to be sought, as a reminder that no deed is counted without it.

﴿those﴾: a demonstrative referring to "man" (whoever), with the title of being characterized by faith and righteous deeds. The plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular was used earlier in view of its wording; and the sense of distance in it (the demonstrative) is, as has been mentioned more than once, an indication of the high rank of the one referred to and the distance of his station in nobility.

﴿will enter Paradise﴾. It is also read as "yudkhalūn" (they will be admitted), in the passive voice, from "idkhāl" (admission).

﴿and they will not be wronged the slightest bit (naqīr)﴾: they will not have anything, however small and insignificant, deducted from the reward of their deeds. For "naqīr" is an idiom for smallness and insignificance. If the reward of the obedient is not diminished, then it is all the more fitting and proper that the punishment of the disobedient not be increased. How could it not be so, when the One who recompenses is the Most Merciful of the merciful? And this is the secret of confining the mention to it immediately after the reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 125:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾ That is: who sincerely devotes himself to Him, the Exalted, recognizing no lord other than Him. It has also been said: who lays his face down for Him in prostration. It has also been said: who makes his deed sincere for Him, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: who entrusts his affair to Him, the Exalted. This is a denial and a rhetorical expression of improbability, that anyone should be better in religion than one who does this, or equal to him. Although the structure of the sentence does not explicitly address the denial or the negation of equality, the prevalent usage and common idiom guide you to it. For when it is said, "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "Is there no one more excellent than so-and-so?", what is meant, definitively, is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. It is on this pattern that the words of the Exalted go, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾, and their like. "Dinan" (in religion) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of "ahsanu" (better), transferred from the subject. The implied sense is: and whose religion is better than the religion of one who submitted, etc. Thus the preference is in reality between the two religions, not between their two adherents. In this there is an indication that this is the utmost to which human capacity can attain.

﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ That is: one who performs good deeds and abstains from evil deeds, or one who performs righteous deeds in the proper manner, which is their descriptive goodness that necessitates their intrinsic goodness. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it by saying: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "aslama" (submitted).

﴿And follows the religion of Abraham﴾ the one that agrees with the religion of Islam, whose correctness and acceptance are agreed upon.

﴿Hanifan﴾ inclining away from the deviant religions. It is a circumstantial clause either from the subject of "ittaba'a" (followed) or from "Abraham."

﴿And Allah took Abraham as a khalil (intimate friend)﴾ He chose him and singled him out with honours resembling the honours of an intimate friend with his friend. The use of the explicit noun (Abraham) in a place where a pronoun could have been used serves to magnify his station, to specify that he is the one being praised, and to emphasize the independence of this parenthetical clause. "Khullah" (intimate friendship) is from "khilal" (interstice), for it is a love that penetrates the soul and mingles with it. It has also been said: it is from "khalal" (deficiency), since each of the two friends fills the deficiency of the other; or from "khall," which is a path in sand, since the two agree in the way; or from "khallah" (trait) in the sense of "khaslah," since the two agree in their qualities. The benefit of this parenthetical clause is abundant, among which is encouragement to follow his religion, peace be upon him. For whoever attains to such nearness to Allah, the Exalted, as to be rightly called a khalil, is worthy that following his way should be the most important matter to which the necks of resolve stretch and the most noble object toward which the eyes of nations gaze. It is said that he, peace be upon him, sent to a friend of his in Egypt during a famine that afflicted the people, seeking provisions from him. His friend said: "If Abraham were seeking provisions for himself, I would have done it, but he wants them for guests, and we too have been afflicted with what has afflicted the people of hardship." So his servants, peace be upon him, returned, passing by a soft valley, and they filled sacks from it out of shame before the people, and brought them to the house of Abraham, peace be upon him, and cast them there and dispersed. One of them came and informed Abraham of the story, and he was greatly grieved by this, especially since people had gathered at his door hoping for food, and his eyes overcame him. Sarah went to the sacks, and found in them the finest of wheat flour, and she baked bread (in another narration, she fed the people). Abraham, peace be upon him, awoke and smelled the aroma of bread, and said: "From where did you get this?" Sarah said: "From your Egyptian friend." He said: "Rather, it is from my Friend, Allah, Mighty and Majestic." So Allah, the Exalted, named him khalil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 126:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This is an independent clause (jumlah mubtada'ah), brought to affirm the obligation of obedience to Allah, the Exalted, upon the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, by explaining that all the existent things in them belong to Him, the Exalted, in creation and in ownership, and that nothing of them lies outside His dominion (malakut), so that He recompenses each one according to what its deeds require, good and evil. It has been said: it is to explain that His taking Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as a khalil (intimate friend) is not because He, glorified be He, has any need for that in any of His affairs, as is the custom of human beings, for the basis of their friendship (khullah) is that some of them need others in their interests; rather, it is merely for the honouring and ennobling of him, peace be upon him. It has been said: it is to explain that the khullah does not remove him from the rank of servanthood ('ubudiyyah). It has been said: it is to explain that his, peace be upon him, being chosen for the khullah is by the sheer will of Allah, the Exalted, i.e., to Him belongs whatever is in them, all of it, and He chooses from them whatever He wills.

And the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing.﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) that affirms the content of what precedes it in the aforementioned respects, for His encompassing, in knowledge and power, of all things, of which is included what is in the heavens and the earth, among the accountable beings and their deeds, affirms that with the most complete affirmation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, verse 127:**

﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women.﴾ That is, concerning their rights in general, as the rulings that follow indicate, and not concerning their inheritance alone. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about many matters relating to women. The ruling on what had already been explained earlier was referred back to what had been revealed about it in the Book. As for what had not yet had its ruling explained, it is addressed here, and this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and [so does] what is recited to you in the Book."﴾ The giving of the ruling (*ifta'*), which is the clarification of what is ambiguous and the elucidation of what is obscure, is attributed to Him and to what was recited from the Book earlier, on two accounts, following the pattern of your saying, "Zayd and his generosity have enriched me." Here *ma* (what) is conjoined either to the subject (*mubtada'*) or to its pronoun in the predicate, because of the separation by the object and the prepositional phrase (*al-maf'ul wa al-jarr wa al-majrur*). The use of the present tense (*al-mudari'*) signals the continuity and permanence of the recitation. The phrase ﴿in the Book﴾ may be connected either to ﴿is recited﴾ or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the implicit pronoun within it, meaning: "recited, being in it." It is also permissible for ﴿what is recited to you﴾ to be the subject (*mubtada'*), with ﴿in the Book﴾ as its predicate, where by "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*). In that case the clause is a parenthetical insertion (*mu'taridah*) intended to show the great importance of what is recited to them, and that justice in the rights stated therein is among the great matters that must be observed and preserved. Thus what is recited covers both what has been recited and what will be recited. It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive case as an oath (*qasam*), which indicates the exaltation and magnification of the one sworn by, as though it were said: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and I swear by what is recited to you in the Book." Thus His statement, ﴿gives you a ruling﴾, means His earlier and later clarification. There is no justification for conjoining it to the genitive pronoun in ﴿concerning them﴾, because that is faulty both in wording and in meaning. As for His statement, ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾, according to the first mode, which is the most evident, it is connected to ﴿is recited﴾, meaning: what is recited to you concerning their affair. According to the latter two modes, it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿concerning them﴾. This idafa (construct) is in the sense of "from" (*min*), since it is the attribution of a thing to its own kind. It has also been read as *yaYama* (with *ya*), by changing the hamza of *ayama* into *ya*.

﴿To whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them.﴾ That is, what has been decreed for them of inheritance and other things.

﴿And you desire﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause (*silah*), as a conjunction of an affirmative clause to a negative clause. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of ﴿you give them﴾, interpreted as: "while you desire." There is no doubt that the restriction of the non-giving to this condition has no evident benefit unless what has been prescribed for them is understood to mean their dowry (*sadaq*).

﴿To marry them﴾ means: in marrying them, not for the sake of enjoying them, but for consuming their wealth. Or it means: marrying them without completing the dowry. This is what has been reported from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), that the orphan girl would be under the guardianship of her guardian (*waliyy*), who would desire her wealth and beauty and wish to marry her for less than the customary dowry of her peers. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they dealt justly with them in completing the dowry. Or it means: [forbidden] from marrying them. This is what has been reported from her (may Allah be pleased with her): that she was an orphan whose guardian was averse to marrying her and did not marry her off, withholding her out of greed for her inheritance. In another report from her (may Allah be pleased with her): it is a man who has an orphan girl in his charge, who is also his heir and his partner in the property, even in a date palm cluster, so he desires to marry her and dislikes giving her to another man, lest he share with him in his property by the share she holds, so he withholds her. Thus what has been prescribed for them, in the first and last modes, means their inheritance, and what is recited concerning them. In the second mode it means their dowry, and what is recited concerning them. His statements, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ and ﴿And do not consume it﴾, and similar texts that indicate the prohibition of encroaching upon their property, relate to the first mode. The second mode concerns their dowry, and what is recited concerning them in His statement, ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans﴾, and the verse that follows.

﴿And the weak among the children﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the orphan women﴾ and to what is recited concerning them. His statement, ﴿Allah instructs you﴾, and so on. In the Jahiliyyah they did not give them inheritance, just as they did not give women inheritance; they gave inheritance only to the men who were capable of managing affairs. It has been reported that 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "We have been informed that you give the daughter half and the sister half, while we used to give inheritance only to one who fights in battle and takes the spoils." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Thus I have been commanded."

﴿And that you stand up for the orphans with justice﴾ is in the genitive case (*bi al-jarr*) as a conjunction to what precedes it, and to what is recited concerning them. His statement, ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property﴾, and similar things that are almost countless, is for the case where ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ is connected to ﴿is recited﴾. As for the case where it is a substitute for ﴿concerning them﴾, the correct reading is that it is in the accusative case (*nasb*), as a conjunction to the position of ﴿concerning them﴾, meaning: "He gives you a ruling that you should stand up." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by implying a verb, meaning: "and He commands you," and this is an address to the rulers, or to the guardians and executors.

﴿And whatever good you do﴾ concerning the rights of those mentioned.

﴿Of good﴾, as you have been commanded, or whatever good you do in general, so that what relates to them falls within it by primary inclusion (*indiraj awwali*).

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾, so He will recompense you according to it.

(p-239) ﴿And if a woman fears﴾ This begins an explanation of matters not clarified in the rulings previously mentioned, meaning: if a woman anticipates

﴿ill-treatment (nushuz) from her husband﴾ That is, his turning away from her and his haughtiness toward her companionship, out of dislike for her and withholding of her rights.

﴿or aversion﴾ That is, by his speaking with her and being companionable with her less, due to what such inclinations and causes require.

﴿there is no blame upon them both﴾ at that time

﴿if they reconcile between themselves in reconciliation﴾ That is, in reconciling between themselves, by her remitting to him part or all of the dower, or part of her turn (qasm), as Sawda bint Zam'a did when she feared that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she gave her day to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Or by her giving him something to win his affection. The reading "yaṣṣālaḥā" (from yatasālaḥā) and "yaṣṣalliḥā" (from yaṣṭalliḥā) and "yuṣālliḥā" (from the form of mufā'ala) were also recited, and the word "ṣulḥan" (reconciliation) is either in the accusative governed by the verb mentioned, under every reading, being a verbal noun (maṣdar) of it with its augmenting letters dropped (the verbal noun, maṣdar, being the basic noun of action derived from the verb). It may also be expressed by the noun of the verbal action (ism al-maṣdar), as if it were said: "iṣlāḥan" (reforming), "tasalluḥan" (reconciling) or "iṣṭilāḥan" (making peace), according to how the verb was read. Or it is governed by a verb following from what was mentioned, meaning: "so he reforms their condition by reconciliation." "Baynahumā" (between them) is either an adverbial complement of the verb or a circumstantial (ḥāl) qualifier of "ṣulḥan." The mention of the negation of blame from them both, although blame does not fall on her from taking (the dower or part of her turn), which is what would usually be the cause of blame, is to show that this reconciliation is not of the kind of forbidden bribery (rishwa) for the giver and the taker alike.

﴿And reconciliation is better﴾ That is, better than separation, or better than bad companionship, or better than enmity. Thus the definite article (al-) is for a specific reference, or it means: it is better than [all] goods, so the article is generic. This clause is a parenthetical statement confirming what precedes it. Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And souls have been made present to stinginess﴾, meaning: they have been made ever-present to it, inherently disposed to it, never separating from it at all. So a woman does not readily give up her rights from the man, nor does a man generously give up good companionship with her when she is plain. In this there is a confirmation and establishment of reconciliation, by urging each of them toward it. But not by looking at one's own condition, for that would call for prolonged haggling and dispute. Rather it is by looking at the condition of the other party: the man's stinginess and his lack of inclination away from his natural disposition, without being won over, is what moves the woman to yield some of her rights to him in order to win him over. Likewise, the woman's stinginess with her rights moves the man to be content on her part with something small and not to demand that she give up much. Thus that reconciliation is realised.

﴿And if you do good﴾ in companionship.

﴿and are mindful (of God)﴾ regarding ill-treatment and aversion, even if the causes calling to them combine, and you are patient with that, observing the rights of companionship, and you do not compel them to give up any of their rights.

﴿then indeed Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ That is, of the good and the mindfulness, or of what you do altogether, so that this enters into it primarily.

﴿All-Aware﴾ So He will reward you and recompense you for that, definitely, since it is impossible that He should waste the reward of the good-doers. In the address to the husbands by way of iltifat (shift from third to second person), and the expression of observing their rights with good conduct, and the word "taqwā" (mindfulness), which indicates that ill-treatment and aversion are things to be guarded against, and the placement of the generous promise upon it, there is an evident gentleness of winning them over and encouragement toward good treatment. It was narrated that it was revealed concerning Amra bint Muhammad ibn Maslama and her husband Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', who married her when she was young. When old age overtook her, he married a young woman, preferred her over her, and neglected her. So she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him about that. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Sa'ib. He had a wife who had grown old, and he had children from her. He wanted to divorce her and marry someone else. She said: "Do not divorce me, and leave me with my children. Allot me a turn every two months if you wish, and if you wish, do not allot me a turn." He said: "If that is acceptable, it is dearer to me." So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and this verse was revealed. (p-240)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 129:

﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you strive to do so﴾. That is: it is impossible for you to be able to be equitable between them in such a way that no inclination at all occurs toward one of them in any matter whatsoever. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to divide his time among his wives and act justly, then he would say: "O Allah, this is my division in what I control, so do not hold me accountable for what You control and I do not control." And in another narration: "And You know best what I do not control," meaning his excessive love for Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

﴿Even if you are eager﴾: that is, eager to establish justice and exerting yourselves in that.

﴿So do not incline with complete inclination﴾: that is, do not act with complete injustice toward the one you are averse to, and be just as much as you are able. For your inability to achieve the true reality of justice only establishes that you are not obligated to it, not that you are excused from what falls short of it among the levels within your capacity.

﴿So that you leave her﴾: that is, the one toward whom you have inclined.

﴿Like one suspended﴾: who is neither married nor divorced. It was also read as "like one imprisoned." And in a hadith: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides leaning."

﴿And if you amend﴾ what you used to corrupt of their affairs.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding inclination in the future.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, forgiving you for the inclination that has passed from you, ﴿Merciful﴾, bestowing His favor upon you by His mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 130:

﴿And if they separate﴾ It is also read "yatafaraqa" (with the verb in the form that means mutual separation). That is: if each of them parts from his companion, such that no agreement is reached between them in any respect, whether by reconciliation or otherwise.

﴿Allah will make each of them independent﴾ of the other, meaning: He will make him free of need of the other, and will suffice him in his affairs.

﴿out of His abundance﴾ out of His wealth and power. In this there is a deterrence for both of them from separation, despite the other's displeasure.

﴿And Allah is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise﴾ Almighty, perfect in His acts and His judgments.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 131:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, that is, of the existing things, whatever creatures there are and their provisions and other things. It is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) drawing attention to the perfection of His vastness and the greatness of His power.

﴿And We have certainly enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, that is, We commanded them in their Scripture, and they are the Jews and the Christians and those before them of the nations. The lam in "al-kitab" is for the genus (li-l-jins), and "min" (from) is connected to "wassaynā" (We enjoined) or to "ūtū" (were given).

﴿And [you]﴾ is a conjunction with the relative clause (ma'tuf 'ala al-mawsul).

﴿That fear Allah﴾, that is: We enjoined each of you and them with "an ittaqu Allah" (that fear Allah), on the basis that "an" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah) from which the preposition has been omitted. It is also permissible for it to be an explanatory particle (mufassirah), since the enjoining carries the sense of saying. Then His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is, in that case, a continuation of the reported speech, that is: "And We indeed said to them and to you, 'Fear Allah; and if you disbelieve…'" to the end of the verse. And on the assumption that "an" is masdariyyah, the construction implies the intention of speech, that is: We commanded them and you with piety and said to them and to you, ﴿if you disbelieve﴾ — the verse. It has also been said that it is a resumptive sentence addressed to this community. In any case, what is consequent upon their disbelief is not the content of His saying ﴿then indeed to Allah belongs﴾ — the verse — but rather the command to know it. As if it were said: "And if you disbelieve, then know that to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" (p-241) of the creatures entirely, who are in need of Him for existence and all the blessings that branch from it, and who cannot be independent of His overflow even for the blink of an eye. So His right is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, that His punishment be feared, and that His reward be hoped for. This He has established by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is ever Free of need﴾, that is, free of the creatures and their worship.

﴿Praiseworthy﴾, praised in His essence, whether they praise Him or not. So He is not harmed by their disbelief and their disobedience, just as He does not benefit from their gratitude and their piety. He enjoined them with piety only out of His mercy, not out of need.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 132:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This is an independent statement, addressed to the audience, serving as a preface (tawti'ah) to what follows of the conditional clause (al-shartiyyah), and it is not included within the reported speech. That is: to Him, glorified is He, belongs whatever is in them of creatures, by creation and by ownership; He disposes of them as He wills, bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Guardian (wakil).﴾ In managing the affairs of all things and all matters. Therefore one must place one's reliance (yatawakkal) upon Him alone, and not upon anyone other than Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 133:

﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people,﴾ i.e., destroy you and utterly uproot you.

﴿and bring others﴾ i.e., and immediately produce in your place another people from mankind, or other creatures in place of humankind. The object of the will (mashi'ah) is omitted because it is implied by the conditional response (al-jaza'), i.e., "If He wills your annihilation and the bringing into being of others, He will remove you," and so on. The meaning is that your being left in your disobedience is only due to His complete independence from your obedience and to His will, which is founded on profound wisdoms, not being related to your annihilation, not because of any incapacity on His part, exalted is He, far above that by a great exaltation.

﴿And God is over all that﴾ i.e., over annihilating you utterly and bringing others into being in your place at once.

﴿Capable﴾: of perfect power. In it, especially in placing the address (khitab) between the conditional clause and what is conjoined to it, there is an intensification of the threat that is not hidden. It has been said: it is an address to those Arabs who opposed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), i.e., "If He wills, He will cause you to die and will bring other people who will support him." Its meaning is the same as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be the likes of you.﴾ It is also related that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck the back of Salman with his hand and said: "They are the people of this one," meaning the sons of Persia.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 134:

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ — like the warrior who, in his struggle, desires the spoil of war.

﴿Then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter﴾ — that is: with Him, exalted is He, is the reward of both for him, if he desires it. Why then would he seek the lowlier of the two? Let him seek both, like one who says: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾. Or let him seek the nobler of the two, for whoever struggles sincerely for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, the spoil will not miss him, and for him in the Hereafter is that which, in comparison to it, is as nothing. That is: with Allah is the reward of both abodes, and He gives each what he desires, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth﴾, and so on.

﴿And Allah is ever Hearing, Seeing﴾ — knowing all that is heard and seen, so that the words and deeds that proceed from them, which relate to their intentions, are included in that knowledge in the first place.

(p-242) ﴿O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice﴾, exceeding in justice and in establishing equity in all matters, striving in that with the utmost striving.

﴿Witnesses for God﴾, establishing your testimonies for the sake of God Most High, with truth. This is a second predicate (khabar thani); it has also been said to be a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Even if it be against yourselves﴾, i.e., even if the testimony is against yourselves, by acknowledging it, since testimony is an expression for informing of another's right, whether that right is owed by the witness himself or by a third party, such that the testimony entails consequences from the side of the one testified against.

﴿Or parents and relatives﴾, i.e., even if it is against your parents and relatives.

﴿Whether he be rich﴾, i.e., the one testified against, ﴿rich﴾: his pleasure is ordinarily to be sought and his anger to be feared.

﴿Or poor﴾: he is ordinarily to be pitied. It is read "If there be a rich one or a poor one" (in ghaniyyun aw faqirun), with kana being complete (tammah), and the answer of the condition omitted, indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿God is more appropriate to both of them﴾ over it. That is: do not refrain from it out of seeking the pleasure of the rich or out of pity for the poor, for God Most High is more worthy of the two kinds of rich and poor indicated by what was mentioned. Had the testimony against them not been a benefit for them, He would not have legislated it. It is also read "awla bihim" (more appropriate to them).

﴿So do not follow desire, lest you deviate﴾, i.e., lest you swerve from the truth, for following desire is among the sources of injustice, which must be feared and guarded against. It has also been said: out of aversion to being just among people, or intending to deviate from the truth.

﴿And if you distort﴾, i.e., your tongues from the testimony of truth or the judgment of justice, by delivering it not in its proper form. It is read "wa in talu" (from wilaya and taṣaddi, i.e., to take charge), meaning: if you take charge of establishing the testimony.

﴿Or refuse﴾, i.e., to establish it altogether.

﴿Then indeed God is ever, of what you do﴾, of distorting of tongues and outright refusal, or of all deeds, of which this is among the parts.

﴿Acquainted﴾: He will certainly recompense you for that. So on the well-known reading it is a pure threat, and on the last reading it contains a threat.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 136:**

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an address to all Muslims. So the meaning of His, the Exalted's, words, ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before﴾, is: remain steadfast in faith in these things, persist in it, and increase in tranquility and certainty regarding it. Or it means: believe in what has been mentioned in detail, on the basis that the faith of some of them was general (ijmali). By "the second Book" is meant the category (jins) that encompasses all the heavenly books, in accordance with His words, ﴿and His books﴾. Believing in it means believing that each of those books was sent down from Him, the Exalted, upon a particular messenger, to guide his community to the religion He prescribed for them through commands and prohibitions. However, this does not mean that the basis of faith in each of those books is the specific character of that book, nor that the rulings and laws of those books remain in full force, nor that what remains of them is valid in relation to them. Rather, it means that faith in all of them is included within faith in the Book sent down upon His Messenger, that the rulings of each of them were true and established until the arrival of what abrogated them (naskh), and that whatever of their laws and rulings has not been abrogated up to now is established insofar as it is among the rulings of this glorious and preserved Book, which is safe from abrogation and alteration, as has passed in the commentary on the end of Surah al-Baqarah.

"Nuzzila" and "unzila" have also been read in the passive voice.

It has been said that the address is to the believers among the People of the Book, because Abdullah ibn Salam, his nephew Salama, his nephew Salama, Asad, Usayd, the two sons of Ka'b, Tha'labah ibn Qays, and Yamin ibn Yamin came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you, in your Book, in Musa, in the Torah, and in Uzayr, and we disbelieve in anything other than that of the books and messengers." So he ﷺ said: "Nay, believe in Allah and His Messenger Muhammad, and in his Book, the Qur'an, and in every Book that came before it." They said: "We will not do that." So it was revealed: ﴿Believe﴾, and they all believed. So He commanded them to believe in the Book that encompasses the Torah, although they had already believed in it before. This is not because the meaning of faith is that which includes its initiation and steadfastness in it, nor because the object of the command in reality is faith in what is other than the Torah, as if it were said: "Believe in all of them and do not single out some over others." Rather, it is because what is commanded is faith in them within faith in the Qur'an, in the manner indicated just above, not their previous faith. Also, it involves urging them to treat those (the Torah and the Gospel) and the other books equally in confirmation, since all of them share in what requires it, namely descent from Allah, the Exalted.

It has also been said that it is an address to the People of the Two Books (Jews and Christians). The meaning then is: believe in all of them, not in some to the exclusion of others. He commanded each group to believe in its own book within the command to believe in the category of Book, for the reason mentioned.

It has also been said that it is addressed to the hypocrites, and the meaning is: believe with your hearts, not merely with your tongues.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day﴾ means: in any one of these things.

﴿Then he has strayed far astray﴾ from the goal, to the extent that he is hardly likely to return to the path. The mention of the angels and the Last Day on the side of disbelief is because disbelief in either of them means that faith is not realized at all. The plural of "books" and "messengers" is because disbelief in one book or one messenger is disbelief in all of them. The messenger is mentioned first in the earlier part because the Book is referred to in terms of its being sent down upon him, while the angels and the books are mentioned before the messengers because they are intermediaries between Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the messengers in the sending down of the books.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 137:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾ Qatada said: They are the Jews, who believed in Musa (Moses).

﴿Then they disbelieved﴾ by their worship of the calf.

﴿Then they believed﴾ when he (Musa) returned to them.

﴿Then they disbelieved﴾ in Isa (Jesus) and the Injil (Gospel).

﴿Then they increased in disbelief﴾ by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: they are a people among whom apostasy was repeated, who persisted in disbelief and increased in persistent error.

﴿Allah would not be one to forgive them, nor to guide them to a way﴾ because it is deemed unlikely of them that they would repent from disbelief and remain steadfast in faith, for their hearts have been stamped with disbelief and accustomed to apostasy, and faith had become for them the least and lowliest of things. This does not mean that if they sincerely professed faith it would not be accepted from them or that they would not be forgiven. The predicate of "kana" is omitted, meaning: "wanting to forgive them."

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that for them there is a painful punishment﴾ indicates that what is meant by those mentioned are those who professed faith outwardly, while disbelieving in secret, time after time, then they increased in disbelief and hypocrisy. And He placed "give good news" (bashshir) in the place of "warn" (andhir) as a mockery of them. (p-244)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 139:

﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies﴾ is in a position of accusative or nominative, by way of censure, in the sense of "those who are meant by them" or "they are the ones who". It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an attribute of "the hypocrites". His words, exalted is He, ﴿rather than the believers﴾, are a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yattakhidhun" (take), meaning: they take the disbelievers as helpers, passing beyond the guardianship of the believers. They used to befriend them, and some of them would say to others: "The affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) will not be completed, so let us turn to the Jews."

﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾ is a rebuke of their opinion, a refutation of it, a declaration of the failure of their hope, and a cutting off of their empty greed. The sentence is parenthetical, confirming what precedes it. That is, do they seek through allegiance to the disbelievers power and dominance? Al-Wahidi said: the original meaning of "'izza (honour) is strength, and from it comes the saying "'azaz" for hard, firm ground. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, honour belongs to Allah entirely﴾, are a justification for what the rebuking interrogative implies, namely the falsity of their opinion and the failure of their hope. For the entirety of the individual instances of honour is confined to His presence, may He be mighty and exalted, such that none attains it except His allies, to whom He has decreed honour and dominance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, which decides the invalidity of seeking strength through other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, and the impossibility of benefiting from it. It has also been said that it is the response to an omitted condition, as if it were said: "If they seek honour with them, then indeed honour belongs to Allah." And "jami'an" (entirely) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in His words, exalted is He, ﴿lillah﴾ (belongs to Allah), because it depends on the subject (mubtada').

**﴿And He has already sent down to you﴾** This is an address to the hypocrites by way of *iltifat* (a shift from third person to second person), which serves to intensify the rebuke that the enumeration of their misdeeds calls for. It is also read in the passive voice, *nuzzila* (from *tanzil* and *inzal*), and *nazala* is read as well, with the lighter form. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun in ﴿they take﴾. It also serves to express the utter repugnance of their condition and the extreme extent of their defiance against Him, glorified is He, by stating that they did what they did, namely taking the disbelievers as allies, even though there was in place what should have prevented them from doing so: the explicit prohibition against sitting with them. That prohibition necessarily implies a prohibition against allying with them, expressed in the most emphatic and forceful manner, following an interjected clause (*jumla mu'tarida*) that states the absence of what would have prompted them to it. It is as if it were said: "You take them as allies, while God, exalted is He, has already sent down to you before this, in Mecca,"

**﴿in the Book﴾** That is, the Noble Qur'an.

**﴿that when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse﴾** This corresponds to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs, turn away from them﴾ (6:68). This requires withdrawing from their company in that disgraceful condition, so how much more so from allying with them and seeking their honor. The word *"an"* (أنْ) here is the lightened form of *inna* (أنَّ), and the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), which is its noun, is omitted, and the conditional clause is its predicate. The phrase ﴿is disbelieved in by them﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to "God's signs," and His words ﴿and mocked by them﴾ are coordinated with it and fall under the same circumstantial function. The idafa (construction) of "signs" to the Glorious Name serves to honor them, to demonstrate their importance, and to magnify the enormity of disbelieving in them. The meaning is: He has sent down to you in the Book that when you hear God's signs being disbelieved in and mocked. This indicates that what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, even though addressed to him specifically, is revealed for the whole community, and that the basis for turning away from them is knowledge of their engaging in discourse about the signs. For this reason, that matter is expressed at one time by "seeing" and at another by "hearing." It also indicates that the intended turning away is the manifestation of opposition by rising from their gatherings, not mere aversion in the heart or the face alone. The pronoun in ﴿with them﴾ refers to the disbelievers implied by His words ﴿is disbelieved in by them and mocked by them﴾.

**﴿Indeed you would then be like them﴾** This is a resumptive clause (*jumla musta'nafa*), brought in to give the reason for the prohibition, and it does not fall under the revelation. The word *idhan* (إذَنْ) is nullified from governing, since it occurs between the subject and the predicate. The meaning is: do not sit with them at that time, for if you do, you would be like them in disbelief and in incurring punishment. The singular "like" (*mithl*) is used either because it functions like a verbal noun (*masdar*), or because it is sufficient with the plural construction that follows. It is read anomalously as *mithlahum* with a fatha, because it is attached to a noun that is indeclinable (*ghayr mutamakkin*), as in His words: ﴿just as you speak﴾ (51:23). It has also been said that it is in the accusative of place (*zarfiyya*), meaning: in the likeness of their condition.

**﴿Indeed God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them﴾** This is the reason for their being like them in disbelief, by stating what that entails of sharing with them in the punishment. By "the hypocrites" is meant either the addressees, and the apparent noun has been placed in the position of their pronoun to brand them with hypocrisy and to give the ruling a reason derived from its etymology; or it refers to the category (*jins*), and they are included within it in the first place. The placing of "the hypocrites" before "the disbelievers" serves to intensify the threat against the addressees. "All of them" is in the accusative in the same way as what precedes it.

﴿الَّذِينَ يَتَرَبَّصُونَ بِكُمْ﴾ ("those who wait in expectation of you") is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning towards the believers, enumerating another of the hypocrites' misdeeds and vile acts. It is either a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitute) for ﴿الَّذِينَ يَتَّخِذُونَ﴾ ("those who take"), or a qualifier (sifah, a descriptive attribute) applying to the hypocrites alone, since they are the ones who wait, not the disbelievers. It may also be in the nominative or the accusative in censure (dhamm), meaning: they wait for your affair and for what happens to you of victory or defeat. The "fa" (the particle فَ) in His words ﴿فَإنْ كانَ لَكم فَتْحٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So if there comes to you a victory from God") serves to make its content follow from what precedes it, since the report of their waiting entails the report of what happens after it, just as the waiting itself calls for something the one who waits expects to occur.

﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they say"), i.e., to you.

﴿ألَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ﴾ ("Were we not with you?"), i.e., supporting you, so give us a share of the spoils.

﴿وَإنْ كانَ لِلْكافِرِينَ نَصِيبٌ﴾ ("and if the disbelievers have a share") of the war, for it is alternating (sijal, turns of fortune).

﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they say"), i.e., to the disbelievers.

﴿ألَمْ نَسْتَحْوِذْ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("Did we not gain mastery over you?"), i.e., did we not overcome you and gain the power to fight you and take you captive, so that we spared you.

﴿وَنَمْنَعْكم مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and protect you from the believers"), by discouraging them from you, and by making them imagine what weakened their hearts, so they became sick in fighting you, and we were lax in supporting them; otherwise you would have been plunder for calamities. So hand over to us a share of what you have gained. The naming of the Muslims' triumph as "fath" (victory) and of the disbelievers' portion as merely "nasib" (a share) serves to magnify the Muslims' standing and belittle the disbelievers' lot. "وَنَمْنَعَكُمْ" ("and protect you", with the naṣb form) was also read, with the implied "an" (idmar an, the understood particle أنْ) before the verb.

﴿فاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ ("So God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection"), with a judgment befitting each of you regarding reward and punishment. As for this world, He has applied to whoever utters the word of Islam its ruling, and He did not lay the sword upon those who spoke it hypocritically.

﴿وَلَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لِلْكافِرِينَ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلا﴾ ("And God will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers") then, just as He may grant it in this world by way of trial (ibtila', testing) and gradual lure (istidraj, drawing on step by step), or it may refer to this world, with the meaning of "sabil" (way) being proof (hujjah).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 142:**

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites think they deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them.﴾ This is a fresh statement (*mubtada'*, an independent sentence) brought to explain another aspect of their ugly deeds. That is: they do what a deceiver does, by displaying faith and concealing its opposite. Allah, for His part, does to them what the dominant party does in deception: He leaves them in this world with their lives and property protected, and He has prepared for them in the Hereafter the lowest level of the Fire. The detailed discussion of this has already passed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. It has also been said: they will be given a light upon the Path (*al-Sirat*) as the believers are given light. They will proceed by their light, then their light will be extinguished while the light of the believers remains, and they will call out: "Wait for us, that we may borrow some of your light."

﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily﴾, heavy and sluggish, like one who is compelled to do the act. It is recited with the *kaf* vowelled with a *fatha* (*kusala*), and both forms (*kusali* and *kusala*) are plurals of *kaslan* (lazy).

﴿They show off to people﴾, so that they may think them to be believers. The word *al-muraa'ah* is a form of *mufa'alah* with the meaning of *tafil* (intensive form), like *na'ima* and *na'im*; or it is for reciprocity, since the one who shows off displays his deed to another, and that other displays to him his approval. The clause is either a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) built upon a question arising from the preceding speech, as if it were said: "What do they intend by standing for it lazily?" and it was answered: "They show off," and so on; or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun in "*qamu*" (they stood).

﴿And they remember Allah only a little﴾. This is coordinated (*'atf*) upon "they show off." That is: they do not remember Him, glorified is He, except with a little remembrance, namely their remembrance with the tongue, since compared with remembrance by the heart, it is little. Or it means: only for a little time. Or it means: they pray only a little, since they pray only in the sight of people, and that is little. It has also been said: they do not remember Him, exalted is He, in the prayer except a little, at the *takbir* (saying "Allahu akbar") and at the *taslim* (the closing salutation).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 143:

﴿Wavering between that⦆ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject of "yurā'ūn" (they show off), or it is in the accusative of censure (manṣūb ʿalā al-dhamm). "That" (dhālika) is a reference to faith and disbelief, which are understood from the context (bi-ma'ūnat al-maqām). That is: wavering between them, bewildered, whom Satan has made to waver (dhabdhabahumu al-shaytān). The true meaning of mudhabdhab is what is pushed and repelled from both sides, time after time. It was also read with a kasra on the dhāl, meaning mudhabdhibīna qulūbahum (making their hearts waver), or their opinion, or their religion; or it has the meaning of mutadhabdhibīna, just as ṣalṣala has the meaning of nuṣalṣilu. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, the reading is "mutadhabdhibīn." It was also read as "mudabdibīn" with an undotted dāl, and it seems the meaning is that they were seized in one way (dubba), that is, one path, and then in another.

﴿Neither to these nor to those⦆ That is: neither attributed to the believers nor attributed to the disbelievers; or neither inclining toward the former nor toward the latter. Its place is in the accusative, as it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "mudhabdhabīn," or as an apposition (badal) from it, or as an explanation and clarification of it.

﴿And whomever Allah sends astray⦆ because of his lack of readiness for guidance and success.

﴿you will not find for him any way⦆ leading to the truth and rightness, let alone that you guide him to it. The address is to everyone who is fit for it, whoever he may be.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 144:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾. They are forbidden explicitly from allying with the disbelievers (kafara), although the description of the state of the hypocrites contains a deterrent from that, [given] the exaggeration in warning and caution.

﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority over you?﴾ That is: do you wish, by that, to give Allah a clear proof against you that you are hypocrites, for their alliance is the most evident proof of hypocrisy; or an authority by which He would impose His punishment upon you? The denial is directed at the wish itself rather than at its object, by saying: "Do you make...?" The emphasis in denying it and magnifying its gravity lies in showing that it is something that a sensible person would not wish, let alone that it would proceed from him, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger?﴾.

(p-247) ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾. This is the stratum at the very bottom of Jahannam. The reason it is so is that they are the most wicked of the disbelievers, for they added to their disbelief mockery of Islam and its people, and deception of them. As for his saying ﷺ: "Three qualities whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he fasts, prays, and claims that he is a Muslim: whoever, when he speaks, lies; whoever, when he promises, breaks his promise; and whoever, when he is entrusted, betrays," and similar narrations, these come under the category of emphasis, severe warning and intensification, for the sake of hyperbole in deterrence. The naming of its seven levels as "darakat" (ranks/degrees of descent) is because they follow one another in succession, each beneath the other. It has also been read with a fatha on the rā' (darak), which is a dialectal variant, like siṭr and siṭar (line), and what supports it is that its plural is adrāk.

﴿And you will not find for them any helper﴾, one who will rescue them from it. The address here is as it was previously.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 146:

﴿Except those who repent﴾, i.e., from hypocrisy (nifaq). This is an exception from the hypocrites, or rather from their pronoun in the predicate (khabar).

﴿And amend﴾ what they had corrupted of their states during the state of hypocrisy.

﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾, i.e., they trust in Him and cling to His religion.

﴿And make their religion sincere﴾, i.e., they make it pure (khalis).

﴿For Allah﴾: they do not seek by their obedience anything but His countenance.

﴿Then those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in view of its being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause (silah), and the meaning of distance in it is to indicate the great distance of their rank and the loftiness of their level.

﴿With the believers﴾, i.e., the known believers who never displayed hypocrisy at all since they believed. Otherwise, they too are believers, i.e., they are with them in the high degrees of Paradise. This is clarified by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾, whose measure cannot be estimated, so they will share it with them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 147:

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) brought to explain that the basis of their punishment, in both its existence and its non-existence, is only their disbelief and nothing else. Thus it confirms what came before it concerning their reward for repentance. The "ma" (what) is interrogative, conveying negation in its most emphatic and forceful form. The meaning is: what thing does Allah, glorified is He, do by punishing you? Does He seek to satisfy His anger through it, or to exact vengeance through it, or to draw benefit through it, or to repel harm through it, as is the custom of kings? He is the Self-Sufficient, exalted above the like of these things. Rather, it is a matter required by your disbelief, so when that is removed by faith and gratitude, the punishment is inevitably dropped. The mention of gratitude before faith is because it is a path leading to it: the mind first perceives the bounties upon it, both those within the self and those in the horizons, and so it gives thanks in a general way, then it advances to knowledge of the Bestower and thus believes in Him. The answer to the conditional is omitted, being indicated by what precedes it.

﴿And Allah is ever Shakir (All-Appreciative)﴾ Allah's gratitude, glorified is He, is His being pleased with the little obedience of His servants and multiplying the reward in return for it.

﴿Alim (All-Knowing)﴾ Intensive in knowledge of all things known, among which are your gratitude and your faith, so it is impossible that He would not give you your rewards in full.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 148:

﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech﴾. His not loving something (ʿadam mahabbatihi taʿala li-shayʾin) is a metonym (kinayah) for His displeasure with it. The bāʾ (preposition) is connected to "al-jahr" (public utterance), and "min" (from) is connected to a omitted element that stands as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "al-sūʾ" (evil). That is: Allah, exalted is He, does not like that anyone should publicly utter evil, being of the nature of speech.

﴿Except one who has been wronged﴾. That is: except the public utterance of one who has been wronged, by calling down curses upon his oppressor, or by complaining about him and reminding him of the evil that is in him, for such is not displeasing to Him, glorified is He. It has been said: it means that one is first insulted and then retorts against the one who insulted him. ﴿And whoever defends himself after he has been wronged﴾, etc. It has been said: a group of people hosted a man and did not feed him, so he complained about them, and he was rebuked for the complaint, whereupon this was revealed. It is also read "illa man ẓalama" (with ẓalama in the active voice), in which case the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: rather, the wrongdoer commits what Allah, exalted is He, does not love, and so he publicly utters evil.

﴿And Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of all things heard, so the speech of the wronged and of the wrongdoer is included in this.

﴿Knowing﴾ of all things known, among which is the condition of the wronged and of the wrongdoer. Thus the sentence is a concluding affirmation (tadhyīl muqarrir) confirming what the exception conveys.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 149:

﴿If you show goodness﴾ — whatever goodness it may be, of words and deeds.

﴿Or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾ — along with what has been permitted to you of holding the wrongdoer to account. The explicit mention of it [pardoning evil], although it is included in showing and concealing goodness, is because it is the one most deserving of clarification. The showing and concealing of goodness were mentioned by way of it being a cause (tasbib) for it, as His saying, mighty and majestic, indicates:

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ — its being placed in the position of the answer to the conditional (jawab al-shart) indicates that the principal matter is pardon together with capability; that is, He was exceedingly forgiving while having complete power to hold to account. Al-Hasan said: He pardons the transgressor while having power to take revenge, so you should follow the practice of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Kalbi said: He is more capable of pardoning your sins than you are of pardoning the sins of one who wronged you. It was also said: [He is] Pardoning toward those who pardon, and Competent to deliver the reward to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 150:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ That is: their creed leads to it and their opinion necessitates it, not that they explicitly declare it, as indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾, that is: by believing in Him, exalted is He, and disbelieving in them. But not by explicitly declaring belief in Him, exalted is He, and disbelief in all of them; rather by way of implication, as expressed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾, that is: we believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others of them, as the Jews said: "We believe in Musa (Moses) and the Tawrah (Torah) and 'Uzayr ('Ezra), and we disbelieve in what is beyond that." And that is nothing but disbelief in Allah, exalted is He, and His messengers, and a distinction between Allah, exalted is He, and His messengers in faith. For He, exalted is He, has commanded them to believe in all the prophets, peace be upon them, and there is no prophet among the prophets except that he informed his people of the truth of the religion of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon them all be peace. So whoever disbelieves in one of them has disbelieved in all of them, and in Allah, exalted is He, too, from a direction he does not reckon.

﴿And they want﴾ by their saying that.

﴿to take a path between that﴾ That is: between faith and disbelief.

﴿a way﴾ which they travel, although there is certainly no intermediary between them, for the truth does not vary, and what is beyond the truth but error?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 151:

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by the ugly attributes.

﴿They are the disbelievers﴾ who are complete in disbelief; their claim and what they call faith carries no weight whatsoever.

﴿Truly (ḥaqqan)﴾ is an infinitive serving as an emphasis for the content of the sentence, meaning: that is established as true, namely, their being complete in disbelief is established as truth. Alternatively, it is an adjective of the verbal noun of "the disbelievers," meaning: they are those who truly disbelieved, (p-249) established, certain, with no doubt about it.

﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers﴾ meaning, for them. The explicit noun was placed in the place of the pronoun to censure them and to remind of their description, or to refer to all disbelievers, of whom they are included in the group from the first entry.

﴿A humiliating punishment﴾ which they will taste when it descends upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 152:

﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, i.e., in the manner that was explained in the tafsir of His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ and so on.

﴿And do not make distinction between any of them﴾, by believing in some of them and disbelieving in others, as the disbelievers did. The use of "bayn" (between) with "aḥad" (any one) has already been thoroughly verified in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, so there is nothing more to add.

﴿Those﴾, the ones described with the sublime attributes mentioned.

﴿Soon He will give them their rewards﴾, those promised to them. The opening of this with "sawfa" (soon) serves to emphasize the promise and to indicate that it will certainly come to pass, even if delayed. It was also read as "nu'tīhim" (We will give them) with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah).

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from them.

﴿Merciful﴾, exceeding in mercy towards them by multiplying their good deeds.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, verse 153:

﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven.﴾ It was revealed concerning the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews when they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If you are a prophet, then bring us a Book from heaven all at once, as Moses (peace be upon him) brought." It was also said: a Book written in a heavenly script on the Tablet, as the Torah was revealed; or a Book we can see with our own eyes as it descends; or a Book sent to us, naming each of us, stating that you are the Messenger of God. Their purpose in this great demand was nothing but domineering and obstinate defiance. Al-Ḥasan said: "Even if they had asked Him in order to clarify the truth, He would have given them, and what He gave them is sufficient."

﴿So they had asked Moses for something greater than that.﴾ This is the answer to an implied conditional: that is, "If you consider what they asked of you to be great, then they had asked Moses for something greater." It was also said that it is a justification for the answer, meaning: "Do not be concerned about their question, for they asked Moses for something greater." Although this request came from their ancestors, since they followed them in everything they did and did not do, it was attributed to them. The meaning is that they have a deep-rooted inclination in this matter, and that what they proposed to you is not the first of their follies.

﴿Then they said, "Show us God openly."﴾ That is: "Show Him to us so that we see Him openly," meaning, face to face, or as those who openly and visibly witness Him. The fā' here is explanatory (tafsīriyya).

﴿So the thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqa) seized them﴾ That is, the fire that came from the sky and destroyed them. It was also recited as "al-ṣa'qa" (الصعقة).

﴿for their wrongdoing.﴾ That is, because of their wrongdoing, which was their obstinacy and their asking for what was impossible in the state they were in. This does not imply that seeing God is absolutely impossible.

﴿Then they took the calf (al-'ijl) after clear proofs had come to them.﴾ That is, the miracles He showed to Pharaoh: the staff, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, and others. It does not refer to the Torah, because it had not yet been sent down to them.

﴿Yet We pardoned that.﴾ And We did not uproot them, though they deserved it. It was said: this is an invitation to repentance, as if it were said: "Those people committed sin and repented, and We pardoned them; so you too repent, that We may pardon you."

﴿And We gave Moses clear authority.﴾ A manifest authority over them, when he commanded them to kill (p-250) themselves as repentance for their disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 154:

﴿And We raised over them the Mount (al-Tur) because of their covenant﴾, i.e., because of their covenant, that they would accept it. It is related that they refused to accept the law of the Torah, so God Most High raised the mountain over them, and they accepted it. Or [it was raised] so that they would fear and not break it. It is related that they intended to break it, so God Most High raised the mountain over them, and they became afraid and desisted from breaking it. This latter is the more fitting, in light of the words of the Mighty and Majestic later: ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾.

﴿And We said to them﴾, through the tongue of Musa (peace be upon him), while the mountain was overshadowing them:

﴿Enter the gate﴾. Qatada said: "We were told that it is one of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)." It was also said: it is Iliya. It was said: it is Ariha. It was said: it is the name of a village. It was said: it is the gate of the dome toward which they used to pray, for they did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis during the lifetime of Musa (peace be upon him).

﴿Prostrating﴾, i.e., bowing low and humbly submissive.

﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress﴾, i.e., do not wrong by hunting fish.

﴿on the Sabbath﴾. It was also read as "lā taʿaddū" with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal, on the basis that its original form is "taʿtadū," and the tā was assimilated into the dal because they are close in place of articulation, after the transfer of its vowel to the ʿayn.

﴿And We took from them﴾, in exchange for their obedience to what they were charged with.

﴿a solemn covenant﴾, emphasized. It is the pact that God took from them in the Torah. It was said: they gave the covenant on the condition that if they intended to turn back from the religion, God Most High would punish them with whatever kind of punishment He wished.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 155:

﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ "Ma" (mā) is either a *zā'idah* (redundant, emphatic particle) or a *nakirah tāmmah* (indefinite noun of complete meaning), and "naqḍihim" (their breaking) is in apposition (*badal*) to it. The "bā'" (bā', the preposition "for/because of") is connected to a verb omitted from the sentence, meaning: "Because of their breaking their covenant, We did to them what We did, namely the curse and the transformation and the other punishments that descended upon them or upon their descendants." It is narrated that they transgressed on the Sabbath during the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), so they were cursed and transformed into apes. It has also been said that the phrase is connected to "We forbade" (ḥarramnā), on the basis that God's words ﴿so for wrongdoing﴾ are an apposition (*badal*) to His words ﴿so for what﴾ and what is conjoined to it. In that case the prohibition is explained by all of these causes together. It is not hidden that their statement, "We killed the Messiah," and their saying against Maryam a grave slander, came after the prohibition, and there is no justification for connecting the phrase to what is indicated by God's words ﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾, because that is a rejection of their statement, "Our hearts are uncovered," so it would be part of the relative clause of God's words ﴿and their saying﴾, which is conjoined to the genitive noun, and so it would not govern its own preposition.

﴿and their disbelief in the signs of God﴾ That is, in the Qur'an, or in what is in their scripture.

﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ such as Zakariyya and Yahya (peace be upon them both).

﴿and their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered"﴾ *Ghulf* is the plural of *aghlaf*, meaning: they are covered with natural coverings, so that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought cannot reach them. Or it is a lightened form of *ghulaf*, the plural of *ghilaf* (covering/sheath), meaning: they are vessels for knowledge, so we are content with what we have and need nothing else. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'. Al-Kalbi said: they mean that our hearts are such that no speech reaches them without being retained, and if there were any good in your speech, they would have retained it too.

﴿Rather, God has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (*kalām mu'taridh*) placed between the two conjoined items, brought in as a digression (*istiṭrād*), hastening to refute their corrupt claim. That is: their disbelief, and the truth not reaching their hearts, is not because their hearts are naturally uncovered. Rather the matter is the reverse: God has sealed them because of their disbelief. Or: their hearts are not as they claimed, but are sealed (p-251) because of their disbelief.

﴿so they do not believe, except a few﴾ Among them, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like. Or: except a faith that is slight and of no account.

﴿وَبِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾, that is, [their disbelief] in Jesus, peace be upon him. It is conjoined (ʿatf) to their saying [in the preceding phrase]. The repetition of the preposition (al-jarr) is due to the long separation between them, caused by the digression (istitrad). It has also been permitted to conjoin it to "bi-kufrihim" [the earlier phrase], so that it and what is conjoined to it are among the causes of the sealing (tabʿ) [of their hearts].
