It has also been said that this whole group is conjoined to the whole group preceding it, and the repetition of the mention of disbelief serves to indicate that their disbelief was repeated: they disbelieved in Moses, then in Jesus, then in Muhammad, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿وَقَوْلِهِمْ عَلى مَرْيَمَ بُهْتانًا عَظِيمًا﴾: a tremendous slander against Mary, whose magnitude cannot be measured, since they attributed to her what is a thousand stations removed from her.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 4, verse 157:**

﴿And their saying: "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa, son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah."﴾ The placement of their statement within the series of their other transgressions that were censured is not merely because it is a lie, but because it includes their delight in killing the Prophet, peace be upon him, and their mockery of him. Their describing him with the title of "Messenger" is said in mockery of him, peace be upon him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾, etc. It also indicates their mention of him, peace be upon him, in a disgraceful manner. This is according to what has been said: that this is a placing of a beautiful mention from Him, exalted is He, in place of their ugly mention. It has also been said: it is a description of him, peace be upon him, from Him, exalted is He, as praise for him, an elevation of his station, pebe upon him, and a manifestation of the extreme boldness of their undertaking to kill him and the utmost shamelessness of their boasting of that.

﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾: this is a circumstantial clause and an interjection.

﴿But it was made to appear to them﴾: It is narrated that a group of Jews insulted him, peace be upon him, and his mother. He prayed against them, and Allah, exalted is He, transformed them into apes and swine. The Jews then agreed to kill him. Allah, exalted is He, informed him that He would raise him to the heavens. He said to his companions: "Which of you is content to have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed, crucified, and enters Paradise?" A man among them said: "I am." So Allah, exalted is He, cast his likeness upon him, and he was killed and crucified. It has also been said: there was a man who was a hypocrite toward 'Isa, peace be upon him. When they intended to kill him, he said: "I will show you where he is." He entered the house of 'Isa, peace be upon him, and 'Isa, peace be upon him, was raised up, and his likeness was cast upon the hypocrite. They entered upon him, killed him, and they thought that he was 'Isa, peace be upon him. It has also been said: Tituanus the Jew entered a house in which he (i.e., 'Isa) was, but did not find him. Allah, exalted is He, cast his likeness upon him, and when he came out he was thought to be 'Isa, peace be upon him, so he was seized and killed. Such extraordinary events are not improbable in the age of prophethood. It has also been said: when the Jews intended to kill him, peace be upon him, and Allah, exalted is He, raised him to the heavens, the leaders of the Jews feared that strife would break out among their common people. So they seized a man, killed him, and crucified him, and they confused the people, showing them that he was the Messiah, though they knew him only by name, because he had not mixed with them except briefly. Here "it was made to appear" (shubbiha) is attributed to the prepositional phrase (lahum), as if it were said: "But the resemblance occurred to them between 'Isa, peace be upon him, and the one killed," or "in the matter," according to the view of one who said that no one was killed but a rumor of his killing was spread and spread among the people; or it is attributed to the pronoun of the one killed, since "Indeed, we killed" indicates that there was someone killed.

﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him﴾: that is, concerning the affair of 'Isa, peace be upon him. When that event occurred, people differed. Some of the Jews said: "He was a liar, so we killed him definitively." Others were hesitant, and some of them said: "If this is 'Isa, then where is our companion?" Some of them said: "The face is the face of 'Isa, but the body is the body of our companion." Those who had heard from him, peace be upon him, that Allah would raise him to the heavens said: "He was raised to the heavens." And some people said: "The human nature (al-nasut) was crucified, and the divine nature (al-lahut) ascended."

﴿They are in doubt about it﴾: that is, they are in hesitation. Doubt (shakk), as it is applied to what neither of its two sides is preponderant, is also applied to hesitation in general, and to what is opposed to knowledge. For this reason it was emphasized by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "But they follow assumption." It is also permissible to interpret doubt as ignorance and knowledge as belief upon which the soul is settled, whether it is certain or otherwise; in that case the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil).

﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾: that is, a killing with certainty, as they claimed by their saying: "Indeed, we killed the Messiah." It has also been said: its meaning is: "And they did not know him with certainty," as in the saying of one who said:

*Thus do the knowing women speak of her,*
*and by my knowledge I have killed that certainty.*

From their saying: "I killed the thing by knowledge" and "I slaughtered it by knowledge," when your knowledge of it is complete. In this there is mockery of them, since it implies that they had some knowledge in general, whereas this has been totally negated from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 158:

﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself.﴾ This is a rejection and denial of his killing, and an affirmation of his elevation.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ (ʿAzīz), that He cannot be overcome in what He wills.

﴿Wise﴾ (Ḥakīm) in all His acts, so that His arrangements concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, enter into this in the first place.

﴿And there is none among the People of the Book﴾ — that is, among the Jews and the Christians. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿except that they will surely believe in him before his death﴾ is a sentence in the form of an oath, which functions as a qualifier (ṣifah) of an omitted antecedent to which the second pronoun refers, and the first pronoun refers to 'Isa (peace be upon him). The meaning is: there is none among the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in 'Isa (peace be upon him) before his soul departs, that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger. But it will be too late for faith, because the time of accountability will have ended. This is reinforced by the reading "*layu'minunna bihi qabla mawtihim*" (with the pronoun in the plural and a *ḍamma* on the nūn), since *aḥad* (anyone) carries the sense of the plural. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) that he explained it in this way. 'Ikrimah said to him: "If someone comes to him and strikes his neck?" He said: "His soul does not leave until he moves his lips with it." He said: "What if he falls from the top of a house, or is burned, or is eaten by a predator?!" He said: "He speaks it in the air, and his soul does not leave until he believes in him."

It is also reported from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: al-Hajjaj said to me: "There is a verse that I have never recited without something troubling my soul about it," meaning this verse. He said: "I am brought a prisoner from among the Jews and the Christians, and I strike his neck, yet I do not hear from him that [statement]." I said: "When death comes to a Jew, the angels strike his back and his face and say: 'O enemy of Allah, 'Isa (peace be upon him) came to you as a prophet, but you denied him!' And he says: 'I believe that he is a servant and a prophet.' And they say to the Christian: ''Isa (peace be upon him) came to you as a prophet, but you claimed that he is God and the son of God!' And he believes that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger, at a time when his faith will not benefit him." He said: "He was reclining, then he sat up straight, looked at me and said: 'From whom did you hear this?' I said: 'Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hanafiyyah related it to me.' He began to scratch the ground with his staff, then said: 'You have taken it from a pure spring.'"

The informing about their state in this way is a warning to them and an exhortation to hasten to faith in him before they are compelled to it, at a time when it no longer benefits them.

It has also been said: both pronouns refer to 'Isa, and the meaning is: there is none among the People of the Book who are alive at the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him) but that he will surely believe in him before his death. It has been related that he (peace be upon him) will descend from the sky at the end of time, and then no one among the People of the Book will remain but that he will believe in him, so that the religion (*milla*) will be one, which is the religion of Islam. Allah will destroy the Dajjal (the Antichrist) in his time, and security will prevail, so that lions will graze with camels, panthers with cows, wolves with sheep, children will play with snakes, and he will remain on the earth for forty years. Then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him and bury him. (p-253)

It has also been said: the first pronoun refers to Allah, exalted is He. It has also been said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾ — that is, 'Isa (peace be upon him).

﴿against them﴾ — against the People of the Book.

﴿a witness﴾ — so he will testify against the Jews for their denial, and against the Christians that they called him the son of Allah, may Allah be exalted far above that, greatly exalted.

﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾ Perhaps their mention with this designation is to signal the complete enormity of their wrongdoing, by recalling its occurrence after they had become Jews, that is, repented from worshipping the calf. That repentance was conditioned upon the crushing of souls, and the magnitude of the wrongdoing is established in itself through the *tanwin al-tafkhim* (the tanwin of magnification). That is: because of a great wrong, beyond the bounds of likenesses and forms, issuing from them.

﴿We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ and for those before them, not for any other reason as they claimed. Whenever they committed one of the sins they had perpetrated, a kind of the good things that had been lawful for them and for their forefathers would be forbidden to them as a punishment. Yet they used to fabricate against God, exalted is He, and say: "We are not the first to whom they were forbidden; they were forbidden to Noah, Abraham and those after them, until the matter reached us." God, exalted and majestic, refuted them in many places and rebuked them with His saying: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel forbade himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾, that is, in your claim that it is an ancient prohibition. It is related that when he (peace be upon him) commanded them to bring out the Torah, none dared to bring it out, because the fact that the prohibition was due to their wrongdoing was inscribed in it. So they were confounded and turned back humbled.

﴿and their hindering many from the way of God﴾, that is, many people, or hindering with many instances of hindrance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 161:

﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾. For usury was prohibited for them just as it is prohibited for us, and in this there is evidence that a prohibition indicates the prohibited thing's being forbidden (al-nahy yadullu 'ala hurmat al-manhi 'anh).

﴿And their consuming of people's wealth by falsehood﴾: by bribery and all other forbidden means.

﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them﴾: that is, for those who persist in disbelief, not for those among them who repent and believe.

﴿a painful punishment﴾. They will taste it in the Hereafter, just as they tasted in this world the punishment of prohibition ('uqubat al-tahrim).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 162:

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ is a resumption (istidrak) from His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We have prepared﴾ etc., and an explanation that some of them are contrary to their state, sooner or later. That is: but those firmly established in knowledge among them, the precise and insightful in it, who do not follow conjecture like those ignorant ones, and by them is meant ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

﴿And the believers﴾, that is, among them. They are described as believers after they were described with what requires it, namely firmness in knowledge, by way of conjunction (ʿatf), which indicates difference between the two conjoined items, treating the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence. His, exalted and majestic is He, saying: ﴿who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the believers," explaining the manner of their belief. It has been said: it is an interposed clause emphasizing what precedes it. His, exalted and majestic is He, saying: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾. It has been said: it is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being: "and I mean those who establish prayer," so that the sentence is interposed between the subject and the predicate. It has been said: it is conjoined to "what has been sent down to you," so that the intended ones are the prophets, peace be upon them, meaning: they believe in the books and in the prophets or the angels. Makki said: that is, and they believe in the angels whose attribute is establishing prayer, according to His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, and do not tire﴾. It has been said: it is conjoined to the kaf in "to you," meaning: they believe in what was sent down to him and to those who establish prayer. It was also read in the nominative, as conjoined to "the believers," on the basis of what has passed concerning treating the designational difference as the essential difference; the same applies to the conjoined items that follow, for His saying: ﴿and those who give zakat﴾ is conjoined to "the believers" while all are one in essence. Likewise the statement of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and the believers in God and the Last Day﴾, for by all of them are meant the believers among the People of the Book. They were first described as being firm in the knowledge of the Book, to signal that this necessarily entails faith, and that those other than them only persisted in disbelief because they were not firm in it; then by their being believers in all the Books sent down to the prophets; then by their acting upon what is in them of laws and rulings, and only the mention of establishing prayer and giving zakat was singled out from among them, as these entail all the bodily and financial acts of worship; then by their being believers in the origin and the return, confirming their possession of faith in both its directions and their encompassing it from both its ends, and as an implicit indication that those other than them among the People of the Book are not believers in either of them in reality, for by their saying: "ʿUzayr is the son of God" they are associators with God, glory be to Him, and by their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" they are disbelievers in the Last Day. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Those﴾ is an indication to them with regard to their being characterized by the excellent attributes enumerated, and the distance implied in it serves to signal the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence; it is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying: ﴿We will give them a great reward﴾ is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the subject which is "those firm in knowledge" and what is conjoined to it. The sin (sa) is for emphasizing the promise, and the indefiniteness of "reward" is for magnification. This is more fitting to the correspondence of the two sides of the resumption, since the first were threatened with a painful punishment and the others were promised a great reward, as if it were said after His saying: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾: "But the believers among them in God and the Last Day, We will give them a great reward." As for what the majority inclined to, making His saying: ﴿who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ etc. a predicate of the subject, it is entirely sound, except that it does not address the correspondence of the two sides. It was also read "sa-yu'tihim" with the ya', in consideration of the apparent sense of His saying: ﴿and the believers in God﴾.

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ This is a reply to the People of the Book concerning their request that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bring down a book from the sky to them, and an argument against them: he is not an innovation among the messengers. His situation, in the reality of sending and the essence of revelation, is like that of all the well-known prophets whose prophethood no one doubts. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position, either as an adjective (نَعْتٌ) of a deleted verbal noun (مَصْدَر), i.e., a revelation "like Our revelation to Noah." Or it is a circumstantial clause (حالٌ) of that implied, definite verbal noun, as is the view of Sibawayh, i.e., "We revealed the revelation in a state of resembling Our revelation to Noah, etc." The phrase ﴿مِن بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("after him") is connected to ﴿أوْحَيْنا﴾ ("We revealed"). Noah is mentioned first because he is the father of mankind and the first prophet through whose tongue Allah the Exalted prescribed laws and rulings, and the first prophet whose community was punished for rejecting his call. Allah destroyed the people of the earth through his supplication.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾: this is coordinated (عَطْفٌ) with ﴿أوْحَيْنا إلى نُوحٍ﴾ ("We revealed to Noah") and is included with it under the ruling of comparison. I.e., "and as We revealed to Abraham ﴿and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes (al-Asbat)﴾, who are the sons of Jacob, peace be upon them."

﴿and Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon﴾: they are singled out for mention, although their inclusion in the line of the prophets is evident, in order to honor them and show their excellence, as in the Exalted One's words: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael﴾. It is also to name explicitly those prophets whom the Jews claim descent from. Repeating the verb (أوْحَيْنا) serves to further confirm the revelation and to draw attention to the fact that they are a distinct group, specially set apart with a particular kind of revelation.

﴿And We gave David the Psalms (Zabur)﴾: Al-Qurtubi said: It contained one hundred and fifty chapters, none of which contained a ruling of the rulings. They were only wisdoms, admonitions, praise, glorification, and commendation of Allah the Exalted. It is also read with a ḍamma on the zāy (زُبورًا), and it is the plural of zibr (زِبْر) in the sense of maznūr (مَزْبُور, "written"). The clause is coordinated with ﴿أوْحَيْنا﴾ and falls under its ruling, because giving the Zabur is one form of revelation, i.e., "and as We gave David the Zabur." Choosing this phrasing rather than ﴿وَأوْحَيْنا إلى داوُدَ﴾ ("We revealed to David") serves to establish the similarity in a specific matter, namely the giving of a scripture, after establishing it in general revelation. Then it is pointed out that the similarity is also established in a matter necessarily attached to both of them, namely the sending as messengers (الإرْسال), in a comprehensive way.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 164:

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿and messengers﴾ (wa-rusulan), it is in the accusative (nusiba) governed by an implied verb indicated by "We revealed" (awhayna), and it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with that verb, falling under the same rule of comparison (hukm al-tashbih) as what precedes it. The meaning is: "And just as We sent messengers." It is not governed by what explains it, His words, exalted is He, ﴿We have related them to you﴾ (qad qasasnahum 'alayka). That would mean "and We related messengers," as some have said. They built on this: the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿We have related them﴾ (qad qasasnahum), on the first reading, are in the accusative as an attribute (sifa) of "messengers" (rusulan). On the second reading they have no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), since that reading is untenable, as you will see. It has also been read with nominative "messengers" (rusulun). His words, exalted is He, ﴿before﴾ (min qablu) are connected (muta'allaq) to "We related" (qasasna), meaning: "We related them before this surah," or "before today."

﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾ (wa-rusulan lam naqsusshum 'alayka) is coordinated with "messengers" (rusulan) and is in the accusative by the same governing element. It has been said that both are in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), and the implied meaning is: "As We revealed to Noah and to the messengers, etc." The correct view is that both are governed by "We sent" (arsalna), because this establishes the parallel between the Prophet's (ﷺ) condition and the conditions of the prophets, peace be upon them, whose prophethood they acknowledge, in the general matter of revelation (ilha'), then in giving the Book, then in sending. The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you﴾ (inna awhayna ilayka) are understood to mean "We have given you" (atayناka) and "We have sent you" (arsalnaka) necessarily. It is as if it were said: "Indeed We have revealed to Abraham and those after him, and We have given you and sent you necessarily." It is as if it were said: "Indeed We have revealed to you a revelation like what We revealed to Noah, and like what We revealed to Abraham and those after him, and We have given you the Criterion (al-Furqan) a giving like what We gave David, a Psalter (zaburan), and We have sent you a sending like what We sent messengers, whom We have related to you before, and messengers whom We have not related to you, without any difference between you and them in the reality of revelation and the essence of sending." So why do the disbelievers ask you for something that none of these messengers, peace be upon them, was given? From here it becomes clear that "messengers" (rusulan) cannot be governed by "We related" (qasasna), for its governing element must be coordinated with "We revealed" (awhayna) and fall under the same rule of comparison on which the argument against the disbelievers revolves. There is no doubt that "We related" (qasasna) has no connection to any part of revelation or giving, so that it could be considered within the scope of (p-256) His words, ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you﴾, and then a similarity that justifies the comparison could be considered between it and what was mentioned. Moreover, its implied form in the first "messengers" requires its implied negation in the second, and that is far more impossible and more evidently false.

﴿And God spoke to Moses﴾ (wa-kallama Allahu Musa): Allah is in the nominative (raf') and "Moses" (Musa) in the accusative (nasb). It has also been read in reversed form ('ala al-qalb). His words, exalted is He, ﴿with direct speech﴾ (taklimān) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) that removes the possibility of metaphor (majaz). Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call whatever reaches a person "speech" by whatever means it reaches him, as long as it is not emphasised with the verbal noun. If it is emphasised with it, it is only the literal reality of speech. The sentence is either coordinated with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you﴾, as a narrative coordinated with a narrative and not with "We gave" and what is coordinated with it, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, as the change of style through the turn (iltifat) indicates. The meaning is: speech without intermediary, which is the highest level of revelation, was specifically given to Moses among them. That did not detract from the prophethood of the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them. How then can it be imagined that the descent of the Torah upon him, peace be upon him, all at once, detracts from the validity of the prophethood of one to whom the Book was revealed in detail, when it is evident that its descent in that manner was for wise purposes that required it? Among them: the Children of Israel were so stubborn and obstinate that, had it not descended in that way, they would not have believed in it. Yet even so, they did not believe in it except after great hardship and repeated trials. God, exalted is He, has favoured our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) by giving him the like of what He gave each of them (ﷺ), a great salutation (taslimān kathiran).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 165:**

﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners﴾. It is in the accusative (nusiba) either as an accusative of praise (al-madh, a form of emphatic commendation), or by implying a verb, "We sent," or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), in that "rusulan" prepares the ground for what follows, or as a fresh starting point (al-bidaya) from the first "rusulan." That is: bearers of good news to the people of obedience of Paradise, and warners to the disobedient of the Fire.

﴿So that people would have no argument against God﴾. That is, no excuse by which they might plead, saying: "If only You had sent us a messenger, so that he might explain Your laws to us and teach us what we did not know of Your rulings, because human power falls short of grasping the particular benefits (juz'iyyat al-maslaha), and most people are unable to grasp their universal principles (kulliyyatuha)." This is as in His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs?"﴾ ...to the end of the verse. It is called an "argument" (hujja) although it is impossible that anyone should have an argument against Him, glorified be He, regarding any of His acts; rather, He may do what He wills, as He wills. This is to draw attention to the fact that the excuse, in its acceptance with Him, exalted be He, in accordance with His generosity and mercy toward His servants, has the standing of a decisive argument that cannot be repelled. For this reason, exalted be He said: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No one is more jealous than God, which is why He forbade indecencies, whether apparent or hidden. No one loves praise more than God, which is why He praised Himself. No one loves excuse more than God, which is why He sent the messengers and revealed the books."

The lam (ل) is connected to "arsalna" (We sent). It has also been said that it is connected to His words, ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾. "Hujja" is the ism (subject) of kana (was), "lil-nas" is its khabar (predicate), and "ʿala Allah" is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial phrase (hal) describing "hujja," meaning: "being against God." Or the khabar is "ʿala Allah," and "lil-nas" is a circumstantial phrase in the aforementioned manner. It is permissible for each of the two to be connected to what the other is connected to, which is the khabar. It is not permissible to connect either to "hujja," because the complement of a verbal noun (masdar) may not precede it.

His words, ﴿after the messengers﴾, mean: after their sending and their conveying of the laws to the nations through their tongues. It is connected to "hujja," or to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier (sifa) of it, because adverbial expressions (zuruf) may be used to describe events, just as events may be predicated of them, as in the phrase "the fighting is on Friday."

﴿And God is ever Mighty﴾, not overcome in any of His affairs. Part of His decree is that He refrains from answering the requests of those who seek to trip up the messengers.

﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts, among which are the sending of messengers and the sending down of books. The multiplicity of messengers and books, and their differences in the manner of revelation and in some of the laws and rulings, are only due to the differences among the nations in the circumstances upon which the sphere of obligation revolves. Just as He, glorified be He and exalted be He, created them in various modes and different stages in accordance with what wisdom in creation requires, so too He imposed upon them worship suited to their condition, in accordance with their differing circumstances and varying capacities, through laws and rulings as wisdom in legislation demands. In sending messengers, revealing books, and in other matters relating to their livelihood and their hereafter, He has taken into account what is in their benefit. Therefore, the request that the Book be sent down all at once is a corrupt proposal, for then the obligations would become overwhelming, and it would be burdensome for the one obligated to accept them and to fulfil them. But gradual revelation, occurring according to the matters that call for it, is easier to accept and simpler to comply with.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 166:

﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ — read with the nun lightened and the name of Allah in the nominative (Allah). It is also read with the nun doubled and the name of Allah in the accusative. It is an istidrak (a corrective qualification, a "but" that qualifies what has been understood from what precedes), as if they, when they tormented him with the questions that had gone before and he argued against them with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Surely We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾ and so on, were told: they do not bear witness to that, but Allah bears witness.

﴿to what He has sent down to you﴾ — read in the active voice; it is also read in the passive voice, with the preposition bi being a complement of the testimony (shahada). That is, He bears witness to the truth of what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, the inimitable, which speaks to your prophethood. It is said: when the words of the Exalted ﴿Surely We have revealed to you﴾ were sent down, they said, "We do not bear witness to this for you," and so ﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ was revealed.

﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ — that is, accompanied by His special knowledge, which no one else knows, namely its composition in a wondrous pattern which every eloquent person is unable to match; or with His knowledge of the state of the one to whom it was sent down and his readiness to receive the holy lights; or with His knowledge of what people need for their livelihood and their hereafter. The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject according to the first two interpretations, and from the object according to the third; and the sentence is in the position of an explanation of what precedes it. It is also read "nazzalahu" (with doubled zay). The words of the Exalted ﴿and the angels bear witness﴾ — that is, to that — are a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), and the clause is coordinated with what precedes it. It is said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object of "anzalahu," meaning: He has sent it down while the angels bear witness to its truthfulness and its being true.

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ — as a witness to the soundness of your prophethood, since He established for it striking miracles and manifest proofs, which suffice without the need to call upon anything else as witness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 167:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ That is, in what Allah the Exalted revealed and bore witness to, or in everything that it is obligatory to believe in, and this is included in it in the first instance. The intended people here are the Jews, since they disbelieved in it.

﴿and barred [others] from the way of Allah﴾, which is the religion of Islam, from anyone who wished to follow it, by their saying: "We do not recognize the description of Muhammad in our Book." It has also been read as "ṣuddū" (passive voice).

﴿They have certainly gone astray﴾ by what they did of disbelief and of barring [others] from the path of truth.

﴿[into] far-reaching error﴾ Because they combined going astray with leading others astray, and because the one who misguides is more deeply rooted in error and further from giving it up.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 168:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ i.e., in what was mentioned just now.

﴿and wronged﴾ i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ) by denying his prophethood and concealing his sublime attributes and substituting others in their place; or wronged people by barring them from that which is good for them in this life and the Hereafter.

﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ because it is impossible for forgiveness to attach to a disbeliever.

﴿nor would He guide them to a path﴾. (p-258)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 169:

﴿Except the path of Hell﴾ because of their lack of readiness for guidance to the truth and for the righteous deeds which are the path of Paradise. The guidance understood from the exception by way of allusion is God's, exalted is He, creation of their evil deeds, which lead them to Hell, when their power and choice are directed to acquiring them; or their being driven to it on the Day of Resurrection by means of the angels. The "path" is taken in its generality and the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil). It has also been said: it is specific to the path of truth, and the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati').

﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun in the accusative, and its governing element is what the exception clearly indicates, as if it were said: "He will cause them to enter Hell, abiding therein," and so on. God's, exalted is He, words ﴿forever﴾ are in the accusative of time (nasb 'ala al-zarfiyyah), removing the possibility of taking abiding (khulud) to mean a long stay.

﴿And that is﴾, i.e., their being made to abide in Hell,

﴿for God easy﴾ because it is impossible that anything of His willed purposes should be difficult for Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 170:

﴿O mankind﴾ After He related to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the Jews' pretexts with falsehoods and their baseless demands made out of obstinacy, and refuted them by establishing his prophethood (peace be upon him) and affirming his messengership by explaining that his (peace be upon him) situation regarding revelation and sending was like the situation of the famous prophets (peace be upon them), whom they acknowledge as prophets; and He confirmed this by His own testimony (glorified is He) and the testimony of the angels. The obligated ones, all of them, were commanded, by way of varying the address, to believe in this, with a command accompanied by the promise of acceptance and the threat for rejection, as a warning that the proof has become binding and no excuse remains for anyone in not accepting. And His saying (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿Indeed the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord﴾ is a repetition of the testimony, an affirmation of the truth of what is testified to, and a preparation for what follows of the command to believe. Mentioning him (peace be upon him) by the title of messengership is to emphasize the obligation to obey him. The "truth" (al-haqq) refers to the noble Qur'an. The preposition "bi" (with) is connected to "jaa'akum" (has come to you), so it is for transitivity, or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of ﴿the Messenger﴾, meaning: coming while bound with the truth. "Min" (from) is also connected either to the verb or to an omitted element that is a circumstantial state of "the truth", meaning: he came to you with it from Him (exalted is He), or: he came to you with the truth existing from Him (exalted is He). The mention of the title of lordship (rububiyya) together with the attribution to the pronoun of the addressees indicates that this is for their nurturing and their bringing to the perfection appropriate to them, as an encouragement for them to comply with the command that follows. The "fa" (then) in His saying (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿So believe﴾ indicates that what precedes necessitates what follows, meaning: so believe in him and in what he has brought of the truth. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿better for you﴾ is in the accusative as an object of a verb that must be omitted, as is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, meaning: intend or bring about a matter better for you than what you are in of disbelief; or it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, as is the view of al-Farra', meaning: believe a belief better for you; or it is the predicate of an omitted "kana" (be) that occurs as a response to the command, not as a conditional response in the technical sense, and this is the view of al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda, meaning: let belief be better for you.

﴿And if you disbelieve﴾ meaning: if you persist and continue in disbelief in Him.

﴿then indeed to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of existing things, whether they are within their very reality, by which the state of the two themselves is known in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, or outside of them but settled within them, of rational beings and others, so the addressees enter among them by primary inclusion. That is, all of it belongs to Him (mighty and majestic is He) in creation, possession and disposal; nothing of it goes out of His dominion and subjugation. So whoever has this status is capable of punishing you for your disbelief without doubt. Or: whoever is such is free of need of you and of others; he is not harmed by your disbelief nor benefited by your belief. It has been said: whoever is such has servants who worship Him and submit to His command.

﴿And God is ever Knowing﴾ exceeding in knowledge, so He is most knowledgeable of the states of all, and thus His knowledge of their disbelief is included in this by primary inclusion.

﴿Wise﴾ observing wisdom in all His acts, among which is His punishing them for their disbelief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 171:

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ is a turning of the address away from the general and a specification of it to the Christians, as a rebuke to them for the disbelief and misguidance they are in.

﴿Do not go to excess in your religion﴾ by overstating the rank of Jesus, peace be upon him, and claiming his divinity. As for the excess of the Jews in lowering his rank, peace be upon him, and their accusation that he was born out of wedlock, this has already been censured against them earlier.

﴿And do not say about Allah except the truth﴾ meaning: do not ascribe to Him what is impossible for Him to be described with, such as incarnation, union, taking a consort, or a son; rather, declare Him free of all of that.

﴿The Messiah﴾ His explanation has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran. It has also been read with a kasra on the mim and a shadda on the sin, like al-Sikkit, in the intensive form (sighat al-mubalagha). It is the subject (mubtada'), and His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Isa﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for it or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to it. His statement, ﴿son of Mary﴾, is an attribute of it, indicating the invalidity of what they ascribed to him, peace be upon him, of being a son of Allah, exalted is He. His statement, ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾, is the predicate (khabar) of the subject, and the sentence is resumed (mustanafa), brought to give the reason for the prohibition of the false saying, which necessarily entails the command to its opposite, namely the truth; that is: he is restricted to the rank of messengership and does not transcend it.

﴿And His word﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾; that is: he was brought into being by His word and command, which is "Be," without an intermediary father or a drop of semen.

﴿Which He conveyed to Mary﴾ meaning: He delivered it to her and placed it in her by the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him. It was said: He informed her of it and told her of it by way of glad tidings, and that is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary﴾. It was said: the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from his pronoun, peace be upon him, concealed in what is indicated by "and His word" of the meaning of the derived noun which is the operator in it, with "qad" implied along with it.

﴿And a spirit from Him﴾ It was said: he is the one whom Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the garment of Mary, so she conceived by the permission of Allah, exalted is He. The breath was named a spirit because it is a wind that comes out of the spirit, and "from" (min) is for the beginning of the end figuratively, not partitive, as the Christians claim. It is related that a skilled Christian physician of al-Rashid debated 'Ali ibn Husayn al-Waqidi al-Marwazi one day, and said to him: "In your book is what indicates that Jesus, peace be upon him, is a part of Him, exalted is He," and he recited this verse. Al-Waqidi recited: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾. He said: "Then it would follow that all those things are a part of Allah, exalted is He, highly exalted." The Christian was silenced and became Muslim, and al-Rashid rejoiced greatly and gave al-Waqidi a magnificent reward. The phrase is connected to an omitted element that falls as an attribute of "a spirit," meaning: existing from His side, exalted is He; it is made from Him, exalted is He, even though it was by the breathing of Gabriel, peace be upon him, because the breathing was by His command, glorified is He. It was said: he was named a spirit because he gives life to the dead. It was said: because he gives life to hearts, just as the Qur'an was named so for that reason in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾. It was said: by the spirit is meant the revelation which was revealed to Mary with the glad tidings. It was said: the custom is that when they wish to describe something with the utmost purity and cleanliness, they say: "it is a spirit"; so when Jesus, peace be upon him, was formed by the breath and not from a drop of semen, he was described as a spirit. The placement of his being a messenger of Allah in the mention before his being His word and a spirit from Him in existence is for establishing the truth from the outset with what is explicit and not open to interpretation, and for determining the outcome of what is open to interpretation and closing the door to deviant interpretation.

﴿So believe in Allah﴾ and single Him out for divinity.

﴿And His messengers﴾ all of them; describe them with messengership and do not remove any of them from their line by ascribing divinity to him.

﴿And do not say "Three"﴾ meaning: the gods are three: Allah, the Messiah, and Mary, as His statement, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ * Or: "Allah is three," if it is established that they say: Allah is one essence, three hypostases: the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit; and that by the first they mean the essence. It was said: the existence; and by the second, knowledge; and by the third, life.

﴿Desist﴾ meaning: from trinitarianism.

﴿It is better for you﴾ the aspects of its accusative status have already passed.

﴿Indeed, Allah is one God﴾ meaning: singular in essence, exalted above plurality in any respect. So "Allah" is the subject, "God" is its predicate, and "one" is an adjective, meaning: singular in His divinity.

﴿Glory be to Him; [He is above] having a son﴾ meaning: I glorify Him with a glorification free of that, for it is only conceivable of one who has a like and to whom annihilation can occur, while Allah, glorified is He, is exalted above such likenesses. It has been read "in yakūn" (that it be), meaning: glorified is He; there is not for Him a son. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, is a resumed sentence brought to give the reason for the declaration of His transcendence and to confirm it: that is, to Him belongs whatever is in them of existent things, by creation, ownership, and disposal, and nothing among things, of which Jesus, peace be upon him, is one, departs from His dominion; so how could it be imagined that he is a son of His, exalted is He?

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Guardian﴾ to Him all creatures entrust their affairs, and He is independent of the worlds. So how could taking a son be conceived of in regard to Him, which is the characteristic of the weak and needy who need someone to succeed them and stand in their place in managing their affairs?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 172:

﴿Never will the Messiah disdain﴾ is a resumptive clause confirming what preceded of the declaration of God's transcendence (tanzih). Al-istinkaf (disdain) means arrogance and haughtiness, from nakaftu al-dam'a, meaning when you wipe the tear away from your face with a finger; i.e., he will never be too proud or too haughty.

﴿to be a servant of God﴾: that is, from being a servant of Him, Exalted is He, constantly devoted to His worship and obedience, as is the duty of servanthood. How could he not, since that is the highest of ranks of honour? The mention of his peace be upon him not disdaining this, rather than something else, is because it is his peace be upon him habit to take pride in it, as his states indicate and his statements make clear. Do you not see that the first statement he made to the people was his saying: "Indeed I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a Prophet" (Q. 19:30), because it fell in the position of a response to what the disbelievers had said? It is narrated that the delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Why do you disparage our companion?" He said: "Who is your companion?" They said: "Jesus." He said: "What should I say?" They said: "You say that he is the servant of God." He said: "There is no shame in his being a servant of God." They said: "Yes, indeed," and so this verse was revealed. This is the secret in making the object of disdain his being a servant of Him, Exalted is He, rather than saying "from the worship of God" and the like, while conveying a noble benefit, namely the complete freedom of his peace be upon him from disdain altogether. For his being a servant of God, Exalted is He, is a state that persists, since worship is continuous, so that non-disdain of it necessarily entails non-disdain of worshipping God, Exalted is He, as has been indicated. This is in contrast to worshipping God, Exalted is He, which is a renewed state that does not necessarily imply continuity; for its bearer to be described by it, it suffices that it be realized once. Thus non-disdain of it does not entail non-disdain of its continuity.

﴿nor do the favoured angels﴾: a conjunction upon "the Messiah," meaning: nor do the favoured angels disdain to be servants of God, Exalted is He. It has been said: if by "the angels" each one of them is meant, no supposition is needed, and whoever claims the superiority of the angels over the prophets, peace be upon them, has argued from the verse, saying: its context is to refute the Christians regarding raising the Messiah above the station of servanthood, and this requires that the conjoined be higher in rank than the conjoined-to, so that the non-disdain of them necessarily entails the non-disdain of his peace be upon him. It is answered that since the basis of the Christians' disbelief and their elevating him, peace be upon him, above the rank of servanthood was that his peace be upon him distinction and uniqueness over the rest of mankind lay in being born without a father, in knowledge of the unseen, and in being raised to heaven, the conjunction is made upon his non-disdain of worshipping God, Exalted is He, with the non-disdain of one who is higher in rank than him in these respects. For the angels were created without father or mother, know what humans do not know of the unseen, and their abode is the highest heavens. No one disputes their high rank from this aspect; the dispute is only about their superiority in terms of the abundance of reward for acts of obedience. Also, the verse is not only for refuting the Christians but also for refuting those who worship the angels, so there is no force to what they said in that case. And even if its being specifically for refuting the Christians is granted, perhaps the conjunction was intended for hyperbole in terms of multiplicity and detail, not in terms of magnification and preference, as in your saying: "The emir has become such that no superior and no subordinate opposes him." And even if the intention of preference is granted, the utmost that follows is the indication of the superiority of the favoured ones among them, namely the Cherubim who surround the Throne, or whoever is higher in rank among the angels, peace be upon them, over the Messiah among the prophets, peace be upon them; and it does not follow from that the superiority of one of the two kinds over the other absolutely. And is there any dispute except about this?

﴿And whoever disdains His worship﴾: that is, His obedience, so it includes all the disbelievers, since they do not obey Him, Exalted is He. The reason the object of disdain here is His worship, Exalted is He, and not what preceded, is to attach the threat to an attribute that is manifestly established for the disbelievers, for their not obeying Him, Exalted is He, is something they have no way to deny being characterized by.

If it is asked: why did He express their not obeying Him, Exalted is He, by disdaining it, when that from them was by way of denying that the command came from Him, Exalted is He, not by way of disdain? We say: because they used to disdain obeying the Messenger of God ﷺ, and is that anything other than disdaining the obedience of God, Exalted is He? For he, peace and blessings be upon him, has no command except the command of God, Exalted is He: "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God" (Q. 4:80).

﴿and is arrogant﴾: al-istikbar (arrogance) is pride in what one should not be proud of. Its root is seeking greatness for oneself without deserving it; not in the sense of seeking to attain it while believing one lacks it, but in the sense of counting oneself great and believing oneself to be so. He expressed it with what indicates seeking, to signal that its outcome is pure seeking without attaining what is sought. He expressed a similar thing with seeking itself in His saying, Exalted is He: "They bar from the way of God and seek to make it crooked" (Q. 7:45). For they did not seek to establish crookedness in the way of God while believing it straight; rather they counted it and believed it crooked and judged accordingly. But he expressed that by seeking, for the reason mentioned, namely the indication that there is nothing beyond seeking and arrogance, and not disdain, which suggests the supposition of shame and deficiency attaching to the one disdained.

﴿Then He will gather them all to Himself﴾: that is, the disdainful and their counterparts, indicated by the mention of the non-disdain of the Messiah and the angels, peace be upon them. The mention of one of the two groups has been omitted in the detailed statement, relying on the detail's indication of it and confidence in the evident requirement that gathering one of them entails gathering the other, since the gathering is general to all creatures. Likewise, the mention of one of the two groups is omitted in the detail at His saying, Exalted is He: "As for those who believed in God" (Q. 4:173), together with the generality of address to both, relying on the evident requirement that rewarding one of them entails punishing the other, since reward encompasses all. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the disdainful, and there is an implied conjoined clause, the estimate being: "He will gather them and others." It has also been said: the meaning is: He will gather them to Himself on the day He gathers the servants for recompense. But it is objected that what is more fitting to the detail that follows is to consider the gathering of all in summary in a single manner. It was read "fa-sayahshiruhum" with a kasra on the shin, which is a dialect; and it was read "fa-sanahshuruhum" with the royal "we," by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 173:

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾: an explanation of the state of the group whose mention was folded into the general statement. It is placed before the explanation of the state of their opposites, to make clear their excellence and to hasten to explain that their gathering (to God) is also taken into account in the general statement. Its presentation under the heading of faith and righteous deed, rather than under the description of not disdaining (worship), which would suit what precedes and follows it, is to draw attention to the fact that it is what brings about the fruits that follow it.

﴿He will pay them their wages in full﴾: without any reduction from them at all.

﴿And He will increase them from His bounty﴾: by multiplying them manifold, and by giving what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

﴿But as for those who disdained﴾: that is, from His worship, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿and were arrogant, He will punish them﴾: because of their disdain and arrogance.

﴿with a painful punishment﴾: whose painfulness no description can encompass.

﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any protector﴾: one who will manage their affairs and direct their interests.

﴿or any helper﴾: one who will help them against His might, the Exalted, and rescue them from His punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 174:

﴿O mankind﴾ is a shift in the mode of address (talwin al-khitab) and a directing of it to all who are legally accountable (al-mukallafin), following the demonstration of the falsity of the many forms of disbelief and misguidance that the disbelievers hold to, and the imposition upon them of decisive proofs before which even solid mountains would crumble, and the removal of their feeble doubts by clear evidence, and an alert to them that the proof has been completed, so that after this there remains no excuse for one who would make pretexts nor any justification for one who would offer apologies.

﴿There has certainly come to you﴾ means: it has reached you and been firmly established in your hearts, such that there is no way for you to deny it.

﴿a proof (burhan)﴾. The burhan is that by which the object sought is demonstrated. What is meant by it is the Qur'an, which indicates the truth of the Prophet's prophethood (ﷺ), and which establishes, through the rulings it contains, among which is what has been pointed to, what the noble verses have affirmed of the truth of the Truth and the falsity of falsehood. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that the Prophet (ﷺ) was referred to by it, because of the miracles he possessed that bear witness to his truthfulness. It has also been said: it is the miracles which he manifested. And it has been said: it is the religion of Truth which he brought. The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿from your Lord﴾, are either connected to "there has come to you" or to an elided element occurring as a qualifying attribute, honouring "a proof," confirming what the nunation conveyed of intrinsic grandeur through added grandeur, meaning: it is originating from Him, the Exalted, with "min" denoting the starting point of the source in a metaphorical sense. It has also been permitted, on the second reading, that "min" be partitive, with the genitive elided, meaning: it is one of the proofs of your Lord. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the addition to the pronoun of the addressees serves to show kindness toward them and to announce that its coming to them is for their nurture and perfection.

﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾. By it is also meant the noble Qur'an, referred to at one time as "the proof," for the reason already indicated, and at another as "the radiant light," which illuminates others by its own nature, as an announcement that it is clear in itself, self-sufficient in establishing its truth and its being from Allah the Exalted through its inimitability, not needing anything else, and clarifying for others the matters mentioned, and as an indication of its guidance for creation and its bringing them out of the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. It has been treated in the manner of coordination based upon the difference of the two terms, considering the difference of title as if it were a difference of essence. Its association with the addressees has been expressed at one time by "coming," attributed to it, which indicates the full strength of its demonstrative power, as though it comes by itself and establishes its rulings without anyone bringing it, and comes against the doubts of the disbelievers to nullify them; and at another time by "sending down," which is applied to it, suitable to the aspect of its being light, as a mark of honour for it, in consideration of each of its titles and its appropriate share. The attribution of its sending down to Himself, the Exalted, is by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) for the completeness of its honour. This is on the assumption that "the proof" refers to the noble Qur'an; but if it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to the manifest miracles upon his hand, or to the true religion, then the matter is easy. The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿to you﴾, are connected to "We have sent down," for although its sending down in essence was to the Prophet (ﷺ), it is also sent down to them through his mediation, upon him be blessings and peace. The condition of its being through mediation was taken into account rather than its condition in essence, as in the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book with truth, that you may judge between the people﴾, and its parallels, to show the completeness of kindness toward them and to make explicit its reaching them, exceeding in establishing their excuse. Its placement before the direct object, although its proper place is after it, is because of the concern with what is placed first and the arousing of desire for what is delayed, as has been explained more than once, and for the preservation of the rhyme-endings (fawasil) of the noble verses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 175:

﴿Then as for those who believed in Allah﴾ according to what the proof that came to them requires.

﴿And held fast to Him﴾ i.e., they protected themselves through Him from what would ruin them, namely the deviation of Satan and other things.

﴿Then He will admit them to mercy from Him and bounty﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is Paradise and what He bestows upon them of things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have not occurred to the heart of any human being. He expressed the outpouring of bounty by "admission" in the manner of the saying of the poet: [I fed her straw and cold water]. The tanwin of "mercy" (raḥmah) and "bounty" (faḍl) is for magnification, and "from Him" (minhu) is attached to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifying attribute of "mercy" that ennobles it.

﴿And guide them to Himself﴾ i.e., to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said: to the promised reward; and it has been said: to His worship.

﴿A straight path﴾ It is Islam and obedience in this world, and the path to Paradise in the Hereafter. The mention of the promise of admission to Paradise before the promise of being guided to it is contrary to the order of occurrence between the two promised things, for the sake of hastening to give the good news of what is the principal aim. It has been said that the accusative of "a path" (ṣirāṭan) is because it is an object of an omitted verb indicated by "He will guide them," i.e., "He will make them know a path, straight."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 4, verse 176:**

﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾ — i.e., concerning the *kalala* (one who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants as heirs). Its mention is dispensed with because it occurs in His saying, ﴿Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalala."﴾ Its explanation has already passed at the beginning of the noble surah. The one who asked was Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him. It is related (p-264) that "he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the road to Mecca in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage and said: 'I have a sister; how much of her inheritance do I take if she dies?'" It is also said that "he was ill, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited him, and he said: 'I am a kalala, so how should I dispose of my property?'" And it is narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited me while I was ill and unconscious. He performed ablution and poured some of his ablution water upon me, and I regained consciousness, and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, to whom does the inheritance belong, since only a kalala inherits from me?' Then it was revealed."

His saying, ﴿If a man dies﴾: this is a resumptive clause explaining the ruling. "Man" (*imru'un*) is in the nominative by a verb implied by what is mentioned. His saying, ﴿he has no child﴾, is a qualifier of him. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "died." It has been objected that it explains an omitted element that is not intended in the statement, i.e., "If a man dies, one who has no child, male or female." The absence of a child is mentioned alone, although the absence of a child is also a condition for the kalala, out of reliance on the matter being clear and on the detailing of the heirs indicating it.

His saying, ﴿and he has a sister﴾, is coordinated with His saying, ﴿he has no child﴾, or is a circumstantial clause. By "sister" is meant one who is not a sister on the mother's side only, for her prescribed share is one-sixth, and its explanation has passed at the beginning of the noble surah.

﴿Then for her is half of what he leaves﴾: i.e., by the prescribed share, and the remainder goes to the 'asabah (residuary heirs), or to her by radd (return) if he has no 'asabah.

﴿And he﴾: i.e., the man for whom the share is prescribed.

﴿inherits from her﴾: i.e., his sister for whom the share is prescribed, if it is supposed that she dies while he survives.

﴿if she has no child﴾, male or female. So the meaning of his inheriting from her is his taking all of what is hers, since that is what is conditioned on the complete absence of a child; it does not mean that he inherits from her in general, for that is realized even with the presence of her daughter. The verse contains nothing indicating that brothers are excluded by anyone other than a child, nor that they are not excluded; it is only the noble Sunnah that indicates their exclusion by a father.

﴿If there are two (sisters)﴾: this is coordinated with the first conditional clause, i.e., two or more.

﴿then for them are two-thirds of what he leaves﴾: the pronoun refers to those who inherit through siblingship, and the feminine and dual forms are according to meaning. It is said: the benefit of describing them as "two" along with the dual suffix indicating two-ness is to draw attention to the fact that what is considered in the difference of ruling is the number, not youth, age, or other things.

﴿And if they are﴾: i.e., those who inherit by way of siblingship.

﴿siblings﴾: i.e., mixed.

﴿men and women﴾: this is a substitute for "siblings." The original would be: "and if they are siblings, brothers and sisters," but the masculine was given precedence over the feminine.

﴿then for the male﴾: i.e., for the male among them.

﴿is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾: they divide the estate according to the method of 'asabah. This is the last thing revealed from the Book of Allah concerning rulings. It is related that al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his sermon: "Behold, the verse which Allah revealed in Surat al-Nisa' concerning the inheritance shares: its first is concerning the child and the parent; its second concerns the husband and wife and the siblings from the mother's side; and the verse with which He concluded the surah concerns the siblings and sisters of full or paternal blood; and the verse with which He concluded Surat al-Anfal He revealed concerning *uli al-arham* (blood relatives)."

﴿Allah makes clear to you﴾: i.e., the ruling of the kalala, or its rulings and laws, of which its ruling is one.

﴿lest you go astray﴾: i.e., out of dislike that you go astray in that matter. This is the view of the Basrans, as stated explicitly by al-Mubarrad. But al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and others of the Kufans held that a *lam* (meaning "so that") is to be assumed, and that "la" is in both positions of "an," i.e., *li-'allā tadillū* ("so that you do not go astray"). Abu 'Ubayd said: "I narrated to al-Kisa'i the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, which is: *la yad'uwanna aḥadukum 'alā waladihi an yuwāfiqa min Allāhi ijābatan* (let none of you invoke against his child that it coincide with an answer from Allah), meaning *li-'allā yuwāfiqa* ("so that it does not coincide"), and he approved of it." But what is mentioned from the verse and the hadith is not explicit in favor of what al-Kisa'i and his like held, for the assumed element in both, according to the Basrans, is: "out of dislike that you go astray," and "out of dislike that it coincide," etc. It has also been said: there is no omission or assumption here; rather it is the object of "makes clear," i.e., He makes clear to you your going astray, which is part of your nature when you are left to yourselves and your dispositions, so that you may guard against it (p-265) and seek its opposite. You know well that this is only fitting when His making clear is a specification of the places of error and misguidance, without explicitly stating what is true and right, and this is not the case.

﴿And Allah is, of everything﴾: among things, of which your circumstances connected with your living and dying are a part.

﴿Knowing﴾: intensely knowing, so He makes clear to you what contains your welfare and benefit.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surat al-Nisa', it is as if he gave charity to every believing man and woman, and he inherits an inheritance, and he is given a reward like one who frees a slave, and he is free from polytheism, and he is, in the will of Allah, among those who will be forgiven."

And Allah knows best.
